HTML Mastery

HTML is the language that tells a browser what is on a page: this is a heading, this is a link, this is a form. This course takes you from "I can write a div" to "I can be trusted with the markup of a production application." It covers the parser (the part of the browser that reads your text) and the two trees it builds from it, the rules that decide what your markup actually becomes, forms and how the browser checks them, the accessibility tree that screen readers receive, and HTML as a security boundary.

How to use this course

  • This course assumes you have written some HTML. You should recognise a tag, an attribute and a stylesheet link. It does not assume you know why <p><div>x</div></p> produces four nodes instead of one, what a content model is (the rule for which elements may go inside which), or what a browser hands to a screen reader. Those are what the course is for.
  • HTML is not a small language. It has:
  • around 115 elements;
  • a parser whose way of recovering from mistakes is written down step by step in the standard;
  • a second tree, computed from the first, that assistive technology reads;
  • a whole security story of its own.

This course covers all four, because the parts people skip are exactly where the expensive defects live. - Every measurement here was taken, not recalled. Each accessibility tree, DOM tree and focus order printed below was produced by rendering the markup in a real Chromium and reading the result out of the browser. Several of them are not what the markup suggests, and those are the ones worth the most. - Read the trees. When a block of markup is followed by a block headed AX TREE, DOM TREE or TAB ORDER, that block is the browser's answer, not the author's opinion. The prose around it explains why the browser answered that way. - Each section is Concept → Mechanism → Practice → Exercises with solutions. The mechanism (how the browser actually handles your markup) matters more here than in most languages, because HTML never reports an error. It recovers silently, and the page you get is not always the page you wrote. - The only setup you need is a browser and its developer tools:

mkdir ~/html-mastery && cd ~/html-mastery
printf '<!doctype html>\n<html lang="en">\n<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Scratch</title></head>\n<body>\n<h1>Scratch</h1>\n</body>\n</html>\n' > index.html
python3 -m http.server 8000

Open http://localhost:8000, then open the developer tools. Keep the Elements panel and the Accessibility pane visible while you work through the course. They are where you can check every claim it makes.

Every example was checked against the parsing algorithm of the WHATWG HTML standard (the living specification browsers follow), through parse5 7.3.0 and jsdom 26.1.0. ARIA roles and properties come from WAI-ARIA 1.3, and the conformance language (what "accessible" formally requires) from WCAG 2.2.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of elements. Four mechanisms, each of which explains a kind of defect that never shows up as an error:

  1. The parser recovers instead of failing. A tag in your text is not yet an element, and HTML has no parse errors that stop the page. Instead, a recovery algorithm written into the standard decides what you actually get. Implied end tags (the browser closing an element for you), foster parenting (stray content moved out of a table) and the empty <p> that appears from nowhere are all that algorithm working as designed (§1–§2, §10).
  2. Content models decide what may go where. Every element belongs to categories such as phrasing, flow and transparent content, and each has permitted parents. Those rules explain every case where the DOM disagrees with the source, including why a <div> ends up outside the <p> you put it in (§2).
  3. The accessibility tree is the real output. The browser computes a second tree from the first, and that second tree is what a screen reader receives. A native element brings its role, name, states and keyboard behaviour together. ARIA (attributes that describe meaning to assistive technology) brings only one of those and leaves the rest to you, which is why <button> beats role="button" (§13–§14).
  4. Markup is an execution boundary. It decides what gets sent and what gets run. Forms submit an entry list you can predict (§11–§12). sandbox is the only deny-by-default mechanism on the page, meaning everything is forbidden until you allow it (§9). And anything built from user input must be escaped for the place it lands in, with a Content Security Policy underneath in case one spot was missed (§3, §16).

By the end you should be able to:

  • predict the DOM a piece of markup produces;
  • write documents that can be navigated by heading, landmark and keyboard;
  • build forms that submit what you think they submit;
  • audit a page four ways: parser, validator, accessibility tree and keyboard (§16).
SECTION 1

The Document, the Parser and the DOM

HTML is the only language in common use that cannot fail to parse. Give a compiler a syntax error and it stops. Give a browser one and it produces a document anyway. The alternative, a blank page with an error message, is what XHTML actually did, and everyone who ever had to ship a web page rejected it.

That one design decision is the source of nearly everything surprising about HTML, and it is why this course starts here rather than with a list of tags. The markup you write and the tree the browser builds are two different things. An algorithm connects the two, and that algorithm never refuses. When the two differ, nothing warns you: the page renders, the tests pass, and one paragraph has silently become three siblings. You cannot reason about the rest of this course (content models, forms, tables, the accessibility tree) without knowing which of the two you are looking at.

Every DOM tree in this section was produced by handing the markup beside it to Chromium and printing what came back.

1.1 From Bytes to Pixels

Bytes
A stream of octets arrives over HTTP. Nothing yet says what they mean.
Characters
Decoded using the character encoding declaration (§1.3). Get this wrong and every non-ASCII character is wrong.
Tokens
The tokenizer turns characters into start tags, end tags, comments, doctypes and character runs.
Tree
Tree construction turns the token stream into a DOM, using the insertion mode and the stack of open elements (§1.6).
Render
Style is matched, boxes are laid out, pixels are painted. That half is css_mastery's; everything above it is this course's.

The two halves talk to each other through the DOM, and only through the DOM. CSS selectors match against the tree, not against your source. JavaScript reads the tree. The accessibility tree (§13) is computed from the tree. So a mistake in building the tree spreads into all three at once, and none of them will tell you where it came from.

HTML Living Standard is the specification, maintained by the WHATWG (the group of browser makers that writes it). It is living in the literal sense: there are no versions. "HTML5" was a marketing name for a period of time, not a document you can point to. The parsing algorithm in it is specified down to the character. That is why every browser builds the same tree from the same bytes, a property that did not exist before 2008 and that this whole section depends on.

The specification for all of this is the html living standard, published by the whatwg and revised continuously rather than in numbered versions. When this course says "the specification", that is the document it means. Its parsing section defines the insertion mode, the stack of open elements and the character encoding declaration precisely enough that every browser recovers from mistakes in the same way. The html living standard is unusually readable for a specification of its size, and the whatwg publishes a developer edition alongside it with the requirements for browser makers stripped out.

1.2 The Doctype and the Three Modes

<!doctype html>

That is all of it. It is not a version number, it says nothing about the document, and the fifteen-word strings with URLs in them that older pages carry are all obsolete. The doctype has exactly one job: to choose the rendering mode.

Standards mode
What <!doctype html> selects. The layout rules the specifications describe.
Quirks mode
No doctype, or an unrecognised one. The browser emulates the bugs of 1998 browsers: the box model measures widths differently, line-height behaves differently inside table cells, and a dozen other differences that will make a modern stylesheet wrong.
Limited-quirks mode
Also called almost-standards mode. Triggered by a few transitional doctypes; differs from standards mode in one place — the space under an image in a table cell.

The failure it prevents is not subtle, but it is confusing, because nothing announces it. A page loses its doctype during a change to a template, and every width on the site shifts by the size of the border and padding. The fastest way to check is document.compatMode: it returns CSS1Compat in standards mode and BackCompat in quirks mode.

The doctype must come before any content: it should be the first thing in the file. Blank lines and comments above it are harmless; the parser skips them and still sees the doctype. Text is not: any characters before it, such as output your server accidentally printed, put the page in quirks mode.

The third mode is limited-quirks mode. A small set of old doctypes trigger it, and it differs from standards mode in only a couple of layout details. In practice limited-quirks mode is a curiosity: write the modern doctype and you are in standards mode, the only mode worth designing for.

1.3 Character Encoding

Before the browser can split the bytes into tags, it has to know which characters those bytes stand for. It decides in this order:

1
A byte order mark at the start of the file.
2
The HTTP Content-Type header's charset parameter.
3
A <meta charset> in the first 1024 bytes of the document.
4
A guess, from the bytes themselves and the user's locale.
<meta charset="utf-8">

Put it as the first thing inside <head>. utf-8 is the only encoding worth using. It covers every writing system, it is the encoding the specification requires, and every other choice leads to mojibake (garbled characters). The 1024-byte limit is real. If the declaration comes after a kilobyte of comments and inline scripts, the browser will already have guessed, and when it finds out it guessed wrong it parses the whole document again from the beginning.

The symptom of getting it wrong is familiar: café shows up as cafÃ©. Those are the UTF-8 bytes for é read as Latin-1, one byte at a time. It is a decoding fault, not a font fault, and no amount of escaping in the source fixes it. The fix is always the declaration.

1.4 Tags Are Not Elements

The tokenizer (the first stage of the parser) reads text and produces tags. Tree construction (the second stage) turns tags into elements. Keep those three words, text, tag and element, apart, and the rest of this section is straightforward.

A start tag is <p>. An end tag is </p>. An element is the node that exists between them in the tree, together with everything inside it. A tag is a piece of syntax; an element is a piece of the document.

An attribute is a name, optionally followed by = and a value. The value may be in double quotes, in single quotes, or unquoted. An unquoted value ends at the first space, which is a trap that really bites:

<img src=cat.png alt=A cat>

DOM TREE
<img src="cat.png" alt="A" cat="">

The tokenizer read alt=A, then treated cat as a second attribute with an empty value. The alt text is "A", the element carries a meaningless cat attribute, and nothing anywhere reports a problem. So quote attribute values. This is not a style preference: an unquoted value cannot contain a space, a quote, an equals sign or a backtick, and the day one of them turns up in a value filled in by a template is the day the page breaks.

Duplicate attributes are resolved the same silent way:

<input name="a" name="b" value="v">

DOM TREE
<input name="a" value="v">

The first one wins and the second one disappears. That matters when markup is put together from a template plus a set of overrides: the override written last is the one that gets thrown away.

1.5 Void Elements and the Self-Closing Slash

Thirteen elements have no content and therefore no end tag. They are called void elements: area, base, br, col, embed, hr, img, input, link, meta, source, track, wbr.

Writing <br/> instead of <br> is allowed and means exactly the same thing: the slash is ignored. The confusion starts when you write the slash on anything else:

<div/>Text

DOM TREE
<div>
  #text "Text"

The <div/> is an ordinary start tag: the slash is thrown away, and the text becomes the div's child instead of its sibling. HTML has no self-closing syntax for non-void elements at all. The habit comes from JSX and from XML, where the slash does mean something, and in HTML it produces a document whose structure is off by one level, with no error anywhere.

The exception is foreign content, meaning SVG and MathML embedded in the page. Inside <svg> and <math>, XML rules apply and <circle r="1"/> really does close itself. That is why the same syntax is correct in one part of a document and misleading in another.

1.6 Tree Construction

Tree construction keeps track of two things, and knowing their names makes the specification readable.

The stack of open elements is exactly what it sounds like: the elements whose start tags have been seen and whose end tags have not. A start tag pushes an element onto the stack; a matching end tag pops it off. Each new element becomes a child of whatever is on top.

The insertion mode is a state machine (a set of named states with rules for moving between them): "before html", "in head", "in body", "in table", "in row", "in cell" and about twenty more. The current mode decides how each token is handled. That is why the same tag behaves differently in different places: a <td> in body content is ignored, while in "in row" mode it opens a cell.

Most of what looks arbitrary about HTML follows from these two. Take the most quoted example in the language:

<p>Before<div>Inside</div>After</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "Before"
<div>
  #text "Inside"
#text "After"
<p>

Four nodes where the author wrote one. The rule is that a <div> start tag, seen while a <p> is on the stack, closes the paragraph first, because <p> may contain only phrasing content (§2.7) and <div> is not phrasing content. "After" then becomes a sibling of the div. And the eventual </p> has no open paragraph to close, so it opens an empty one and immediately closes it.

Nothing warned. The CSS rule p { margin: 1rem } now applies to two paragraphs, one of them empty, and document.querySelectorAll('p').length is 2.

1.7 The DOM

The output of tree construction is a tree of nodes. Four kinds of node matter for this course.

Document node
The root. document in JavaScript. Not an element.
Element node
A tag pair and its attributes: <p>, <img>, <html>. document.documentElement is the <html> one.
Text node
A run of characters. Elements do not contain strings — they contain text nodes, and there can be several in a row.
Comment node
A comment. Really in the tree, reachable from script, and delivered to the client.

The point about text nodes is easy to skim past, and it is behind a whole family of bugs. Text is not a property of the element around it. It is a child of its own, alongside the other children, and runs of text separated by an element are separate nodes:

<p>Some <em>emphasis</em> here</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "Some "
  <em>
    #text "emphasis"
  #text " here"

Three children, and two of them are text. That is why whitespace between elements is real content. A newline in your source between </a> and <a> is a text node containing a newline, and it is why a row of inline-block elements has gaps that no CSS margin explains.

Four node types cover almost everything you will meet:

  • an element node is a tag that became an element;
  • a text node is a run of characters;
  • a comment node is an HTML comment, which stays in the tree even though nothing draws it;
  • the document node is the root, and documentelement names its one element child, the <html> element.

So document.documentElement is the <html> element and document.body is the <body> element. A stray comment node between two elements is a real sibling that nextSibling will land on. That is the usual reason a script written with nextSibling instead of nextElementSibling skips an element.

1.8 Error Recovery

There is no such thing as invalid HTML that fails to parse. There is markup that breaks the specification's authoring rules, which is what a validator reports (§16.4). And there is the parsing algorithm, which spells out an exact recovery for every possible input.

Four recoveries worth recognising, all measured:

<form action="/a"><input name="x"><form action="/b"><input name="y"></form></form>

DOM TREE
<form action="/a">
  <input name="x">
  <input name="y">

A nested form is dropped entirely. It is not merged, and it is not flattened with a warning: the inner start tag is ignored, so y becomes a control of the outer form and is submitted with it (§12.2). This is the most consequential repair the parser makes anywhere in the language, because you cannot see it and it changes what gets submitted.

<table><tr><td>Cell</td>Stray text</tr></table>

DOM TREE
#text "Stray text"
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "Cell"

Text inside a table is foster-parented out of it, and ends up before the table in the tree. The operation has its own name in the specification precisely because it is so strange. Text in a table must be inside a cell; anything else is moved out.

<p>Text</span> more</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "Text more"

A stray end tag for an element that is not open is ignored. It simply disappears, leaving a single text node. The typo has no effect at all, which is why it survives code review.

<p class="one>Text</p>

DOM TREE
(nothing)

An unterminated attribute value swallows everything after it up to the next quote character. Here that is the rest of the fragment, and the result is nothing: no paragraph, no text, no error. A missing quote is the one typo that can silently delete part of a page.

1.9 Optional and Implied End Tags

Some end tags may be left out, because the parser can work out where they belong. This is legal, specified and widely used:

<ul><li>One<li>Two</ul>

DOM TREE
<ul>
  <li>
    #text "One"
  <li>
    #text "Two"

The <li> start tag implies the end of the previous item, </li>. That is an implied end tag. The same holds for <p>, <tr>, <td>, <th>, <dt>, <dd>, <option> and several others, and it is why an unclosed <p> (§1.6) does not end up nested inside the next one.

The parser also adds elements you did not write. <tbody> is the famous one:

<table><tr><td>A</td></tr></table>

DOM TREE
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "A"

There is a <tbody> in that tree and none in the markup. That is why table > tr matches nothing as a CSS selector, and why a script that walks table.children finds a section rather than a row. Both cause endless confusion, and both are this one rule.

The optional end tag rules are worth knowing but not worth exploiting. Leaving out </li> saves five characters and costs the next reader a moment of doubt. The real value of knowing the rules is being able to read minified and machine-generated HTML without assuming it is broken.

An optional end tag is a convenience, not an invitation. The parser closes the element for you at a point the specification fixes, and that point is occasionally not where you would have closed it. The ones you will meet are <li>, <p>, <tr>, <td>, <th>, <option> and <optgroup>. Note <option> in particular: an <option> left unclosed inside a <select> is closed by the next <option>. That is why leaving the end tag out is safe there, and why nobody writes </option>.

1.10 Scripts Block the Parser

A classic <script> stops tree construction. The parser must pause, download the file if it is external, run it, and only then continue. It has to, because the script might call document.write and change the stream of tokens underneath it.

Plain
<script src> is parser-blocking: fetch, execute, then resume. In <head> this delays the entire page.
defer attribute
Fetch in parallel, execute after parsing finishes, in document order. The right default for application code.
async attribute
Fetch in parallel, execute the moment it arrives, in whatever order they finish. Correct only for scripts that depend on nothing and that nothing depends on.
type="module"
Deferred by default — no attribute needed. Adding async to a module opts back into "as soon as ready".

Two mechanisms limit the damage:

  • The preload scanner reads ahead through the raw bytes while the parser is blocked, finds src and href values, and starts those downloads early. That is why moving a stylesheet link earlier can still help even though the parser has not reached it yet.
  • document.write is the reason none of this can be optimised away. It is effectively deprecated: browsers now ignore it for parser-blocking scripts injected into a document that is already loading, and there is no good reason to use it.

Two events mark the end. DOMContentLoaded fires when parsing is complete and every deferred script has run. load fires when every subresource, images included, has finished. Application code almost always wants the first.

Collected: the defer attribute runs the script after parsing, in document order; the async attribute runs it as soon as it arrives, in no particular order; and type="module" is deferred by default, so a module script needs neither. Meanwhile the preload scanner is reading ahead for the resources it can see, which is why a script that writes markup defeats it. The event to hang start-up code on is domcontentloaded, which fires once the document is parsed and every defer attribute script has run. The async attribute deliberately makes no promise about being finished by then.

Two more parser behaviours belong here. speculative parsing is what the browser does while a blocking script runs: it keeps tokenising past the blocked point to discover resources to download, and throws that guessed-ahead tree away if the script writes markup. That is speculative parsing and the preload scanner working together, and document.write is what defeats both.

And the parser is a streaming parser: it builds the tree from bytes as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole document, which is why a slow response paints bit by bit. A streaming parser is also why the <meta charset> deadline in §1.3 exists at all: the decision has to be made before most of the bytes have arrived. The load event fires later than DOMContentLoaded. DOMContentLoaded means the document is parsed, while the load event waits for every stylesheet, image and frame as well, which on a page full of images can be seconds later.

1.11 View Source Is Not the DOM

View source shows the bytes the server sent. The DevTools element inspector shows the current DOM. They differ for three reasons, from least to most surprising: a script has changed the tree; the parser rewrote something, as in §1.8; or the page's HTML was generated entirely by script, so its source is nearly empty.

Going the other way, from tree back to text, is called serialisation, and it does not round-trip in the way people assume:

<p>a &amp; b <br> <input disabled></p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "a & b "
  <br>
  #text " "
  <input disabled="">

innerHTML on that paragraph returns a &amp; b <br> <input disabled="">. The entity comes back escaped because the text node contains a literal ampersand, and the boolean attribute has gained an explicit empty value. Neither changes the meaning, but both mean that comparing innerHTML with a source string is not a reliable test. textContent, by contrast, gives you the joined text of every descendant with no markup at all. That is also what makes it the safe way to insert text a user supplied (§16.9).

1.12 The Other Serialisation

The same DOM can be written out as XML instead of HTML, and a document served as application/xhtml+xml is read by an XML serialization parser instead of the HTML one. Under those rules there is no error recovery: a missing end tag is a fatal error, and the browser shows a parse-error page instead of a document.

XHTML was the attempt to make that the norm. It failed for a reason worth understanding rather than mocking. The web is written by everyone, much of it is assembled by templates and by gluing strings together, and a system where one unescaped ampersand in a comment takes the page down does not survive contact with reality. HTML's error recovery is not sloppiness. It is the specification of what to do when, not if, the input is malformed.

In practice, you will not serve XHTML, and text/html is the content type for everything in this course. What survives from that era is the habit of quoting attributes and closing elements. It is good practice for the reasons in §1.4 and §1.5, not because any parser demands it. The two places XML rules still apply inside an HTML document are <svg> and <math>, the foreign content where <circle r="1"/> closes itself and letter case matters again (viewBox is the attribute everyone gets wrong).

That form is xml serialization. The practical reason to know it exists is that a .xhtml file served as application/xhtml+xml is read by an XML parser with no error recovery at all: a single unclosed tag is a fatal error and the page does not render. xml serialization is therefore strict where §1.8 is forgiving. That is occasionally useful in a pipeline that generates files, and almost never what you want to serve.

Exercises

1. A colleague writes <p>Introduction<div class="callout">Note</div>Rest of paragraph</p> and asks why the callout's margins collapse strangely and why p:last-child matches an empty element. Answer both.

Solution

Both symptoms come from the same rewrite (§1.6). The DOM is not one paragraph containing a div; it is four siblings:

<p>Introduction</p>
<div class="callout">Note</div>
"Rest of paragraph"
<p></p>

The <div> start tag closed the paragraph, because <p> accepts only phrasing content and <div> is flow content (§2.7). "Rest of paragraph" is then a bare text node between the div and an empty <p>, which the trailing </p> created — an end tag with no matching open element opens one and closes it.

Why the margins look wrong: the callout is not inside the paragraph, so it is not indented or constrained by it, and its margins collapse against the paragraph above and the empty paragraph below rather than being contained.

Why p:last-child matches something empty: there really is an empty paragraph, and it is the last one.

The fix depends on the intent. If the callout is an aside within the flow, take it out of the paragraph:

<p>Introduction</p>
<div class="callout">Note</div>
<p>Rest of paragraph</p>

If it must be inline within the sentence, it has to be phrasing content — a <span>, or a <mark> if the meaning is highlighting (§4.9).

The general lesson is the one this section exists for: check the DOM, not the source. DevTools' element inspector would have shown four nodes immediately, and document.querySelectorAll('p').length returning 2 is a one-line diagnosis.

2. Why does the CSS selector table > tr never match anything, and what should it be?

Solution

Because there is a <tbody> between them that you did not write. The parser inserts one around any row that is not already inside <thead>, <tbody> or <tfoot> (§1.9), so the real tree is table > tbody > tr even for the simplest possible table.

Write table tr — the descendant combinator, which does not care how many levels intervene — or name the section explicitly with table > tbody > tr.

The same rule explains three other confusions:

  • table.children[0] is a <tbody>, not a <tr>, so a script walking rows should use table.rows or querySelectorAll('tr').
  • A <tbody> appears in DevTools that is nowhere in view source, which is §1.11's difference in its most common form.
  • In a <template> (§15.2) the rule does not apply the same way, because the template's contents are parsed in a fragment context.

And it is worth noting the converse: <thead> and <tfoot> are not inserted for you. Only <tbody> is implied, so a table with header cells but no <thead> really does have its header row inside the body section.

3. Given <img src=logo dark.png alt=Company logo>, describe the element the parser produces.

Solution

An <img> with four attributes, none of them what was intended:

<img src="logo" dark.png="" alt="Company" logo="">

An unquoted attribute value ends at the first whitespace (§1.4). So src is logo, and then dark.png is read as a new attribute name with no value; alt is Company, and logo becomes a fourth attribute.

The consequences: the image requests a file called logo, which almost certainly 404s; the alt text is "Company", which is wrong but not obviously wrong; and two junk attributes are attached, which nothing will ever report. A validator flags the junk attributes (§16.4) and that is the only automated signal.

<img src="logo dark.png" alt="Company logo">

A filename with a space is legal but poor practice — it must be percent-encoded as logo%20dark.png in some contexts — so the better fix is to rename the file.

The rule to take away: always quote attribute values. Unquoted values cannot contain a space, a quote, an apostrophe, an equals sign or a backtick, and the moment a value comes from a variable rather than being typed by hand, you cannot guarantee it contains none of them. This is also an injection path: a templated unquoted value containing a space can inject an attribute — onmouseover=... — into the tag (§16.9).

4. A page renders correctly in development and every width is 20 pixels wider in production. Nothing in the CSS changed. What is the first thing to check?

Solution

Quirks mode (§1.2). Check document.compatMode in the console: CSS1Compat is standards mode, BackCompat is quirks.

Quirks mode changes the box model — width includes padding and border rather than excluding them — so a box with width: 200px plus 10px of padding on each side measures 200px in quirks and 220px in standards. A whole page shifting by exactly twice a padding value is that difference.

The cause is nearly always that the doctype is no longer the first thing in the file (§1.2). Production adds something that development does not: a templating engine emitting a blank line with a BOM, a caching layer prepending a comment, a PHP file with whitespace before its opening tag, or a proxy injecting a banner. Any content before <!doctype html> other than whitespace puts the document into quirks mode.

How to confirm in thirty seconds: view source in production and look at the very first bytes — not DevTools' element inspector, which shows the DOM and will happily display a doctype the parser inferred (§1.11). curl -s https://… | head -c 100 | xxd shows a byte order mark or stray characters that no visual inspection will.

Once found, the fix is to remove whatever precedes the doctype. Setting box-sizing: border-box would make the numbers agree again and would leave the page in quirks mode, where a dozen other differences are waiting.

5. Explain why <div /> does not do what a developer coming from JSX expects, and name the one place in an HTML document where the same syntax does work.

Solution

Because HTML has no self-closing syntax. In the HTML parser the trailing slash on a start tag is parsed and then discarded, so <div /> is exactly <div> — an open element with no end tag, which then takes everything after it as its children until something closes it (§1.5).

So <div/>Text produces a <div> containing "Text", not a <div> followed by "Text" — the tree in §1.5 is the measurement. In a real page the consequences compound: <div/><div/><div/> is three nested divs, each inside the last, and a layout built on that will be wrong in a way that looks like a CSS problem.

The slash is permitted on void elements — <br/>, <img/>, <input/> — where it is equally meaningless but harmless, since those elements cannot have children anyway. That is why the habit survives: it works everywhere you happen to have tried it.

The one place it genuinely works is foreign content: inside <svg> and <math>, XML parsing rules apply, and <circle cx="5" cy="5" r="4"/> really does close itself (§1.12). This is also where case sensitivity comes back — viewBox must be spelled with its capital B in SVG, while class and id on an HTML element are matched case-insensitively.

JSX is not HTML. It is a JavaScript syntax that compiles to function calls, and its rules — self-closing tags, className, {} interpolation — are its own. Markup copied out of a component into an HTML file needs converting, and this is the conversion people forget.

SECTION 2

Elements, Attributes and Content Models

§1 followed the bytes of a page through the parser until they came out as a tree. This section is about the pieces that tree is built from: what an element is, what an attribute is, and the rules that say which elements may contain which others. Almost nobody learns that last part on purpose.

It is worth a section of its own because it is enforced in a way no other part of HTML is: there is no error message. A <div> inside a <p> does not fail. It silently produces a different tree from the one you wrote, and every piece of CSS and JavaScript you write afterwards is aimed at a structure that does not exist. §1.8 showed how that happens. This section gives you the rules that predict it.

2.1 What an Element Is

An element is a node in the tree. It has a name, a set of attributes and, unless it is a void element (§1.5), a list of children. Tags are the syntax that produce it; the element is the thing that exists afterwards (§1.4).

Three properties of the name are worth stating once:

It is a fixed vocabulary
HTML defines roughly 115 element names. You cannot invent one — except by the rules in §2.11, which are precise and narrow.
It is case-insensitive
<DIV> and <div> are the same element, and the parser stores it lowercase.
It carries meaning, not appearance
The default styling is a convention of the browser's stylesheet, not part of the element. <strong> is not "bold"; it is "important", which a browser happens to render bold and a screen reader may render as emphasis in the voice.

The third is the one that changes how you write. Choosing an element means choosing what the content is. That choice matters to the browser's default behaviour, to the accessibility tree (§13.2), to search engines, to reader modes, to translation tools, and to the next person reading the markup. Choosing how it looks is CSS's job. The two decisions can be made separately precisely because an element's name says nothing about its appearance.

2.2 Attribute Syntax: Quoting, Escaping, and Duplicates

An attribute is a name/value pair on the start tag. The syntax allows more than most people write, and knowing exactly how much it allows is what lets you read other people's markup.

<a href=/about class="nav link" title='A "quoted" word' data-id=42>About</a>

DOM TREE
<a href="/about" class="nav link" title="A \"quoted\" word" data-id="42">
  #text "About"

All four of those are legal. A value may be unquoted when it contains no space, quote, =, <, > or backtick; href=/about and data-id=42 qualify. It may be in double quotes or in single quotes. Single quotes are how you write a value that itself contains double quotes without escaping anything, which §9.3's codecs parameter needs.

Whatever you wrote, the DOM stores one form: a string. The quoting was syntax, and it is gone by the time the tree exists.

Quote everything anyway. The unquoted form fails in a genuinely nasty way: a value that later gains a space, or a value filled in by a template that comes back empty, silently merges with the next attribute. The rule "always quote" costs nothing and removes a whole class of bug. This is one of the few places where the strictest style available is clearly right.

Attribute names are case-insensitive; attribute values are not:

<input type="TEXT" NAME="q" ID="search" value="hi">

DOM TREE
<input type="TEXT" name="q" id="search" value="hi">

NAME and ID were turned into lowercase, and type="TEXT" was left exactly as written. Attribute names are case-insensitive; values are plain strings that each attribute interprets however it likes. type happens to compare its value without regard to case, so this input is still a text field. class does not, so class="Nav" and class="nav" are two different classes.

A value that must contain <, >, & or the quote character that surrounds it needs a character reference (§2.13). &amp; and &quot; are the two that come up, and §9.13's srcdoc is the extreme case: a whole document escaped into one attribute value.

What happens when the same attribute appears twice is worth knowing, because it is completely silent:

<p class="one" class="two" id="x">Text</p>

DOM TREE
<p class="one" id="x">
  #text "Text"

The first one wins and the second is discarded. No error, no warning, nothing in the console. This is a real bug in generated markup. A template that emits class="card" and a component that also emits class="{{extra}}" produce an element with only the first, and the second author's styling simply never applies. It is one of the few things a validator (§16.4) catches that nothing else does.

One vocabulary note for the rest of the course: an unquoted attribute value is the form with no quotes at all, href=/about. An unquoted attribute is legal, and it is the one form this course will never write.

2.3 Attributes Are Not Properties

This is the distinction that causes the most confusion in the DOM, and one example is enough to learn it.

An attribute is what is written in the markup. It is stored as a string and read with getAttribute(). A property is a field on the JavaScript object that represents the element. Many properties reflect an attribute: reading one reads the other, and writing one writes the other. A handful deliberately do not.

document.body.innerHTML = '<input id="q" type="text" value="start">';
const q = document.querySelector('#q');
console.log('getAttribute("value"):', JSON.stringify(q.getAttribute('value')));
console.log('.value              :', JSON.stringify(q.value));

q.value = 'typed';
console.log('after q.value = "typed"');
console.log('getAttribute("value"):', JSON.stringify(q.getAttribute('value')));
console.log('.value              :', JSON.stringify(q.value));

q.setAttribute('value', 'reset');
console.log('after setAttribute("value", "reset")');
console.log('.value              :', JSON.stringify(q.value));

getAttribute("value"): "start"
.value              : "start"
after q.value = "typed"
getAttribute("value"): "start"
.value              : "typed"
after setAttribute("value", "reset")
.value              : "typed"

Read that last pair twice. The value attribute is the field's starting value; the value property is its current one. Once the user or a script has changed the current value, the element sets its dirty value flag, and from then on the attribute no longer feeds the property at all. setAttribute('value', 'reset') changed the markup, and the field on screen still says typed.

This is not a quirk; it is what makes a form resettable. form.reset() puts every control back to its attribute value, which it could not do if typing had overwritten that value. It is also the mechanism behind §12.7's measured surprise that minlength does not apply to a value written in the markup: the constraint is defined in terms of the dirty value.

The general rule: the attribute is the initial state written in the document; the property is the live state. For href, class and id the two stay in step, because nothing else writes them. For value, checked and selected they separate the moment a user touches the control, and those are exactly the three you will reach for.

One more difference is worth memorising, and href shows it. getAttribute('href') returns the string as written, "/about", while the .href property returns the resolved absolute URL, "https://example.com/about". Reflected properties are allowed to tidy up what they return, and properties that hold a URL always do.

Two more consequences worth naming. The value attribute and the value property are the pair this subsection measured, and the same split exists for checked and for selected. And a URL-valued property is normalised: getAttribute('href') gives the string as written while .href gives the absolute url it resolves to. So a comparison against an absolute url must read the property, and a comparison against what the document said must read the attribute.

2.4 Boolean Attributes

A boolean attribute is true when it is present and false when it is absent. The value is never consulted.

<label><input type="checkbox" checked> bare</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" checked=""> empty</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" checked="checked"> its own name</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" checked="false"> the string "false"</label>

All four are checked. checked="false" is checked; checked="no" is checked; checked="" is checked. The only way to make a checkbox unchecked is for the attribute not to be there.

The correct spellings are the empty string and the attribute's own name, so checked and checked="checked" are the two standard forms. Anything else is conforming-invalid: it works, and a validator will complain.

This trips up every templating language on earth, because the natural thing to write is:

<input type="checkbox" checked="{{isSubscribed}}">

When isSubscribed is false, that renders checked="false", which is checked. Every framework has a special syntax for this (Vue's :checked, React's checked={...}, Angular's [checked]), and they all exist because the attribute has no way to say "false". If you are building markup as strings, the fix is to emit the attribute or leave it out, never to give it a value.

The boolean attributes you will meet: checked, selected, disabled, readonly, required, multiple, hidden, inert, open, async, defer, autofocus, novalidate, formnovalidate, controls, autoplay, loop, muted, playsinline, default, reversed, ismap and allowfullscreen. download on a link looks like one, because its presence is what makes the link download, but strictly it is not: its value, when there is one, is the suggested file name. §9.2 measured the consequences for media; §12.7 the ones for forms.

Two on the list are worth singling out. type="checkbox" is where the trap bites hardest, because a checkbox's state is exactly what a template is most likely to set from a variable, and type="checkbox" with checked="false" is checked. And autofocus is a boolean whose presence moves the page's focus when it loads. A stray autofocus left in a partial template gives you a page that scrolls itself somewhere unexpected; autofocus on more than one element applies to the first.

2.5 Enumerated Attributes and What Invalid Values Do

An enumerated attribute takes one keyword from a fixed list. The interesting question is what happens when it gets something else, and the answer has two parts that are easy to mix up.

<article dir="middle" translate="maybe" contenteditable="sure">
  <p>Text</p>
</article>

DOM TREE
<article dir="middle" translate="maybe" contenteditable="sure">
  #text "\n  "
  <p>
    #text "Text"
  #text "\n"

The DOM keeps the string exactly as written. Parsing does not check values. dir="middle" is stored, because an attribute value is just text and the parser has no idea what dir means.

Turning the string into a state happens later, when something asks. Each enumerated attribute defines an invalid value default (the state for an unrecognised keyword) and a missing value default (the state when the attribute is absent), and an unrecognised keyword gets the first:

document.body.innerHTML = '<article id="a" dir="middle" translate="maybe">Text</article>';
const a = document.querySelector('#a');
console.log('getAttribute("dir"):', JSON.stringify(a.getAttribute('dir')));
console.log('.dir              :', JSON.stringify(a.dir));
console.log('.translate        :', a.translate);

getAttribute("dir"): "middle"
.dir              : ""
.translate        : true

The attribute still says middle. The reflected property says the empty string, because .dir reflects only the keywords it knows and reports "no state" otherwise. translate="maybe" produced true, because translate's invalid value default is to inherit from the parent, and with no ancestor saying no, inheriting means yes.

That difference is the practical point: a typo in an enumerated attribute is invisible from the markup and visible from the property. §9.9's kind="caption" is the same failure with expensive consequences. An invalid kind falls back to metadata, which is never displayed, so a typo in a caption track silently produces captions nobody sees. When an enumerated attribute is not doing what you expect, read the reflected property, not the markup.

Common enumerated attributes: type on <input> (§11.3), dir, translate, contenteditable, spellcheck, autocapitalize, enterkeyhint, inputmode, loading, decoding, fetchpriority, referrerpolicy, crossorigin, preload, kind, wrap, method, enctype, autocomplete, scope and shadowrootmode.

Three of the global ones are worth a sentence each, because all three are enumerated and none is boolean:

  • spellcheck takes true or false, and spellcheck="false" is right for a field holding a code or an identifier.
  • autocapitalize takes none, sentences, words or characters and controls the on-screen keyboard; autocapitalize="none" belongs on a username field.
  • enterkeyhint (enter, done, go, next, search, send) changes the label on the on-screen keyboard's action key, so enterkeyhint="search" on a search field is a one-attribute improvement on every phone.

2.6 Content Categories

HTML sorts elements into overlapping content categories. Each element's specification says which categories it belongs to, and which categories its children may come from. This is the machinery behind the question "where may this go?".

Metadata content
Sets up presentation or behaviour, or the relationship to other documents. <title>, <base>, <link>, <style>, <meta>, <script>, <noscript>, <template>. Mostly in the head (§3).
Flow content
Nearly everything that goes in the body. If an element has no more specific rule, it accepts flow content.
Sectioning content
Defines a scope for headings. <article>, <aside>, <nav>, <section> — exactly four (§6).
Heading content
<h1>–<h6> and <hgroup>. Defines the header of a section.
Phrasing content
Text and the elements that mark up text at the level of a sentence. A strict subset of flow content (§2.7).
Embedded content
Content from outside the document: <img>, <video>, <audio>, <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, <canvas>, <svg>, <math> (§8, §9).
Interactive content
Specifically intended for user interaction: <a href>, <button>, <input> (except hidden), <select>, <textarea>, <details>, <label>, and <img usemap>, <video controls>, <audio controls>.

Two of these categories carry rules that bite in ordinary code.

No interactive content inside interactive content. A <button> may not contain an <a href>, and an <a href> may not contain a <button>. This is not pedantry. There is no sensible answer to what a click does, no sensible focus behaviour, and the accessibility tree ends up with a control inside a control, which screen readers report inconsistently. When a card is clickable and contains a "Save" button, the answer is a link on the title with the card styled around it, not a link wrapped around the whole thing.

metadata content mostly cannot appear in the body. <style>, <script> and <template> are the exceptions. That is why <link rel="stylesheet"> in the body is a mistake people make, and <script> at the end of the body is not.

An element's permitted parent is the other side of all this: the set of elements whose content model accepts it. Some elements have only one:

  • <li> requires <ul>, <ol> or <menu>;
  • <td> requires <tr>;
  • <option> requires <select>, <optgroup> or <datalist>;
  • <figcaption> requires <figure>.

When you put one somewhere else, §1.8's recovery rules decide what happens, and the answer is rarely what you wanted. §10.4's foster parenting is the worst of them.

A few category memberships are worth memorising, because they are the ones that decide real markup. heading content is <h1>–<h6> and <hgroup> and nothing else. <meta> is metadata content, which is why it belongs in the head. <canvas>, like <img> and <video>, is embedded content, so <canvas> may appear inside a paragraph. <textarea> and <datalist> are phrasing content, which is what lets <textarea> sit inside a <label> and <datalist> go almost anywhere. <optgroup> belongs to no category at all: it may appear only where an element's content model names it, which is inside a <select>. Of the categories in this paragraph, heading content is the one a <p> will not accept.

2.7 Phrasing Content, and Where Text May Go

phrasing content is the category you will look up most, because it answers the question "can I put this inside a paragraph?".

It is text, plus the elements that mark up text at the level of a sentence: <a>, <em>, <strong>, <code>, <span>, <br>, <img>, <button>, <input>, <label>, <select>, <textarea>, <time>, <abbr>, <cite>, <q>, <mark>, <sub>, <sup>, <small>, <b>, <i>, <u>, <s>, <data>, <bdi>, <bdo>, <ruby>, <wbr>, <svg>, <video>, <audio>, <canvas>, <output>, <progress>, <meter>, <datalist>, <template>, <slot> and <script>.

What is not in it is the short list that matters: <p>, <div>, <ul>, <ol>, <dl>, <table>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <nav>, <header>, <footer>, <main>, <figure>, <blockquote>, <pre>, <hr>, <form>, <fieldset>, <details>, <dialog> and <h1>–<h6>.

<p> accepts phrasing content and nothing else, which is why this happens:

<p>A paragraph <div>with a div inside</div> and more text.</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "A paragraph "
<div>
  #text "with a div inside"
#text " and more text."
<p>

Four siblings where the source had one element with three children. The parser reached <div> and saw that a <p> cannot contain it. So it closed the paragraph implicitly (§1.9), added the <div> as a sibling, and put the trailing text after it. Then it met </p> with no open paragraph, which by the recovery rules opens and immediately closes an empty one. That fourth node is a real empty paragraph on the page, and it will pick up your paragraph margin.

Nothing reported an error. CSS written as p > div matches nothing; p:last-child matches the empty one; document.querySelector('p').textContent returns "A paragraph ". This is the most common case of §1.8 in practice, and knowing that <p> takes phrasing content only is the whole defence. When you need a block inside something, that something must be a <div> or a container with meaning, never a <p>.

The same rule explains why <label> may wrap an <input> but not a <table>, and why <button> may contain an <img> and a <span> but not a <ul>.

Eight of those are easy to get wrong, so they are worth repeating. <hr> is not phrasing content: it is a thematic break at the level of whole blocks, so it cannot go inside a paragraph. <u>, <small>, <abbr>, <sub>, <sup>, <ruby> and <output> all are phrasing content, so all seven may appear inside a <p>: <abbr> around an acronym, <sub> and <sup> in a formula, <small> around small print, <u> around an annotation, <ruby> around an annotated character, and <output> where a form's calculated result belongs (§11.13).

2.8 The Transparent Content Model

A few elements have no content model of their own. Instead they take their parent's. The specification calls this transparent, and it is what lets <a> do something that looks as if it should be illegal:

<a href="/a"><h2>A heading inside a link</h2><p>and a paragraph</p></a>

DOM TREE
<a href="/a">
  <h2>
    #text "A heading inside a link"
  <p>
    #text "and a paragraph"

The tree is exactly what was written. Nothing moved, because <a> is transparent: inside a <div>, an <a> may contain whatever a <div> may contain. Wrapping a whole card (image, heading, paragraph) in one link is legal markup, and it is how "the entire card is clickable" is done without JavaScript.

Two limits survive transparency, and both come from §2.6. There must still be no interactive content inside, so a <button> in there is not allowed. And an <a> inside a <p> is still bound by the paragraph's rules, so there it may contain only phrasing content. Transparency passes the parent's restriction down; it does not escape it.

The transparent content model also applies to <ins>, <del>, <map>, <object>, <video>, <audio>, <slot>, <canvas> and <noscript>. For <ins> and <del> it is why the same element can mark either a phrase or three whole paragraphs as inserted (§5.9).

The card-wrapping pattern comes with a practical warning, which §7.10 develops. A link's accessible name (what a screen reader announces) is everything inside it, so a link wrapping an image, a heading, a date and two paragraphs is announced as one enormous run of text. The pattern that keeps the large click area and a short name puts the <a> around the heading only and stretches it over the card with CSS.

2.9 Permitted Parents, and Reading a Specification Entry

Every element's reference page carries a short technical summary. Once you can read it, you never have to guess about nesting again. The entry for <li> says, in effect:

Content categories
None. An <li> is not flow content, which is why it may not appear on its own.
Permitted content
Flow content — so a list item may contain paragraphs, tables and nested lists.
Tag omission
The end tag may be omitted (§1.9).
Permitted parents
<ul>, <ol>, <menu>. Nothing else.
Implicit ARIA role
listitem when inside a list, generic otherwise — which is §13.2's point that a role can depend on context.

The permitted parent line is the one to check when markup mysteriously rearranges itself. A <div> between a <ul> and its <li> elements is a natural thing to reach for when you want a wrapper, but it is not allowed, and what happens next is up to each browser's recovery. §5.2 measures it: Chrome is forgiving and keeps the list role and both listitem nodes. That is how one browser recovers, not a guarantee. Nothing in the specification says what the tree should be, so the answer may differ between engines and may change, which is the reason not to rely on it.

Four nesting rules cover most real mistakes:

  • <ul> and <ol> may contain only <li> (plus <script> and <template>). To nest a list, put the inner <ul> inside an <li>, not between two of them.
  • <table> may contain only <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> and <tr>. Anything else is foster-parented out of the table (§10.4).
  • <dl> may contain <dt> and <dd>, optionally wrapped in <div>, the one place where the specification explicitly allows a wrapper (§5.6).
  • <form> may not contain another <form>. The inner one is dropped outright, which is a silent way to lose a whole feature.

2.10 Global Attributes

A global attribute may appear on any element. There are about thirty; these are the ones that earn their place.

id
A document-unique identifier. The target of a fragment link (§7.5), of <label for> (§11.2) and of every aria-labelledby (§13.3).
class
A space-separated list of names, for CSS and for scripts. Carries no meaning to the browser at all — class="button" makes nothing a button.
title
Advisory text, shown as a tooltip on hover. See the warning below.
style
Inline CSS for this element. Highest specificity short of !important, which is why it is a poor default and a fine escape hatch for a computed value.
hidden
Boolean. Not rendered, not in the accessibility tree, not a focus stop (§13.8). hidden="until-found" is the enumerated form that find-in-page can reveal.
tabindex
Focusability and focus order (§14.3).
contenteditable
Enumerated: true, false, plaintext-only. Makes the subtree editable in place.
draggable
Enumerated true/false — not boolean, so bare draggable is invalid and draggable="false" is meaningful.
spellcheck
Enumerated true/false. Worth setting to false on fields holding codes, IDs and names.
autocapitalize
none, sentences, words, characters. Controls the on-screen keyboard's shift behaviour; none is right for usernames and codes.
nonce
A one-time token matching the page's Content Security Policy, letting this specific inline script or style run (§16.10).

Two of those need a warning rather than a description.

The title attribute is not a substitute for a label, and is not reliably reachable. Some screen readers announce it and others do not. It does not appear on touch devices at all, it cannot be reached by keyboard, its timing cannot be adjusted, and it cannot be styled. It is genuinely useful in exactly one place, giving an <iframe> a name (§9.11), where the specification asks for it, and otherwise only for extra detail nobody needs. Anything a user must read belongs in the page. §13.3 measures where the title attribute sits in the order of sources for an accessible name: dead last, behind everything.

The nonce attribute is unusual in that reading it back is deliberately blocked. When the page's Content Security Policy arrives in an HTTP header, getAttribute('nonce') returns the empty string from script. A nonce that an injected script could read out of the DOM would defeat the policy it enforces. The value stays available as a property to code in the same document and is hidden from the attribute API, a rare case of the two deliberately disagreeing (§2.3). (Measured in Chromium: with the header, "" from the attribute and the value from .nonce; without one, the value from both.)

The nonce attribute is also the one global attribute with a lifetime: it means something only for the response it was generated for. A nonce attribute reused across responses, or baked into a static file, lets an attacker who has read one page satisfy the policy on every other. That is why §16.10 insists the value be fresh and unguessable for every response.

Three on the list carry no meaning at all, and it is worth saying so plainly. The class attribute is a list of names for CSS and scripts, and nothing in the browser reads it: class attribute values do not create roles, landmarks or behaviour. The style attribute holds CSS declarations for this one element; a style attribute beats every stylesheet rule short of !important, which makes it a poor default but a good escape hatch for a value computed at runtime. And the id attribute is the one identifier the platform itself uses: <label for>, aria-labelledby, headers, popovertarget and every fragment link (a URL ending in #name) find their target through the id attribute. So a duplicated id attribute breaks all of them at once.

2.11 Custom Elements, data-*, and the Naming Rules

You cannot invent an element name, but you can extend the vocabulary in two approved ways, and both have precise naming rules.

A custom element name must contain a hyphen. That is the entire rule. It guarantees that no name you invent can ever collide with a future standard element, because standard element names never contain one.

<my-widget level="3">Content</my-widget>

DOM TREE
<my-widget level="3">
  #text "Content"

Both a hyphenated and an unhyphenated unknown name parse: the parser accepts any name and builds an element from it (§1.8). The difference appears afterwards. A hyphenated name is a valid custom element name, so customElements.define() can attach behaviour to it, and the browser will upgrade every instance already on the page (§15.3). An unhyphenated one can never be defined. It becomes an HTMLUnknownElement, and if the standard later adds that name, your markup silently means something else. A handful of names are reserved even though they have hyphens: annotation-xml, color-profile, font-face and a few other old SVG and MathML names.

Custom attributes have their own convention: start them with data-. A custom data attribute is guaranteed never to collide with a standard attribute, has its own API, and is the approved place to attach data to an element.

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="d" data-user-id="42" data-role="admin"></div>';
const d = document.querySelector('#d');
console.log('dataset.userId :', d.dataset.userId);
console.log('dataset.role   :', d.dataset.role);
console.log('keys           :', Object.keys(d.dataset).join(', '));
d.dataset.lastSeen = 'now';
console.log(d.outerHTML);

dataset.userId : 42
dataset.role   : admin
keys           : userId, role
<div id="d" data-user-id="42" data-role="admin" data-last-seen="now"></div>

dataset maps data-user-id to userId and back: strip the prefix, then remove each hyphen and capitalise the letter after it. Writing dataset.lastSeen created data-last-seen. The mapping works perfectly in both directions as long as your attribute names are lowercase with hyphens, which is the only form the specification allows.

Three limits on data-* worth knowing before you build on it:

  • Every value is a string. dataset.userId is "42", not 42, and a JSON blob in an attribute has to be parsed on every read.
  • It is visible to everyone, in view source and in devtools, so nothing secret goes there.
  • It is not a state store. A component whose truth lives in the DOM will disagree with itself the first time two scripts write to it.

Use it for what it is good at: a small value that can be written as text, that must survive server rendering, and that travels with the element.

Do not use data-* to express meaning HTML already has. data-hidden, data-disabled and data-required all exist as real attributes without the prefix, and the real ones inform the accessibility tree (§13.5) while the prefixed ones inform nobody.

Three names to keep straight. customelements.define is the call that attaches behaviour to a hyphenated name, and it is what makes customelements.define the reason the hyphen rule exists at all (§15.3). A custom data attribute is any data-*, and every custom data attribute on an element appears in dataset under its camel-cased name. And outerhtml is the serialisation of an element including its own tags, as against innerHTML, which leaves them out. The measurement above used outerhtml precisely so the new data-last-seen attribute would be visible.

2.12 lang, dir, and translate

Three global attributes describe the document's language and writing direction, and each has a concrete, visible effect.

The lang attribute names the language of an element's content as a BCP 47 tag (the standard format for language codes): en, en-GB, pt-BR, ar, zh-Hans. It is inherited, so <html lang="en"> is the one that matters most, and any passage in another language should say so:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Autumn</title></head>
  <body>
    <p>The French call it <span lang="fr">la rentrée</span>.</p>
  </body>
</html>

Several things depend on it:

  • a screen reader chooses its pronunciation rules and voice from it, and mispronouncing an entire page is the difference between usable and not;
  • the browser picks hyphenation and line-breaking rules;
  • lang-sensitive typography such as quotation marks and case conversion follows it;
  • spell-checking follows it;
  • translation tools use it to decide which language to translate from.

<html lang> is WCAG 3.1.1 at Level A, and a passage's lang is 3.1.2 at Level AA.

The dir attribute sets the base direction: ltr, rtl or auto. It does not translate anything or mirror your layout. It tells the bidirectional algorithm (the browser's rules for mixing left-to-right and right-to-left text) which way the paragraph runs, and that decides where punctuation lands and how mixed-direction runs are ordered. dir="auto" looks at the first character with a strong direction and is exactly right for user-generated content, where you do not know in advance which way a comment runs (§4.12).

The translate attribute is enumerated, yes or no, and marks content that must not be machine-translated: a product name, a code sample, a person's name:

<p>Deploy with <code translate="no">git push origin main</code> when ready.</p>

Google Translate and the browser's built-in translation both respect it. Without it, a code sample on a translated page comes back with its keywords translated, which is a real and frequent way for documentation to turn into nonsense. As §2.5 measured, an invalid value falls back to inheriting from the parent, which on a page that says nothing else means yes, so a typo silently means "translate this".

To summarise the three: the lang attribute names the language and is the one that changes pronunciation, hyphenation and spell-checking; the dir attribute names the base direction and changes only layout; and the translate attribute says whether machine translation should touch the content at all. Only the lang attribute is a WCAG requirement: 3.1.1 at Level A for the document and 3.1.2 at level aa for a passage. The level aa criterion is the one most organisations' accessibility commitments are written against.

2.13 Character References

A character reference is how you write a character that the markup syntax would otherwise swallow. There are two kinds.

A named character reference is &, a name, and ;: &amp;, &lt;, &gt;, &quot;, &nbsp;, &copy;. There are about 2,200 of them.

A numeric character reference is &#, the code point (the character's number in Unicode) in decimal, and ;, or &#x and the number in hexadecimal. &#169; and &#xA9; are both ©.

<p>&copy; 2026 &#169; &#xA9; &amp;copy;</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "© 2026 © © &copy;"

The first three produced the same character. The fourth is the useful trick: &amp;copy; escapes the ampersand, so the literal text &copy; appears on the page. That is how you write about entities. It is also the fix when a page displays &amp; where an & should be: someone escaped a string that was already escaped.

Only three references are truly required, and they are required in different places. In text, &lt; for < and &amp; for &. In an attribute value, &amp; for & and &quot; for a double quote inside a double-quoted value. Everything else is optional, because in a UTF-8 document (§1.3, §3.3) you can simply type the character. ©, →, — and 😀 are all fine as literal bytes, and far easier to read in source than &#128512;.

The one that is not optional in practice is &amp; in a URL:

<a href="/search?q=cats&amp;page=2">Next page</a>

A bare & in an attribute value is legal HTML when it cannot be read as the start of a reference, and &page= is in fact left alone. But whether a given &name gets decoded depends on rules nobody keeps in their head, and it is a gamble you do not need to take. Always write &amp; in a URL. It costs nothing: in jsdom 26.1.0 both spellings of the link above resolve to the same https://example.com/search?q=cats&page=2.

&nbsp; deserves its own paragraph because it is so often used for the wrong reason. It is U+00A0, an ordinary character that happens to be a space the line-breaking rules will not break at. That makes it right for keeping a unit with its number (5&nbsp;km, Chapter&nbsp;4) and wrong for indentation or for pushing things apart, which is CSS's job. As §2.14 explains, a run of &nbsp; is the one kind of whitespace that does not collapse, which is exactly why it gets abused as a layout tool.

The two kinds have different strengths. A named character reference is readable (&copy; says what it is), but there are about 2,200 of them to look up. A numeric character reference needs no lookup at all, because the code point is the name. So a numeric character reference is what a generator emits, and what you fall back to for a character with no named character reference.

2.14 Whitespace Collapsing

The last piece of vocabulary, and one the DOM tree makes unusually clear:

<p>one    two
three</p>

DOM TREE
<p>
  #text "one    two\nthree"

The parser preserved every character. Four spaces and a newline are still there in the text node. textContent returns them, and a regular expression over the DOM will see them.

The collapsing happens later, during rendering. CSS's white-space property, whose starting value is normal, says that a sequence of whitespace characters is drawn as a single space, and that a newline counts as whitespace. So the reader sees "one two three" while the DOM holds something else. That is why comparing textContent with what you see on screen so often fails.

Two consequences follow, and both are frequent bugs.

Whitespace between inline elements is a real space. Written on separate lines, <a> elements in a list are separated by a newline in the source, and that newline is drawn as a gap between them. It is not a margin, and no amount of CSS on the links will remove it. The classic fixes are to remove the whitespace from the source, or to lay the container out with flexbox so whitespace between elements stops taking part.

<pre> is where it stops. <pre> (§4.11) carries white-space: pre from the browser's stylesheet, so its whitespace is drawn exactly as written, which is what makes it right for code and for captured tool output. The element itself does not preserve whitespace; the CSS does, and the same declaration applied to a <div> behaves identically. The parser has one real whitespace rule of its own: a newline immediately after the <pre> start tag is dropped, so that writing the opening tag on its own line does not put a blank first line in the output.

Exercises

1. A component library emits <div class="card" class="{{theme}}" data-id="{{id}}" hidden="{{isHidden}}">. Three bugs. Find them, and say what each looks like in production.

Solution

The duplicate class attribute. §2.2 measured it: the first occurrence wins, the second is discarded silently. So the card class applies and the theme class never does. In production this looks like "the theme prop does nothing" — the value is correct in the template, correct in the props, and absent from the DOM. Nothing logs, and the fix is to compose one string: class="card {{theme}}".

hidden="{{isHidden}}" on a boolean attribute. §2.4: presence is truth and the value is never consulted, so hidden="false" hides the element. This one is worse than the first because it fails in the direction that removes content — the element is not rendered, not in the accessibility tree, and not a focus stop (§13.8). Someone will spend an afternoon on "the card disappears when isHidden is false". The fix is to emit the attribute or not emit it; every framework has syntax for exactly this.

data-id="{{id}}" is a lesser problem, and it is real. Whatever id is, dataset.id reads back a string. If the surrounding code does if (el.dataset.id === someNumber) it never matches, and dataset.id > 10 is a string comparison. §2.11: every data-* value is a string, in both directions.

There is a fourth thing that is not a bug but is worth flagging in review: if theme can ever be empty, class="card " is harmless, but the same template shape with an unquoted value — class=card {{theme}} — would merge into the next attribute. That is why §2.2's advice is to quote unconditionally.

2. Why is <p><div>x</div></p> four nodes rather than one, and why is <a href="/x"><h2>Title</h2><p>Body</p></a> exactly what it looks like? Give the rule that distinguishes them.

Solution

The rule is the content model of the containing element, and the two cases sit on opposite sides of it.

<p> accepts phrasing content only (§2.7). <div> is flow content and not phrasing content, so it cannot be a child of a paragraph. The parser cannot report an error — HTML has no mechanism for that — so it applies §1.8's recovery: implicitly close the <p>, emit the <div> as a sibling, continue. The measured result in §2.7 is four nodes: the original <p> holding the text before the div, the <div>, a bare text node, and a fourth empty <p> created by the stray </p> that now has no open paragraph to close.

<a> is transparent (§2.8). It has no content model of its own and takes its parent's, so an <a> sitting in the body may contain anything the body may contain — headings and paragraphs included. Nothing is rewritten because nothing was violated. The measured tree is the source tree.

The distinguishing question is therefore never "is this element inline or block" — that is CSS vocabulary and it does not decide anything here. It is "what does the specification say this element's permitted content is", and there are three answers that matter: a fixed category (<p>: phrasing), a specific list (<ul>: only <li>), or transparent (<a>, <ins>, <del>, <object>, <video>).

Two riders on the transparent case. Interactive content still may not nest, so a <button> inside that <a> is invalid regardless. And transparency inherits restrictions rather than escaping them — put the same <a> inside a <p> and it may only contain phrasing content, because that is what its parent permits.

3. document.querySelector('input').setAttribute('value', 'reset') does not change what the user sees. Explain precisely, and give the correct code.

Solution

The value attribute and the value property are two different things (§2.3). The attribute is the field's initial value; the property is its current value. They agree until the field's dirty value flag is set — which happens the first time the user types or a script assigns to .value — and after that the attribute no longer feeds the property at all.

§2.3 measured the whole sequence: with value="start" in the markup, both read start; after q.value = 'typed', getAttribute('value') still returns start while .value returns typed; and setAttribute('value', 'reset') changes the attribute and leaves .value at typed.

The correct code is to assign the property:

document.body.innerHTML = '<input value="start">';
const input = document.querySelector('input');
input.value = 'typed';                 // the user types

input.setAttribute('value', 'reset');  // changes the document, not the field
console.log('after setAttribute:', input.value);

input.value = 'reset';                 // changes the field
console.log('after assignment  :', input.value);

after setAttribute: typed
after assignment  : reset

This is a design decision, not an oversight. It is what makes form.reset() possible: reset restores every control to its attribute value, which it could not do if typing had overwritten it. The same split explains checked versus .checked and selected versus .selected, and it is why a "reset this field" button implemented with setAttribute works perfectly in tests — which never type — and never in production.

The general rule: read the property for live state, the attribute for what the document said. And when debugging, getAttribute() and devtools' Elements panel both show you the document; the property is the only thing that shows you the state.

4. Design the markup for a "recently viewed product" card that must be entirely clickable, carry a product ID for analytics, contain a "Add to basket" button, and be announced sensibly by a screen reader. Justify every decision against a rule in this section.

Solution

<article class="card" data-product-id="A-4021">
  <img src="/p/A-4021.jpg" alt="" width="200" height="200">
  <h3><a class="card__link" href="/products/A-4021">Cast iron skillet, 26cm</a></h3>
  <p>Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260&nbsp;°C.</p>
  <p class="card__price">£48.00</p>
  <button type="button" class="card__buy">Add to basket</button>
</article>

The link wraps the heading only, not the card. The obvious approach — an <a> around everything — is legal, because <a> is transparent (§2.8). It is still wrong here for two reasons. First, §2.6: interactive content may not contain interactive content, and there is a <button> inside, so the whole-card link is actually invalid markup. Second, §7.10: a link's accessible name is all of its text, so a card-wrapping link is announced as "Cast iron skillet 26cm pre-seasoned oven safe to 260 degrees £48.00, link" — useless in a list of links.

The whole card is still clickable, via CSS, by stretching the link's box over the card — .card { position: relative } and .card__link::after { position: absolute; inset: 0 }. The click target is the card, the accessible name is nine words, and the DOM stays valid. The technique belongs to css_mastery; the reason it has to be a technique rather than markup is this section's content model rules.

data-product-id, not productid. §2.11: the data- prefix is the sanctioned way to attach data to an element, it is guaranteed not to collide with a current or future standard attribute, and it reads back as dataset.productId. An invented bare attribute has neither guarantee. The value is a string on the way out, which is fine — an analytics identifier is a string.

alt="" on the image. §8.3: the image is decorative here, because the product name is already the heading immediately below it. An alt repeating the name would make a screen reader announce the product twice.

<article>, not <div>. §6: a self-contained, independently distributable item is what <article> means, and it gives the card an article role in the accessibility tree so a user can navigate between cards.

type="button" on the button. §11.8: a <button> inside a <form> defaults to type="submit", and an <article> that later gets wrapped in a form would start submitting it. Stating the type costs eleven characters and removes the possibility.

&nbsp; between the number and the unit. §2.13: it is the one legitimate use of a non-breaking space — keeping 260 and °C on the same line — rather than as a layout tool.

5. A colleague says "<span> is inline and <div> is block, that is the difference". What is wrong with that answer, and what is the real one?

Solution

It confuses a CSS fact with an HTML one, and the two are independent.

"Inline" and "block" name values of the CSS display property. The browser's default stylesheet gives <div> display: block and <span> display: inline, and one line of CSS reverses either. If that were the whole difference, div { display: inline } would make a <div> interchangeable with a <span>, and it does not.

The real difference is the content model (§2.6). <span> is phrasing content and accepts phrasing content; <div> is flow content and accepts flow content. That is a property of the document language, and no stylesheet changes it. The consequences are the ones this section measured:

  • A <span> may appear inside a <p>; a <div> may not, and putting one there produces the four-node tree of §2.7 rather than an error.
  • A <div> may contain a <ul> or a <table>; a <span> may not, and the parser will not rewrite that one — it simply produces markup a validator rejects and a specification does not define.
  • Both are valid parents in different places, and neither is decided by how they are painted.

There is a second thing wrong with the answer, which matters more in practice. It implies the choice between them is a visual one, and the choice is not visual at all: §4.14's point is that <div> and <span> both mean nothing, and the actual decision is whether some element with meaning — <section>, <article>, <nav>, <p>, <em>, <time> — fits. <div> and <span> are what you reach for once you have established that none does.
