Picking between the two meaningless elements is the last and least interesting step, and by then the answer is dictated by where the element has to live.

SECTION 3

The Head: Metadata, Encoding and the Resource Graph

The <head> is the part of the document nobody sees and everything reads. It decides:

  • how the bytes are turned into characters;
  • what the page is called in a search result and a browser tab;
  • what a link to the page looks like when someone pastes it into a chat;
  • which stylesheet arrives, and when;
  • what colour the browser paints around the page;
  • and, on a phone, whether the page is laid out at the screen's real width or squeezed out of a pretend 980-pixel desktop.

It is also the part of a document that piles up over the years. A ten-year-old site's head is forty lines of tags nobody dares delete. This section is organised so you can tell which of those forty actually do something.

One structural note before anything else. <head> is a real element with real rules about what it may contain, but its tags are almost always left out (§1.9). Everything up to the first element that belongs in the body goes into the head automatically. That is why a stray <div> placed before your <link> tags quietly moves them into the body.

3.1 What Belongs in the Head

The head holds metadata content (§2.6) and nothing else. Exactly eight elements belong to that category:

<title>
The document's name. Required — it is the only element the specification says every document must have (§3.2).
<meta>
Name/value metadata, or the character encoding, or an HTTP-header-like pragma (§3.3, §3.5, §3.6).
<link>
A relationship to another resource: a stylesheet, an icon, a canonical URL, a hint (§3.9).
<base>
The base URL for every relative reference in the document. At most one (§3.4).
<style>
Inline CSS.
<script>
Inline or external JavaScript. Blocks the parser unless deferred (§1.10).
<noscript>
Content for a browser with scripting off (§3.15).
<template>
Inert markup (§15.2). Legal in the head, rarely put there.

Order matters for two of them, and for nothing else. <meta charset> must come first, for the reason §3.3 gives. <base> must come before any element that uses a URL, because it only affects references that come after it.

A minimal, complete head is four lines, and a surprising number of sites never need a fifth:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Cast iron skillet, 26cm — Acme</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>
</body>
</html>

One structural reminder from §1.9 while we are here. <head> and <body> are real elements whose tags are almost always left out, and the parser decides where one ends and the other begins. Everything from the start of the document up to the first element that belongs in the body goes into <head>; that element and everything after it go into <body>. So a stray <div> written above your <link> tags does not sit in the <head>. It opens the <body>, and every metadata element after it ends up in the body too, where <link rel="stylesheet"> still works and <meta charset> does not.

3.2 title

<title> is the document's name, and it appears in more places than anyone expects:

  • the browser tab and the window title;
  • the bookmark and the history entry;
  • the headline link of a search result;
  • the text a screen reader announces when the page loads;
  • the fallback title of a link shared into a chat application.

It is plain text only (markup inside it is not treated as markup), and there is exactly one per document.

Writing it well is a small discipline with disproportionate returns:

  • Most specific first. Cast iron skillet, 26cm — Acme, not Acme — Shop — Cookware — Cast iron skillet. A browser tab shows about twenty characters and a search result about sixty, so the front of the string is the part that survives.
  • Unique per page. Two pages with the same title cannot be told apart in history, in bookmarks or in a search result, and search engines flag duplicate titles.
  • Say what the page is, not what the site is. "Home" is a bad title; "Acme — hand-forged cookware" is a good one.
  • Update it on a client-side route change. A single-page application (one that swaps views with JavaScript instead of loading new pages) that does not set document.title leaves the user's tab, history and back button all saying whatever the first page said (§14.6).

The title is also the first thing a screen reader announces after a navigation, which makes it the user's confirmation that the page they clicked is the page that loaded.

3.3 meta charset

The single most important line in the head:

<meta charset="utf-8">

§1.3 explained why the encoding must be known before the bytes can become characters. This is the declaration, and three details about it are non-negotiable.

It must be within the first 1024 bytes of the document. The browser searches that first stretch for it; if it is not there, the parser falls back to a guess. The rule in practice is simpler: make it the first thing inside <head>, before the title, before anything.

Getting it wrong is silent and ugly. A UTF-8 file read as Windows-1252 shows é as Ã© and — as â€". That pattern is called mojibake, and once you have seen it you recognise it instantly. The file is not corrupted: the same bytes, decoded correctly, are fine.

The HTTP Content-Type header wins over the meta tag. If the server sends Content-Type: text/html; charset=iso-8859-1, that is the encoding, and no meta tag overrides it. So a page that shows mojibake despite a correct <meta charset> has a server configuration problem, not a markup one. Check the response header first.

Always use UTF-8. It encodes every character in Unicode, the overwhelming majority of the web uses it, every tool defaults to it, and there is no situation in current practice where anything else is the right answer. Make sure your editor and your build pipeline agree: a UTF-8 declaration on a file saved in some other encoding is worse than no declaration at all.

Note the syntax: <meta charset="utf-8"> is a special short form. The older <meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=utf-8"> still works and says the same thing at four times the length.

3.4 base

<base> sets the URL that every relative reference in the document is resolved against. It can also set a default target for links and forms.

<base href="https://cdn.example.com/v2/" target="_blank">

Its effect is easiest to see by measuring it. With that <base> in the head of a document served from https://www.example.com/products/skillet, four links and an image resolve like this:

document.baseURI  : https://cdn.example.com/v2/

href="about"                         ->  https://cdn.example.com/v2/about
href="/about"                        ->  https://cdn.example.com/about
href="https://other.example.com/x"   ->  https://other.example.com/x
href="#top"                          ->  https://cdn.example.com/v2/#top
src="logo.png"                       ->  https://cdn.example.com/v2/logo.png

Read the fourth line twice, because it is the reason <base> has a bad reputation. A fragment-only link resolves against the base too. So href="#top", which every reader expects to scroll to the top of the current page, becomes a link to a different document entirely. Every in-page anchor, every skip link (§6.10) and every href="#" on the page silently starts navigating away.

The other rules follow from the same mechanism. A root-relative /about keeps its path but takes the base's origin (its scheme, host and port), and an absolute URL is left alone. document.baseURI tells you what is actually in effect.

There is at most one <base> per document, and it must come before any element that uses a URL. A <link rel="stylesheet"> written above it resolves against the document, not the base, which gives you a page where some assets moved and others did not.

The honest summary: <base> solves a problem almost nobody has, and creates one everybody notices. Use absolute or root-relative URLs, or generate the prefix at build time. The one genuinely good use is inside an <iframe srcdoc> (§9.13). There the frame has no URL of its own, so relative references would otherwise have nothing to resolve against.

3.5 The Named Metas

<meta name="..." content="..."> is a name/value pair about the document. The HTML specification defines eight names, and these are the useful ones.

<meta name="description" content="A 26cm pre-seasoned cast iron skillet, oven safe to 260°C. Free UK delivery.">
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
<meta name="author" content="Dana Okonjo">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0b3d2e">
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
<meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">

description meta. A one- or two-sentence summary. Search engines do not use it for ranking, but they often show it as the snippet under the result, so it is a piece of writing aimed at a person deciding whether to click. Around 150 characters is what survives being cut short. It is also the fallback description for a social card when Open Graph is missing (§3.13). Write a different one for each page: a site-wide description is worse than none, because it makes every result look the same.

robots meta. Instructions for crawlers (the programs search engines use to read pages), separated by commas:

  • index/noindex says whether this page may appear in results;
  • follow/nofollow says whether its links should be crawled;
  • noarchive suppresses the cached copy;
  • max-snippet, max-image-preview and max-video-preview limit what may be shown.

noindex is the one that matters, and the one to be careful with. A noindex left in a template after a staging deploy removes a site from search results, and that is a genuinely common outage. googlebot is the variant aimed at one specific crawler.

Two limits worth knowing. A noindex only works if the crawler can fetch the page. Blocking the page in robots.txt stops the crawler from ever seeing the tag, so a page that is blocked and marked noindex can stay in the index. And noindex is not access control: it is a request, honoured by the major crawlers and by nobody else. Anything that must not be public needs authentication.

author meta names the document's author. Some readers, feed tools and content pipelines read it.

theme-color suggests a colour for the browser's own interface around the page: the address bar on mobile, the title bar of an installed app. It accepts a media attribute, so a site can offer one colour for each colour scheme:

<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" content="#ffffff">
<meta name="theme-color" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" content="#0b1120">

color-scheme declares which colour schemes the page supports: light, dark, or light dark. It is what makes the browser's own drawing follow suit: form controls, scrollbars and the default background colour behind the page. A dark-themed site that styles everything itself but leaves this out gets white scrollbars and white form controls, which gives it away. The equivalent CSS property is color-scheme and belongs to css_mastery. The meta version applies before any stylesheet arrives, which is exactly when a flash of white would otherwise happen.

referrer sets a referrer policy for the whole document: how much of this page's URL is sent to the next site in the Referer header. It takes the same values as the referrerpolicy attribute on individual elements (§9.11): no-referrer, origin, same-origin, strict-origin, strict-origin-when-cross-origin and others. Current browsers already default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so this is for tightening the policy, not for matching the default.

keywords is defined and ignored. No major search engine has used it for two decades. Delete it.

To summarise the six: write a distinct description meta per page, because it is the snippet a human reads before deciding to click; use the robots meta deliberately and check it before every release, because a stray noindex in a robots meta removes a site from search; set author meta if your pipeline uses it; set theme-color and color-scheme so the browser's own interface matches the page; and set a referrer policy only when you want something tighter than the modern default. Note also that media is not limited to <link>: a theme-color may carry a media attribute, and the media attribute is how one page offers a different colour for each scheme.

3.6 http-equiv

<meta http-equiv> imitates an HTTP response header from inside the document. It exists because authors have not always had access to the server's configuration, and today headers are better in nearly every case.

Three values are still in use.

<meta http-equiv="content-security-policy" content="default-src 'self'">
<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="5; url=/new-location">
<meta http-equiv="x-ua-compatible" content="IE=edge">

content-security-policy is a real, enforced CSP (a list of rules saying which scripts, styles and other resources the page may load), and it is the one legitimate reason to reach for http-equiv: it works on static hosting where you cannot set headers. It has two limits that matter. It cannot carry frame-ancestors (§9.14), report-uri or sandbox; browsers ignore those directives in a meta tag, so a clickjacking defence written this way silently does not exist. And it only takes effect from the point in the document where it appears, so anything above it has already been fetched with no policy at all. Put it first, and prefer the header when you can send one.

meta refresh reloads the page or redirects after a delay. Avoid it. With a non-zero delay it moves the page out from under a reader with no warning and no way to stop it, which fails WCAG 2.2.1. With a zero delay it is a redirect done in the wrong layer, and it breaks the back button because the original page stays in history. A server-side 301 or 302 is correct, faster, cacheable and understood by crawlers. The one defensible use is a "this page has moved, you will be taken there in ten seconds" page that also contains a real link, and then the link is what people will use.

x-ua-compatible told Internet Explorer which rendering engine to use. Internet Explorer is gone. Delete it.

http-equiv cannot set arbitrary headers. Content-Type, default-style, refresh, content-security-policy and x-ua-compatible are the whole list. In particular, you cannot set caching, CORS or X-Frame-Options this way, and a line in someone's head that appears to do so is doing nothing at all.

Of the three, meta refresh is the one you are most likely to inherit and most reliably should remove. A meta refresh with a delay moves the page under the reader with no way to stop it, which fails WCAG 2.2.1; with no delay it is a redirect in the wrong layer that breaks the back button. Replace it with a 301 or 302.

3.7 The Viewport

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

This is the second most important line in the head, and the reason is historical. When phones first came with browsers, the whole web was designed for desktop widths. So mobile browsers pretended to be about 980 pixels wide and scaled the result down. The page was more or less legible, everything was tiny, and the user pinched to zoom. Without a viewport meta that is still what happens: a responsive stylesheet on a page with no viewport tag has all its media queries checked against a fake 980-pixel viewport, and none of them match.

width=device-width says: lay the page out at the device's real width. initial-scale=1 says: start at 100% zoom, do not scale it down. Together they are the line every responsive page needs, and there is essentially no reason to write anything else in it.

The other properties exist and are mostly traps.

width=device-width
Layout viewport equals the device width. Always.
initial-scale=1
Start unzoomed. Always.
user-scalable=no
Never. Disables pinch-to-zoom, which is a direct WCAG 1.4.4 failure and makes the page unusable for anyone with low vision.
maximum-scale=1
Never, for the same reason — it is user-scalable=no with extra steps.
viewport-fit=cover
Extends the layout under a notch or rounded corner. Needed only when you also handle the safe-area insets in CSS.

user-scalable=no gets the emphasis because it is still copied into new projects from old templates, usually to stop iOS zooming in when a form field is focused. That zoom has a different cause and a different fix: iOS zooms when an input's font size is below 16 pixels, so setting font-size: 16px on inputs removes the behaviour without taking zoom away from everyone. Some browsers now ignore user-scalable=no outright, which tells you what the platform thinks of it.

There is no situation in current practice where a viewport meta should say anything other than those two properties. Write the viewport meta once, in your base template, and never think about it again.

3.8 Icons and the Manifest

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">

Those four lines are a complete, current set of icons, and the reasoning behind each is worth having.

favicon.ico is the old fallback. Browsers request /favicon.ico from the site root whether you declare it or not, so it exists mainly to stop a 404 in your logs. A single 32×32 image inside is enough.

An SVG icon covers every other case at any size, because it is a vector image. It can even contain a prefers-color-scheme media query and change with the user's theme.

apple-touch-icon is what iOS uses when a page is added to the home screen: a 180×180 PNG, with no transparency and no rounded corners, because the system rounds it.

The web app manifest is a JSON file that describes the site as an installable application: its name, its icons at several sizes, its theme and background colours, its start URL and its display mode. rel="manifest" is how the document points at it, and it is what makes "Add to home screen" produce something that looks like an app instead of a bookmark.

{
  "name": "Acme Cookware",
  "short_name": "Acme",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#0b3d2e",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-maskable.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png",
      "purpose": "maskable" }
  ]
}

The maskable purpose matters more than it looks. Without one, Android crops your icon into a circle and cuts off the edges. A maskable icon keeps its important content inside the central 80%, so any shape the platform cuts it into leaves that content intact.

The old alternative to all of this was twenty lines of apple-touch-icon-precomposed, msapplication-TileImage and PNGs in a size for every device that ever existed. Those are safe to delete.

The web app manifest is the only one of the four that describes the site rather than an image, and rel="manifest" is the single line that connects the page to it. Without rel="manifest" the web app manifest is a JSON file nothing points at, and "Add to home screen" falls back to a bookmark with a favicon.

On the first line specifically: rel="icon" is the modern spelling, and it replaces the rel="shortcut icon" of twenty years ago ("shortcut" was never a real link type). Give rel="icon" a sizes and a type when you offer more than one, and the browser picks.

3.9 link and the Resource Graph

<link> states a relationship between this document and another resource. The rel attribute names the relationship and decides everything the element does; a <link> with no rel does nothing at all.

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/produits/poele">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

rel="stylesheet" is the one that blocks. A stylesheet is render-blocking by design: the browser will not paint until it has the CSS, because painting first would show unstyled content and then rearrange it. That is the right trade-off, and it makes the number and size of stylesheets in the head the main factor in how quickly a page appears.

The media attribute is the lever. A stylesheet whose media does not currently match is still downloaded, at low priority, and does not block rendering:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/wide.css" media="(min-width: 60em)">

That is the honest way to split a large stylesheet. Note that the download still happens: media changes the priority and the blocking, not whether the file is fetched.

The rel values worth knowing, beyond those already covered:

stylesheet
A CSS file. Render-blocking unless media excludes it.
icon, manifest
§3.8.
canonical, alternate
§3.12.
preload, preconnect, prefetch, dns-prefetch, modulepreload
§3.10.
next, prev
Position in a sequence of pages. Read by some readers and crawlers; harmless and occasionally useful.
author, license, help
Relationships to a person, a licence, a help document. Also valid on <a> (§7.9).
search
An OpenSearch description, which lets a browser offer search-from-the-address-bar for your site.

3.10 Resource Hints: preload, preconnect and prefetch

A resource hint tells the browser to do now some work it would otherwise do later. The four kinds solve genuinely different problems and are routinely confused.

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://analytics.example.com">

rel="preconnect" opens the TCP connection and completes the TLS handshake (the encryption setup) to another origin now, so that when the browser finds a resource there, those round trips are already paid for. It saves 100–300 milliseconds on a font or API host on another origin. It costs a connection, so use it for two or three origins at most; beyond that you are competing with the requests you actually have.

rel="preload" fetches one specific resource at high priority. It is the only hint that requires an as attribute (font, style, script, image, fetch), because as decides the priority, the Accept header and which CSP directive applies. Its purpose is to fix late discovery. A font referenced from inside a CSS file is not discovered until the CSS has been downloaded and parsed, which can be two round trips into the page load. Preloading it moves the request to the first round trip.

A preload that is never used is a wasted download, and the browser logs a console warning about it, which makes this the easiest hint to get wrong. Two specific traps. crossorigin is required for fonts, even ones from your own origin, because fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, and a preload without it fetches the file twice. And preload does not apply the resource: a preloaded stylesheet still needs its <link rel="stylesheet">.

rel="prefetch" fetches something at low priority for a future navigation: the checkout page from the basket page, the next page of results. It is a bet on where the user goes next, paid for out of spare bandwidth. Do not use it for anything on the current page; that is what preload is for.

rel="dns-prefetch" only looks up a hostname's address. It is a weaker, cheaper preconnect, and mostly useful alongside it for origins you are less sure about.

The rule that keeps these useful: hints are a scarce resource, not a checklist. Every hint competes with real requests for the same bandwidth. A head with fifteen preloads is slower than a head with none, because the browser's own priorities were better than the ones you overrode. Preload the font the page cannot paint without, preconnect the one third-party origin that matters, and leave the rest alone.

Collected, in one line each: rel="preconnect" pays for a connection to an origin before you need it; rel="preload" fetches one resource this page cannot paint without, and is the only one of the four that needs an as attribute; rel="prefetch" fetches something for the next navigation at idle priority; and dns-prefetch resolves a name and nothing else. The as attribute is worth restating because omitting it is the usual cause of a double fetch — it determines the priority, the Accept header and the CSP directive, so a rel="preload" without it is a request the browser cannot match to the real one.

3.11 Subresource Integrity and crossorigin

When you load a script or stylesheet from someone else's server, you run whatever they serve. subresource integrity closes that gap by pinning the exact bytes:

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib-3.2.1.js"
        integrity="sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kPzQho1wx4JwY8wC"
        crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

The integrity attribute holds a hash (a fingerprint) of the expected content: sha256, sha384 or sha512, base64-encoded, with the algorithm name in front. The browser fetches the file, hashes it, and refuses to execute it if the two hashes differ. A compromised CDN, an injected line, a truncated download and a silently updated file all fail safely, by not running.

Two mechanical requirements come with it.

crossorigin is required for a resource from another origin. Without CORS (the rules that let one origin read another's responses), the browser cannot read the response body well enough to check it, so the check cannot run. crossorigin="anonymous" sends no credentials and is what you want; the server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

The hash pins one exact version. That is the point, and also the maintenance cost. A URL like /lib@3/latest.js cannot have an integrity hash, because its content is meant to change. So SRI forces you to pin an exact version, which is good practice anyway: a third-party script that updates itself is an unreviewed deploy to production every time its author pushes.

Generate the hash rather than typing it:

curl -sS https://cdn.example.com/lib-3.2.1.js |
  openssl dgst -sha384 -binary |
  openssl base64 -A

The crossorigin attribute appears on <script>, <link>, <img>, <video> and <audio> (not on <iframe>, which has no such attribute), and it always means the same thing: fetch this in CORS mode. Its values are anonymous (no cookies or credentials) and use-credentials (send them). It is required for SRI, for reading an image into a <canvas> without tainting it (§8.14), for a <track> from another origin (§9.9), and for fonts.

3.12 canonical, alternate and hreflang

The same content can often be reached at several URLs: with and without a trailing slash, with tracking parameters, under a print path, on a staging domain. A canonical link says which one is the real one:

<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">

Search engines merge their signals onto the canonical URL, which is why a page with ?utm_source=newsletter in the address does not compete with itself in the index. Three rules:

  • make it absolute;
  • make it self-referential on the canonical page itself;
  • make sure it points at a page that actually exists and returns 200.

A canonical pointing at a redirect or a 404 is worse than none.

rel="alternate" names a different version of the same content: a translation, a feed, a print version:

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-GB" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/produits/poele">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">
<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" title="Blog" href="/feed.xml">

hreflang names the language, and optionally the region, of the linked document as a BCP 47 tag (§2.12). Two rules make the difference between it working and not. The set must be complete and reciprocal: every page in the group lists every page in the group, including itself, and if the French page does not point back at the English one, the pair is ignored. And x-default names the page to serve when none of the languages matches the user's, usually a language picker or the main market's page.

hreflang on a <link> describes the whole document. The same attribute on an <a> (§7.9) describes the language of one link's destination, which is a different and much smaller claim.

The two are not alternatives. A canonical link says "this is the same content as that"; rel="alternate" says "that is a different version of this". So a translated page has both: a self-referential canonical link naming itself, and a rel="alternate" for every language including its own.

This is also the part of the head that search engine optimization actually depends on. Most of what is sold as search engine optimization is content and links. The markup half is small and mechanical: a unique title, a real description, a correct canonical, valid structured data, and headings that describe the page.

3.13 Open Graph and Social Cards

When a URL is pasted into a chat application, a social network or a messaging app, that application fetches the page and builds a preview from its metadata. open graph is the vocabulary nearly all of them read.

<meta property="og:title" content="Cast iron skillet, 26cm">
<meta property="og:description" content="Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260°C. Free UK delivery.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og/skillet.png">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="A cast iron skillet on a gas hob">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/products/skillet">
<meta property="og:type" content="product">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="Acme Cookware">

Note property, not name. Open Graph is an RDFa vocabulary rather than a meta name defined by the HTML specification, and some consumers ignore a tag written with name="og:title". Both spellings appear in the wild; property is the one the specification asks for.

og:title, og:description, og:image and og:url are the four that matter. The image is the one with real requirements: an absolute URL, at least 1200×630 for a large card, under about 5MB, and served from a URL that does not require a login, because a crawler is not logged in. og:image:alt is its alternative text, and it is as necessary here as anywhere else.

The twitter card tags are the same idea in a different vocabulary, and today they are mostly redundant, because the platform falls back to Open Graph. Two are still worth sending:

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:site" content="@acmecookware">

twitter:card chooses the layout, and summary_large_image is the difference between a thumbnail and a full-width picture. Note that these use name, not property.

Two practical points. Nothing here has a fallback chain you control. Each consumer decides what to read and what to substitute, and most fall back to <title> and <meta name="description">, which is a good reason to get those right first. And previews are cached aggressively by every platform, so a corrected card can take days to appear unless you use the platform's own cache-clearing tool.

The practical position on the twitter card tags is that they are a small, cheap supplement, not a second system: send twitter:card to choose the layout, and let Open Graph supply the content. A twitter card block that repeats every Open Graph value is two sets of strings to keep in step for no gain.

3.14 Structured Data

structured data describes a page's content in a vocabulary machines can read, so that a search engine can show it as a rich result: a recipe with its cooking time, a product with its price and rating, an event with its date, a breadcrumb trail.

The vocabulary is schema.org, and there are two syntaxes for putting it in a page.

json-ld is the recommended one. It is a JSON block in a <script> whose type is application/ld+json, and it is entirely separate from the markup:

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Product",
  "name": "Cast iron skillet, 26cm",
  "image": "https://example.com/img/skillet.png",
  "description": "Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260°C.",
  "brand": { "@type": "Brand", "name": "Acme" },
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "price": "48.00",
    "priceCurrency": "GBP",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock"
  }
}
</script>

The block is not executed. application/ld+json is a data type, not a script type, so the browser runs nothing. Its advantages all come from being separate: it can be generated from the same data that renders the page, it does not constrain the markup, and it can be validated on its own.

microdata is the other syntax. It annotates the markup in place with itemscope, itemtype and itemprop:

<div itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Product">
  <h1 itemprop="name">Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>
  <img itemprop="image" src="/img/skillet.png" alt="A cast iron skillet" width="400" height="400">
  <div itemprop="offers" itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Offer">
    <span itemprop="price">48.00</span>
    <meta itemprop="priceCurrency" content="GBP">
  </div>
</div>

itemscope starts an item, itemtype gives its type as a schema.org URL, and each itemprop names a property whose value is the element's text, or its content, href or src for elements that have one. A <meta itemprop> inside the body is the usual way to give a value that has no visible text.

Microdata's advantage is that it cannot drift out of date: the price in the markup is the price in the data. Its disadvantage is that it forces the markup into the shape of the vocabulary, which is why JSON-LD's problem of keeping two copies is usually judged the lesser evil. Whichever you choose, the structured data must describe what is actually on the page. Inventing a rating or a price that the page does not show is against every search engine's guidelines and is penalised.

Both syntaxes can be checked with Google's Rich Results Test and with the schema.org validator, and it is worth doing: a single mistyped property name means the whole item is thrown away.

3.15 noscript

<noscript> holds content that is shown only when scripting is unavailable, either because it is turned off in the browser or because an extension or a network policy blocks it.

<noscript>
  <p>This page needs JavaScript for the interactive chart.
     The same figures are in the <a href="/reports/2025.csv">CSV download</a>.</p>
</noscript>

DOM TREE
<noscript>
  #text "\n  <p>This page needs JavaScript for the interactive chart.\n     The same figures are in the <a href=\"/reports/2025.csv\">CSV download</a>.</p>\n"

In the head it may contain only <link>, <style> and <meta>; in the body it may contain anything. The tree above shows the part that surprises people: with scripting enabled the contents are not parsed as elements at all. There is no <p> and no <a> in the DOM, only a single text node holding the markup word for word. That is why document.querySelector('noscript a') returns null, and why a script cannot reach inside one. With scripting disabled, the same bytes are parsed normally and the elements exist.

Realistically, very few users turn JavaScript off on purpose, and <noscript> is not a substitute for progressive enhancement (§12.14), the practice of building a page that works without JavaScript and improves with it. Such a page needs no <noscript>. A page that is a blank white rectangle without JavaScript is not fixed by a paragraph apologising for that.

Where it genuinely earns its place is narrow but real: offering an alternative to a feature that only works with scripts, and supplying a tracking pixel or a stylesheet variant for when JavaScript is off. Treat it as a courtesy, not a strategy.

Exercises

1. Audit this head. There are six problems.

<head>
  <title>Home</title>
  <meta name="keywords" content="cookware, pans, skillet, cast iron, kitchen">
  <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, user-scalable=no">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'none'">
</head>
Solution

1. <meta charset> is last. §3.3: it must be within the first 1024 bytes, and everything above it has already been decoded under a guess. Move it to the first line of the head. On this small head the guess would probably be right, which is what makes the bug survive to production and appear the day someone adds a long comment above it.

2. user-scalable=no. §3.7: it disables pinch-to-zoom, which is a direct WCAG 1.4.4 failure and makes the page unusable for many people with low vision. Some browsers ignore it now. If it was added to stop iOS zooming on focused inputs, the fix is font-size: 16px on the inputs.

3. <title>Home</title>. §3.2: this is the tab, the bookmark, the history entry, the search result headline and the first thing a screen reader announces. "Home" identifies nothing and is not unique. Acme — hand-forged cookware says what the page is.

4. frame-ancestors in a <meta> CSP. §3.6 and §9.14: browsers explicitly ignore frame-ancestors in a meta tag. This is the worst bug in the list, because it looks like a clickjacking defence and provides none. It must be a response header.

5. X-UA-Compatible. Internet Explorer no longer exists. Dead code in the critical path of every page load.

6. <meta name="keywords">. §3.5: no major search engine has used it in about twenty years. It is a list of the site's commercial intentions, published to competitors, achieving nothing.

There is also an omission worth flagging: no <meta name="description">, so search results and social previews will show whatever the engine extracts from the page. It is one of the few pieces of metadata that reliably affects whether people click.

The corrected head:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Acme — hand-forged cookware</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Cast iron cookware made in Sheffield. Free UK delivery.">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hand-forged cookware</h1>
</body>
</html>

with Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' moved to a response header.

2. A page adds <base href="https://cdn.example.com/assets/"> to fix its image paths. Assets load. What breaks, and why?

Solution

Every in-page anchor on the page becomes a link to a different origin. §3.4 measured it: with that base, href="#top" resolves to https://cdn.example.com/assets/#top. Clicking it does not scroll — it navigates the browser to the CDN, which almost certainly returns a 404 or a directory listing.

That is not a corner case. It hits the skip link (§6.10), every table-of-contents link, every accordion or tab implemented with fragment links, and every href="#" used as a placeholder — which is to say most of a real page's internal navigation.

Every root-relative URL moves to the CDN's origin. href="/about" becomes https://cdn.example.com/about, because a root-relative URL keeps its path and takes the base's origin. So the site's own navigation now points at the asset host.

And anything above the <base> is unaffected, since a base only applies to references after it. A <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/style.css"> written above it resolves against the document and one below it resolves against the CDN — two identical-looking lines fetching from two different hosts, which is a genuinely nasty thing to debug.

Why it seemed to work: relative asset URLs like src="logo.png" were exactly the case the author was testing, and they do resolve correctly. The failure is in a different category of URL, on a different part of the page, and it looks like a routing bug rather than a head bug.

The fix is to remove the <base> and make the asset URLs absolute — at build time, from a configured origin. If the asset host must be switchable, that is a build-time substitution or a CSS custom property, not a document-wide rewrite of every URL on the page.

<base> has one genuinely good use: inside an <iframe srcdoc> (§9.13), where the frame has no URL of its own and relative references would otherwise resolve against nothing.

3. Distinguish preload, prefetch, preconnect and dns-prefetch, and give a page where all four are justified.

Solution

They differ along two axes: how much work the browser does, and which navigation the work is for.

Hint Does For
dns-prefetch Resolves a hostname A later request to that origin
preconnect DNS + TCP + TLS A later request to that origin
preload Fetches one resource, high priority This page
prefetch Fetches one resource, idle priority The next page

The most important distinction is the last two: preload is for something this page needs and would otherwise discover late; prefetch is a bet on where the user goes next, paid for out of spare bandwidth. Using preload for a next-page resource makes the current page slower for a benefit that may never be collected.

A basket page justifies all four:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout">
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://analytics.example.com">

preconnect to the font origin, because the connection cost — DNS, TCP, TLS — is three round trips that would otherwise be paid at the moment the font is discovered.

preload the font file itself. §3.10: a font referenced from inside a CSS file is not discovered until that CSS has been fetched and parsed, which is late. as="font" sets the priority and the Accept header, and crossorigin is required even for a same-origin font — fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, and without it the browser fetches the file twice.

prefetch the checkout page, because from a basket the next navigation is highly predictable. Idle priority means it does not compete with anything on the current page.

dns-prefetch for analytics, which is a lower-confidence, lower-cost hint for an origin that is requested late and is not on the critical path.

The discipline that keeps this working is restraint. Every hint competes for the same bandwidth as real requests, and a head with fifteen preloads is slower than one with none, because the browser's own priority ordering was better than the one you overrode. Preload what the page cannot paint without, preconnect the one origin that matters, and measure rather than assume — an unused preload produces a console warning, which is the fastest way to find the ones that were guesses.

4. A product page must look right when pasted into a chat app, appear correctly in search with price and availability, and not compete with its own tracking-parameter URLs. Write the head metadata, and say which mechanism does each job.

Solution

Three jobs, three different mechanisms, and they do not substitute for each other.

<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Cast iron skillet, 26cm — Acme</title>
<meta name="description" content="A 26cm pre-seasoned cast iron skillet, oven safe to 260°C. £48, free UK delivery.">

<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">

<meta property="og:title" content="Cast iron skillet, 26cm">
<meta property="og:description" content="Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260°C. £48, free UK delivery.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og/skillet.png">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="A cast iron skillet on a gas hob">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/products/skillet">
<meta property="og:type" content="product">
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Product",
  "name": "Cast iron skillet, 26cm",
  "image": "https://example.com/img/skillet.png",
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "url": "https://example.com/products/skillet",
    "price": "48.00",
    "priceCurrency": "GBP",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock"
  }
}
</script>

The chat preview is Open Graph (§3.13). property, not name — some consumers ignore the name spelling. The image must be an absolute URL, at least 1200×630, and reachable without authentication, because the crawler is not logged in. twitter:card with summary_large_image is the one non-Open-Graph tag still worth sending, and it uses name.

The rich search result is JSON-LD (§3.14). Open Graph cannot express a price or an availability state; schema.org can, and JSON-LD is the syntax search engines recommend. The values must match what the page actually shows — inventing a price or a rating is against every engine's guidelines.

The duplicate-URL problem is rel="canonical" (§3.12). ?utm_source=newsletter produces a distinct URL that would otherwise compete with the clean one for the same query. Absolute, self-referential, and pointing at a URL that returns 200 rather than a redirect.

And <title> plus <meta name="description"> underneath all three, because every consumer that does not find the specialised metadata falls back to them — which includes a surprising number of chat applications and every search engine that decides your Open Graph description is worse than the page's own text.

One thing deliberately absent: <meta name="keywords">. §3.5 — no major search engine has used it for about twenty years.

5. Your site loads a charting library from a public CDN. Security review asks you to make that "supply-chain safe". Explain what SRI does and does not protect against, and what else you would change.

Solution 
<script src="https://cdn.example.com/chart-4.4.1.min.js"
        integrity="sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kPzQho1wx4JwY8wC"
        crossorigin="anonymous" defer></script>

What subresource integrity protects against. The browser hashes the delivered bytes and refuses to execute the file if the hash differs (§3.11). That covers a compromised CDN serving modified code, a network attacker injecting into the response, a corrupted or truncated download, and — the underrated one — the library's author silently republishing a different file under the same URL. All of them fail closed: the script does not run.

What it does not protect against. It pins bytes, not behaviour. If version 4.4.1 was already malicious when you generated the hash, SRI faithfully guarantees you receive that exact malicious file forever. It does nothing about the library's own dependencies loaded at runtime, nothing about data the script chooses to exfiltrate, and nothing about the CDN going down — the failure mode of a hash mismatch is a page with no chart, which is availability traded for integrity.

Two mechanical requirements come with it. crossorigin="anonymous" is required, because without CORS the browser cannot read the body well enough to verify it and the check silently cannot run. And the URL must name an exact version — a latest URL cannot have a hash by construction, which is a useful forcing function: an auto-updating third-party script is an unreviewed deploy to production every time its author pushes.

What else I would change, in order of value:

  • Self-host it. This removes the third party from the request path entirely: no cross-origin connection, no CDN outage, no third-party access to your users' IP addresses and referrers, and the file goes through your own build and review. Cross-CDN caching stopped being a real benefit when browsers partitioned their caches per site, which removed the main argument for the CDN.
  • Add a Content Security Policy (§16.10) with an explicit script-src. SRI checks one file you already knew about; CSP constrains what any script on the page may load and where it may send data, which is the layer that limits the damage if something does get in.
  • Add defer so the script does not block the parser (§1.10) — unrelated to security, and free while editing the tag.
  • Pin and audit the dependency in the build, so that upgrading 4.4.1 to 4.5.0 is a reviewed change with a regenerated hash, rather than an edit to one attribute.

The honest summary for the review: SRI is a cheap, real integrity control and is not a supply-chain strategy. Self-hosting plus a CSP is.

SECTION 4

Text-Level Semantics

This section is about the elements that mark up text inside a paragraph: the ones that say a phrase is emphasised, or is a piece of code, an abbreviation, a date, or a quotation from another language.

This is the part of HTML where the temptation to choose an element by how it looks is strongest. These elements come with visible default styling, and the difference between two of them is often invisible. <b> and <strong> both render bold. <i> and <em> both render italic. So the obvious conclusion is that they are two spellings of the same thing, and the obvious conclusion is wrong: one pair carries meaning into the accessibility tree (what a screen reader receives) and the other does not.

The measurements in this section make that concrete. Every element below was rendered in a real browser, and you can see which ones produce a node in that tree and which produce nothing at all.

4.1 Semantic and Presentational Markup

semantic markup says what content is. presentational markup says how it should look. HTML contains both, for historical reasons. Today the view is that presentation belongs in CSS, and the presentational elements survive only where they carry a real, specific meaning that no other element expresses.

Here is the distinction, measured:

<p><em>emphasis</em> <strong>strong</strong> <b>b</b> <i>i</i> <u>u</u> <s>s</s> <small>small</small> <mark>mark</mark></p>

AX TREE
paragraph
  emphasis
    text "emphasis"
  text
  strong
    text "strong"
  text
  text "b"
  text
  text "i"
  text
  text "u"
  text
  deletion
    text "s"
  text
  text "small"
  text
  mark
    text "mark"

Eight elements, four nodes. <em> produced an emphasis node, <strong> a strong, <s> a deletion, and <mark> a mark. <b>, <i>, <u> and <small> produced nothing at all. Their content appears as bare text, impossible to tell apart from unmarked prose.

That is the whole difference, and it is not a matter of taste. A screen reader may change its pitch or add a pause for emphasis, and it can announce deletion and mark. For <b> it has nothing to work with, because there is nothing there.

None of this makes <b> wrong. It makes it specific: §4.3 describes the narrow jobs those four elements still have. The rule is simply that when you mean "this is important", you write the element that means it.

The practical form of the rule: reach for semantic markup when the distinction matters to a reader who cannot see the page, and for CSS when it does not. semantic markup does not mean "more elements". A <div> used honestly is semantic in the only sense that counts, because it claims nothing untrue.

4.2 em and strong

The two carrying elements, and the distinction between them is real.

<em> is stress emphasis: the word you would say louder. It changes the meaning of a sentence, and moving it moves the meaning:

<p>We <em>need</em> this by Friday.</p>
<p>We need this by <em>Friday</em>.</p>

The first says the requirement is not negotiable. The second says the day is not negotiable. That is a difference in meaning, and it is exactly what the element records. <em> can be nested, and nesting increases the emphasis.

<strong> is importance, seriousness or urgency. It does not change what the sentence means. It marks part of it as mattering more than the rest: a warning, a deadline, a caveat:

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> the pan will be extremely hot.</p>

<strong> can be nested too, and the outer one is less strong than the inner one.

The practical test: would you say it differently, or is it just more important? Said differently is <em>; more important is <strong>. When neither is true and the text is only bold for design reasons, the answer is CSS on a <span>, or, more often, that the design does not need it.

4.3 b, i, u, s and small

These four produce no accessibility node, as §4.1 measured, and each survives for one specific job that no meaningful element covers.

<b>
Text drawn to attention without extra importance: a keyword in a summary, a product name in a review, the lead-in of an article.
<i>
Text in an alternate voice or mood: a technical term, a taxonomic name, a phrase in another language, a thought, a transliteration.
<u>
A non-textual annotation: a spelling error marked by a checker, a proper name in Chinese. Rare, and easily mistaken for a link.
<s>
No longer accurate or relevant: a superseded price, a cancelled item. Produced a deletion node.
<small>
Side comments and small print: legal disclaimers, licensing, attribution, copyright.

Two of these are worth extra care.

<i> for a foreign phrase should carry lang (§2.12), because lang is the part a screen reader can act on: <i lang="fr">la rentrée</i> gets French pronunciation, while the <i> alone gets nothing.

<s> is the odd one out. It did produce a node, deletion, so it is announced. Do not confuse it with <del> (§5.9): <s> means "no longer accurate", while <del> means "removed from the document in an edit". A crossed-out old price is <s>; a paragraph struck out in a tracked revision is <del>.

And the general warning: because these produce no node, a page that uses <b> for every warning and <i> for every emphasis is a page where none of that reaches anyone using assistive technology. Use them for their meanings, not their looks.

4.4 code, kbd, samp and var

Four elements for writing about computing, and the measurement is instructive:

<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> and <dfn id="d">a definition</dfn> and <code>code</code> and <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> and <samp>output</samp> and <var>x</var></p>

AX TREE
paragraph
  Abbr "HyperText Markup Language"
    text "HTML"
  text "and"
  term "a definition"
  text "and"
  code
    text "code"
  text "and"
  text "Ctrl"
  text "and"
  text "output"
  text "and"
  text "x"

<code> produced a code node; <kbd>, <samp> and <var> produced none. That does not make the other three pointless. They still mean something to anyone reading the markup, to a stylesheet and to tooling. But they carry nothing to a screen reader.

<code>
A fragment of computer code — a function name, a filename, an attribute. Inline; wrap it in <pre> for a block (§4.11).
<kbd>
Input from the user: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd>. Nests to show a key within a shortcut within a menu.
<samp>
Output from a program: an error message, a printed result.
<var>
A variable — in code, in mathematics, or a placeholder in a command such as git help <command>.

The four combine. A key combination inside a sentence about a program's output is <samp>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop</samp>, and a documented command is <code>cp <var>source</var> <var>destination</var></code>.

4.5 abbr and dfn

<abbr> marks an abbreviation or acronym, and its title gives the full form. The measurement above shows why that matters. The tree records Abbr "HyperText Markup Language": the title became the element's accessible name, replacing the visible text. So a screen reader announces the full form instead of the letters.

That is a real benefit and a real risk in one attribute:

<p>The <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> specification.</p>

The benefit is that "HTML" is announced as the full phrase. The risk is the same thing: a full form that is wrong, wordy or repeated in every paragraph becomes a sentence the user cannot skip. And title still cannot be reached by keyboard and is invisible on touch screens (§2.10), so a sighted mouse user gets a tooltip and nobody else sees anything.

The practical convention: expand an abbreviation in the text the first time it appears, as in "HyperText Markup Language (HTML)", and use <abbr title> sparingly after that, or not at all. The written-out form serves every reader; the attribute serves one kind.

<dfn> marks the defining instance of a term: the one place where a term is introduced, not every use of it. It produced a term node. Its content is the term being defined, and the surrounding text is the definition:

<p><dfn id="foster">Foster parenting</dfn> is the parser's rule for moving disallowed
content out of a table.</p>
<p>See <a href="#foster">foster parenting</a> for the mechanism.</p>

Giving it an id makes it linkable, which is what turns a scattered set of definitions into a glossary. If the term itself is an abbreviation, <dfn><abbr title="…">…</abbr></dfn> is the correct nesting.

4.6 time and data

Two elements that attach a machine-readable value to human-readable text.

<p>Published <time datetime="2026-03-14T09:00">14 March</time>, <data value="4021">order</data>, H<sub>2</sub>O, 10<sup>3</sup>.</p>
<address>Acme, Sheffield</address>

AX TREE
paragraph
  text "Published"
  time
    text "14 March"
  text ","
  text "order"
  text ", H"
  subscript
    text "2"
  text "O, 10"
  superscript
    text "3"
  text "."
group
  text "Acme, Sheffield"

<time> produced a time node. The datetime attribute holds the value in a format machines can read, while the element's text stays readable for people:

<time datetime="2026-03-14">14 March</time>
<time datetime="2026-03-14T09:00:00Z">9am UTC</time>
<time datetime="2026-03">March 2026</time>
<time datetime="09:00">nine in the morning</time>
<time datetime="PT2H30M">two and a half hours</time>
<time datetime="2026-W11">the second week of March</time>

The formats are a fixed list: a date, a time, a date and time with a time-zone offset, a year, a year and month, a month and day, a week, and a duration starting with P. Anything else is invalid, and, as with every attribute of this kind, nothing tells you.

<time> is what makes "last Tuesday" something search engines can index, and it is where a calendar or a feed reader gets an event's date from. When the visible text is relative ("three days ago"), the datetime is the only place the actual moment exists.

<data> is the same idea for anything that is not a time. <data value="4021">order</data> pairs a display string with a value for machines: a product SKU behind a product name, a numeric rank behind "first", a standard spelling behind a variant. It produced no node, which is expected: the value is for machines, and the text is what a person gets.

Note also <sub> and <sup>, which did produce subscript and superscript nodes. They are for real subscripts and superscripts (chemical formulae, mathematical exponents, ordinal suffixes, footnote markers), not for making text small and raised as a visual effect.

And <address>, which produced a group. It marks contact details for the nearest <article> or for the document, not any postal address. The author's email under a blog post is an <address>; a customer's delivery address in a table is not.

The datetime attribute is where the machine-readable value lives, and it is the reason <time> exists at all: the element's text can say "three days ago" while the datetime attribute says 2026-03-11, and only one of those is still correct next week.

4.7 Presentational Traps

Three habits produce markup that looks right and means nothing. They are worth naming together because they have the same cause.

Using a heading for size. An <h3> on a line that is not a section heading puts a fake entry in the outline (§6.3). Use CSS.

Using <br> for spacing. Two or three <br> elements to make a gap between blocks is layout done with the wrong tool; the blocks should be separate elements with a margin. §4.8 has the narrow case where <br> is right.

Using &nbsp; for indentation. As §2.13 explained, it is a character, not a spacing instruction, and it is the one whitespace that does not collapse. That is why it gets abused for this, and why the result does not adapt to the screen and is awkward to select.

The pattern in all three is choosing an element for what the browser's default stylesheet does with it. The default stylesheet is only a convention (§2.1), and each of these has a CSS answer that is shorter, adjustable, and does not lie to the accessibility tree.

4.8 br, wbr and hr

Three elements are about breaks rather than meaning, and each has a narrow correct use.

<p>One<br>Two</p><hr><p>Super<wbr>califragilistic</p>

AX TREE
paragraph
  text "One"
  LineBreak
  text "Two"
separator orientation=horizontal
paragraph
  text "Super"
  text "califragilistic"

<br> produced a LineBreak node. It is correct where a line break is part of the content: a postal address, a poem, a song lyric, a line of dialogue. It is wrong as spacing between paragraphs, which is CSS's job.

<hr> produced separator orientation=horizontal, a real ARIA role, so it is announced. It means a thematic break: a scene change in a story, a change of subject within a section. It is not a decorative line. A page that uses it to draw lines between cards puts a separator announcement between every pair. Use a CSS border for a line.

<wbr> produced no node, but look closely at what it did: the text is split into two nodes, "Super" and "califragilistic". That is a word break opportunity: a point where the browser may break a long word if it needs to, and where nothing appears if it does not. It is right for a long URL, a long identifier or a chemical name, and it is invisible when unused. Copying the text still gives you the whole word, because no character was inserted.

4.9 mark

<mark> marks a run of text as relevant in some context that is not part of the original text. It produced a mark node in §4.1's measurement, so it is announced.

Two uses, and both are about relevance-to-a-reason rather than importance:

<p>Showing results for <b>cast iron</b>:</p>
<p>The <mark>cast iron</mark> skillet retains heat better than steel.</p>

Highlighting a search term in a result is the standard case. The highlight is not part of the sentence; it is a note from the software about why this text is here.

Drawing attention to a passage in a quotation, for the sake of the commentary around it: the equivalent of a highlighter pen on someone else's page. The original author did not emphasise it; you did.

The distinctions that matter:

  • Not <strong>. <strong> says the author considers this important. <mark> says it is relevant to what the reader is doing right now. The search term is not important; it is what you searched for.
  • Not <em>. <em> changes how a sentence would be spoken.
  • Not a highlighted style. If the yellow background is decoration, it is CSS on a <span>. <mark> puts an announcement in the accessibility tree that nothing justifies.

<mark> can be placed inside a quotation without changing what the quotation says, and that is what makes it the right element for annotating text you did not write.

4.10 The Shape of the Tree

Putting the measurements above together, this is which text-level elements produce an accessibility node and which do not:

Produce a node
<em> → emphasis, <strong> → strong, <mark> → mark, <s> → deletion, <code> → code, <abbr> → Abbr, <dfn> → term, <time> → time, <sub>/<sup> → subscript/superscript, <br> → LineBreak, <hr> → separator, <address> → group, <ruby> → Ruby
Produce nothing
<b>, <i>, <u>, <small>, <kbd>, <samp>, <var>, <data>, <wbr>, <bdi>, <bdo>, <span>, <div>

Two lessons follow, and neither is "only use the first list".

The second list is not useless. <kbd> and <var> mean something to a reader of the markup, to a stylesheet and to any tool that processes the document. <bdi> and <wbr> change how text is drawn rather than what it means, which is exactly their job. <data> exists for machines other than screen readers.

But a node is the only thing a screen reader can act on. So when the meaning matters to a listener (this is emphasised, this is important, this is a search hit, this is a date), the element must come from the first list. That is the single practical rule this section comes down to.

The exact set varies between browsers at the edges, and the tree above is Chrome's; some other engines do expose <kbd> and <var>. Where the meaning is essential rather than merely helpful, put it in the text.

4.11 pre

<pre> shows its content with whitespace kept and in a monospace font. §2.14 explained the mechanism: the parser keeps whitespace everywhere, and it is CSS white-space that normally collapses it. <pre> gets white-space: pre from the browser's stylesheet.

<pre><code>def f(x):
    return x * 2
</code></pre>

DOM TREE
<pre>
  <code>
    #text "def f(x):\n    return x * 2\n"

The DOM confirms that the indentation and the newlines are ordinary text; they never were anything else.

Four points about using it.

A code block is <pre><code>, both elements. <pre> says "whitespace matters"; <code> says "this is code". Either one alone is incomplete, and the pair is what every documentation tool produces.

The first newline after <pre> is dropped. A parser rule does this so that writing the opening tag on its own line does not produce a blank first line. The closing tag has no such rule, so a newline before </pre> is real and will show.

Content must be escaped. < and & inside a <pre> are still markup, so a code sample containing HTML needs &lt; and &amp; (§2.13). This is the most common way a code block on a page swallows the rest of the document.

Long lines overflow. A <pre> does not wrap, so a wide block makes the whole page scroll sideways unless it sits in a container with overflow-x: auto, the same requirement as a wide table (§10.13). For a screen reader user a long code block is also a long unbroken run of text, so a <figure> with a <figcaption> saying what it is (§8.12) is a real courtesy.

<pre> is also correct for anything else where the spacing is the content: captured terminal output, ASCII-art diagrams in a text file, fixed-width data.

4.12 Bidirectional Text

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu are written right to left. A document that mixes them with a left-to-right language is laid out by the Unicode bidirectional algorithm, a set of rules that decides the order of mixed-direction text. It works from the characters themselves plus a base direction, and getting the base direction right is HTML's part of the job.

<p dir="ltr">The user said <bdi>مرحبا</bdi> in the review.</p>
<p><bdo dir="rtl">abc def</bdo></p>
<ruby>漢<rp>(</rp><rt>kan</rt><rp>)</rp>字<rp>(</rp><rt>ji</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby>

AX TREE
paragraph
  text "The user said"
  text "مرحبا"
  text "in the review."
paragraph
  text "abc def"
Ruby
  text "漢"
  text "字"

Neither <bdi> nor <bdo> produced a node, which is correct: both change how text is drawn, not what it means.

The dir attribute (§2.12) sets the base direction to ltr, rtl or auto. It is inherited, so <html dir="rtl"> is the main declaration for a right-to-left site.

<bdi> isolates a run of text whose direction you do not know in advance. It is the element for user-generated content, and the problem it solves is real. An Arabic username placed inside an English sentence can drag the surrounding punctuation to the wrong side, so a list of comments shows its counts and separators visibly scrambled, because of the data and not because of a bug in your code. <bdi> is dir="auto" plus isolation, and it is the correct wrapper for any name, title or string that came from a user.

<bdo> overrides the algorithm entirely for its content and forces a direction. It is a blunt tool for the rare case where the characters' own direction is wrong for the display: showing a string in a debugging tool, or a deliberate typographic effect. It is not for laying out a right-to-left page; that is dir on a container.

Two more rules make a bidirectional page work. Never build a bidirectional string by concatenation (gluing pieces together): name + ": " + message produces exactly the scrambling above. Use separate elements, with <bdi> around the parts that vary. And dir="auto" is the right default for any field a user types into, so the input's direction follows what they write.

4.13 ruby

Ruby annotations are the small pronunciation or meaning notes printed above (or beside) text, used mainly for Japanese furigana and Chinese pinyin.

<ruby>漢<rt>kan</rt>字<rt>ji</rt></ruby>

Three elements make it up. <ruby> wraps the whole thing. <rt> holds each annotation. <rp> holds fallback parentheses that are shown only by a browser that does not support ruby, so the annotation falls back to 漢(kan)字(ji) instead of running together:

<ruby>漢<rp>(</rp><rt>kan</rt><rp>)</rp>字<rp>(</rp><rt>ji</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby>

Every current browser supports ruby, so <rp> is a compatibility measure rather than a requirement. But it costs little, and it is what the specification asks for.

One honest limitation from the measurement above. The tree shows a Ruby node containing the base characters, and the <rt> annotations, "kan" and "ji", do not appear in it. So in this browser the reading is not passed to assistive technology through this interface. Ruby's value is therefore mainly visual, and for readers learning the script. Do not rely on it to give a pronunciation to a screen reader user; put anything essential in the text.

Ruby is not only for East Asian text. It is legal, and occasionally useful, for any short annotation printed above a run of text: a transliteration, a gloss, a stress mark.

4.14 div and span

These are the two elements that mean nothing, and knowing that they mean nothing is what makes them useful.

<pre><code>def f(x):
    return x * 2</code></pre>
<div>div</div><span>span</span>

AX TREE
code
  text "def f(x): return x * 2"
text "div"
text "span"

Neither produced a node. Their content is bare text, exactly as if the tags were not there. That is by design: <div> is a generic block container and <span> a generic container for text within a line. Their whole purpose is to give CSS or JavaScript something to hold on to without claiming anything about the content.

The difference between them is the content model (§2.7), not the appearance. <span> accepts phrasing content and may live inside a <p>; <div> accepts flow content and may not. Putting display: block on a <span> changes neither fact.

Reach for them last, and without embarrassment. The decision procedure is:

  1. Is there an element that means what this content is? <article>, <nav>, <time>, <em>, <button>, <table> — use it.
  2. Is it a thematic group that has a name? <section> with aria-labelledby (§6.5).
  3. Otherwise: <div> or <span>.

Step 3 is not a failure. A flex container, a grid cell, a card wrapper, a scroll container (§10.13), a framework's mount point: all of these exist for layout or scripting and claim nothing about the content. <div> is the honest element for them. Using <section> instead adds no meaning while hinting at one that is not there.

The failure mode is the opposite one: <div class="button"> with a click handler, <div class="heading"> styled large, <div class="nav"> holding the site's links. Each looks right, and §16.5's list shows what they cost: no role, no keyboard support, no landmark, and no place in any of the lists a screen reader user moves around by. Nothing reads the class name (§2.10).

So the summary of this whole section: choose the element that says what the content is; when nothing does, choose the element that says nothing. The mistake is never using <div> as such. It is using <div> where a meaningful element existed, or using <b> where <strong> was meant.

Exercises

1. For each, name the correct element and say why.

1. The word "must" in "the pan must be dry before storing".
2. "Warning:" at the start of a safety note.
3. A search term highlighted in a result snippet.
4. A price that has been reduced, shown crossed out.
5. A paragraph removed in a tracked revision of a policy.
6. A French phrase in an English sentence.
Solution

1. <em>. Stress emphasis — the word you would say louder, and moving it changes what the sentence means (§4.2). "The pan must be dry" versus "the pan must be dry" are different claims. It produces an emphasis node, which a screen reader can act on.

2. <strong>. Importance, not a change of meaning (§4.2). The sentence would be spoken the same way; the word marks the note as one to take seriously. Produces a strong node.

3. <mark>. §4.9: relevance to the reader's current purpose rather than the author's emphasis. The original text did not emphasise "cast iron"; the search did. Not <strong>, which would claim the author thought it important, and not a CSS highlight, which conveys nothing to a listener.

4. <s>. "No longer accurate or relevant" (§4.3). It produces a deletion node, so the state is announced rather than only drawn. Note this is one of the two struck-through elements and the two are not interchangeable — see 5.

5. <del> (§5.9), with datetime and cite if the revision is documented. The distinction from <s> is the reason both exist: <s> means the content is out of date, <del> means the document was edited. A superseded price is a fact about the world; a struck paragraph in a policy is a fact about the document's history.

6. <i lang="fr">. §4.3: <i> is the alternate-voice element, and a foreign phrase is its canonical case. The important half is the lang (§2.12): <i> alone produces no accessibility node at all, so on its own it conveys nothing to a listener, while lang="fr" makes a screen reader switch to French pronunciation. If the phrase is emphasised as well as foreign, that is <em lang="fr">.

The pattern across all six: four of them produce a node and two do not, and the two that do not (<i>, and <b> had it appeared) are exactly the ones where the meaning has to be carried by something else — lang, or the surrounding words.

2. Why is <b> not simply a shorter <strong>? Answer with reference to what the browser produces.

Solution

Because <strong> produces an accessibility node and <b> produces nothing. §4.1 measured both in one tree: <strong>strong</strong> became strong with a text child, and <b>b</b> became a bare text "b" — indistinguishable from unmarked prose.

They render identically, which is the entire reason for the confusion. The default bold is a convention of the browser's stylesheet (§2.1) and is not what either element means.

What that costs in practice. A screen reader can announce, change pitch for, or let a user navigate by strong. It has nothing to work with for <b> — the user hears the words with no indication that they were marked at all. So a page using <b> for every warning has warnings that exist only for people looking at the screen. The same argument applies, more sharply, to <em> versus <i>.

<b> is still a real element with a real job, and this is not an argument for never using it (§4.3). It marks text drawn to attention without conveying extra importance: a keyword in a summary, a product name in a review, an article's lead-in sentence. That is a genuine editorial category, and no other element expresses it.

The test is the one from §4.2: would you say it differently, or is it just more important? Differently is <em>. More important is <strong>. Neither, and merely visually distinct, is <b> — or, more often, a <span> with a class, because the distinction is a design decision rather than an editorial one.

The general principle this is an instance of: choosing an element for what the default stylesheet does with it is choosing appearance and getting semantics as an accident. The appearance is one line of CSS either way; the semantics is the only part that cannot be added later.

3. A comment system shows username: message. Users report that comments from Arabic-speaking members render with the punctuation in the wrong place, and sometimes the whole line appears reversed. Diagnose and fix.

Solution

This is a bidirectional-text bug, and it is in the concatenation. The Unicode bidirectional algorithm decides the visual order of a run of text from the characters themselves plus a base direction. When an Arabic username is dropped into a left-to-right line, the algorithm sees a right-to-left run adjacent to neutral characters — the colon, the space, any trailing punctuation — and those neutrals take their direction from what surrounds them. The colon that was meant to separate the name from the message ends up on the wrong side, and with enough right-to-left content the whole line reorders.

Nothing is wrong with the data or with the code. The rendering is the algorithm working correctly on a string that did not say where its parts began and ended.

The fix is <bdi> around every value that came from a user (§4.12):

<p><bdi class="user">مرحبا</bdi>: <bdi class="body">Great pan, thanks.</bdi></p>

<bdi> is dir="auto" plus isolation: it computes each run's direction from its own first strong character, and it prevents that direction from leaking into the surrounding text. The colon then belongs to the outer paragraph's direction and stays where it was written.

And the rule the bug came from: never build a bidirectional string by concatenation. name + ': ' + message produces one text node with no boundaries in it, and there is nothing for the algorithm to isolate. Separate elements are the fix, not a cleverer string.

Three related changes worth making at the same time:

  • dir="auto" on the comment <textarea>, so the field's own direction follows what the user is typing rather than the site's.
  • lang on the comment body where it is known (§2.12), so a screen reader uses the right pronunciation rules.
  • Not <bdo>. It forces a direction rather than detecting one, so it would render Arabic text left-to-right — the opposite of what is wanted. <bdo> is for the rare case where the characters' own directionality is wrong for the presentation.

One more place the same bug appears: anywhere a user-supplied string is interpolated into a sentence — a page title, an email subject, a notification, a breadcrumb. All of them need the same treatment.

4. Write the markup for a documentation page fragment containing: a defined term, a keyboard shortcut, a command with a placeholder, a code block, and program output. Explain each choice.

Solution 
<p>A <dfn id="reflow">reflow</dfn> is the browser recalculating the geometry of part
   of the page. Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> to open the
   command palette and run <code>Show Rendering</code>.</p>

<p>Copy a profile with <code>cp <var>source</var> <var>destination</var></code>.</p>

<figure>
  <pre><code>function measure(el) {
    return el.getBoundingClientRect().height;
}</code></pre>
  <figcaption>Reading a layout property forces a reflow.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The profiler prints <samp>Recalculate Style: 14ms</samp>.</p>

<dfn> for the defining instance, with an id so other pages can link to it (§4.5). It produced a term node in the measurement. Only the defining occurrence — later uses of "reflow" are plain text, or links to #reflow.

<kbd> per key, not per combination (§4.4). Three elements with literal + between them, so a stylesheet can draw each as a key cap and the structure says what it is.
