<var> for the placeholders in the command. This is the documented convention for "replace this with your own value", and it is more precise than the angle-bracket convention because it is markup rather than punctuation the reader has to interpret.

<pre><code> for the block, both elements (§4.11). <pre> says whitespace is significant, <code> says it is code; either alone is incomplete. Note the closing </code></pre> sits immediately after the last character — a newline before it is real content and renders as a blank line, whereas the newline after the opening tag is dropped by the parser.

Wrapped in a <figure> with a <figcaption> (§8.12), because a code block is self-contained content referenced from the text, and the caption names it for everyone. This also gives the block somewhere to hang the overflow-x: auto a long line needs.

<samp> for the program's output (§4.4), distinguishing it from <code>, which is code you would write. Both are monospace by default and they are not the same thing.

One honest note. §4.4's measurement shows <code> produces a code node while <kbd>, <samp> and <var> produce none in this browser. They remain worth writing — they are meaningful to a reader of the markup, to the stylesheet, and to documentation tooling — but where the distinction is essential to understanding, say it in the prose as well. "Press Ctrl+Shift+P" and "the profiler prints…" already do that here, which is why the markup can carry the rest.

5. A designer asks for a large, bold, coloured line of text above a paragraph. A developer writes <h2 class="lede">. Assess, and give the alternatives.

Solution

It is the wrong element, and the cost is in the outline rather than on the screen.

A heading element means "this begins a section" (§6.2). The page's heading list — which is how a screen reader user navigates within a page, and how a reader-mode view builds its table of contents — now has an entry for something that begins nothing. The user selects it expecting a section and lands on a decorative line. If the surrounding page uses <h2> for real sections, the outline (§6.3) is also structurally wrong: this lede either interrupts a section or claims to open one.

The cause is §4.7's pattern: choosing an element for what the browser's default stylesheet does with it. Large and bold is a convention (§2.1), not what <h2> means.

The alternatives, in order:

1. If it is the article's opening summary — a lede or standfirst — and sits under the real heading: the meaning is "this paragraph is an introduction", and the honest markup is a paragraph with a class.

<h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>
<p class="lede">Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260&nbsp;°C, and heavier than it looks.</p>

<p class="lede"> with the styling in CSS. The class carries no meaning (§2.10), which is correct — there is no meaning to carry beyond "paragraph".

2. If it is a subtitle or tagline attached to the heading above it: <hgroup> is the element built for exactly this (§6.2), and it associates the two without letting the tagline become a heading:

<hgroup>
  <h1>Acme Cookware</h1>
  <p>Hand-forged in Sheffield since 1994</p>
</hgroup>

3. If part of it is genuinely important — a warning, a deadline — then <strong> inside the paragraph (§4.2), which does produce a node.

4. If it really is purely visual and none of the above applies: a <span> with a class, or nothing at all. §4.14 — <div> and <span> mean nothing, and meaning nothing is the correct thing to mean here.

What to say to the designer: nothing changes visually in any of these. Every version renders identically once the CSS is written, because the size, weight and colour were always going to come from CSS. The choice is only about what the markup claims, and <h2> claims something false.

SECTION 5

Lists, Quotations and Editorial Semantics

This section covers three families of element with one thing in common: each turns something the reader would otherwise only see into a structure the browser can report.

  • A bulleted list looks like a list because of the bullets. Marked up as a list, it also is one: the browser knows how many items there are and how deeply each is nested, and announces all of that before a reader starts going through it.
  • A quotation looks like a quotation because it is indented. Marked up as one, it carries its source, and the reader is told where it starts and ends.
  • An edit looks like an edit because of the strikethrough. Marked up as one, it carries the date and the reason.

The pattern is the same each time: the CSS shows it to one audience, and the markup tells everyone. Everything below was measured against a real accessibility tree.

5.1 What a List Gives You

<ul><li>One</li><li>Two</li></ul>

AX TREE
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    text "One"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    text "Two"

A list node containing listitem nodes, each with a level and a marker. From that, assistive technology can tell a user "list, 2 items" on the way in, "item 1 of 2" on each item, and "out of list" on the way out, and it can offer a command to skip the whole thing.

That count is the useful part, and it is why a list is not decoration. A reader who can see a list judges its length at a glance and decides whether to read it. A reader who cannot see it needs to be told, and the only place that number exists is the structure.

The same argument works the other way round. A sequence of <div> elements styled with bullets is not a list. It looks identical, announces nothing, and gives the user no way to skip past it: the bullets are drawn by CSS, and CSS does not reach the accessibility tree.

5.2 ul and ol

Two list types, and the difference is meaning rather than appearance.

<ul> is an unordered list: the items belong together, and their order is not part of the information. Ingredients, features, tags, a navigation menu.

<ol> is an ordered list: the order is information. Steps in a procedure, a ranking, a breadcrumb trail, a numbered specification.

The test is whether reordering the items would make the content wrong. Reordering a list of ingredients does not; reordering the steps of a recipe does. That is the whole decision, and it does not depend on whether the design shows numbers. An <ol> styled list-style: none is still ordered, and a <ul> numbered with CSS counters is still not.

Two rules on the markup itself.

A <ul> or <ol> may contain only <li>, plus <script> and <template> (§2.9). Text, <p> and <div> are not allowed between the list and its items.

All the content goes inside the <li>. A list item may contain flow content (paragraphs, images, tables, nested lists), so there is never a reason to put anything directly at the list level.

Browsers are forgiving about the first rule, which is why breaking it survives in real markup:

<ul><div><li>Wrapped item</li></div><li>Plain item</li></ul>

AX TREE
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    text "Wrapped item"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    text "Plain item"

Chrome kept the list role and both listitem nodes despite the wrapper. That is how it recovers, not a guarantee: the specification does not say what the tree should be for markup it does not allow, so the result may differ between engines and may change. Write it correctly and the question never comes up. A validator (§16.4) reports the wrapper, which is the reason to run one.

5.3 li, value, start and reversed

<li> is a list item. In an <ol> it carries an implicit number, and three attributes control the numbering.

<ol reversed><li>Third</li><li>Second</li><li>First</li></ol>
<ol start="4"><li>Four</li><li>Five</li></ol>

AX TREE
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "3."
    text "Third"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "2."
    text "Second"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "1."
    text "First"
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "4."
    text "Four"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "5."
    text "Five"

The reversed attribute counts down, starting from the number of items: three, two, one. It is the one for a countdown, or a "top ten" presented from tenth to first.

The start attribute sets the first number. The measurement shows start="4" producing markers 4 and 5. This is how you continue a list that a paragraph or a code block interrupted, so the second half does not restart at one.

value on an <li> sets that item's number and renumbers everything after it. It is the escape hatch for a list whose numbering really is irregular.

All three carry through to the marker text that assistive technology reports, as the tree shows, so the numbers a listener hears are the numbers on the screen. All three also work on <ol> only (and take whole numbers): start and reversed on a <ul> do nothing.

The type attribute (1, a, A, i, I) chooses the numbering style. It belongs in CSS as list-style-type unless the style is part of the content, as in a legal document whose clauses are cited as "(a)".

In summary: the start attribute chooses where the numbering begins, value overrides one item and renumbers what follows, and the reversed attribute counts down instead of up. The start attribute is the one you will actually use, for a list interrupted by prose. The reversed attribute is for a countdown, and it takes its starting number from the item count rather than from start.

5.4 Nested Lists

A nested list goes inside an <li>, never between the list and its items:

<ul><li>Top<ul><li>Nested</li></ul></li></ul>

AX TREE
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    text "Top"
    list
      listitem level=2
        ListMarker "◦"
        text "Nested"

The level is the reward. The inner item reports level=2, and the marker changes from • to ◦, so both a sighted reader and a listener are told the depth. A screen reader announces something like "list, 1 item, level 2" when entering the inner list, which is how a user keeps their place in a deep structure.

Two rules.

The nested list is a child of the <li>, and it is the parent item's content. <ul><li>Top</li><ul>…</ul></ul>, with the inner list as a sibling of the items, is invalid, and it loses the parent/child relationship that level expresses.

A nested list is a real hierarchy, so use it only for one. A three-level nested list of navigation is a menu with submenus. A three-level nested list used to indent things is a structure claiming a relationship that does not exist.

Nesting has no limit in principle, and it becomes unreadable in practice past about three levels. When it goes deeper, the content usually wants headings and sections (§6) instead of a list.

5.5 menu

<menu> is a list of interactive items: commands, actions, tool buttons. Structurally it is a <ul>: it contains <li> elements and produces the same tree.

<ul style="list-style:none"><li>One</li><li>Two</li></ul>
<menu><li><button>Copy</button></li><li><button>Paste</button></li></menu>

AX TREE
list
  listitem level=1
    text "One"
  listitem level=1
    text "Two"
list
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    button "Copy"
  listitem level=1
    ListMarker "•"
    button "Paste"

<menu> produced list and listitem, exactly as <ul> does. So the choice between them is editorial: <menu> says "these are commands", <ul> says "these are items". Neither changes what a user hears, and <ul> is what nearly all existing markup uses.

It is not the ARIA menu role. role="menu" describes an application menu with a specific keyboard contract (arrow keys between items, one tab stop, Escape to close), and using it commits you to building all of that (§14.6). A toolbar of buttons is a <menu> or a <ul>, not a role="menu".

The first list above shows something else worth knowing. list-style: none removed the ListMarker nodes and left the list and listitem roles intact in this browser. That is Chrome. Safari removes the list semantics entirely when the markers are removed, reasoning that a list without markers was not meant to be a list. The consequence is real: a navigation menu styled without bullets, which is nearly all of them, is announced as a list in one browser and not in another. The standard fix is to state the role explicitly on lists whose markers are styled away:

<ul role="list" style="list-style:none">
  <li>Shop</li>
</ul>

This is one of the few places where restating a native role (§13.9's second rule) is accepted advice rather than a mistake. It compensates for a known browser behaviour instead of changing the meaning.

5.6 Description Lists

A description list pairs terms with descriptions. It is the element people forget exists, and it is the right answer far more often than it is used.

<dl>
  <dt>Reflow</dt><dd>Recalculating geometry.</dd>
  <dt>Repaint</dt><dt>Redraw</dt><dd>Redrawing pixels.</dd>
</dl>

AX TREE
DescriptionList
  term "Reflow"
  definition
    text "Recalculating geometry."
  term "Repaint"
  term "Redraw"
  definition
    text "Redrawing pixels."

<dl> is the list, <dt> a term, <dd> a description. The measurement shows how they are linked: two term nodes followed by one definition, which is how you say that "Repaint" and "Redraw" are two names for the same thing. It works the other way too: one <dt> followed by several <dd> elements, for a term with several meanings.

What it is for, beyond glossaries:

  • Metadata: an article's author, date and category; a product's specifications; a commit's fields.
  • Key/value pairs of any kind, the case where people reach for a two-column table. §10.1's test settles it: a table's cells need both a row header and a column header to mean anything. A term and its description need only each other, so it is a description list.
  • Question and answer, with the question as the <dt>.
  • Dialogue, with the speaker as the <dt>.

Two structural rules. A <dl> may contain <dt>, <dd>, and — uniquely — <div> wrapping a group of them. That is the one place the specification approves a wrapper (§2.9), and it exists precisely because styling a term/description pair would otherwise take awkward CSS tricks. And the pairs are positional: a <dd> describes the <dt> elements immediately before it, so order is the only thing that links them.

What it is not for: two-column layout, and, despite the name, a set of definitions where each <dfn> (§4.5) sits in surrounding prose. <dl> is for the pairing structure, and when a description is three paragraphs of discussion, headings work better.

5.7 blockquote

<blockquote> marks a quotation that forms a whole block. The cite attribute on it gives the URL of the source.

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/report">
  <p>Revenue rose in every quarter.</p>
  <footer>— <cite>Annual report 2025</cite></footer>
</blockquote>
<p>She called it <q cite="https://example.com/r">a good year</q>.</p>

AX TREE
blockquote
  paragraph
    text "Revenue rose in every quarter."
  contentinfo
    text "—"
    text "Annual report 2025"
paragraph
  text "She called it"
  text "“"
  text "a good year"
  text "”"
  text "."

Two measured surprises in six lines, and both change how the markup should be written.

The <footer> inside the blockquote became a contentinfo landmark. That is the role of the page's footer (§6.7). It happens because a <footer> belongs to the nearest sectioning element (<article>, <aside>, <nav> or <section>), and <blockquote> is none of those. So an attribution written this way puts a spurious page-level landmark in the landmark list, and a page with three quotations has three contentinfo entries where there should be one.

The cite attribute is a second problem of the same kind. It holds the source's URL, and no browser exposes it to the user: not as a link, not as a tooltip, not in the accessibility tree. It is metadata for machines and nothing more.

So the attribution has to be real content, outside the quotation:

<figure>
  <blockquote cite="https://example.com/report">
    <p>Revenue rose in every quarter.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <figcaption>— <cite><a href="https://example.com/report">Annual report 2025</a></cite></figcaption>
</figure>

<figure> and <figcaption> (§8.12) are the specification's own recommendation for exactly this, and the reasons add up:

  • the caption sits outside the <blockquote>, so it is not part of the quotation, which matters because the source's name is not something the source said;
  • it produces no landmark;
  • the <cite> wraps a real link, so the URL is available to everyone, not only to a parser.

The other rule about <blockquote> is that its content is flow content, so quoted paragraphs go in <p> elements inside it, not as bare text.

5.8 q and cite

<q> is an inline quotation, and the measurement above shows what it does: the browser added “ and ” as generated content. Those quotation marks are not in the DOM. They come from the browser's stylesheet and follow the element's lang (§2.12), so a <q lang="fr"> gets « and » and a <q lang="de"> gets German quotation marks.

That is the argument for using it, and it comes with a trap: do not type the quotation marks as well. <q>"a good year"</q> renders as ““a good year””. The element supplies them.

<q> also handles nesting correctly, switching to the inner quotation style, which is genuinely awkward to do by hand.

<cite> names a work, not a person: a book, an article, a film, a report, a specification, a song. It is shown in italics by default, and it produced no node of its own in the tree above, so its value is editorial and visual rather than announced.

The distinction that catches people: <cite> is for the title of the work, and the specification says explicitly that a person's name is not a citation. So the attribution to a person is plain text, and the work they wrote is <cite>:

<figcaption>— Dana Okonjo, <cite>Cast Iron: A History</cite></figcaption>

5.9 del and ins

Two elements mark an edit to the document, as opposed to marking content as no longer accurate.

<p>The rate is <del datetime="2026-01-01">4.5%</del> <ins datetime="2026-01-01">5.0%</ins>.</p>
<del><p>A whole removed paragraph.</p></del>

AX TREE
paragraph
  text "The rate is"
  deletion
    text "4.5%"
  text
  insertion
    text "5.0%"
  text "."
deletion
  paragraph
    text "A whole removed paragraph."

<del> produced a deletion node and <ins> an insertion, so both are announced. The strikethrough and the underline are not the only signal.

Both are transparent (§2.8), as the second block shows: a <del> at the top level wrapped a whole <p>, and the tree kept the paragraph inside the deletion. So the same element can mark a word, a sentence or six paragraphs, which is what a revision-tracking system needs.

Both take two attributes. datetime records when the change was made, in the same formats as <time> (§4.6). cite gives a URL explaining the change: an issue, a changelog entry, a meeting record. No browser shows either to the user, so, as with <blockquote cite>, they are metadata, and anything the reader needs to know must be in the text.

The distinction from <s> (§4.3) is worth stating precisely, because both are drawn struck through:

<s>
The content is no longer accurate or relevant. A superseded price, a cancelled event, a completed to-do item. A fact about the world.
<del>
The document was edited and this was removed. A fact about the document's history.

A crossed-out old price on a sale item is <s>. A clause struck from a policy in an amendment is <del>. Both produce a deletion node, so the difference is not what a listener hears. It is whether your markup is telling the truth, which matters to anyone reading or processing it later.

5.10 Lists in Interfaces

Most lists on a modern page are not lists in prose. They are navigation menus, card grids, search results, comment threads, tag clouds and toolbars, and marking them up as lists is the most valuable habit in this section.

<nav aria-label="Main">
  <ul role="list">
    <li><a href="/shop">Shop</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

The reason is §5.1's: the count. A navigation with fourteen links is announced as "list, 14 items", and the user decides whether to go through it or skip to the next landmark. Without the list, they find out how long it is by reaching the end.

Four patterns worth marking up as lists, all of which often are not:

  • Navigation: <ul> for a menu, <ol> for a breadcrumb, because a breadcrumb's order is the hierarchy (§7.13).
  • A grid of cards: visually a grid, structurally a list of items. Flexbox and grid both work perfectly well on a <ul>.
  • Comments and search results: a list of <article> elements (§6.5), one per <li>.
  • Tags and filters: a list of links or buttons.

And the role="list" in that example is deliberate. As §5.5 measured and explained, removing the markers with list-style: none (which every one of these designs does) makes some browsers drop the list semantics, and stating the role puts them back.

5.11 When Not to Use a List

Three cases where a list is the wrong structure, each with the right one.

When the items are records with fields. Three lines, each showing a name, a date and a status, are a <table> (§10): each cell has a meaning from both its row and its column, which is exactly what a list cannot express.

When the items are term/description pairs. Use <dl> (§5.6), not a <ul> of "Term: description" strings, and not a two-column table.

When it is one thing, or prose. A single <li> is a paragraph with a bullet. And a list of full sentences that read as an argument is prose that has been chopped up: the bullets add nothing, and the reader loses the linking words that made it an argument.

There is also a fourth, more common than the others: a list used for indentation. A <ul> with one item, or a nested list whose nesting expresses no hierarchy, is claiming a structure to get a margin. That is CSS's job.

5.12 The Tree, Collected

Every element in this section and what it produces, as measured:

<ul> <ol> <menu>
list, with listitem children carrying level and a ListMarker.
<dl>
DescriptionList, with term and definition children.
<blockquote>
blockquote. A <footer> inside it becomes a contentinfo landmark — put the attribution outside.
<del> <ins>
deletion and insertion, wrapping whatever they contain.
<q> <cite>
No node of their own. <q> contributes the browser's generated quotation marks as text.

And the two attributes that look useful and are not: cite on <blockquote>, <q>, <del> and <ins> is invisible to every user in every browser. It is worth writing as provenance for machines, and it never replaces a visible, linked attribution.

Exercises

1. Choose the correct structure for each, and justify it.

1. Steps for seasoning a cast iron pan.
2. A product's dimensions, weight and material.
3. A site's primary navigation, styled with no bullets.
4. Search results, each with a title, snippet and date.
5. A recipe's ingredients.
6. Three lines each showing a customer, an order date and a status.
Solution

1. <ol>. The sequence is the information — §5.2's test: reordering the steps makes the content wrong. Whether the design shows numbers is irrelevant; an <ol> with list-style: none is still ordered.

2. <dl>. Term/description pairs (§5.6). Not a two-column table: §10.1's test is that a table's cells need both a row and a column header to mean anything, and "2.1 kg" needs only "Weight". Not a <ul> of "Weight: 2.1 kg" strings either, because that throws away the pairing the tree records as term and definition.

3. <ul role="list"> inside <nav aria-label="…">. A list because of the count — "list, 14 items" is what lets a user decide whether to walk it (§5.1, §5.10). <ul> rather than <ol> because the order is a design choice, not the hierarchy. And role="list" explicitly, because §5.5 measured that list-style: none removes the markers, and while Chrome keeps the roles, Safari drops the list semantics entirely when the markers go — which is the case for essentially every navigation menu ever styled.

4. <ul> (or <ol>) of <article> elements, one per <li>. A list, for the count. <article> for each result because a search result is self-contained and would make sense alone (§6.5), and it gives each an article node the user can navigate between. <ol> if the ranking is meaningful, <ul> if it is not.

5. <ul>. Reordering ingredients does not make the recipe wrong, so it is unordered — this is the canonical contrast with 1, and the pair is worth remembering because it shows the test does not depend on the content being "list-like".

6. <table> (§10). Each cell means "this customer, this field", which is the two-dimensional relationship §10.1 defines a table by and which no list can express. With <caption> and <th scope="col"> — and §10.10 measured what happens without them: Chrome demotes a table with no headers and no caption to LayoutTable, which is not exposed as a table at all.

2. A blockquote is written with its attribution in a <footer> inside it. What is wrong, and what is the correct markup?

Solution

Two things, and the first is measured in §5.7: the <footer> becomes a contentinfo landmark.

<footer> is scoped by the nearest sectioning element — <article>, <aside>, <nav> or <section> (§6.4). <blockquote> is not one of those, so the footer is scoped to the document and takes the page-level contentinfo role (§6.7). The measurement shows exactly that. A page with three quotations therefore has three contentinfo entries in its landmark list, where there should be one, and the user's landmark navigation is polluted with attributions.

The second is editorial: the attribution is inside the quotation. "Annual report 2025" is not something the annual report said. Anything inside <blockquote> is asserted to be part of the quoted material, and a screen reader reading the blockquote reads the attribution as though the source had signed itself.

And a third thing that is not wrong but is worth knowing: the cite attribute on <blockquote> holds the source's URL and no browser exposes it to anyone — not as a link, not as a tooltip, not in the accessibility tree. It is machine-readable provenance and nothing more, so if the reader should be able to reach the source, that has to be a real link.

The correct markup is the one the specification itself recommends:

<figure>
  <blockquote cite="https://example.com/report">
    <p>Revenue rose in every quarter.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <figcaption>
    — <cite><a href="https://example.com/report">Annual report 2025</a></cite>
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<figure> groups the quotation with its caption (§8.12). The <figcaption> is outside the <blockquote>, so it is not part of the quotation and produces no landmark. <cite> names the work — and note it wraps the title, not a person: the specification is explicit that a person's name is not a citation, so an attribution to a human is plain text with the work in <cite>. The <a> makes the source reachable by everyone rather than only by a parser.

Keep the cite attribute as well. It costs nothing and it is real metadata; it simply is not a user-facing feature.

3. Explain why role="list" is sometimes correct on a <ul>, given that §13.9's second rule of ARIA says not to restate a native role.

Solution

Because it is not restating a role that is present — it is restoring one the browser removed.

What happens: §5.5 measured a <ul style="list-style:none"> in Chrome, and the ListMarker nodes disappeared while list and listitem survived. Safari behaves differently: removing the markers removes the list semantics, on the reasoning that a list styled with no bullets was not intended as a list. The behaviour was introduced deliberately, because the web is full of <ul> elements used purely as layout containers, and announcing every one of them as a list made VoiceOver noisier without helping.

Why that matters so much: essentially every navigation menu, card grid, tag list and toolbar on the web sets list-style: none. So the elements most worth announcing as lists — the ones where the count genuinely helps a user decide whether to walk it (§5.1) — are exactly the ones affected.

Why it does not violate the second rule of ARIA. That rule says not to change native semantics — <button role="link"> is the failure it is aimed at. Here the role being stated is the element's own role, and the effect is to keep it rather than to override it. Nothing is changed; something is prevented from being dropped. This is one of a small number of accepted exceptions, alongside role="presentation" on a genuine layout table (§10.12), and it is accepted precisely because it compensates for a known browser behaviour rather than expressing a design opinion.

When to use it: on lists whose markers are styled away and whose item count is useful to a reader — navigation, results, cards, comments. Not on a <ul> that is only a flex container with nothing list-like about it; that one should probably not be a <ul> at all (§5.11).

The honest caveat, which is why this is an exception and not a rule: it is a workaround for one browser's heuristic, and heuristics change. It costs eleven characters and does no harm anywhere, which is what makes it worth doing rather than reasoning about per site.

4. Distinguish <s>, <del> and <strike>, and give a case for each of the first two.

Solution

All three render struck through and two of them are still in the language.

<strike> is obsolete. It was purely presentational, it has been removed from the specification, and it should not appear in new markup. Browsers still render it, which is why it survives in old pages. There is no case for it.

<s> means the content is no longer accurate or relevant (§4.3). A fact about the world. It produces a deletion node.

<p>Cast iron skillet, 26cm — <s>£64.00</s> <strong>£48.00</strong></p>

The old price was correct and is not any more. Nothing about the document was edited; the price changed. Other cases: a cancelled event in a schedule, a sold-out size, a completed item in a to-do list.

<del> means this was removed from the document in an edit (§5.9). A fact about the document's history. It also produces a deletion node, and it carries datetime and cite.

<p>Refunds are available within <del datetime="2026-01-15">14</del>
   <ins datetime="2026-01-15">30</ins> days.</p>

A policy was amended and the change is being shown. <ins> marks the replacement, and both carry the date of the amendment. Other cases: a tracked revision, a changelog, a published erratum, a wiki diff.

Why the distinction matters given that both produce deletion. A listener hears the same thing either way, so this is not an accessibility difference — it is whether the markup is true. The consumers that care are the ones that read the document later: a diff tool, a content pipeline, an editor, a legal review, and the next person maintaining it. <del datetime> on a sale price claims the document was amended on that date, which is false and will confuse whoever relies on it.

The rule of thumb: ask what changed. If the world changed, <s>. If the document changed, <del> — and then it should have a datetime, and there is usually an <ins> nearby.

5. A design shows an FAQ as a series of bold questions each followed by a paragraph. Give three possible markups and choose one.

Solution

Option A — a description list.

<dl>
  <dt>Is the pan pre-seasoned?</dt>
  <dd><p>Yes. It arrives ready to use, and improves with each cook.</p></dd>
  <dt>Can it go in the dishwasher?</dt>
  <dd><p>No. Wash by hand and dry immediately.</p></dd>
</dl>

Question/answer is one of the cases <dl> is explicitly for (§5.6). The tree records term and definition nodes, so the pairing is machine-readable, and the whole set is announced as one structure a user can skip. Costs: <dd> may contain flow content but the pairing is positional, so an answer containing a heading or an aside starts to strain; and styling a <dl> needs the <div> wrapper the specification blesses for exactly that reason.

Option B — headings and paragraphs.

<section aria-labelledby="faq-h">
  <h2 id="faq-h">Frequently asked questions</h2>
  <h3>Is the pan pre-seasoned?</h3>
  <p>Yes. It arrives ready to use, and improves with each cook.</p>
</section>

Each question becomes a heading, so all of them appear in the page's heading list (§6.3) and a user can navigate directly to the one they want. That is a genuine advantage for a long FAQ. The cost is that the outline fills with twenty level-3 entries, which is right if the FAQ is the page and noisy if it is one section of a product page.

Option C — <details> per question.

<details>
  <summary>Is the pan pre-seasoned?</summary>
  <p>Yes. It arrives ready to use, and improves with each cook.</p>
</details>

Collapsible with no JavaScript, and the keyboard behaviour, the expanded state and the focus stop all come free (§14.7). It matches how most FAQ designs actually behave. Two costs, both measured in §14.7: a closed <details> removes its contents from the accessibility tree and from find-in-page, so a user searching the page for "dishwasher" finds nothing; and the questions are not headings, so they are absent from the heading list.

Choice: B, with C's mechanism where the design requires collapsing. For a standalone FAQ page the headings are the deciding factor — navigating a long FAQ by heading is exactly how someone uses one, and it is the only option that supports it. If the design requires collapsed answers, the two combine, with the heading inside the summary:

<details>
  <summary><h3>Is the pan pre-seasoned?</h3></summary>
  <p>Yes…</p>
</details>

When A is right instead: a short FAQ embedded in a larger page, where twenty new headings would swamp the outline. Then the <dl> gives the pairing without adding to the heading list, which is precisely the trade.

What is wrong in all cases is the markup the design implies literally: <p><b>Is the pan pre-seasoned?</b></p> followed by <p>Yes…</p>. §4.1 measured that <b> produces no node at all, so nothing anywhere records that the first paragraph is a question and the second its answer. It renders correctly and means nothing.

SECTION 6

Document Structure: Sectioning and Landmarks

A page has two structures at the same time, and confusing them causes nearly every mistake in this section.

The first is the heading hierarchy, <h1> through <h6>. It is how a reader, sighted or not, understands what the page is about and how its parts relate. The second is the set of landmarks: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer> and a few others. Landmarks are how someone using a screen reader jumps between the regions of a page without reading all of it.

They are not the same structure, neither is derived from the other, and a page needs both. A screen reader user typically arrives, presses a key to list the landmarks and find the main content, then presses another key to list the headings inside it and find the part they want. Neither list is usable without the other. And CSS produces neither, which is why a beautifully laid-out page can have no structure at all as far as a screen reader is concerned.

Everything below was measured against a real accessibility tree, and two of the results are ones the markup alone would not lead you to predict.

6.1 The Two Structures, Measured

<header><a href="/">Acme</a></header><nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/shop">Shop</a></nav><main><h1>Title</h1><article><h2>An article</h2></article><section aria-label="Related"><h2>Related</h2></section><aside><h2>Sidebar</h2></aside></main><footer><p>© 2026 Acme</p></footer>

AX TREE
banner
  link "Acme"
navigation "Main"
  link "Shop"
main
  heading "Title" level=1
  article
    heading "An article" level=2
  region "Related"
    heading "Related" level=2
  complementary
    heading "Sidebar" level=2
contentinfo
  paragraph
    text "© 2026 Acme"

Six elements, six landmark roles, and none of the roles written in the markup. <header> became banner, <nav> became navigation, <main> became main, <aside> became complementary, <footer> became contentinfo, and <section aria-label> became region. The headings kept their level, which is what a list of headings is built from.

That is the whole reward for using the sectioning elements instead of <div>: you get the landmark structure for free, and you get it right. §13.9's first rule of ARIA, use the native element, is nowhere cheaper to follow than here.

6.2 Headings

There are six ranks, <h1> to <h6>, and heading rank is the only thing that sets them apart. <h1> is the most important and <h6> the least. The default text sizes are a habit of the browser's stylesheet, not what the element means (§2.1).

Three rules make headings work.

Every heading is a real heading, and nothing else is. Text that is large and bold because of a CSS class is not a heading. It does not appear in a list of headings, does not get a level, and tells nobody anything. The reverse holds too: do not use a heading element to make text big. That is what CSS is for, and an <h3> used for its size puts a fake entry in the outline.

One <h1> per page, naming what the page is about. This is a convention rather than a rule of the specification, and it is a good one. The <h1> is the page's headline, it usually matches the <title> (§3.2), and a page with six of them has no headline at all.

Do not skip a level going down. An <h2> may be followed by an <h3>, and an <h3> may be followed by an <h2>. Going back up any number of levels is fine, because it closes sections. Going down by more than one is a skipped heading level:

<hgroup><h1>Acme Cookware</h1><p>Hand-forged in Sheffield</p></hgroup><h2>Products</h2><h4>Skipped a level</h4>

AX TREE
group
  heading "Acme Cookware" level=1
  paragraph
    text "Hand-forged in Sheffield"
heading "Products" level=2
heading "Skipped a level" level=4

The tree records level=4 after level=2, exactly as written. Nothing corrects it and nothing warns. To a user reading the list of headings, a jump from 2 to 4 says "there is a level-3 section here that I have missed", and they will go looking for it. The fix is always to change the number, never to add a fake heading.

The measurement also shows <hgroup>, which exists for one narrow job: grouping a heading with a subtitle or tagline, so the subtitle does not become a heading of its own. It contains exactly one heading plus any number of <p> elements, and it produces a group node. The <p> is connected to the heading without competing with it in the outline. Before <hgroup>, the usual workaround was a second heading element for the tagline, which put a fake section in every page's outline.

So heading rank is the whole vocabulary of this structure, and a skipped heading level is the only way to get it wrong. Two habits keep the heading rank honest. Choose it by asking whether the content is a subsection of what comes before it. And re-read the list of headings after any restructuring, because a skipped heading level is invisible on the page and obvious in that list.

6.3 The Document Outline

The document outline is the tree implied by the heading ranks: each heading opens a section that runs until the next heading of the same or higher rank.

h1  Cast iron skillet, 26cm
    h2  Specifications
    h2  Care and seasoning
        h3  First use
        h3  Cleaning
    h2  Reviews
        h3  Most helpful

This outline is what a screen reader's list of headings shows, indented. It is what a reader-mode view builds its navigation from, and it is a large part of how a search engine understands what a page is about. Getting it right is mostly a matter of asking "is this a subsection of the thing above it?" and choosing the rank to match.

There is an important piece of history here, because it still misleads people. HTML once specified an outline algorithm in which a heading's effective rank came from how deeply it was nested in sectioning elements. An <h1> inside two nested <section> elements would act as a level-3 heading, so you could write <h1> everywhere and let the nesting sort it out. It was a genuinely nice idea. No browser ever implemented it, no screen reader ever used it, and it has been removed from the specification. Advice recommending it is out of date, and following it produces a page whose entire outline is a flat list of level-1 headings.

So: the rank you write is the rank you get. Nesting a <section> does not lower the rank of the headings inside it. The measurement in §6.2 shows the levels reported exactly as written, and that is all there is to it.

6.4 Sectioning Content

sectioning content is a category of exactly four elements: <article>, <aside>, <nav> and <section>. Each one sets a scope for the headings and for the <header>/<footer> inside it (§6.7).

Choosing between them is a question about content, not layout, and there is a procedure for it:

<article>
Self-contained: it would still make sense if it were syndicated, printed alone or shown in a feed.
<nav>
A block of major navigation links (§6.6).
<aside>
Tangentially related to the content around it: a pull quote, a related-links box, an advertisement, a glossary note.
<section>
A thematic grouping that is none of the above — and, per §6.5, one that has a heading.
<div>
None of the above applies. A grouping that exists for styling or scripting and means nothing (§4.14).

Work down that list in order and stop at the first match. The last row is not a failure: a <div> is the right answer for a flex container, a grid cell, a card wrapper, or anything that exists only for CSS. Reaching for <section> because <div> feels unsophisticated is the most common mistake here, and §6.5 measures what it costs.

6.5 article, section and aside

This is the measurement that settles the <section> question:

<article><header><h2>Post title</h2></header><p>Body</p><footer><p>Posted 2026</p></footer></article><section><h2>Unlabelled section</h2><p>x</p></section>

AX TREE
article
  sectionheader
    heading "Post title" level=2
  paragraph
    text "Body"
  sectionfooter
    paragraph
      text "Posted 2026"
heading "Unlabelled section" level=2
paragraph
  text "x"

The <article> produced an article node. The <section> produced nothing at all. Its heading and paragraph are direct children of the document, with no container between them.

That is not a bug. A <section> maps to the region role only when it has an accessible name (a label a screen reader can announce), because an unnamed region is a landmark with nothing to say: "region" appears in the landmark list and the user has no idea what it holds. Without a name, the browser leaves it out of the tree entirely. Compare §6.1, where <section aria-label="Related"> produced region "Related".

So the rule is mechanical: a <section> needs a name, or it is a <div> with extra characters. The best way to give it one is aria-labelledby pointing at the heading it already has:

<section aria-labelledby="related-h">
  <h2 id="related-h">Related products</h2>
</section>

aria-label works too and duplicates the string; aria-labelledby cannot drift.

<article> is the more useful of the two, and it is underused. The test is syndication: would this content make sense on its own, in a feed reader, in an email digest, printed by itself? A blog post, a news story, a product card, a comment, a forum reply, a review: all articles. Articles nest naturally. A comment is an <article> inside the post's <article>, which is exactly how the relationship reads.

<aside> means "tangential", not "in the sidebar". A pull quote in the middle of a paragraph is an <aside>. A sidebar containing the site's main navigation is a <nav> that happens to be placed at the side. When an <aside> is a direct child of <body>, it is a complementary landmark, as §6.1 measured. Nested inside an <article>, it belongs to that article and is not a page-level landmark.

The mechanism is worth stating once more, because it is easy to half-remember: <section> maps to role="region" only when it has an accessible name. role="region" is one of the two landmark roles that behave that way; form is the other. Name it, or use a <div>.

6.6 nav

<nav> marks a block of major navigation links and produces the navigation landmark. §7.13 covers writing navigation; two structural points belong here.

It is for major blocks, not for every group of links. A site's main menu, a breadcrumb, a table of contents, pagination and the big block of footer links are all <nav>. Three links inside a paragraph are not. Overusing it fills the landmark list with entries that are not destinations.

More than one <nav> on a page must be labelled, with aria-label or aria-labelledby. Two unlabelled navigation landmarks cannot be told apart. §6.12 has the labelling rules.

A footer's block of links is a genuine judgement call. If it is a real site map with forty links, <nav aria-label="Footer"> helps a user find it. If it is four links to the privacy policy and the terms, it is not navigation, and the <footer> landmark already covers it.

6.7 header and footer

<header> and <footer> are the two elements whose meaning depends on where they are, and the measurements above show both cases.

At the top level, as direct children of <body>, they are the page's banner and its footer:

banner
  link "Acme"
...
contentinfo
  paragraph
    text "© 2026 Acme"

Inside a sectioning element they belong to that section, and their roles are different:

article
  sectionheader
    heading "Post title" level=2
  ...
  sectionfooter
    paragraph
      text "Posted 2026"

banner and contentinfo are page-level landmarks and appear in the landmark list. sectionheader and sectionfooter are not landmarks. They are structural roles that describe an introduction and a conclusion within their own section. So there is exactly one banner and one contentinfo per page, and as many sectionheader and sectionfooter elements as you have sections.

That scoping is what makes both elements useful inside an <article>. The byline, date and tags at the top of a post are its <header>; the tags, share links and "posted in" line at the bottom are its <footer>. Neither clutters the page's landmark list.

What goes in a page <header>: the site's name or logo, the main navigation, a search box, the account menu. What goes in a page <footer>: the copyright, the legal links, the contact details, secondary navigation. Neither has to be at the visual top or bottom; the roles are about what the content does.

One constraint worth knowing: a <header> may not contain another <header> or a <footer>, and the same is true the other way round.

6.8 main

<main> contains the content that is unique to this page: everything that is not the parts repeated across the site.

<main id="main">
  <h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>
</main>

It is the most valuable landmark on the page, because it answers the question every screen reader user asks first: where does the actual content start? Without it, they must get past the banner, the navigation and the cookie notice on every page of the site.

Four rules:

  • One per page, and only one may be visible at a time. Several <main> elements are invalid, and a router that renders several views at once must hide all but the current one.
  • It must not be inside an <article>, <aside>, <footer>, <header> or <nav>. It is the page's content, not part of one section of it.
  • It is the skip link's destination (§6.10), which is why it usually carries an id.
  • It is not a wrapper for everything. The page header, the main navigation and the footer go outside it.

<main> has no equivalent in the vocabulary from before HTML5, and no default styling. That is why it is often missing from older markup: it is the one landmark that has to be added on purpose, rather than replacing a <div> that was already there.

6.9 The search Landmark

<search> is the newest element in this section. It groups the controls that search the site or the current page, and it produces a search landmark:

<search><form role="search"><label for="q">Search</label><input id="q" type="search" name="q"><button>Go</button></form></search>

AX TREE
search
  search
    LabelText
      text "Search"
    searchbox "Search"
    button "Go"

Look carefully at what that tree shows: two nested search nodes, because the example has both the <search> element and role="search" on the form inside it. That is a duplicate landmark, and it is the one mistake to avoid while this element is new. The user's landmark list gets two identical entries, and neither tells them anything the other did not.

Write one or the other. The element is the better choice:

<search>
  <form action="/search">
    <label for="q">Search products</label>
    <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
    <button>Search</button>
  </form>
</search>

role="search" on the <form> is still the compatible fallback, and it is what every page written before this element existed uses. Both produce the same landmark; the element describes itself and needs no ARIA (§13.9).

<search> is not only for a site-wide search box. It is just as correct around a filter panel, a faceted-search sidebar, or any group of controls whose job is to narrow down what is shown. It is not for a form that creates or edits something.

Two smaller points. <input type="search"> differs from type="text" in small, platform-specific ways (a clear button, a different on-screen keyboard, sometimes a history dropdown), and it produces the searchbox role, as the tree shows. And a search field still needs a real <label>; a placeholder is not a label (§11.2).

One more detail belongs with the element: type="search" on the input. type="search" produces the searchbox role instead of textbox, and gives the user a clear button and a keyboard suited to searching. These are small platform conveniences that cost nothing and that a plain type="text" does not get.

6.10 Skip Links

A keyboard user arriving at a page starts at the top and presses Tab to move forward. On a site with thirty navigation links, reaching the content costs thirty presses, on every single page. A skip link is the fix, and it is the oldest accessibility pattern on the web:

<a href="#main" class="skip">Skip to content</a><nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/a">A</a><a href="/b">B</a></nav><main id="main" tabindex="-1"><h1>Title</h1><button>First control</button></main>

TAB ORDER
<a> "Skip to content"
<a> "A"
<a> "B"
<button> "First control"
(leaves the page)

The measurement shows the skip link is the first stop on the page, and that is the entire requirement. A skip link that is not first is useless, because you have to tab through the thing you wanted to skip in order to reach it.

Four details make it work.

It is a fragment link to <main> (§7.5). Activating it moves the point where the browser's Tab sequence starts to the target, so the next Tab continues from inside the content.

The target carries tabindex="-1". Not every browser reliably moves focus to a fragment target that cannot normally take focus. tabindex="-1" makes the element focusable by script without adding it to the Tab sequence (§14.1), which makes the behaviour certain everywhere.

It is visible when focused, and only then. The convention is to position it off-screen and bring it back on :focus. It must not be hidden with display: none or visibility: hidden, because both remove it from the tab order and from the accessibility tree entirely (§13.8). The link then exists in the markup but can never be used, which is the most common way this pattern is broken.

Its text says where it goes. "Skip to content" or "Skip to main content", not "Skip".

A long page with several major regions may reasonably offer more than one ("Skip to content", "Skip to search", "Skip to footer") as a small list at the very top. Beyond three, the skip links become navigation in their own right and are worse than the problem they solve.

6.11 The Landmark Roles

Eight landmark roles exist. Six come free with an element, and knowing which is which is all this table is for:

banner
From <header> at the top level. The site's masthead. One per page.
navigation
From <nav>. Many per page, each labelled.
main
From <main>. The page's own content. Exactly one.
complementary
From a top-level <aside>. Supporting content.
contentinfo
From <footer> at the top level. Copyright, legal, contact. One per page.
search
From <search>, or role="search" on a form (§6.9).
region
From a named <section>. Unnamed, it is not a landmark at all (§6.5).
form
From a named <form>. Same rule as region: no name, no landmark.

Two of the eight, region and form, appear only when the element has an accessible name. That is deliberate: an unnamed entry in a landmark list is noise, so the platform declines to create one.

Two rules keep the list useful.

Every part of the page should be inside a landmark. Content that sits between landmarks can only be reached by reading straight through, which is what landmarks exist to avoid. The target is a page of banner, navigation, main and contentinfo with nothing in between.

Do not create landmarks you do not need. Eight is a small, memorable list precisely because a landmark is a top-level destination. A page with fifteen region landmarks has replaced a useful list with a second table of contents.

Three of those roles are worth writing out in their ARIA spelling, because you will meet them on <div> elements in older markup: role="banner" is what <header> gives you, role="contentinfo" is what <footer> gives you, and role="complementary" is what <aside> gives you. Seeing role="banner" or role="complementary" on a <div> is not wrong; it produces the same landmark. But it is the long way to say what the element already says. And role="contentinfo" on a <div> inside an <article> produces a page-level landmark where the element would have produced none.

6.12 Labelling Landmarks

When there is more than one landmark of a kind, each one needs a name. Otherwise the user's list shows "navigation, navigation, navigation".

<nav aria-label="Main">…</nav>
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">…</nav>

<section aria-labelledby="specs-h">
  <h2 id="specs-h">Specifications</h2>
</section>

Three rules, and each has a wrong version that is common.

Do not repeat the role in the label. aria-label="Main navigation" is announced as "Main navigation navigation". The role is already spoken; the label supplies only what tells this one apart.

Prefer aria-labelledby when a heading already exists. It cannot drift out of step with the visible text the way a copied aria-label string can, and it means one fewer invisible string in the markup. Use aria-label when there really is no visible text to point at.

Do not label a landmark of which there is only one. A single <main> needs no label, and neither does a single <nav>. The name adds a word to every announcement and distinguishes it from nothing.

§13.3 covers the full calculation of an accessible name, and its order of priority applies here too: aria-labelledby beats aria-label, which beats the element's own content.

6.13 A Complete Page

Putting the section together, this is the structural skeleton that almost every content page should have:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Cast iron skillet, 26cm — Acme</title>
</head>
<body>
  <a href="#main" class="skip-link">Skip to content</a>

  <header>
    <a href="/"><img src="/logo.svg" alt="Acme" width="120" height="40"></a>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/shop" aria-current="page">Shop</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
    <search>
      <form action="/search">
        <label for="q">Search products</label>
        <input id="q" type="search" name="q">
        <button>Search</button>
      </form>
    </search>
  </header>

  <main id="main" tabindex="-1">
    <h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>

    <section aria-labelledby="specs-h">
      <h2 id="specs-h">Specifications</h2>
      <p>Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260&nbsp;°C.</p>
    </section>

    <section aria-labelledby="reviews-h">
      <h2 id="reviews-h">Reviews</h2>
      <article>
        <header><h3>Excellent heat retention</h3></header>
        <p>Six months in and it only gets better.</p>
        <footer><p>Posted March 2026</p></footer>
      </article>
    </section>
  </main>

  <aside aria-labelledby="related-h">
    <h2 id="related-h">Related products</h2>
  </aside>

  <footer>
    <p>&copy; 2026 Acme Cookware</p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Read it as a landmark list and it is short and complete: banner, navigation, search, main, complementary, contentinfo. Read it as a heading outline and it is a level-1 page title with two level-2 sections and a level-3 review inside one of them. CSS produced neither structure, and both are what a user actually moves around the page by.

The two things that look optional and are not: the skip link must be first, and every <section> and every second <nav> must be named.

Exercises

1. A page is built entirely from <div> elements with descriptive class names — .page-header, .main-nav, .content, .sidebar, .page-footer. The CSS is excellent and the page looks right. What exactly is missing, and what does a screen reader user experience?

Solution

Every landmark is missing, and the class names contribute nothing. §2.10: class carries no meaning to the browser at all. class="main-nav" produces a plain generic node — a <div> named main-nav is not a navigation landmark by any mechanism.

What the user experiences, concretely: pressing the key that lists landmarks returns nothing, or only the document itself. There is no way to jump to the content, so on every page of the site they must tab or read past the header, the entire navigation, and any promotional content before reaching what they came for. On a site with thirty header links that is thirty keystrokes per page, and the fact that the visual design makes the content obviously central helps them not at all.

If the headings are also <div class="heading">, the second navigation mechanism is gone too, and the page is one undifferentiated run of text.

The fix is a rename, and the diff is small:

From To Landmark
<div class="page-header"> <header> banner
<div class="main-nav"> <nav aria-label="Main"> navigation
<div class="content"> <main id="main"> main
<div class="sidebar"> <aside aria-labelledby="…"> complementary
<div class="page-footer"> <footer> contentinfo

Every one of those roles comes free from the element, as §6.1 measured — no ARIA required. The CSS need not change at all: the class names can stay on the semantic elements, so this is a genuinely low-risk refactor, which is worth saying because it is often deferred as though it were a rewrite.

Two additions beyond the rename. A skip link as the first focusable element (§6.10), pointing at the <main id="main" tabindex="-1">. And, if the headings are also faked, real <h1>–<h3> elements — because the landmark list gets the user to the content and the heading list gets them around inside it, and they need both.

What is explicitly not the fix: adding role="navigation" and role="main" to the <div> elements. It works, and it is more markup for the same result, which is what §13.9's first rule of ARIA is about.

2. When should you use <section> and when <div>? Answer with reference to what the accessibility tree actually does.

Solution

Use <section> when the content is a thematic group that has a name; use <div> otherwise. The measurement in §6.5 is what makes that rule concrete rather than a matter of taste.

An unnamed <section> produced no node at all — its heading and paragraph appeared as direct children of the document, with nothing between them. A <section aria-label="Related"> produced region "Related" (§6.1). So a <section> maps to the region landmark only when it has an accessible name, and without one the element is precisely as meaningful as a <div>: zero.

That is deliberate. A landmark exists so a user can jump to it from a list, and an unnamed entry in that list says "region" and nothing else — so the platform declines to create one rather than filling the list with noise.

Therefore:

<section aria-labelledby="specs-h">
  <h2 id="specs-h">Specifications</h2>
</section>

aria-labelledby pointing at the heading the section already has, rather than aria-label duplicating the string — one string, no possibility of drift.

And <div> for: a flex or grid container, a card wrapper, a scroll container (§10.13), a styling hook, anything a JavaScript framework needs a root for. None of these are content groupings, none has a name, and none belongs in a landmark list. Reaching for <section> because <div> feels unsemantic is the common error, and the honest answer is §4.14's: <div> means nothing, and meaning nothing is frequently correct.

One more distinction worth having. Before reaching for <section> at all, check the other three sectioning elements (§6.4): is it self-contained enough to be an <article>? Is it navigation, so <nav>? Is it tangential, so <aside>? <section> is the one to use when the answer to all three is no — and then only with a name.

And the rule that follows from all of it: do not use a landmark to convey "this bit is important". A page with eight named region landmarks has replaced a short, useful list of destinations with a second table of contents, which is worse than having none.

3. A design has a page title, a tagline under it, and three sections whose sub-headings are styled smaller than their bodies require. Write the heading markup, and explain the two traps.

Solution 
<hgroup>
  <h1>Acme Cookware</h1>
  <p>Hand-forged in Sheffield since 1994</p>
</hgroup>

<section aria-labelledby="skillets-h">
  <h2 id="skillets-h">Skillets</h2>
  <h3>Seasoning</h3>
</section>

Trap one: the tagline must not be a heading. The instinct is <h2>Hand-forged in Sheffield since 1994</h2>, which puts a phantom section in the outline — a reader browsing the heading list sees a level-2 entry that contains nothing and leads nowhere. <hgroup> exists for exactly this: one heading plus any number of <p> elements, producing (as §6.2 measured) a group node containing heading "Acme Cookware" level=1 and a paragraph. The tagline is associated with the heading without competing with it.

Trap two: the rank is the meaning, not the size. "Styled smaller than their bodies require" is a CSS problem with a CSS answer. Picking <h4> because it looks right produces the skipped heading level §6.2 measured — the tree recorded level=4 straight after level=2, exactly as written, with nothing to correct it. A user reading the heading list concludes there is a level-3 section they have missed and goes looking for it.

The heading rank answers "is this a subsection of the thing above it?" and nothing else. Size is h3 { font-size: 1rem }.

A third trap worth naming, because it is the one that produces the worst outcome: do not reach for the old outline algorithm. The specification once said a heading's effective rank came from its nesting depth in sectioning elements, so <h1> everywhere would sort itself out. No browser ever implemented it and it has been removed (§6.3). Following that advice gives a page whose entire outline is a flat list of level-1 headings, which is strictly worse than the skipped level it was meant to avoid.

The rank you write is the rank you get, and nesting a <section> demotes nothing.

4. Write the landmark structure for an application shell: a top bar with a logo and account menu, a collapsible left sidebar of navigation, a main work area, and a right panel showing details of the selected item. State every label and say why.

Solution 
<a href="#work" class="skip-link">Skip to content</a>

<header>
  <a href="/"><img src="/logo.svg" alt="Acme" width="110" height="32"></a>
  <nav aria-label="Account">
    <ul><li><a href="/settings">Settings</a></li><li><a href="/help">Help</a></li></ul>
  </nav>
</header>

<nav aria-label="Sections" id="sidebar">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/invoices" aria-current="page">Invoices</a></li>
    <li><a href="/customers">Customers</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

<main id="work" tabindex="-1">
  <h1>Invoices</h1>
</main>

<aside aria-labelledby="details-h">
  <h2 id="details-h">Invoice details</h2>
</aside>

Landmark list: banner, navigation "Account", navigation "Sections", main, complementary "Invoice details". Five entries, each naming a destination.

Two <nav> elements, both labelled. §6.12: two unlabelled navigation landmarks are indistinguishable. The labels are "Account" and "Sections" — not "Account navigation", because the role is already announced and the longer label reads as "Account navigation navigation".

The right panel is <aside>, not <section>. It is supporting content about the thing selected in the main area — the definition of tangential. Named with aria-labelledby pointing at its own <h2>, so the string exists once (§6.12).

<main> wraps the work area only, not the sidebar and not the top bar. §6.8: one per page, and the page chrome goes outside it.

The skip link targets the work area, because that is where the user wants to land — not the sidebar, which is the thing they are skipping. §6.10 measured that it must be the first focus stop, and its target carries tabindex="-1" so focus lands reliably.

The collapsible sidebar has a requirement the markup above does not yet meet, and it is the interesting part of this question. When it is collapsed, hiding it with CSS alone leaves its links in the tab order and in the accessibility tree — a keyboard user tabs into an invisible menu. Use hidden or display: none, both of which remove it from both trees (§13.8), and give the toggle button aria-expanded and aria-controls:

<button type="button" aria-expanded="true" aria-controls="sidebar">Sections</button>

One thing deliberately absent: any role="banner", role="navigation" or role="main". Each element already carries its role, as §6.1 measured, and adding it is the thing §13.9's first rule of ARIA tells you not to do.

5. A single-page application renders three views at once and shows one with CSS, so there are three <main> elements in the DOM. Explain every problem and give the fix.

Solution

Three <main> elements is invalid, and the rule is not arbitrary: <main> is the answer to "where does this page's content start", and three answers is no answer. §6.8 — one per page, and only one may be visible at a time.

What actually breaks, in order of severity:

The landmark list has three identical main entries. A screen reader user's first action on arriving is to jump to the main content; they now choose between three, two of which are the wrong view.

Two views' content is in the accessibility tree and the tab order. This is the worst of it, and it depends entirely on how they are hidden. Hidden with opacity: 0, visibility: hidden on a parent's descendant, height: 0, or by moving them off-screen with position: absolute, the hidden views' controls remain focusable — so a keyboard user tabs from the visible form into an invisible one and their focus disappears. Only display: none and hidden remove an element from both trees (§13.8).

Two extra <h1> elements. The heading list shows three level-1 headings, and the outline (§6.3) has three top-level entries where there should be one.

Duplicate id attributes, if the views share a template — so document.getElementById, every <label for> (§11.2), every aria-labelledby (§13.3) and every fragment link (§7.5) resolves to whichever comes first, which is generally the wrong view.

The fix, in order of preference.

Render one view. This is a rendering-strategy question, and pre-rendering all three is a performance optimisation whose measured benefit is usually smaller than assumed. One <main>, one <h1>, no duplicate IDs, no hidden focus traps.

If they must all be in the DOM, keep one <main> and swap its contents; the inactive views become plain <div> elements with hidden:

<main id="main" tabindex="-1">
  <div data-view="invoices">…</div>
  <div data-view="customers" hidden>…</div>
</main>

hidden — not a CSS class — because it removes the subtree from rendering, from the accessibility tree and from the tab order in one attribute, with no possibility of a stylesheet change resurrecting it.

And the thing this application is almost certainly also missing: on a view change, move focus to the new view's heading and update document.title (§14.6, §3.2). A real navigation does both; a client-side one does neither, so a screen reader user hears nothing at all when the view changes and their focus stays where it was — possibly on an element that no longer exists.

SECTION 7

Links, URLs and Navigation

The link is the web's defining invention. Everything else in HTML has a counterpart in some earlier document format. What turned a collection of documents into a web is that any document can point at any other, across machines and organisations, without asking permission or coordinating with anyone.

Mechanically, it is also one of the simplest elements: one tag, and one attribute that matters. So most of this section is not about syntax. It is about the three things that go wrong:

  • links that are not really links;
  • links whose text says nothing;
  • target="_blank", which has more consequences than any two-word attribute should.

7.1 What a Link Is

An <a> element with an href attribute is a hyperlink: it takes you somewhere. Without href it is not a link at all, and the accessibility tree leaves no doubt about it:

<a href="/about">About us</a><a>No href</a><a href="/docs" download>Handbook</a><a href="#top">Back to top</a>

AX TREE
link "About us"
text "No href"
link "Handbook"
link "Back to top"

Three link nodes and one bare text node. The second <a> has no href, so it is not a link, not focusable, has no role, and does nothing on Enter. It is a <span> that happens to be spelled <a>. This is one of the most common accidental defects in generated markup: a template's href that comes out empty produces exactly this, and the styling still makes it look like a link.

Notice what the third and fourth show too: download and a fragment-only href are both still links. The specification calls the no-href case a "placeholder link", and the only reason it exists at all is to hold a spot in a navigation for a page that does not exist yet.

A link is interactive content and phrasing content (§2.6, §2.7), and it has the transparent content model (§2.8). So it may wrap a heading and three paragraphs, and it may not contain a <button> or another link.

So the href attribute is the whole difference between a link and a decorated span. Everything else in this section (resolution, targets, rel, download) modifies the href attribute, and none of it applies to an <a> that does not have one.

7.2 Links and Buttons

This is the most consequential choice in this section, and it has a one-line rule.

A link goes
It takes you somewhere. It has a URL, it can be bookmarked, copied, opened in a new tab, and put in history.
A button does
It performs an action on this page. Submits, opens a dialog, toggles, deletes, adds to basket.

The two are not interchangeable, and the differences are concrete, not a matter of style:

<a href="/a">Read more</a><button type="button">Read more</button>

AX TREE
link "Read more"
button "Read more"

They have different roles, and the role is what a screen reader announces and what a user's shortcuts navigate by. Most screen readers can list all the links, or jump between buttons, and a control in the wrong list is a control the user cannot find. Beyond that:

  • Keys differ. A link activates on Enter only; a button activates on Enter and Space. A <div> with a click handler responds to neither, and a link styled as a button ignores Space, which is the key a user who thinks it is a button will press.
  • The context menu differs. Right-clicking a link offers "open in new tab", "copy link address" and "open in new window". None of that means anything for an action, and all of it is expected for a destination.
  • Middle-click and ctrl-click differ. A link opens in a background tab; a button does not, and should not.
  • Only a link has a URL. If the thing can be bookmarked or shared, it must be a link.

Two consequences follow, and both are common mistakes.

A <div> or <span> with a click handler is neither. It has no role, cannot take focus, does not respond to the keyboard, and does not appear in any of the user's navigation lists. Making it work means adding tabindex="0", role="button", an Enter handler and a Space handler: four things to rebuild a <button>, and §13.9's first rule of ARIA says not to.

<a href="#" onclick="..."> is a link pretending to be a button. It announces as a link, offers "open in new tab" (which does nothing useful), and if the JavaScript fails, it jumps to the top of the page. Use a <button type="button">.

The test, when it is genuinely unclear: would opening this in a new tab make sense? If yes, it is a link. If the answer is "that would be meaningless", it is a button.

The one case for role="button" is a control you cannot turn into a real <button>: a legacy widget, or an element a framework controls. Then role="button" must come with tabindex="0" and with Enter and Space handlers, because role="button" changes what the element is announced as and nothing about what it does.

7.3 href and URL Resolution

href holds a URL, and the browser resolves it against the document's base URL. That is the document's own URL unless a <base> says otherwise (§3.4).

There are two views of that URL, and they differ:

getAttribute('href')
The string exactly as written in the markup.
element.href
The resolved, absolute URL.

That is §2.3's difference between attribute and property in its most useful form. An <a href="about"> on a page at https://example.com/products/skillet reports "about" from the attribute and "https://example.com/products/about" from the property. A script that compares getAttribute('href') with a full URL will never find a match.

The <a> element also exposes each part of the resolved URL as a property (protocol, host, hostname, port, pathname, search, hash and origin), which makes it the simplest URL parser available without creating a URL object.

7.4 Absolute, Relative and Root-Relative

Three forms, and choosing between them is a real decision.

Absolute
https://example.com/about. Scheme and host included. Resolves to itself, wherever it appears.
Root-relative
/about. Keeps the current origin, replaces the whole path. Independent of where the linking page lives.
Relative
about or ../about. Resolved against the current directory, so its meaning changes with the page it is on.

A relative url is resolved by taking everything up to the last / of the current path and adding the link's text after it. On /products/skillet the directory is /products/, so about becomes /products/about, and ../about becomes /about.

That dependence on the directory is the trap, and it takes a specific form: a trailing slash changes the meaning of every relative link on the page. On /products/skillet a link to reviews goes to /products/reviews; on /products/skillet/ the same markup goes to /products/skillet/reviews. Many routers treat those two URLs as the same page, so a site can work perfectly until someone links to it with a trailing slash.

Use root-relative URLs for links within your own site. They do not depend on the current path, they survive a page being moved, and they are shorter than absolute ones. Use absolute URLs when the markup will be read outside its document: a rel="canonical" (§3.12), an Open Graph image (§3.13), an email, an RSS feed, a JSON-LD block. Use relative URLs for things that really do live side by side, and keep the trailing-slash rule in mind when you do.

A protocol-relative URL (//example.com/x, which takes the page's scheme) was once the way to serve assets over both HTTP and HTTPS. It is obsolete: everything is HTTPS now, and the form really does break when a page is opened from a local file. Write https://.

7.5 Fragment Identifiers

A fragment identifier is the part of a URL after #. It is never sent to the server. The browser handles it locally, after the document loads, by finding the element whose id matches and scrolling it into view.

<a href="#pricing">Jump to pricing</a>
<a href="/faq#refunds">Refunds policy</a>
<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

Four behaviours are worth knowing precisely.

The match is against id, and, historically, against an <a name="...">. Only id matters now.

Two fragments are special. #top and the empty fragment # both scroll to the top of the document when no element has that id. That is why href="#" is such a common placeholder, and also why it is a bad one: it is a real navigation that adds a history entry and moves the reader to the top of the page.

A fragment navigation moves focus, or should. The browser sets the "sequential focus navigation starting point" to the target, so the next Tab continues from there, which is what makes a skip link work (§6.10). If the target cannot normally take focus, some browsers do this reliably and some do not; adding tabindex="-1" to the target makes it certain (§14.1).

:target matches the element the fragment points at, which is how a CSS-only tab or accordion is built. It is also why an element with an id can pick up styling from a URL the author never expected.

Two smaller forms exist. A text fragment (#:~:text=cast%20iron) asks the browser to find and highlight that text instead of an element, and it is what a browser generates for "copy link to highlight". And an <a href> with only a query, ?page=2, keeps the current path and replaces the query, which makes it a relative URL like any other.

The focus behaviour has a name worth knowing: the browser sets the sequential focus navigation starting point to the fragment's target, so the next Tab continues from there instead of from the top. That is the whole mechanism behind a skip link (§6.10), and sequential focus navigation is the same idea §14.1 uses to separate "focusable" from "reachable by Tab".

7.6 target and Named Browsing Contexts

target says where the linked document should open. It names a browsing context: a tab, a window, or a frame (§9.11).

_self
The current context. The default; you never need to write it.
_blank
A new tab or window, every time. See §7.7.
_parent
The containing frame's parent. Same as _self when there is no frame.
_top
The outermost context, breaking out of every frame.
a name
A named frame or window. Reuses it if it exists, creates it if not.

The named form is the one people forget exists, and it is genuinely useful: several links with target="preview" all load into the same <iframe name="preview"> instead of opening six tabs.

target also appears on <form> (§12.1) and, as formtarget, on the submit button. Its most important interaction is with sandbox: a sandboxed frame cannot navigate the top-level page without allow-top-navigation (§9.12), and that is what stops an advertisement from replacing the page around it.

target has a per-button override on forms, just as formmethod and formaction override method and action (§12.5): formtarget on a submit button sends that one submission somewhere else. formtarget is how a "preview" button opens the result of the filled-in form in a new tab while the ordinary submit button stays put.

7.7 The Cost of target="_blank"

Opening in a new tab has a security history worth knowing, because the advice about it changed, and most of what is written online is now out of date.

The historical problem is reverse tabnabbing. When a page opened another with target="_blank", the new document received a window.opener reference to the page that opened it, and could use it to send that page somewhere else.
