So a link to a third-party site could get the original tab quietly replaced with a convincing fake login page. The user returns to it and trusts it, because they opened it themselves. rel="noopener" was the fix.

Here is what current browsers actually do. Three links, opened from a real page served over HTTP, with the new document reporting what it received:

<a href="/child" target="_blank">plain target=_blank</a>
<a href="/child" target="_blank" rel="noopener">with rel=noopener</a>
<a href="/child" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">with rel=noreferrer</a>

plain target=_blank      ->  window.opener is null | document.referrer is http://127.0.0.1:38797/
with rel=noopener        ->  window.opener is null | document.referrer is http://127.0.0.1:38797/
with rel=noreferrer      ->  window.opener is null | document.referrer is (empty)

window.opener is already null without any rel at all. Current browsers apply noopener automatically to every target="_blank", and that is now the specified behaviour. So rel="noopener" on a _blank link is not the live defence it is usually presented as. It is a compatibility measure for browsers too old to do this automatically, and it is harmless to keep.

rel="noreferrer" still does something distinct, and the measurement shows it: it suppresses the Referer header, so the destination is not told which page the user came from. It also implies noopener. Use it when the destination has no business knowing where the link was. Be aware that it also removes the referrer from that site's analytics, which is sometimes exactly the point and sometimes a favour you did not mean to withhold.

The bigger cost of target="_blank" is not security; it is that it takes a decision away from the user. The back button no longer takes them anywhere. A screen reader user may not notice that they are in a new tab. On mobile, the tabs pile up out of sight. The user already has ctrl-click, middle-click and a context menu for opening in a new tab, and they know when they want it.

So the defensible uses are narrow: a link opened from inside a form the user is halfway through filling in, a document that opens in a viewer, a help page meant to sit beside a task. In those cases say so in the link text or with an icon plus a visually-hidden "(opens in a new tab)", because an unannounced change of context is a WCAG 3.2.5 concern and, more simply, a surprise.

To restate the conclusion: reverse tabnabbing was the reason rel="noopener" became standard advice, and current browsers now close reverse tabnabbing themselves for target="_blank". rel="noreferrer" is the attribute that still changes something measurable, and rel="noreferrer" is a product decision about what the destination should be told, not a security default.

7.8 download

The download attribute asks the browser to save the resource instead of navigating to it, and optionally to give the saved file a name:

<a href="/reports/2025.pdf" download>Annual report (PDF, 2.1 MB)</a>
<a href="/exports/tmp-4f2a.csv" download="orders-2025.csv">Download orders as CSV</a>

Three rules govern it.

It is same-origin only. A download on a URL from another origin is ignored, and the browser navigates instead. This is deliberate: without that restriction, any site could make any other site's content be saved under a name of the attacker's choosing.

The filename is a suggestion. The browser cleans it up, and a Content-Disposition header from the server wins over the attribute.

It works on blob: and data: URLs, which is how an export made entirely in the browser works: generate the data, call URL.createObjectURL(blob), set download to the filename, and click the link. That is the standard pattern for "download this table as CSV" with no server involved.

Two courtesies that cost a few characters. Say the format and the size in the link text, as in "Annual report (PDF, 2.1 MB)", because a reader on a metered connection needs to know before tapping. And do not use download for something the browser could display, such as an image or a PDF the user may only want to look at. Navigating there and letting them save it if they want leaves the choice with them.

One last property of the download attribute is worth stating, because it surprises people: the download attribute does not change what is fetched, only what the browser does with the response. The request is an ordinary GET, so the resource must be readable at that URL without a login if you expect a link preview of it to work.

7.9 rel on a Link

rel describes the relationship between the current document and the link's destination. It takes a space-separated list of link types, and only some of them mean anything on <a> as opposed to <link> (§3.9).

noopener
Withhold window.opener. Now implicit for target="_blank" (§7.7).
noreferrer
Send no Referer. Implies noopener.
nofollow
"I do not vouch for this destination." For user-submitted links and anything untrusted.
sponsored, ugc
The two specific reasons: a paid placement, and user-generated content. More informative than a bare nofollow.
next, prev
Position in a sequence — pagination, a multi-part article.
external
Leaves the site. Purely informational; commonly used as a CSS hook for an outbound icon.
author, license, help, alternate, bookmark, tag
Semantic relationships read by feed readers, some crawlers and content tools.

rel="nofollow" is the one with a real practical purpose: it is how a site with comments or user profiles avoids becoming a link farm (a page used to boost other sites in search results). Anywhere a stranger can put a URL on your page, the markup should carry rel="nofollow ugc", and usually target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" as well.

hreflang on an <a> names the language of the destination (§3.12), and type gives its expected MIME type (its file type). Both are hints only; neither changes what the browser fetches.

Of these, rel="nofollow" is the one with a practical consequence rather than an informational one. Put rel="nofollow ugc" on every link a stranger can create, and treat any place a user can type a URL as needing it: rel="nofollow" is what stops a comment field from becoming a link farm.

7.10 Link Text

A link's accessible name is, by default, all of its text content, and the measurement shows it adding up across elements, including an image's alt:

<a href="/a"><span>Read </span><img src="i.png" alt="the 2025 annual report"></a>

AX TREE
link "Read the 2025 annual report"
  text "Read"
  image "the 2025 annual report"

The name is built from everything inside the link. That has two consequences, and between them they decide almost everything about writing links.

A link wrapping a card is announced as the entire card. §2.8 established that <a> is transparent and may legally wrap a heading, an image, a date and two paragraphs. The resulting link is named with all of it, which makes it unusable in a list of links. The pattern that keeps a large click area and a short name is a link around the heading only, stretched over the card with CSS.

"Click here" and "Read more" are meaningless out of context, and out of context is exactly how many people meet them. Screen readers offer a list of every link on the page, and a page of "Read more" gives twelve identical entries. So does a search engine's view, and so does a reader skimming.

The rule is: the link text should say where it goes, on its own.

  • ❌ To read our annual report, <a href="/r">click here</a>.
  • ✅ Read our <a href="/r">2025 annual report</a>.

Five more rules that cover the rest:

  • Do not put the URL in the text, unless the URL itself is the information. A screen reader reads it out character by character.
  • Do not use the same text for two destinations on one page. If two links must both say "Edit", tell them apart (aria-label="Edit invoice 4021") or include the subject in the text.
  • Do not make a whole sentence a link. The name becomes a paragraph, and the click area becomes a wall.
  • An icon-only link needs a name. Use either visually-hidden text inside it or an aria-label on it; title alone is not enough (§2.10).
  • Say when a link is not a page. "(PDF, 2.1 MB)", "(opens in a new tab)": the information a user needs before deciding to press it.

There is one deliberate exception to the "no duplicate text" rule. A list of articles where each has a "Read more" is acceptable if each link carries an aria-label naming its article. But a link around the article's own heading is better, because it needs no ARIA at all and everyone can see what it says.

7.11 mailto, tel and Other Schemes

href takes any URL, not only http and https.

<a href="mailto:hello@example.com">hello@example.com</a>
<a href="mailto:support@example.com?subject=Order%204021&amp;body=My%20order%20has%20not%20arrived">Email about this order</a>
<a href="tel:+441142960000">+44 114 296 0000</a>
<a href="sms:+441142960000">Text us</a>

mailto: opens the user's mail client. It accepts subject, body, cc and bcc as query parameters, all percent-encoded (special characters written as % codes). Remember &amp; between them, since this is an attribute value (§2.13). Several addresses can be separated by commas.

tel: dials a phone number. Write the number in international format, with the + and no spaces or punctuation, in the href, and format it readably in the link text; the two do not have to match. On a desktop it opens whatever program handles calls; on a phone it is the single most useful link a business page has.

Two limitations to be honest about. mailto: depends on the user having a mail program set up, and many people use webmail without one, so for them the link does nothing visible. So always show the address as text as well, so it can be copied. And a long mailto: body is fragile: mail programs cut it short, and line breaks (%0D%0A) are handled inconsistently.

Other schemes you will meet: sms:, geo:, data: (§8.10's inline resources), blob: (§7.8) and a site's own registered scheme via navigator.registerProtocolHandler. A scheme the browser does not recognise simply does nothing, so there is no harm in offering one alongside an ordinary link.

7.12 aria-current

In a navigation, one link is usually the page you are on. aria-current="page" says so:

<nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a><a href="/shop">Shop</a></nav>

AX TREE
navigation "Main"
  link "Home"
  link "Shop"

The tree does not show it, and that is a limitation of the measuring tool rather than of the markup. Chrome's Accessibility.getFullAXTree does not expose aria-current as a property in the build these measurements were made with, the same gap §10.11 records for aria-sort. The attribute does reach real assistive technology through the operating system's accessibility interfaces, where a screen reader announces the link as "Home, current page". This is one of the two claims in this course that the tooling cannot verify for you.

aria-current is an enumerated attribute with six values, and choosing the right one matters:

page
The current page in a set of pages. The common case.
step
The current step in a process.
location
The current position in a breadcrumb or a flow chart.
date, time
Today in a calendar; now in a timeline.
true
Current, unspecified how. The fallback when none of the above fits.

aria-current="false" is the same as leaving it out. And, as with every enumerated attribute, an unrecognised value falls back to a default (§2.5), which here is true, so a typo makes every link "current".

Note what this replaces. The usual approach is a CSS class on the active link, which tells only sighted users about the state. aria-current is the half machines can read. It is also a perfectly good CSS selector, a[aria-current="page"], so using it lets you drop the class entirely.

7.13 Navigation

Links become navigation when they are grouped, and the grouping is done in the markup, not the styling.

<nav aria-label="Main">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop">Shop</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop">Shop</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop/skillet" aria-current="page">Cast iron skillet</a></li>
  </ol>
</nav>

<nav> marks a block of major navigation links and produces a navigation landmark (§6.6, §13.6), which lets a user jump straight to it or straight past it. It is for major groups (the site's main navigation, a breadcrumb, a table of contents, pagination), not for every set of links on the page. A footer with forty links is one <nav>; the three links in a paragraph are not navigation at all.

A page with more than one <nav> must label them, with aria-label or aria-labelledby. Two unlabelled navigation landmarks cannot be told apart in a landmark list. Do not include the word "navigation" in the label: the role already says it, and the user hears "Main navigation navigation".

Navigation is a list, and marking it up as one is not ceremony. It tells a screen reader user how many items there are before they start, which is exactly what they need to decide whether to go through it or skip it. Use an <ol> for a breadcrumb, because the order means something, and a <ul> for a menu, because it does not.

Pagination is navigation too, with rel="prev" and rel="next" on the right links (§7.9) and aria-current="page" on the current page number.

Two things belong here but are covered elsewhere, because they are focus problems rather than link problems: the skip link that lets a keyboard user jump past the navigation to the content (§6.10), and moving focus after a client-side route change, without which a single-page application's navigation is silent to a screen reader user (§14.6).

Pagination deserves the rel types as well as the landmark: rel="next" on the link to the following page and rel="prev" on the previous one. Some crawlers and readers treat rel="next" as a hint about the sequence, and it costs nothing to state.

Exercises

1. For each, say whether it should be a link or a button, and why.

1. "Add to basket" on a product page.
2. "Next page" in a paginated list of results.
3. "Show more" that expands a truncated paragraph in place.
4. "Log out".
5. "Download invoice (PDF)".
6. "Open filters" that shows a modal dialog.
Solution

The test throughout is §7.2's: does it go somewhere, or does it do something? Equivalently — would "open in a new tab" make sense?

1. Button. It performs an action on the current page. There is no URL for "the state after adding a skillet to a basket", and opening it in a new tab is meaningless. <button type="submit"> inside a form that posts the item.

2. Link. It goes to /results?page=2. That URL is bookmarkable, shareable, in history, and openable in a new tab — which people genuinely do with pagination. A button here would break the back button and remove ctrl-click. Add rel="next" (§7.9).

3. Button. The content is already on the page and the control changes its visibility. Prefer <details>/<summary> (§14.7), which needs no JavaScript and gets the keyboard behaviour and the expanded state for free; otherwise a <button aria-expanded="false">.

4. Button, in a form that POSTs. This is the one people get wrong. Logging out changes server state, so it must not be a GET — a link is a GET, and any prefetcher, link scanner, antivirus proxy or "open all in tabs" will eventually follow it and log the user out. <form method="post" action="/logout"><button>Log out</button></form>.

5. Link, with download. It has a URL and it is a resource. <a href="/invoices/4021.pdf" download>Download invoice 4021 (PDF, 240 KB)</a> — and the size in the text, per §7.8, because someone on a metered connection needs it before tapping.

6. Button. A dialog is a state of this page, not a destination. <button type="button">Open filters</button> calling showModal() (§14.8). It becomes a link only if the filters have their own URL — in which case it is a navigation and the dialog is the wrong pattern.

The pattern across the six: anything with a URL that a user might reasonably want to bookmark, share or open in a new tab is a link. Anything that changes state — here, or on the server — is a button. And a state change on the server additionally implies a form and a POST, which is where §12.3's method semantics come in.

2. Someone reviews a pull request and asks for rel="noopener noreferrer" on every target="_blank" link, citing a security article. What is your response?

Solution

The concern was real and has been fixed in the platform. The measurement in §7.7, taken from a current Chromium against a real HTTP origin, shows a plain target="_blank" link giving the opened document window.opener === null — with no rel at all. Current browsers apply noopener implicitly to every target="_blank", and that is now the specified behaviour rather than a vendor choice.

So rel="noopener" is not the live defence the article describes. It is harmless and mildly useful as a compatibility measure for a browser old enough to predate the implicit behaviour, and there is no reason to remove it from code that has it. It is also not worth a review comment demanding it be added.

rel="noreferrer" is a different matter, and the same measurement separates them: it is the only one of the three that suppressed the Referer header. That is a real, current effect and a product decision, not a security default. Suppressing the referrer is right for a link to a competitor, to an unrelated third party, or from a page whose URL is itself sensitive — a URL containing an order number or a token tells the destination something it should not know. It is wrong for a link to a partner who uses referrers to attribute traffic, where withholding it removes credit you meant to give.

The bigger point to make in the review is that the article's premise — that target="_blank" is fine as long as you add a rel — is the part that has not aged well. §7.7: opening a new tab takes a decision away from the user. The back button no longer returns them anywhere, the tab stack fills up invisibly on mobile, and a screen reader user may not notice the context changed at all. The user already has ctrl-click, middle-click and a context menu.

So the review comment I would make instead is: why is this target="_blank" at all? If there is a good reason — the user is part-way through a form, or the destination is a reference to consult alongside a task — keep it and announce it, with an icon plus visually-hidden "(opens in a new tab)", because an unannounced context change is a WCAG 3.2.5 concern. If there is no reason, remove the attribute and the question of rel disappears with it.

3. A page has twelve article cards, each ending in "Read more". Explain the problem precisely and give two fixes with their trade-offs.

Solution

The problem is that a link's accessible name is its text content (§7.10), so the page has twelve links all named "Read more". That matters because of how links get used:

  • Screen readers offer a list of every link on the page, for exactly the same reason a sighted reader skims. Twelve identical entries make that list useless, and the user has to walk the page linearly instead — which is the thing the feature exists to avoid.
  • The same applies to a sighted reader skimming, and to a search engine, which uses link text as a signal about the destination.
  • Reading it in context does not rescue it. The link list, the tab sequence and a search engine's index all see the link without the heading above it.

Fix 1 — make the heading the link. The best answer, and it removes rather than adds:

<article>
  <h3><a href="/articles/cast-iron">How to season a cast iron pan</a></h3>
  <p>Three coats of oil and an hour in the oven…</p>
</article>

Every link is now uniquely and descriptively named, with no ARIA at all. The card is still fully clickable by stretching the link's box over it with CSS (§2.8's exercise), which keeps the large touch target. The trade-off is a design change: the "Read more" affordance disappears, and if the design team wants that visual cue back it becomes a non-interactive span inside the link or a decorative arrow.

Fix 2 — keep "Read more" and give each an accessible name:

<a href="/articles/cast-iron" aria-label="Read more: How to season a cast iron pan">Read more</a>

No design change, and the link list becomes usable. Two costs. The visible text and the accessible name now differ, which WCAG 2.5.3 constrains — the visible text must be contained in the accessible name, and "Read more: How to season…" satisfies that only because "Read more" is at the front, so the order is not arbitrary. And it is a duplicated string that has to be kept in step with the heading; if the heading is edited and the aria-label is not, the two disagree silently.

A third option to reject: title="How to season a cast iron pan" on the link. §2.10 — title is last in the name precedence chain (§13.3), is not announced by all screen readers, is invisible on touch devices, and cannot be reached by keyboard. It looks like a fix and is not one.

Recommendation: fix 1. It is less markup, needs no ARIA, cannot drift out of step, and improves the page for everybody rather than only for the users of one technology.

4. Write a breadcrumb and a primary navigation for a product page, and justify every element and attribute.

Solution 
<nav aria-label="Main">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop" aria-current="page">Shop</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop">Shop</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop/cookware">Cookware</a></li>
    <li><a href="/shop/cookware/skillet" aria-current="page">Cast iron skillet, 26cm</a></li>
  </ol>
</nav>

Two <nav> elements, because both are major navigation blocks and each becomes a navigation landmark (§13.6) a user can jump to or skip.

Both are labelled, and this is required rather than optional: two unlabelled navigation landmarks are indistinguishable in a landmark list. The labels are "Main" and "Breadcrumb" and not "Main navigation" — the role already says "navigation", so the longer label is announced as "Main navigation navigation".

<ul> for the menu, <ol> for the breadcrumb. The distinction is meaning, not appearance (§5.2): a breadcrumb's order is the hierarchy, and reordering it would make it wrong; the menu's order is a design choice. Both are lists so that a screen reader announces "list, 3 items" before the user commits to walking it — which is the information they need to decide whether to.

aria-current="page" on the current item in each (§7.12). This is the machine-readable half of the "you are here" state that a CSS class conveys visually. It is also a perfectly good CSS selector, a[aria-current="page"], so it replaces the class rather than adding to it. Note the breadcrumb's last item is still a link — keeping it a link means it can be copied and shared, and aria-current supplies the state that would otherwise be conveyed by disabling it.

Root-relative URLs throughout (§7.4), so nothing depends on the current path and a page can be moved without rewriting its navigation.

Separators are CSS, not markup. The > between breadcrumb items belongs in li + li::before, because a > in the markup is read aloud as "greater than" by some screen readers and is not content.

What is deliberately absent: any role="navigation", since <nav> already has it (§13.9's second rule); any role="list", since <ul> has it; and the word "You are here", since aria-current conveys it. Each would be reimplementing something the element already provides.

5. A single-page application replaces its <a href="/products/skillet"> links with <div onclick="router.go('/products/skillet')"> for performance. List everything this loses.

Solution

The performance premise is false to begin with — a click handler on an <a> that calls preventDefault() and routes is exactly as fast, and every router does it that way. What the change costs is close to everything a link is:

Role and discoverability. §7.1 measured that an element with no href is not a link and produces no link node. A <div> produces nothing at all. It is absent from the screen reader's link list, absent from the tab sequence, and has no role to announce — so it is not merely worse, it is invisible to an entire navigation mechanism.

Keyboard operation. Not focusable, so it cannot be reached by Tab; and with no key handlers, Enter does nothing. Restoring that means tabindex="0", role="link" and an Enter handler — three things reimplementing an element that had them.

The URL, and everything downstream of it. No middle-click to open in a background tab, no ctrl-click, no context menu, no "copy link address", no drag to the bookmarks bar, and nothing shown in the status bar on hover — so the user cannot see where it goes before committing.

Crawling and sharing. A search engine follows href attributes. A <div onclick> is not a link to any crawler, which means the product page is unreachable by search and by any tool that walks the site.

Progressive enhancement (§12.14). With href, a routing failure — a JavaScript error, a slow chunk, a blocked bundle — degrades to a full page navigation that works. With onclick, it degrades to nothing happening.

The download, rel, target, hreflang and type attributes, and :link/:visited styling, all of which are properties of the element rather than of the handler.

The fix is the ordinary pattern, and it keeps every one of the above:

<a href="/products/skillet">Cast iron skillet, 26cm</a>

with a delegated click handler that calls preventDefault() and routes — while deliberately not intercepting a click with a modifier key or a middle-click, so ctrl-click still opens a new tab.

There is one thing the router must still do that the browser was doing for free, and it is easy to miss: on a route change, move focus and update the title (§14.6, §3.2). A real navigation announces the new page and resets the focus position; a client-side one does neither unless you make it.

SECTION 8

Images and Responsive Images

An image is the most common piece of embedded content on the web, and the one where each attribute has the most consequences. Four attributes, alt, width, height and loading, decide whether the page can be used without sight, whether it jumps around while loading, and how fast it appears. None of them is optional in practice, and three of them are routinely left out.

This section is in two halves:

  • The first is about what an image means: the node it produces in the accessibility tree, and the surprisingly precise craft of writing the text that stands in for it.
  • The second is about which bytes to send. That is where srcset, sizes and <picture> live. These three features look complicated because they solve two different problems with one syntax, and they become simple as soon as you separate the two problems.

8.1 The img Element

<img src="skillet.jpg" alt="A cast iron skillet on a hob" width="200" height="200">

<img> is a void element (§1.5). It is both phrasing content and embedded content (§2.6), and it is replaced (§9.1): its box is filled by the decoded image file, whose own dimensions the browser does not know until the file arrives.

The src attribute is a URL, resolved against the document's base URL (§3.4) exactly like an href (§7.3). A relative src on a page at /products/skillet resolves against that path, which is the usual reason an image works on one route and returns a 404 on another.

Everything else on the element falls into three groups, and the rest of this section covers those three groups: what it means (alt), how big it is (width, height), and which bytes to fetch (srcset, sizes, loading, decoding, fetchpriority).

There are also ismap and usemap, which belong to image maps (§8.13), and crossorigin and referrerpolicy, which behave as they do on <video> (§9.2) and <iframe> (§9.11).

The src attribute is also the one attribute an <img> cannot do without. An <img> with no src attribute is a broken image box with an accessible name and nothing behind it, a state that template bugs produce regularly and that nothing reports.

8.2 What an Image Becomes in the Accessibility Tree

Four images, four ways of handling alt (the third is the one to avoid), and three nodes:

<img src="skillet.jpg" alt="A cast iron skillet on a hob" width="200" height="200"><img src="divider.png" alt="" width="200" height="8"><img src="chart.png" width="200" height="100"><img src="logo.svg" alt="Acme" title="Acme Corporation" width="80" height="30">

AX TREE
image "A cast iron skillet on a hob"
image
image "Acme"

Everything about alt is in that measurement.

alt="text" names the image. The node is an image, and the text is its accessible name: what a screen reader announces where a sighted reader sees the picture.

alt="" removes the image from the tree entirely. There is no second node. This is not a nameless image; it is no image, and that is exactly what an empty alt is for. It tells assistive technology that this picture carries no information the reader needs. The second image is simply absent.

No alt at all leaves a nameless image node, and this is the failure case. The image is announced, so the user knows something is there, but there is nothing to say about it. Most screen readers fall back to reading the filename, so the user hears "chart dot p n g, image". That is noise if the image is decorative and a loss if it is not, and the browser cannot tell which, because the author did not say.

alt beats title. The fourth image has both and is named "Acme". §13.3 has the full order of priority; the short version is that title comes last, behind aria-labelledby, aria-label and alt.

So there are three states, not two: described, deliberately silent, and unspecified. The first two are decisions. The third is an omission, and it is the one thing about images a checker can catch automatically every time, which is why check_html.py reports it and why every accessibility linter leads with it.

The middle case has a name worth using in code review: an empty alt, alt="", is a decision, and the measurement above is why it matters that it is written on purpose. An empty alt removes the image from the tree; a missing alt leaves a nameless node. They look almost identical in the markup and produce opposite results.

8.3 Writing alt Text

The rule is not "describe the image". It is write what the image is there to do, so that replacing the image with your text leaves the page saying the same thing. That one change of viewpoint answers almost every case.

Informative
Carries information not in the surrounding text. Say what that information is. alt="A cast iron skillet on a gas hob".
Decorative
Adds atmosphere, separates sections, illustrates text that already says it. alt="", and the image leaves the tree.
Functional
Inside a link or a button. The alt is the control's name, so it describes the action, not the picture: alt="Search", not alt="Magnifying glass".
Text in an image
The alt is the text, verbatim. A logo's alt is the company name.
Complex
A chart, a diagram, a map. A short alt naming it, and the detail in real text nearby (§8.12).

The functional case is the one that changes most people's habits, and it can be measured:

<a href="/products/skillet"><img src="skillet.jpg" alt="" width="100" height="100"><span>Cast iron skillet</span></a><a href="/products/pan"><img src="pan.jpg" alt="Frying pan" width="100" height="100"></a>

AX TREE
link "Cast iron skillet"
link "Frying pan"
  image "Frying pan"

Two links. In the first, the image has alt="" because the product name is right there in the <span>, so the link is named by its text and there is no image node at all. In the second, the image is the only content, so its alt becomes the link's accessible name. It must therefore describe where the link goes, not what the photograph shows.

Get that backwards and you get the two classic failures: a card where the product name is announced twice, and a link announced as "photograph of a frying pan on a white background, link", which tells the user nothing about what pressing Enter does.

Six rules that cover the rest:

  • Do not start with "image of" or "photo of". The node is already announced as an image, so the words are pure repetition. The exception is when the medium is the point (alt="Oil painting of a harbour"), because then it is information.
  • Do not repeat the caption. If a <figcaption> (§8.12) already says it, the alt should say something else or be empty.
  • Length: a sentence. If it needs a paragraph, it is a complex image, and the paragraph belongs on the page where everyone can read it.
  • Punctuate it. A screen reader uses punctuation for pauses; an alt text with no punctuation is read as one long run.
  • No keyword stuffing. Search engines have penalised it for two decades, and it makes the page worse for the people the attribute exists for.
  • alt is not a tooltip. It is shown only when the image fails to load. The attribute for hover text is title, and §2.10 explains why you probably do not want that either.

The honest test, and the one to actually use: read the page aloud with your alt text in place of each image. If it still makes sense and says nothing twice, the alt text is right.

8.4 width, height and Intrinsic Size

An image has an intrinsic size: the pixel dimensions stored in the file. The browser learns it only after the start of the file arrives, which on a slow connection can be seconds after the text around it has already been laid out.

The width attribute and the height attribute tell it in advance:

<img src="harbour.jpg" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="1600" height="900">

Three things about these two attributes are commonly got wrong.

They are unitless numbers of CSS pixels, not lengths. width="50%" is invalid. Browsers still honour it as a percentage for old pages' sake (in Chromium, an image with width="50%" inside a 400-pixel container rendered 200 pixels wide), but a validator rejects it, and percentages belong in CSS.

They do not fix the display size. Any CSS width overrides them, and the almost universal img { max-width: 100%; height: auto } does exactly that. Sizing the image on screen is not their job.

Their real job is to declare the aspect ratio (the ratio of width to height). Modern browsers compute aspect-ratio: attr(width) / attr(height) from them in the default stylesheet. That is why the pair must match the file's real dimensions, not the size you intend to display it at: the numbers are used as a ratio, not as a size.

So always write the file's true dimensions, and let CSS decide how big it appears. The combination width="1600" height="900" with max-width: 100%; height: auto gives you an image that stretches with the layout and still reserves the right amount of space before it loads, which is the whole point of §8.5.

So the width attribute and the height attribute describe the file, not the layout. Write the file's real pixel dimensions into the width attribute and the height attribute, let CSS size the element, and the browser gets the aspect ratio it needs before a single byte of the image arrives.

8.5 Layout Shift

layout shift is what happens when content that has already been drawn moves because something above it changed size. The classic cause is an image with no dimensions. The browser lays out the text, reserves zero height for the image, draws the page, then the image arrives and everything below it jumps down.

For a reader this is not cosmetic. It is the reason you tap the wrong link: the one you were aiming at moved a moment before your finger landed. It is measured as cumulative layout shift, one of the three core web vitals (Google's main measures of page experience), and Google's published threshold for "good" is a CLS of 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile of page loads. The other two are largest contentful paint, the moment the biggest visible element finishes rendering, which should be within 2.5 seconds, and Interaction to Next Paint, how quickly the page responds to input, which should be 200 milliseconds or less.

Images are at the centre of two of those three, which is why the attributes in this section matter for more than correctness.

Always set width and height
The browser reserves a box of the right shape immediately (§8.4). This is the single largest CLS win available and it costs two attributes.
Do the same for every replaced element
<video>, <iframe> and <canvas> all shift the same way, and an unstyled <iframe> defaults to 150 pixels tall (§9.11).
Reserve space for late content
Banners, advertisements and consent notices inserted above existing content shift everything. Give the container a minimum height before it fills.
Do not lazy-load the LCP image
§8.6. Deferring the fetch of the largest visible image directly delays largest contentful paint, which is the metric it defines.

The largest contentful paint element on a content page is nearly always an image: a hero image, a product photo, an article's lead picture. So the most valuable performance work on most pages is to find that one image, not lazy-load it, give it fetchpriority="high", and serve it in a modern format at a sensible size. Everything else in this section matters less than that.

cumulative layout shift is the metric, and it is one of the three core web vitals alongside Largest Contentful Paint and Interaction to Next Paint. Two things make cumulative layout shift unusual among performance metrics: it measures the page's whole lifetime rather than one moment, and it can almost always be fixed from the markup, which is why the core web vitals appear in an HTML course at all.

8.6 loading, decoding and fetchpriority

Three attributes are hints about when the browser should do the work.

<img src="hero.jpg" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high">
<img src="gallery-7.jpg" alt="The east pier" width="800" height="600" loading="lazy" decoding="async">

loading takes eager (the default) or lazy. loading="lazy" delays the fetch until the image comes close to the visible area, and it is the right default for anything below the fold (the part of the page you must scroll to see): a gallery, a long article's later illustrations, a list of avatars. It is built into the browser, with no library and no scroll listener.

The trap is at the top of the page. loading="lazy" on an image that is visible when the page loads makes things worse. The browser must first lay out the page to discover the image is in view, and only then start the request, which is always later than an eager fetch. On the hero image it delays largest contentful paint by exactly that amount. The rule is mechanical: lazy-load nothing that is visible without scrolling.

decoding takes sync, async or auto. It controls whether the browser may decode the image (turn the file into pixels) off the main thread and show it slightly later, instead of holding up everything else while it decodes. decoding="async" is a reasonable default for images that are not the LCP element. The effect is small, and occasionally noticeable on large images and slow devices.

fetchpriority takes high, low or auto. It reorders the queue of requests. high on the hero image tells the browser to fetch it ahead of the other images it found at the same time; low on decorative or below-the-fold images gets them out of the way. It is relative to other resources of the same type, not absolute, and using high too often makes it meaningless.

Put together, the hero image of a page should carry width, height, fetchpriority="high" and no loading attribute, and every image below the fold should carry width, height, loading="lazy" and decoding="async".

The decoding attribute is the least important of the three and the easiest to set: decoding="async" on everything that is not the LCP element. The decoding attribute only affects whether the page waits for the decode before showing things, so its effect is small, occasionally visible on a large image and a slow device, and never harmful.

8.7 srcset and Resolution Switching

Here is the first of the two problems responsive images solve. Resolution switching means offering the same picture at several sizes, so that a phone does not download a 1600-pixel-wide file to show it 375 pixels wide, and a high-density screen can get more pixels than it displays.

The srcset attribute lists the candidates and lets the browser choose. There are two ways to describe a candidate, and they are not interchangeable.

The simpler one is the pixel density descriptor:

<img src="logo.png" srcset="logo.png 1x, logo@2x.png 2x, logo@3x.png 3x"
     alt="Acme" width="120" height="40">

1x, 2x and 3x say how many image pixels there are per CSS pixel. The browser picks by the screen's device pixel ratio (a typical laptop is 1, most phones are 2 or 3). This form is exactly right for an image shown at a fixed size: a logo, an icon, an avatar. It assumes the CSS size is known and constant, so the only thing that varies is density.

The other is the width descriptor, the one you will use for content images:

<img src="harbour-800.jpg"
     srcset="harbour-400.jpg 400w, harbour-800.jpg 800w, harbour-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(min-width: 40em) 50vw, 100vw"
     alt="A harbour at dusk" width="1600" height="900">

DOM TREE
<img src="harbour-800.jpg" srcset="harbour-400.jpg 400w, harbour-800.jpg 800w, harbour-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="(min-width: 40em) 50vw, 100vw" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="1600" height="900">

400w means "this file is 400 pixels wide". It is a fact about the file, not a condition and not a breakpoint, and reading it as one is the most common misunderstanding of this syntax. It says nothing about when to use the file.

src stays, and it is still required. A browser that does not understand srcset uses it, and it is the candidate chosen when nothing else applies. Point it at a middle-sized file rather than the largest.

The choice is entirely the browser's, and it may use information you do not have: the device pixel ratio, the network conditions, whether the image is already cached, the user's data-saving setting. That is a feature: you supply the menu, and the browser knows the diner. It also means you cannot test "which one gets picked" by resizing a window, because browsers deliberately do not switch down to a smaller file once a larger one is cached.

The two descriptor styles answer different questions. A pixel density descriptor says "use this file on a screen of this density", which works only when the CSS size is fixed, so a pixel density descriptor suits a logo or an avatar. A width descriptor says "this file is this many pixels wide" and leaves the choice to the browser, so a width descriptor suits any image whose displayed size depends on the viewport.

The phrase responsive image covers both this mechanism and §8.9's, and the distinction inside it is the one to keep: a responsive image built with srcset is the browser choosing between interchangeable files, and one built with <picture> is you choosing between different pictures.

8.8 sizes and Why It Is Required

A width descriptor alone is not enough for the browser to choose. It knows each candidate's width in pixels, but it does not know how wide the image will be on this page. That depends on CSS it has not parsed yet, and images are fetched by the preload scanner (§1.10) before layout exists.

The sizes attribute closes that gap by telling it in advance:

sizes="(min-width: 40em) 50vw, 100vw"

Read it as a list of pairs, each a media condition and a length, checked left to right, where the first match wins and a bare length at the end is the default. This one says: on a viewport at least 40em wide, the image will take up half the viewport width; otherwise, the full width.

The browser then does the arithmetic. On a 1000-pixel viewport at density 2, the first condition matches, so the image will be 500 CSS pixels wide and needs about 1000 image pixels. harbour-1600.jpg is the smallest candidate that is big enough.

Three things to know about sizes.

It is a promise about your layout, and nothing verifies it. If the CSS actually makes the image 33% wide and sizes says 50vw, the browser reliably fetches a file that is too big. Keeping the two in step is a real maintenance cost of this feature, and the main argument for generating both from the same source.

sizes="auto" removes the problem for lazy-loaded images. On an <img> that also has loading="lazy", the browser can wait until layout is done and use the real width, because the fetch was delayed anyway. Where it applies, it is always better than a hand-written list. It does not apply to images loaded eagerly, which are exactly the ones fetched before layout.

sizes without srcset does nothing, and srcset with w descriptors without sizes defaults to 100vw, which fetches too much for every image that does not span the full width. The two go together.

So the sizes attribute is not optional decoration on a w-descriptor srcset. Without a sizes attribute the browser assumes 100vw and fetches too much for every image that is not full-width.

8.9 picture and Art Direction

The second problem is a different kind of problem. art direction is when the content of the image should change with the viewport: a wide landscape crop on a desktop, a tight square crop of the same subject on a phone, because the landscape version at 375 pixels is an unreadable smear.

srcset cannot express that, and should not: it hands the choice to the browser, and this is a choice only you can make. <picture> is the element for it.

<picture>
  <source media="(min-width: 40em)" srcset="wide.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="narrow.avif" type="image/avif">
  <img src="fallback.jpg" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="400" height="200">
</picture>

DOM TREE
<picture>
  #text "\n  "
  <source media="(min-width: 40em)" srcset="wide.avif" type="image/avif">
  #text "\n  "
  <source srcset="narrow.avif" type="image/avif">
  #text "\n  "
  <img src="fallback.jpg" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="400" height="200">
  #text "\n"

The mechanism is the same list of sources as <video> (§9.3): the browser takes the first <source> whose media matches and whose type it can decode, and stops. It does not look at the rest, and it does not reconsider.

The <img> is not a fallback in the <video> sense. It is required, and it is the element that actually renders. <picture> is a wrapper that chooses which URL the <img> uses. That has three consequences worth stating:

  • The alt goes on the <img>, and there is only one, because as far as the page is concerned there is only one image.
  • width and height go on the <img> too. If the art-directed crops have different aspect ratios, CSS has to handle it, because the attributes can only declare one ratio.
  • Every CSS selector targets the <img>, not the <picture>, which renders as a plain inline box.

The two features combine: a <source> may carry srcset with w descriptors and sizes, giving you art direction and resolution switching. Reach for <picture> only when you need media or type. For "the same picture at several sizes", srcset on the <img> is less markup and gives the same result.

8.10 SVG: Three Ways to Use It

SVG is a vector format (shapes described by geometry, not a grid of pixels), so it looks sharp at any resolution: no srcset, no 2x file, no blur on a high-density screen. There are three ways to put one on a page, and they differ in what you can do with it afterwards.

As an <img>, when it is a picture:

<img src="logo.svg" alt="Acme" width="120" height="40">

Cached like any image, cannot be styled by the page's CSS, and any script inside it does not run. That last point makes this the safe way to show an SVG you did not write.

Inline, when it must respond to the page:

<svg width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" role="img" aria-label="Download"><path d="M12 3v12m0 0l-4-4m4 4l4-4M4 20h16" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"></path></svg><svg width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9" fill="currentColor"></circle></svg>

AX TREE
image "Download"

Two SVGs, one node. The first has role="img" and an aria-label, so it is an image named "Download". The second has aria-hidden="true" and is gone, which is what you want for an icon next to a text label that already says the same thing (§13.8).

inline svg is the form to use for icons, because fill="currentColor" and stroke="currentColor" take on the CSS color of the surrounding text. One icon file is then correct in light mode, dark mode, on hover and inside a disabled button, with no variants. Nothing else in this section can do that.

Two attributes on an inline <svg> are not optional. viewBox sets up the coordinate system and is what makes the graphic scale; without it the SVG has a fixed size, and resizing it with CSS crops it instead of scaling it. And an inline <svg> needs either role="img" with a name, or aria-hidden="true"; with neither, it is an unnamed node whose role varies between browsers. focusable="false" is an old fix for Internet Explorer, which made SVGs focus stops; it is harmless and no longer needed.

As a sprite, with <use>, when many icons share one file:

<svg width="24" height="24" role="img" aria-label="Download"><use href="/icons.svg#download"></use></svg>

<use> refers to a shape by fragment identifier, either in the same document or in an external file. One request delivers the whole set of icons, and each instance is a few bytes of markup. The costs: CSS reaches inside a <use> only through inherited properties such as currentColor (which is usually all you need), and an external sprite file is subject to CORS.

Of the three, inline svg is the one to use by default for icons, because inline svg is the only form CSS can reach into: currentColor, hover states and a prefers-reduced-motion rule all work on it and on neither of the others.

8.11 Formats and the Fallback Chain

Four raster formats matter, and the choice is mostly mechanical.

JPEG
Photographs. Lossy, no transparency, decoded by everything ever built. The universal floor.
PNG
Lossless, with transparency. Right for screenshots and flat graphics, large for photographs.
WebP
Lossy or lossless, with transparency and animation. Roughly 25–35% smaller than JPEG at similar quality, and supported by every current browser.
AVIF
Smaller again — frequently half the size of a comparable JPEG — with wide colour and transparency. Supported by every current browser; slower to encode.

webp is the safe modern default and avif is the smaller one, so the standard chain offers AVIF, then WebP, then a JPEG or PNG as the floor:

<picture>
  <source srcset="harbour.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="harbour.webp" type="image/webp">
  <img src="harbour.jpg" alt="A harbour at dusk" width="1600" height="900">
</picture>

type is what makes this work: the browser skips a <source> whose MIME type it cannot decode, without fetching anything (§9.3). Order matters and is not negotiable. The first match wins, so the smallest format goes first and the format every browser can decode goes last, as the <img>.

Two notes. Serving one format is a legitimate choice for a small site; the chain saves bandwidth, it is not needed for correctness. And the same choice can be made on the server from the Accept header, which keeps the markup to a single <img>. That belongs to backend_and_api_design_mastery, and the trade-off is more complex markup against a more complex build and cache.

8.12 figure and figcaption

<figure> groups content with a caption that refers to it. <figcaption> is that caption, and it must be the figure's first or last child.

<figure>
  <img src="chart.png" alt="Revenue rose in every quarter, from 1.2M to 1.9M" width="200" height="100">
  <figcaption>Revenue by quarter, 2025. Source: annual report.</figcaption>
</figure>

AX TREE
figure
  image "Revenue rose in every quarter, from 1.2M to 1.9M"
  Figcaption
    text "Revenue by quarter, 2025. Source: annual report."

The measurement makes an important point. In this browser the figcaption did not become the figure's accessible name: the figure node is unnamed, and the caption is a child node, read in order. So the caption and the alt are both announced, one after the other, and they must not say the same thing.

That is how the work is divided, and it is the whole reason both exist:

  • The alt is what the image shows: the information a reader who cannot see it would otherwise lose. For a chart, that is the trend or the finding, not "a bar chart".
  • The figcaption is what a reader sees under the image: the title, the units, the source, the credit. Everyone reads it, sighted or not.

A caption reading "Figure 4" with alt="Figure 4" gives a screen reader user "Figure 4, image, Figure 4" and no data at all.

<figure> is not only for images. It takes any self-contained content the main text refers to: a code listing, a table, a quotation, a video, several images together. The defining property is that it could be moved to an appendix without breaking the sentence around it, and that is the test for whether to use it at all. An illustration the paragraph calls "the diagram below" fails that test; it is part of the flow.

For a truly complex image (a chart with a dozen series, a process diagram, a map), neither attribute is enough. The answer is a real text alternative on the page: a short alt naming the image, the caption naming it for everyone, and a <details> (§14.7) or an adjacent section containing the data table (§10) or the description. That is better for every reader, not only those who cannot see it.

8.13 Image Maps

An image map divides one image into clickable regions. It is the oldest interactive feature in HTML, and it survives for a narrow set of cases: a floor plan, a seating chart, an anatomical diagram, a geographic map.

<img src="offices.png" alt="Our offices in London and Berlin" usemap="#offices" width="600" height="400">
<map name="offices">
  <area shape="rect" coords="0,0,300,400" href="/offices/london" alt="London office">
  <area shape="circle" coords="450,200,90" href="/offices/berlin" alt="Berlin office">
</map>

usemap on the <img> points at a <map> by its name, with a # in front like a fragment identifier (§7.5), and it matches name, not id. Each <area> is a link with a shape.

shape takes rect (four numbers: left, top, right, bottom), circle (three: centre x, centre y, radius), poly (pairs of x,y coordinates) and default (the whole image). The coords are in the image's intrinsic pixels, and that is the feature's fatal flaw: they do not scale. On an image displayed at a size that changes with the screen, an image map's regions are in the wrong place at every size but one, and no attribute fixes it.

Two accessibility rules, both mandatory. Every <area> needs an alt: it is a link, and the alt is its accessible name (§7.10), so an area without one is a link with no name. And the image itself still needs its own alt describing the picture.

The modern alternative is usually better: an inline <svg> (§8.10) with an <a> around each shape. The coordinates scale because the SVG scales, the regions can be styled and given hover and focus states, and each link is an ordinary link. Reach for <map> when the underlying image is a photograph or a pixel-based diagram shown at a fixed size; reach for SVG otherwise.

8.14 canvas

<canvas> is a bitmap that JavaScript draws into. It is embedded content with no content of its own: the element is an empty rectangle, and everything in it is the result of drawing commands.

<canvas id="sparkline" width="200" height="60">
  <p>Signups rose from 12 to 48 over the last 30 days.</p>
</canvas>

width and height here are different from every other element in this section. They set the bitmap's dimensions, in device-independent pixels, and CSS sizing scales that bitmap instead of changing it. Setting only a CSS width on a canvas produces a stretched, blurry drawing, the classic canvas bug. For a sharp result on a high-density screen, set the attributes to the CSS size multiplied by devicePixelRatio, and scale the drawing context to match.

Drawing goes through a context obtained from getContext:

<canvas id="sparkline" width="200" height="60"
        role="img" aria-label="Signups by week, rising from 12 to 48">
  <p>Signups rose from 12 to 48 over the last 30 days.</p>
</canvas>
<script>
  const canvas = document.getElementById('sparkline');
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#3b82f6';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 20, 120, 20);
  console.log('context  :', ctx.constructor.name);
  console.log('bitmap   :', canvas.width + '×' + canvas.height);
  console.log('nonsense :', canvas.getContext('nonsense'));
</script>

context  : CanvasRenderingContext2D
bitmap   : 200×60
nonsense : null

That output was captured from a real Chromium, not from the jsdom the rest of this course's JavaScript runs under, because jsdom has no getContext at all: it throws unless a native canvas package is installed.

getContext('2d') returns the two-dimensional drawing context, whose class name the measurement confirms; getContext('webgl2') and getContext('webgpu') return the three-dimensional ones. Asking for something the browser cannot provide returns null instead of throwing, and that is how you test for support. The same null comes back for webgl2 on a machine with no usable GPU, so the check is worth doing rather than assuming.

The accessibility position is the important part, and it is bad. A canvas is pixels. Nothing drawn into it exists in any tree, so a chart, a game or an editor drawn on a canvas is entirely invisible to assistive technology and to search engines, and none of it is text you can select, find or zoom. The element's children are ignored when the canvas renders, and they are the specified fallback. A screen reader does read them, which makes them the minimum obligation: a real description, or an equivalent table.

That obligation is heavy enough to be a reason not to reach for canvas. For charts, an inline <svg> is accessible, styleable, selectable and scalable; for anything that is really a document, HTML elements are. Canvas earns its place for genuinely pixel-level work: games, image editing, video processing, and visualisations with tens of thousands of points where the cost of that many DOM elements is real. In those cases, the fallback content and a parallel accessible version are part of the job, not an afterthought.

Exercises

1. Assign the correct alt to each of these five images, and justify each in one sentence.

1. A company logo in the site header, inside a link to the homepage.
2. A decorative swirl separating two sections.
3. A photograph of a product, in a card that already shows the product name as a heading.
4. A magnifying glass icon that is the only content of the search button.
5. A bar chart of revenue by quarter, in an article about the annual results.
Solution

1. alt="Acme" — or alt="Acme, home" if the destination is not obvious from context. This is the functional case (§8.3): the image is the only content of a link, so its alt becomes the link's accessible name. Not "Acme logo": the word "logo" describes the picture, and the user needs to know where the link goes.

2. alt="" — the decorative case. §8.2 measured the effect: an empty alt removes the image from the accessibility tree entirely, so it is neither announced nor a nameless node. Omitting the attribute instead would leave a nameless image node and most screen readers would read the filename.

3. alt="" — also decorative here, and this is the case people get wrong. The product name is already the heading beside it, so a descriptive alt makes the card announce the product twice. §8.3's measurement shows exactly this pairing: the image goes, and the link is named by its text.

4. alt="Search" — functional again. The alt names the action the button performs, not the picture on it. alt="Magnifying glass" produces a button announced as "magnifying glass, button", which describes the icon and not what pressing it does.

5. alt="Revenue rose in every quarter, from £1.2M in Q1 to £1.9M in Q4" — the complex case, and the alt carries the finding rather than the form. "Bar chart of revenue by quarter" is a description of the picture that leaves the reader knowing nothing they did not already know from the surrounding text.

For the fifth, the alt is not the whole answer. §8.12: put the chart in a <figure> with a <figcaption> giving the title, units and source for everyone, and put the actual numbers on the page as a data table (§10) — in a <details> if the design will not accommodate them. That serves the reader who wants the figures, the reader using a screen reader, and search indexing, all with the same markup.

2. Explain, precisely, why srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w" without a sizes attribute usually makes a page slower, not faster.

Solution

Because sizes defaults to 100vw, and that default is wrong for nearly every image.

The width descriptor states a fact about the file: 400w means "this file is 400 pixels wide" (§8.7). It is not a condition and not a breakpoint. To choose between candidates the browser needs one more number — how wide the image will be laid out on this page — and it needs it before layout exists, because images are fetched by the preload scanner (§1.10) while the CSS is still being parsed.

sizes is where that number comes from (§8.8). With no sizes, the specification says to assume 100vw: the image will fill the viewport's width.

So on a 1200-pixel viewport at device pixel ratio 2, the browser computes that it needs about 2400 image pixels and picks the largest candidate — even if the image is actually laid out in a 300-pixel-wide sidebar and 400w would have been ample. The result is a file four to six times larger than needed, on every image with a w descriptor and no sizes, which is a page that is slower than the same page with no srcset at all.

The fix is a sizes value that matches the CSS:

<img src="photo-400.jpg" srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w"
     sizes="(min-width: 60em) 300px, 100vw"
     alt="The east pier" width="800" height="600">

Two riders. sizes is an unverified promise about your own layout — nothing checks it against the CSS, and drift between them is a real maintenance cost, which is the argument for generating both from one source. And for a lazy-loaded image, sizes="auto" removes the problem entirely: the fetch is deferred until layout has happened, so the browser can use the real measured width instead of a promise. It does not help eagerly-loaded images, which are precisely the ones fetched before layout.

3. When is <picture> required and srcset insufficient? Give a case, and explain why the browser cannot make the choice itself.

Solution

<picture> is required when the content of the image must change, not merely its resolution — what §8.9 calls art direction.

The case: a hero photograph of two people standing at opposite ends of a wide landscape. At 1600 pixels the composition works. At 375 pixels, scaled down, both faces are a few pixels across and the image conveys nothing. The phone needs a different photograph — a tight crop of one subject — not a smaller copy of the same one.

<picture>
  <source media="(min-width: 40em)" srcset="team-wide.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source media="(min-width: 40em)" srcset="team-wide.jpg">
  <source srcset="team-crop.avif" type="image/avif">
  <img src="team-crop.jpg" alt="Dana and Sam at the harbour" width="600" height="600">
</picture>

Why the browser cannot decide. srcset deliberately hands the choice to the browser, which is right when the candidates are interchangeable — it knows the device pixel ratio, the network conditions, the cache state and the user's data preference, and you do not. That entire arrangement depends on every candidate being the same picture. The moment the candidates differ in what they show, the choice is an editorial one about which crop communicates the subject, and nothing in the browser has any basis for making it. So <picture> inverts the model: media conditions are author-controlled and evaluated in order, first match wins, exactly like <video>'s source list (§9.3).

The two related cases where <picture> is also the answer, both for the same reason — an author-controlled decision rather than a browser one:

  • Format negotiation with type, so the browser skips an AVIF it cannot decode without fetching it (§8.11). Here the ordering is the decision.
  • A different aspect ratio per breakpoint, which srcset cannot express at all because there is one width/height pair on the <img>.

Three things stay on the <img> regardless, because the <img> is what actually renders: the alt, the width and height, and every CSS selector.

4. A page scores badly on both LCP and CLS. Its hero is <img src="hero.jpg" class="hero" loading="lazy"> and its gallery is fifty <img src="…" alt="…"> with no other attributes. Diagnose and fix, in priority order.

Solution

First: loading="lazy" on the hero image is the LCP defect, and it is backwards. §8.6: a lazy image is not requested until the browser has laid the page out far enough to know it is near the viewport, which is strictly later than an eager fetch. The hero is almost certainly the largest contentful paint element, so this attribute delays the exact moment the metric measures. Remove it, and add fetchpriority="high" so the request is made ahead of the fifty gallery images discovered at the same time.

Second: no width or height anywhere is the CLS defect. §8.5: with no dimensions the browser reserves zero height, lays out the text, paints, and then jumps everything down as each image arrives. Fifty images means fifty shifts. Add the files' true intrinsic dimensions (§8.4) — they are used as an aspect ratio, not a size, and max-width: 100%; height: auto in CSS still controls the rendered size.

Third: the hero has no alt. Not a performance defect, and the most serious correctness one: §8.2 measured that an image with no alt leaves a nameless image node, and most screen readers then read the filename. Decide whether the hero is informative or decorative and say so.

Fourth: the gallery should be lazy — the hero should not. The rule is mechanical: lazy-load nothing visible without scrolling, lazy-load everything below the fold. Fifty eager image requests compete with the hero for connections and bandwidth, which is a second, indirect way this page delays its own LCP.

The result:

<img src="hero.jpg" class="hero" alt="A harbour at dusk"
     width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high">

<img src="gallery-1.jpg" alt="The east pier" width="800" height="600"
     loading="lazy" decoding="async">

Fifth, and the largest remaining win: serve fewer bytes. A hero at 1600 pixels wide should have a srcset with sizes (§8.8) so a phone fetches a 400-pixel file, and should be offered as AVIF and WebP before JPEG (§8.11). That is a bigger LCP improvement than any attribute above, but it comes fifth because it is the only one that needs a build pipeline — the first four are edits to the markup and can ship today.

5. A team renders its dashboard's charts on <canvas>. Accessibility review rejects it. What exactly is the problem, what is the minimum fix, and what is the better answer?

Solution

The problem is total, not partial. A canvas is a bitmap (§8.14). Everything drawn into it — axes, labels, series, values, legend — exists only as pixels. There is no DOM inside it, so there are no nodes in the accessibility tree, nothing for a screen reader to read, no text to select or search with find-in-page, nothing for a search engine to index, and nothing that reflows or reacts when the user increases the font size. A user who cannot see the chart gets an unlabelled rectangle. This is not "the labels need better contrast"; there are no labels as far as the platform is concerned.

The minimum fix uses the fallback content, which the element's children provide and which assistive technology does read:

<figure>
  <canvas width="600" height="300" role="img"
          aria-label="Signups by week, rising from 12 to 48 over 30 days">
    <table>
      <caption>Signups by week</caption>
      <tr><th scope="col">Week</th><th scope="col">Signups</th></tr>
      <tr><th scope="row">1</th><td>12</td></tr>
      <tr><th scope="row">4</th><td>48</td></tr>
    </table>
  </canvas>
  <figcaption>Signups by week, last 30 days.</figcaption>
</figure>

The aria-label gives the canvas a name and states the finding; the table inside gives the actual data (§10); the <figcaption> names the chart for every reader (§8.12). This is genuinely better than nothing, and it has a maintenance flaw that is worth naming: the fallback is a second copy of the data, kept in step by discipline alone, and it is invisible during development because nobody looking at the page ever sees it.

The better answer is to draw the chart as inline <svg> (§8.10). Every element is a real node: a <title> on the graphic names it, each series can be a labelled group, values can be text, and the whole thing scales, inherits currentColor, responds to CSS and can be given focus and hover behaviour per element. There is no second copy of anything, because the accessible representation is the chart.

When canvas is still right: genuinely pixel-level work — games, image and video editing — and datasets large enough that tens of thousands of DOM nodes are a real performance problem. In those cases the fallback content and a parallel accessible representation, such as a linked data table, are part of the deliverable rather than an afterthought. A dashboard with a handful of series is not that case, and the review is correct.

SECTION 9

Audio, Video, Tracks and Embedded Content

Everything so far has been markup the browser draws itself. This section is about four elements that hand a rectangle of the page over to something else (a video decoder, another document, a plugin surface), and about the attributes that decide what that something else is allowed to do inside the rectangle.

That handover makes these elements a different kind of thing from <p> and <table>:

  • A <video> is not styled text. It is a decoder with a set of controls attached, and those controls are markup you did not write and cannot see in view source.
  • An <iframe> is not a box. It is a second document with its own DOM, its own origin (the site it comes from), its own focus order and its own security boundary, sharing the screen with yours.

Getting either one wrong produces the two most expensive failures in the section: media nobody can operate without a mouse, and a frame that can reach into the page that embedded it.

So the measurements matter more here than usual. Every accessibility tree, DOM tree and tab order printed below came out of a real Chromium, and two of them are not what the markup suggests.

9.1 Embedded Content, and What "Replaced" Means

HTML's content model (§2.6) has a category called embedded content: elements whose contents come from outside the document. <img>, <video>, <audio>, <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, <canvas> and <svg> all belong to it. CSS has a matching term, a replaced element, for a box whose inside CSS does not lay out, because the box is filled by something with its own built-in dimensions.

Being replaced has the same three practical consequences every time:

It has an intrinsic size
The resource's own dimensions, known only after the resource loads. Until then the browser is guessing, which is where layout shift comes from (§8.5).
Its children are not its content
Markup inside a <video> or an <object> is configuration and fallback, not what the reader sees when the resource works.
It has its own accessibility story
The tree node for the element does not describe the resource. Something in the markup has to.

That third point is the backbone of this section. An <img> gets its name from alt (§8.3). A <video> gets no name from anywhere unless you provide one, and an <iframe> gets nothing but its title. The elements that fetch their content from elsewhere are exactly the ones where the accessibility tree cannot work anything out for itself, because the browser has not read the resource and will not.

9.2 The Video Element

At its smallest, a video is one element and two attributes:

<video controls src="clip.mp4" width="320" height="180"></video>

src names the file; the controls attribute asks the browser for a set of playback controls. Without the controls attribute there are no controls at all, not a reduced set but none, and §9.7 measures exactly what that costs.

width and height behave as they do on <img> (§8.4). They are numbers of CSS pixels, not percentages, and their job is to give the browser the aspect ratio before the file arrives, so the page does not jump. Set them to the video's real dimensions and let CSS scale it.

The rest of the attributes fall neatly into two groups: what plays and how it loads.

controls
Boolean. Give the browser's own player. Present at all means on — controls="false" is still on (§2.4).
poster
A URL for a still to show before playback. Without one the browser shows nothing until the first frame decodes.
preload
none, metadata or auto. A hint about how much to fetch before the user asks.
loop
Boolean. Seek back to the start on reaching the end.
muted
Boolean. The default mute state. The user can unmute; the attribute does not keep it muted.
autoplay
Boolean. Start without being asked — subject to §9.6, which is most of the story.
playsinline
Boolean. Play in the element's own box rather than taking over the screen, which is what mobile Safari does otherwise.
crossorigin
anonymous or use-credentials. Fetch with CORS, which a cross-origin <track> requires and <canvas> reading requires.

Three of those are boolean attributes and carry exactly the same trap as §2.4. muted="false" mutes. autoplay="no" autoplays. controls="" shows controls. The only way to turn a boolean attribute off is to remove it, and a templating language that renders muted="{{isMuted}}" will produce a video that is always muted, starting the first time isMuted is false.

The preload attribute deserves a moment, because it is the one people set carelessly. It is a hint, not an instruction: the specification explicitly allows a browser to ignore it, and mobile browsers on metered connections often do.

  • none means fetch nothing until the user presses play, which is right for a page with twelve videos on it.
  • metadata fetches enough to know the duration and dimensions. That is what makes the progress bar meaningful before playback, and it is the value the specification recommends as the default.
  • auto says the whole file is worth fetching.

The preload attribute is also overridden entirely by autoplay: a browser that intends to start playing has to download, whatever the hint says.

The poster attribute is the cheapest quality win on the list. Without it, a video is a black rectangle until the first frame is decoded, which on a slow connection looks like a broken page. With it, the reader sees a still image immediately. And because the poster is an ordinary image request, it can be served small, cached and preloaded (§3.10). Choose a frame that says what the video is about rather than the first frame, which is often black.

One more note on the poster attribute before moving on: the poster attribute is fetched as an ordinary image, so it counts in §8.5's layout-shift arithmetic and benefits from the same treatment: a sensible size, a modern format, and a preload if it is above the fold.

Two of the boolean attributes are worth naming again, because they are so often set together. The muted attribute sets the starting mute state and nothing more: the user may unmute, and the muted attribute will not switch the sound off again. The loop attribute jumps back to the start on reaching the end, and a loop attribute on anything longer than a few seconds is an animation that WCAG 2.2 requires a way to pause.

9.3 Containers, Codecs, and the Source List

src on the element itself commits you to one file in one format. The alternative is a list:

<video controls width="320" poster="poster.jpg">
  <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  Your browser cannot play this video.
</video>

DOM TREE
<video controls="" width="320" poster="poster.jpg">
  #text "\n  "
  <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
  #text "\n  "
  <source src="clip.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  #text "\n  "
  <track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default="">
  #text "\n  Your browser cannot play this video.\n"

The browser goes through the <source> children in order, takes the first one it believes it can play, and stops. It never comes back to try another after a decoding failure, so the order is a priority list: put the format you would rather serve first. If none matches, the element plays nothing, and the children that are not <source> or <track> become the fallback (§9.4).

type is what makes that decision cheap. Without it, the browser must start fetching each candidate to find out what it is; with it, the decision is made from the string alone. And the string has two halves that people mix up.

A container format is the file's wrapper: MP4, WebM, Ogg. It interleaves the streams, holds the index and carries the metadata. A codec is the compression scheme for one stream inside it: H.264, VP9 or AV1 for video; AAC, Opus or Vorbis for audio. video/mp4 names only the container format, and an MP4 can hold a codec the browser cannot decode, so a type of video/mp4 is a promise the browser cannot fully check.

The codecs parameter closes that gap:

<video controls width="320">
  <source src="clip.mp4" type='video/mp4; codecs="av01.0.05M.08, opus"'>
  <source src="clip.mp4" type='video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E, mp4a.40.2"'>
</video>

Now the browser can reject the first line without any network traffic at all. avc1.42E01E is H.264 Baseline profile, level 3.0, and mp4a.40.2 is AAC-LC: the pair that plays essentially everywhere, which is why it goes last, as the floor. av01.… is AV1, which is dramatically smaller but decoded by fewer devices, which is why it goes first.

Note the quoting: the value itself contains a comma and double quotes, so the attribute is wrapped in single quotes. That is legal HTML (§2.2) and much clearer than escaping.

In practice, a modern source list has two or three entries, cheapest and newest first, ending in H.264/AAC in an MP4. Serving one format only is a defensible choice too (H.264/AAC alone works); it is just larger for every viewer whose browser could have taken AV1.

9.4 Fallback Content, and What It Is Actually For

The text after the last <source> is the element's fallback content. It is worth being precise about when it appears, because the common belief is wrong.

It is shown when the browser does not implement the element at all. A browser that has never heard of <video> treats the tag as unknown, skips it and renders the children, which is exactly what §1.8's error recovery gives you for free. Every browser in current use implements <video>, so in practice almost nobody ever sees this fallback.
