It is not shown when the browser understands <video> but cannot decode any of the sources. In that case the element exists, takes up its box, and shows the browser's own failure state. Your careful paragraph of alternative content sits in the DOM and is never drawn.

That is why the useful thing to put there is a link rather than an apology:

<audio controls src="interview.mp3">
  <a href="interview.mp3">Download the interview (MP3, 4.2 MB)</a>
</audio>

DOM TREE
<audio controls="" src="interview.mp3">
  #text "\n  "
  <a href="interview.mp3">
    #text "Download the interview (MP3, 4.2 MB)"
  #text "\n"

The DOM confirms that the children really are there, as ordinary elements; the parser does nothing special to them. But a reader who needs an alternative to a media element that failed is far better served by the transcript link of §9.10, which is always visible, than by fallback content that only an ancient browser will ever reach.

9.5 The Audio Element

<audio> is <video> with the picture removed, and its attribute list is the same minus the three that only make sense for a picture: no poster, no playsinline, no width/height. src, controls, preload, loop, muted, autoplay, crossorigin, <source> children and <track> children all behave identically.

<audio controls src="interview.mp3"></audio>

AX TREE
Audio "Unable to play media." disabled=true
  button "play" disabled=true
  slider "audio time scrubber" disabled=true orientation=horizontal valuemax=100 valuemin=0 valuetext=0
  button "mute" disabled=true
  button "show more media controls" haspopup=menu

Two differences from the video tree in §9.7 are worth noticing. There is no full-screen button, because there is nothing to make full screen. And the buttons come in a different order (play, progress bar, mute), because the audio player is laid out as a single row rather than a frame with a bar under it. You control neither from markup; both are the browser's own interface, and both differ between browsers.

The name and the disabled=true states are a side effect of the measurement. This tree was produced on a machine that has no interview.mp3, so Chrome is showing the element in its error state and naming it from its own status text. With a real file the structure is the same and the states are live. That side effect is worth leaving in rather than faking a loaded tree, because it also shows the failure of §9.4: a media element that cannot load does not disappear; it sits there announcing that it is broken.

One habit worth forming for audio in particular. Because there is no picture to catch the eye, an <audio> element with no text around it is nearly invisible on the page and gives nothing away in the accessibility tree. Put a heading or a paragraph next to it saying what the recording is, and link the transcript underneath (§9.10).

9.6 Autoplay, and the Rules Browsers Actually Apply

autoplay is the attribute most likely to do nothing. Every current browser applies a policy on top of it, and the policy is roughly the same everywhere:

1
Muted media may autoplay. No sound, no interruption, no policy.
2
Unmuted media may autoplay if the user has already interacted with the document — a click, a tap, a key.
3
Some browsers keep a per-site engagement score and relax the rule for sites the user watches media on often.
4
Otherwise playback is refused, and a scripted play() returns a promise that rejects with NotAllowedError.

So the only reliably-autoplaying media is the muted kind:

<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="320" height="180"
       poster="loop-poster.jpg" src="ambient.mp4"
       aria-label="Ambient background footage of a harbour"></video>

That combination, autoplay muted loop playsinline, is the decorative background video, and each of the four is essential. Drop muted and rule 1 stops applying. Drop playsinline and mobile Safari may take over the whole screen. Drop loop and the page ends up frozen on the last frame.

It is also a pattern to use sparingly. A looping video is a continuous animation, and WCAG 2.2 requires a way to pause, stop or hide any animation that starts automatically and runs for more than five seconds (§13.11). A five-second decorative loop is fine. A thirty-second one needs a pause control, which means it needs controls or a button you write yourself. The prefers-reduced-motion media query is the other half of the answer and belongs to css_mastery.

For anything with sound, the honest conclusion is simpler: do not use autoplay. The user will be somewhere public, on a call or listening to something else, and the browser will very likely refuse anyway.

9.7 What controls Builds

This is the measurement that changes how you think about media elements. Here is a <video controls> and the accessibility tree Chrome builds from it:

<video controls src="clip.mp4" width="320" height="180"></video>

AX TREE
Video "Unable to play media." disabled=true
  group "buffering" live=polite
  button "play" disabled=true
  button "mute" disabled=true
  button "enter full screen" disabled=true
  button "show more media controls" disabled=true haspopup=menu
  slider "video time scrubber" disabled=true orientation=horizontal valuemax=100 valuemin=0 valuetext=0

One element in your markup, six child nodes in the tree: four buttons, a slider, and a polite live region (an area whose updates are announced without interrupting) that reports buffering. Five of the six are interactive. None of it appears in view source, because it is not in your document. It lives in the browser's own shadow DOM (§15.7), built and named by the browser in the user's language. One attribute gets you a substantial, tested, translated, keyboard-operable player.

Now remove the attribute:

<video src="clip.mp4" width="320" height="180"></video>

AX TREE
Video "Unable to play media." disabled=true

Nothing. No buttons, no slider, no live region. A <video> without controls, and without a scripted player of your own, is a rectangle that a keyboard user cannot start, in which a screen reader user cannot find a single control, and that nobody can pause. If you are building a custom player, that empty tree is the hole you have taken responsibility for filling. Every one of those six nodes, with names, states and key handling, is now yours (§14.6).

The third measurement is the surprising one. Six nodes that look focusable, and this is the focus order:

<button>Before</button>
<video controls src="clip.mp4" width="320" height="180"></video>
<button>After</button>

TAB ORDER
<button> "Before"
<video>
<button> "After"
(leaves the page)

A media player is one tab stop, not six. Tab moves to the video as a whole; the arrow keys and space then work inside it, exactly like the radio group and the <select> in §14.6. This is the roving-tabindex pattern, built by the browser, and it is why a page with eight videos on it does not cost forty-eight presses of Tab to get past.

It is also the model to copy. When you build a composite widget (one control made of several parts), the native players are the example to follow: one stop from the outside, arrow keys within.

9.8 Captions, Subtitles and Descriptions

Media is the one place where the accessibility requirement is not a small attribute but a separate piece of content that somebody has to write. It cannot be generated from markup, and this is where media projects run over budget.

Three different alternatives serve three different groups of people, and they are not interchangeable:

Captions
Everything on the audio track, in the same language: dialogue plus speaker identification, sound effects and relevant music. For someone who cannot hear the audio at all.
Subtitles
A transcription or translation of the dialogue, for someone who can hear it but does not understand it. No sound effects — the assumption is that the audio is available.
Descriptions
What is happening on screen and is not conveyed by the audio, for someone who cannot see it. Read out in the gaps between dialogue.

The difference between the first two is the one that gets blurred, and blurring it is a real failure. A deaf viewer given a subtitle track hears nothing, reads the dialogue, and misses the doorbell, the gunshot and the fact that the music has turned ominous. A caption track says [doorbell rings]. A subtitle track does not, because a subtitle track is for a viewer who heard the doorbell perfectly well and simply does not speak the language.

WCAG 2.2 turns this into three graded requirements. They are worth knowing by name, because they are what an audit will cite (§13.11):

  • 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded), Level A — captions for all prerecorded audio in synchronised media.
  • 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative, Level A — either an audio description or a full text alternative.
  • 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded), Level AA — an audio description specifically, the text alternative no longer sufficing.

The Level A/AA split matters commercially. Most public-sector and accessibility-policy commitments are written against AA, which means an audio description is not optional for prerecorded video with meaningful visuals.

Automatic captioning is now good enough to be a genuinely useful starting point, and not good enough to ship without review. It reliably mangles proper names, technical vocabulary and people talking over each other, and it produces no speaker labels and no sound effects at all. In other words, it produces subtitles and labels them captions. Budget for a human to go over it.

The distinction to hold on to is that a caption track and a subtitle track are different pieces of content serving different people, even when the words overlap. A caption track includes speaker labels and sound effects because its reader hears nothing; a subtitle track does not, because its reader hears everything and simply does not speak the language.

9.9 The Track Element and WebVTT

<track> attaches a timed text file to a media element. It is a void element (§1.5), it must be a child of the <video> or <audio>, and it must come after the <source> elements.

<video controls width="320" height="180" src="lecture.mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="lecture-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <track kind="subtitles" src="lecture-fr.vtt" srclang="fr" label="Français">
  <track kind="descriptions" src="lecture-desc.vtt" srclang="en" label="Audio description">
  <track kind="chapters" src="lecture-chapters.vtt" srclang="en" label="Chapters">
</video>

The kind attribute takes exactly five values, and it decides what the browser does with the cues (the timed pieces of text):

subtitles
Displayed over the video. The default when kind is omitted.
captions
Displayed over the video, and announced as captions in the track menu.
descriptions
Not displayed. Intended to be spoken by assistive technology.
chapters
Not displayed. Offered as navigation points in the player's UI.
metadata
Not displayed at all. Cues exist only for scripts to read.

Two details of the kind attribute are easy to get wrong. Leaving it out gives you subtitles, not captions, so a track written as captions and tagged with nothing is mislabelled in every track menu. And an invalid value does not fall back to subtitles; it falls back to metadata, which is not shown at all. A typo like kind="caption" therefore produces a video whose captions are silently invisible, and nothing anywhere reports an error.

The other three attributes are small, and all of them matter. srclang is a BCP 47 language tag naming the language of the cue text, and it is required whenever kind is subtitles. label is what the user sees in the track menu, so write it in the language it names (Français, not French), because the person looking for it is the person who reads that language. The default attribute marks the one track to switch on when the user has expressed no preference, and it may appear on at most one track per media element.

src on a <track> is restricted to the same origin unless the media element carries crossorigin, which is the usual reason a caption file returns 200 and never appears.

The file itself is WebVTT, and it is deliberately simple enough to write and compare by hand:

WEBVTT

00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.500
[door creaks open]

00:00:05.100 --> 00:00:08.000
<v Dana>We shipped it on Friday.

intro
00:00:08.200 --> 00:00:12.000 line:90% align:center
And nobody noticed until Monday.

Four rules cover almost everything:

  • The file must begin with the literal string WEBVTT; a single byte before it and the whole file is rejected.
  • Timestamps are HH:MM:SS.mmm, with the hours optional, separated by --> with spaces around the arrow.
  • A cue may carry an optional identifier on the line above its timing, which is what a script or a chapter menu uses to refer to it.
  • Settings after the timestamp position the cue on screen.

Cue text allows a small amount of markup: <v Speaker> for the voice, <b>, <i>, <u> and <c.classname> for styling, and <00:00:06.000> for karaoke-style timing. Everything else is plain text, and &amp;, &lt; and &gt; are the escapes.

WebVTT is served as text/vtt. A server that has not been told about the extension will send .vtt as text/plain or application/octet-stream, and the browser will refuse the track. That is the second most common reason captions do not appear, after the kind typo above.

The default attribute is the last piece, and the one most often forgotten. A track with no default attribute anywhere in the element loads correctly and stays switched off until the user finds the track menu, which most users never open.

9.10 Transcripts and Audio Descriptions

Captions cover the person watching. A transcript covers everyone else, and it is the most valuable, least technical thing on this page.

A transcript is the whole content of the media as text on the page: dialogue, speaker labels and the visual information a description track would carry, merged into one readable document. It is not a <track>. It is ordinary HTML next to the player.

<figure>
  <video controls width="320" height="180" src="lecture.mp4">
    <track kind="captions" src="lecture-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  </video>
  <figcaption>Dr. Okonjo on cache invalidation, 12 minutes.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
  <summary>Read the transcript</summary>
  <p><b>Dr. Okonjo:</b> There are only two hard problems…</p>
</details>

The reasons to write one are not mainly about disability, which makes it an easy case to make:

  • It is the only alternative that works for someone who is both deaf and blind, through a braille display. Captions do not reach that user, and neither does a description track.
  • It is searchable, by the site's own search and by search engines, which cannot index a video's audio at all.
  • It is skimmable. Many readers would rather scan twelve minutes of text in ninety seconds than watch it.
  • It is linkable. A colleague can quote the paragraph instead of saying "about eight minutes in".
  • On its own, it satisfies WCAG 1.2.3 at Level A, as long as it includes the visual information.

An audio description is the other half of the same problem, and the more expensive one. It is a spoken narration of what can be seen but not heard ("she crosses out the second column"), fitted into the gaps in the dialogue. There are two ways to deliver it:

  • a descriptions track that assistive technology reads aloud, which is cheap but depends on the user's setup supporting it;
  • a second, separately produced audio or video file with the description mixed in, which always works and costs a studio.

The extended form, where the video pauses to make room for a description that does not fit in the gaps, needs the second approach.

The practical order in which to spend a budget: captions first, because they are Level A and can be checked mechanically; then a transcript, because it is cheap and helps everybody; then descriptions, because they are the most expensive and the most specialised. Writing the video's script with description in mind (having the presenter say "the second column" out loud instead of pointing at it) removes most of the need for the third, and costs nothing at all.

9.11 The Iframe: A Document Inside a Document

An <iframe> embeds a whole other browsing context: a separate document with its own DOM, its own URL, its own history entry, its own scripts and its own origin.

<iframe title="Sales dashboard for 2025" src="/dashboard" width="600" height="400"
        loading="lazy" referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></iframe>

title is not optional. It is the only source of an accessible name an iframe has, and the difference shows directly in the tree:

<!-- ❌ no title: the frame is a nameless node -->
<iframe src="about:blank" width="300" height="150"></iframe>
<!-- ✅ -->
<iframe title="Sales dashboard for 2025" src="about:blank" width="300" height="150"></iframe>

AX TREE
Iframe
Iframe "Sales dashboard for 2025"

A screen reader user moving around by frame gets a list of them. The first entry on that list has no name, and its user has no way of knowing whether it is the map, the video or the advertisement without going inside. Write the title as a description of what the frame is for ("Sales dashboard for 2025"), not "iframe" and not the URL.

The focus behaviour is the second thing that catches people out, and it is the opposite of §9.7's:

<button>Before</button>
<iframe title="A small frame" srcdoc="<button>Inside</button>" width="200" height="80"></iframe>
<button>After</button>

TAB ORDER
<button> "Before"
<iframe>
<button> "After"
(leaves the page)

That output is true but incomplete, and the gap is worth understanding, because it is an honest limit of the tool rather than a fact about the platform. The recorder reads document.activeElement in the parent document, and for as long as focus is anywhere inside a frame, the parent reports the <iframe> element itself. Driving the same page and asking each frame separately gives the real sequence:

Tab 1  parent: BUTTON#one          frame: BODY
Tab 2  parent: IFRAME              frame: BUTTON#inner
Tab 3  parent: IFRAME              frame: BUTTON#inner2
Tab 4  parent: BUTTON#two          frame: BODY

An iframe is not one tab stop. It is as many stops as its document has, inserted into the parent's sequence at the frame's position, and the parent cannot see them, count them or change their order. A page that embeds a third-party widget with forty focusable elements has forty extra stops in the middle of it. The parent's only options are removing the frame, making its container inert (§14.10), or asking the widget's author to fix it.

The rest of the attribute list is short.

  • loading="lazy" delays the frame's fetch until it comes close to the visible area. It is worth setting on anything below the fold, because a third-party embed is often the single heaviest thing on a page.
  • referrerpolicy controls what Referer header the frame's request carries. no-referrer sends none, origin sends only the scheme and host, and strict-origin-when-cross-origin, the modern default, sends the full URL to destinations on the same origin and only the origin elsewhere. Set referrerpolicy="no-referrer" when the frame's operator has no business knowing which of your pages the user is on.
  • name gives the frame a name that <a target> and <form target> can aim at (§7.6).
  • width and height are in CSS pixels, and the height defaults to 150, which is why an unstyled iframe is a squat rectangle.

9.12 The Sandbox Attribute

An embedded document is not a picture of a page; it is a running program. By default it can run scripts, submit forms, open pop-ups, navigate the whole window away from your page, and, if it comes from the same origin, read your document's DOM and storage. The sandbox attribute takes all of that away and lets you give back one capability at a time.

<iframe title="Untrusted widget" src="/widget" sandbox width="300" height="150"></iframe>
<iframe title="Untrusted widget, scripts allowed" src="/widget"
        sandbox="allow-scripts" width="300" height="150"></iframe>

The sandbox attribute with an empty value applies every restriction. Each space-separated token then lifts exactly one. The full list is long; these are the ones that come up:

allow-scripts
Run JavaScript. Without it the frame is inert markup.
allow-forms
Submit forms. Without it the form renders and submission silently does nothing.
allow-same-origin
Keep the document's real origin. Without it the frame is placed in an opaque origin: no cookies, no storage, no same-origin access in either direction.
allow-popups
Open new windows and tabs. The pop-up inherits the sandbox unless allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox is also present.
allow-top-navigation
Navigate the whole browser tab. Prefer allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation, which requires a real gesture.
allow-modals
alert(), confirm(), prompt(), print(). <dialog> works regardless (§14.8).
allow-downloads
Start a download, whether from a link or from script.

Here is what those tokens actually do, measured by serving a real page over HTTP, embedding the same frame document four ways, and asking each frame what it managed to do:

parent origin: http://127.0.0.1:39527

sandbox attribute                  script?  location.origin              localStorage
---------------------------------  -------  ---------------------------  ---------------------
(absent)                           runs     http://127.0.0.1:39527       works
sandbox                            blocked  —                            —
sandbox="allow-scripts"            runs     http://127.0.0.1:39527       throws SecurityError
sandbox="allow-scripts
         allow-same-origin"        runs     http://127.0.0.1:39527       works

-- what the parent page can reach, via iframe.contentDocument --
(absent)                            readable
sandbox                             null
sandbox="allow-scripts"             null
sandbox="allow-scripts
         allow-same-origin"         readable

Three things in that table are worth stopping on.

The bare sandbox really does stop scripts. It does not merely restrict them: the script element is parsed and never run.

location.origin is not how you observe the opaque origin. An opaque origin is a unique, anonymous origin that matches nothing, not even itself. location.origin reports the URL's origin in all four rows, because it is worked out from the URL. What actually changed is the document's security origin, and you can see it in the two other columns: storage throws an error, and the parent's contentDocument comes back null instead of a document. If you are debugging a sandboxed frame and reading location.origin to check whether the sandbox took effect, you will wrongly conclude it did not.

allow-scripts allow-same-origin together is worth a second thought. The row shows why: it is the one combination that both runs code and has full access to your origin. When the framed document comes from the same origin as the parent, that combination lets the framed page reach up and remove the sandbox attribute from its own <iframe>, after which it is not sandboxed at all. The rule: if you need both tokens, serve the framed document from a different origin, so that allow-same-origin means "its own origin" and not yours.

The reason to reach for this at all is that sandbox is the only mechanism on the page that is deny by default. Content Security Policy (§16.10) restricts what a document may load; sandbox restricts what an embedded document may do, starting from nothing. For anything user-generated (a preview of a submitted HTML snippet, a rendered email, a third-party template), it is the right building block, and sandbox="allow-scripts" on a frame served from a separate origin is the standard recipe.

9.13 srcdoc, and Permissions Policy

srcdoc supplies the frame's document inline instead of fetching one:

<iframe title="Preview" sandbox srcdoc="&lt;p&gt;Hello from the frame.&lt;/p&gt;"
        width="300" height="80"></iframe>

The whole document goes into an attribute value, so every < must be written &lt; and every " must be written &quot; (§2.2). A srcdoc frame uses the embedding document's URL to resolve relative links, and, critically, it takes on that document's origin unless a sandbox is applied. So srcdoc alone does not isolate anything: pasting user-supplied markup into it gives that markup your origin. srcdoc plus sandbox is the combination that makes a safe preview pane, and it is exactly what a comment-preview or email-rendering feature needs.

Where sandbox governs what the frame may do, the allow attribute governs which powerful features the frame may ask the user for. It holds a Permissions Policy, written in the same syntax as the Permissions-Policy HTTP header but applying only to this frame:

<iframe title="Video call" src="https://calls.example.com/room/42"
        allow="camera 'self' https://calls.example.com; microphone 'self' https://calls.example.com; geolocation 'none'"
        width="600" height="400"></iframe>

Each entry is a feature name and a list of who may use it: 'self' for the frame's own origin, 'none' for nobody, * for any origin, or explicit origins. Features include camera, microphone, geolocation, fullscreen, payment, display-capture, autoplay, clipboard-write and several dozen more. A feature not mentioned uses its default, which for the sensitive ones is 'self', so a frame from another origin gets nothing unless it is granted.

Two properties of permissions policy follow from it being a policy rather than a permission. It only ever narrows what is allowed: a frame cannot be granted more than the embedding document has, so allow="camera *" on a page whose own Permissions-Policy header forbids the camera grants nothing. And it does not replace the user's consent. It decides whether the frame is even allowed to ask; the prompt still happens.

The old attributes allowfullscreen and allowpaymentrequest are the same idea from before the policy syntax existed, and they are now defined as allow="fullscreen *" and allow="payment *". New code should use allow.

So the two attributes split the work cleanly: sandbox governs what the embedded document may do, and the allow attribute governs which powerful features it may ask for. The allow attribute never grants more than the embedding page already has, which is what makes it safe to write generously.

9.14 Being Framed: Clickjacking and frame-ancestors

Everything so far has been about controlling what you embed. The other direction, who may embed you, is a security question with a name.

clickjacking is the attack where a malicious page loads your site in an invisible frame, places it under a decoy, and gets the user to click something they cannot see. The user believes they are clicking "Play video"; the click lands on your "Delete account" button, in their logged-in session, in a real browser, with real cookies. Nothing about the request is forged, which is why the usual server-side defences do not see it: as far as your application can tell, a logged-in user clicked a button.

The defence is to declare who may frame you, and there are two mechanisms.

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example.com

frame-ancestors is a CSP directive (§16.10) listing the origins allowed to embed the document. 'none' forbids framing entirely; 'self' allows your own origin. It replaces the older X-Frame-Options: DENY / SAMEORIGIN header, which is still worth sending alongside it for very old browsers but cannot express a list of more than one allowed origin.

Three properties of frame-ancestors are why it must be a response header and cannot be markup:

  • The browser enforces it before the framed document renders, so there is nothing in the document yet to consult.
  • A <meta http-equiv> CSP (§3.6) is explicitly forbidden from carrying it, and browsers ignore it there. Sending frame-ancestors in a meta tag is a defence that silently does not exist.
  • It applies to the whole chain of ancestors, not just the immediate parent, so a partner you allowed cannot itself be framed by an attacker to pass the embedding along.

The consequence for an embeddable widget is that frame-ancestors turns "embeddable" into a deliberate decision. If your application has any control that changes state behind a session cookie (and every application does), the default should be frame-ancestors 'none', with an explicit list of allowed origins on the specific routes meant to be embedded. Set it once, at the edge, for everything.

SameSite=Lax cookies raise the cost of this attack considerably, since a framed request from another site no longer carries the session by default, and Chromium-based browsers now treat a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax. It is a mitigation, not the fix: it does nothing against an attacker on the same site, and frame-ancestors costs one header.

9.15 Object, Embed and Fencedframe

Three more embedding elements exist. Two are historical and one is new, and the honest summary is that you will rarely reach for any of them.

<object> and <embed> were the elements of the plugin era, when a page might embed Flash, Java or a PDF viewer. <object> takes data and type, and, unlike every other embedding element, it supports real fallback content, because a plugin that fails to start really does fall back to the children:

<object type="image/svg+xml" data="chart.svg" width="200" height="100">
  <p>Revenue rose in every quarter of 2025.</p>
</object>

DOM TREE
<object type="image/svg+xml" data="chart.svg" width="200" height="100">
  #text "\n  "
  <p>
    #text "Revenue rose in every quarter of 2025."
  #text "\n"

<embed> is the same idea as a void element, with src instead of data and no fallback at all. Neither has a useful accessibility story:

<object type="image/svg+xml" data="chart.svg" width="200" height="100"
        aria-label="Revenue by quarter"></object>
<embed type="image/svg+xml" src="chart.svg" width="200" height="100">

AX TREE
PluginObject "Revenue by quarter"
EmbeddedObject

PluginObject and EmbeddedObject are not roles a screen reader does anything useful with, and the <embed> node has no name at all, because no attribute could give it one. For an SVG use <img> or inline <svg> (§8.10); for a PDF use a link; for another document use <iframe>, which has title, sandbox and allow. The one place <object> still earns its keep is embedding a PDF with a link as the fallback, and even there an <iframe> plus a download link is usually better.

<fencedframe> is the new one. It is worth knowing it exists, and not worth using yet. It is a frame designed so that the embedding page and the embedded content cannot communicate at all (no shared storage, no postMessage, no reading of the parent's URL), so that an advertisement can be shown to a user chosen by data neither side is allowed to see. It exists for the privacy-sandbox advertising APIs, ships only in Chromium, and has no cross-browser support. Recognise it in someone else's markup; do not build on it.

A last word on <fencedframe>: it is worth recognising and not worth adopting. <fencedframe> exists to serve one industry's privacy requirements, it ships in one engine, and nothing in an ordinary application needs a frame that cannot communicate with the page that embeds it.

Exercises

1. A page embeds a video with <video src="promo.mp4" width="640" height="360">Your browser does not support video.</video>. List everything wrong with it, in order of how much it matters.

Solution

First, and by a distance: there is no controls attribute. §9.7 measured what that costs — the accessibility tree contains a single Video node with no children at all. No play button, no scrubber, no mute, no live region. Nobody can start it, pause it or seek in it, by any input method. The video is decoration that happens to be a video.

Second: no captions. No <track kind="captions">, so the content is unavailable to anyone who cannot hear it. That is WCAG 1.2.2 at Level A — the lowest conformance bar there is — and for a promotional video it is also the version that plays in a noisy office with the sound off, which is most of them.

Third: no accessible name. The Video node is named from the browser's status string, not from anything the author supplied. Wrap it in a <figure> with a <figcaption> (§9.10), or give it an aria-label.

Fourth: the fallback text will never be seen. §9.4: fallback content is shown when the browser does not implement <video>, not when the file fails to decode. Every browser in use implements <video>. If the intent was "give people something when this does not work", the mechanism is a visible transcript or download link outside the element.

Fifth: no poster. Until the first frame decodes the reader sees a black rectangle 640×360.

Sixth: a single src rather than a <source> list. Not a defect — H.264 in MP4 plays everywhere — but every viewer is being sent the largest of the available encodings.

The fixed version:

<figure>
  <video controls preload="metadata" poster="promo-poster.jpg"
         width="640" height="360">
    <source src="promo.av1.mp4" type='video/mp4; codecs="av01.0.05M.08, opus"'>
    <source src="promo.mp4" type='video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E, mp4a.40.2"'>
    <track kind="captions" src="promo-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  </video>
  <figcaption>What we shipped this quarter — 2 minutes.</figcaption>
</figure>

2. A team ships captions and the QA report says "captions do not appear" for a track that returns HTTP 200. Give four distinct causes, each with the check that distinguishes it.

Solution

The kind attribute has a typo. kind="caption" is an invalid value, and §9.9's rule is that an invalid value falls back to metadata, not to subtitles — and a metadata track is never displayed. Check: read the attribute character by character; the five legal values are subtitles, captions, descriptions, chapters, metadata.

The file is served with the wrong Content-Type. A server that does not know the .vtt extension sends text/plain, and the browser refuses the track. The request is a clean 200, which is what makes this one waste an afternoon. Check: curl -I the track URL and look for text/vtt.

The file does not begin with WEBVTT. A byte-order mark, a blank line, or an editor that added a comment header, and the whole file is rejected as malformed. Check: head -c 16 file.vtt | xxd — the first six bytes must be WEBVTT.

The track is cross-origin and the media element has no crossorigin. A <track src> on a different origin than the document is only fetched when the <video> carries crossorigin, and the server must send the matching CORS headers. Check: compare the track's origin with the page's; look for a CORS error in the console.

There is a fifth that is not a bug: no default attribute on any track. The track loads correctly and is simply switched off until the user chooses it from the menu. Distinguish it by opening the player's own track menu — if the track is listed, the pipeline is fine and only the default is missing.

3. You must render user-submitted HTML — a preview pane in a comment editor. Design the embedding, and justify each token you allow.

Solution 
<iframe title="Comment preview"
        src="https://preview.example-cdn.com/render?id=4021"
        sandbox="allow-scripts"
        referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
        allow="camera 'none'; microphone 'none'; geolocation 'none'"
        width="600" height="300"></iframe>

A frame at all, rather than inserting the markup into the page. Sanitising HTML into your own document means being right every time against an adversary who only has to be right once. A frame moves the problem from "did I catch every vector" to "what can this document do", which is a bounded question with a mechanism attached.

sandbox with only allow-scripts. The bare sandbox attribute denies everything; each token adds one capability back. Scripts are allowed because a preview that silently drops the user's <script> is not a preview of what will be published. Everything else stays denied: no forms, no pop-ups, no top-level navigation, no downloads, no modals.

Not allow-same-origin — and this is the load-bearing decision. §9.12 measured the difference: without it the document is in an opaque origin, localStorage throws SecurityError, and the parent's contentDocument comes back null. Any cookies your users hold for your origin are unreachable from inside the frame.

A separate origin in src. Even with allow-same-origin withheld, serving the preview from your own host means one future engineer adding that token — for a plausible reason, such as measuring the rendered height — turns the frame into same-origin script execution with full access to the session. The separate origin makes that mistake survivable, because "same origin" then means the CDN's origin. This is the pairing rule from §9.12, and it costs a hostname.

referrerpolicy="no-referrer". The preview service has no need to know which page, thread or draft the user is on, and comment bodies frequently contain URLs whose referrers would leak.

allow denying the capture features. Belt and braces: a cross-origin frame gets no camera or microphone by default, but stating it means an accidental future Permissions-Policy change at the edge cannot quietly open them.

What is still missing. The frame's own response needs Content-Security-Policy (§16.10) to restrict what the untrusted markup may load and where it may send data, and the preview origin should serve frame-ancestors naming your site only. Sandboxing bounds what the document may do; CSP bounds what it may reach. Both, or neither is enough.

4. Explain why a <video controls> is one tab stop while an <iframe> containing three buttons is three, and what that difference implies for anyone building a custom media player.

Solution

They are different because only one of them is a single document.

The video is one stop by design. Its six control nodes live in a shadow root the browser owns (§15.7), and the browser implements the roving-tabindex pattern of §14.6 inside it: the player is one entry in the document's focus sequence, and arrows and space operate within it once focus is there. §9.7 measured it — Before, <video>, After, and the page ends. This is the same shape as a radio group or a <select>, and it is deliberate: Tab is the coarse navigation key, and a page of eight players would otherwise cost forty-eight presses to walk past.

The iframe is three stops because there is no single sequence. The frame's document has its own focus order, and the browser splices it into the parent's at the frame's position. §9.11 measured one → inner → inner2 → two. The parent's document.activeElement reports the <iframe> element throughout, which is why a recorder that watches only the parent sees one stop — a limitation of the observer, not a property of the platform.

The implication for a custom player is the one measured in §9.7: a <video> without controls has no children in the accessibility tree. Not a reduced set — none. Everything the browser was providing becomes yours:

  • Six controls with roles, accessible names and states, in the user's language, not just in yours.
  • The live region that announces buffering.
  • One tab stop, with arrow-key and space handling inside it, rather than six separate stops.
  • Space to play/pause, arrows to seek and change volume, and whatever conventions the platform's users already have (§14.11).

That list is why the honest advice is to style the native player where possible and build a custom one only when a requirement genuinely demands it. When you do, the empty tree is the specification: every node the browser used to supply is a thing you now owe.

5. Your product embeds a partner's dashboard, and the partner embeds yours. Someone proposes shipping X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN from both sides. What breaks, what is the fix, and what threat is the whole exercise about?

Solution

What breaks: both embeds, immediately. SAMEORIGIN permits framing only by the same origin. Each side's frame of the other is cross-origin by definition, so each browser refuses to render it. The header has no allowlist form — DENY and SAMEORIGIN are the only useful values, and the ALLOW-FROM variant that once existed is not implemented by current browsers.

The fix is frame-ancestors, the CSP directive that replaces the header and does take a list:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example.com

Sent by your application, on the routes that are meant to be embeddable. The partner sends the mirror image. Everything else on both sites should stay at frame-ancestors 'none', because embeddability should be a decision made per route rather than a site-wide default.

Two details from §9.14 that catch people implementing this. It must be a response header: a <meta http-equiv> CSP is explicitly forbidden from carrying frame-ancestors, browsers ignore it there, and the result is a defence that appears to be deployed and is not. And it constrains the whole ancestor chain, not just the immediate parent — so an attacker cannot frame the partner's page in order to reach yours through it.

The threat is clickjacking. An attacker loads your authenticated page in a transparent frame over a decoy, and the user's click on "Play" lands on your "Transfer funds". The request is genuine in every respect — real session, real cookies, real browser, a real click by the real user — so nothing on the server can distinguish it. That is why the defence has to be enforced by the browser before the document renders, and why it is a header rather than anything in the markup.

SameSite=Lax cookies, the default for a cookie with no SameSite attribute in Chromium-based browsers, mean the framed request often does not carry the session at all, which raises the cost of this attack a great deal. It is not the fix: it does nothing against a same-site attacker, and it depends on a default that a SameSite=None cookie somewhere in your stack quietly opts out of. frame-ancestors costs one header at the edge and does not depend on anyone's cookie policy.

SECTION 10

Tables

A table is the only structure in HTML whose meaning runs in two directions at once. Every other element says "this contains that". A table says "this cell belongs to that column and to that row". This whole section is about how that second relationship is set up, because it is the part people leave out.

Leaving it out has a specific cost. A sighted reader works out the relationship from position: the number is under "Revenue" and beside "Q2", so it is Q2's revenue. A screen reader user gets the cells one at a time, and if nothing in the markup says which header a cell belongs to, they get a stream of numbers. The link between a cell and its headers is not decoration. It is the only copy, for that reader, of information the visual layout gives sighted readers for free.

Tables also have the most aggressive error recovery in the parser, which makes them the place where §1.8's silent repairs do the most damage. §10.4 measures it.

10.1 What a Table Is For

A table presents data with two-dimensional relationships: rows that are records, columns that are fields, and cells whose meaning depends on both.

That definition is narrower than it sounds, and it is worth applying honestly. A list of names is a list, not a one-column table. A key/value pair (a term and its definition, a label and a value) is a description list (§5.6). A form's fields are a form. And a page's overall layout is CSS's problem, not a table's, for reasons §10.12 measures.

What really is a table: a price list by size and colour, a schedule by room and hour, a comparison of plans by feature, a financial statement by line item and quarter, an API's parameters by name, type and default. In every one of those, a cell means nothing without its row and column headers, and that is the test.

Tables earned their bad reputation entirely in the years when they were the only way to lay out a page. The element itself is precise, well specified and extremely well supported by assistive technology. Used for data, it is the right answer, and nothing modern replaces it.

10.2 The Anatomy of a Table

<table>
  <caption>Quarterly revenue</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Quarter</th><th scope="col">Revenue</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">Q1</th><td>1200</td></tr>
    <tr><th scope="row">Q2</th><td>1450</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

AX TREE
table "Quarterly revenue"
  caption
    text "Quarterly revenue"
  rowgroup
    row
      columnheader "Quarter"
      columnheader "Revenue"
  row
    rowheader "Q1"
    cell "1200"
  row
    rowheader "Q2"
    cell "1450"

Nine elements make up every table that exists:

<table>
The container. Its children may only be <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> and <tr> (§2.9).
<caption>
The table's title. Must be the first child (§10.8).
<thead> <tbody> <tfoot>
Row groups (§10.3). Each becomes a rowgroup node.
<tr>
A row. May contain only <th> and <td>.
<th>
A header cell — columnheader or rowheader depending on scope (§10.5).
<td>
A data cell. Becomes cell.
<colgroup> <col>
Column-wise styling hooks (§10.9). They carry no semantics.

Read the tree against the markup and one thing stands out: <thead> produced a rowgroup node and <tbody> did not. That is not an error in the measurement. Chrome exposes the explicit <thead> as a row group and flattens the <tbody> holding the ordinary rows, because a table's body is the default and adds nothing for a user moving around by group. The two <th scope="row"> cells became rowheader, and the two in the head became columnheader, which is the distinction scope exists to make.

Notice also where the accessible name came from: the <caption>. The table is named "Quarterly revenue", and the caption also appears as a child node, so a screen reader announces the title on entering the table and again when reading straight through.

10.3 thead, tbody and tfoot

The three row groups do four things, and only the first happens whether you want it or not.

They are inserted whether you write them or not. The parser creates a <tbody> around any <tr> that is not already in a group, so a table written without one still has a <tbody> in its DOM. §10.4 measures this, and it explains why table > tr never matches anything in CSS.

They label the rows semantically. <thead> marks the rows that are headers for the columns beneath them, <tfoot> the summary rows, <tbody> the data. Assistive technology exposes them as row groups, so a user can be told "row 4 of 30, in the table body".

They let a long table repeat its headers when printed. A browser printing a table that runs across pages repeats the <thead> at the top of each page and the <tfoot> at the bottom. This only happens when the rows really are in those elements.

They give CSS a handle: tbody tr:nth-child(even) for zebra striping without hitting the header row.

HTML 4 required <tfoot> to come before the <tbody> in the source; the current specification requires it after, and browsers draw it last either way. Write it last, because a source order that matches the visual order is one that matches the reading order and the DOM order (§14.4).

A table may have several <tbody> elements. That is the correct way to express a table with grouped sections (a schedule grouped by day, an invoice grouped by category), each with its own heading row.

10.4 Foster Parenting: What the Parser Does to Bad Table Markup

Tables are where §1.8's error recovery does its most surprising work, because the table parsing algorithm has a rule no other element has: content that is not allowed in a table is moved out of it, to just before the table. The specification calls this foster parenting.

<table>
  <tr><td>a</td></tr>
  Stray text
  <div>A div</div>
  <tr><td>b</td></tr>
</table>

DOM TREE
#text "\n  Stray text\n  "
<div>
  #text "A div"
<table>
  #text "\n  "
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "a"
    #text "\n  "
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "b"
    #text "\n"

Both the text and the <div> were evicted from the table entirely and re-inserted before it: not at the top of the table, not in the first cell, but as siblings in front of the whole element. The two rows are intact, and they now sit inside a <tbody> the source never wrote.

This is the most confusing failure in HTML, and it has a recognisable signature: content appears above a table when it was written inside one, and it is unstyled, because none of the table's CSS reaches it. A template that outputs a loading spinner or an {{#if}} comment between rows produces exactly this.

The parser's own insertion is the other half:

<table><td>No row</td></table>

DOM TREE
<table>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "No row"

A <td> with no <tr> gets one, and the <tr> gets a <tbody>. The parser will build missing structure around a cell, but it will not tolerate something that is not a cell inside that structure.

Three rules follow, and between them they prevent every instance:

  • Nothing may sit between <table> and <tr> except a row group, a <caption> or a <colgroup>. No wrapper <div>, no template block that outputs a comment, no helper that outputs markup to make whitespace.
  • Nothing may sit between <tr> and its cells. A conditional that wraps a <td> in anything is a bug.
  • A template rendering rows must emit <tr> elements and nothing else at that level. This is why table rows are the most common place where a templating language needs its "no wrapper element" syntax.

check_html.py reports this kind of problem as PARSER-MOVED, and it is the reason that check exists: the markup is not invalid in any way anything else notices, and the page it produces is not the page that was written.

10.5 th, scope, and How a Cell Finds Its Headers

<th> marks a cell as a header. scope says what it is a header for, and it takes four values.

col
Header for every cell below it in its column. The role becomes columnheader.
row
Header for every cell to its side in its row. The role becomes rowheader.
colgroup
Header for a group of columns — the spanning header above a set of sub-headers.
rowgroup
Header for a group of rows — the section heading inside a <tbody>.

scope="col" and scope="row" cover almost everything. The scope attribute matters because without it the browser guesses: a <th> in the first row is taken as a column header, and a <th> in the first column as a row header. The guess is usually right, but it is not something to depend on. The moment a table has headers in both directions, or a header partway down, the guess and the truth silently part ways.

State the scope attribute on every <th>. It is four extra characters, and it turns a guess into a fact.

Here is what the connection between cells and headers looks like for a table with headers in both directions and cells that span several rows or columns:

<table>
  <caption>Room bookings</caption>
  <tr><th scope="col">Room</th><th scope="col" colspan="2">Morning</th></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row" rowspan="2">Blue</th><td>09:00</td><td>Free</td></tr>
  <tr><td>10:00</td><td>Booked</td></tr>
</table>

AX TREE
table "Room bookings"
  caption
    text "Room bookings"
  row
    columnheader "Room"
    columnheader "Morning"
  row
    rowheader "Blue"
    cell "09:00"
    cell "Free"
  row
    cell "10:00"
    cell "Booked"

Three rows, and the second has three children while the third has two. That is because the rowspan="2" cell appears once, in the row where it starts. The accessibility tree does not copy a spanned cell into the rows it covers; the connection is worked out and reported when the user asks about a cell, not by cloning nodes. The same is true of the colspan="2" header: one columnheader "Morning", spanning two columns.

What a screen reader does with this is the point of the whole exercise. Moving to the "Booked" cell announces something like "Blue, Morning, Booked": the row header, the column header, then the content. The algorithm walked left to the nearest rowheader and up to the nearest columnheader. Take the scope attributes away and it announces "Booked".

Two spellings to keep straight when reading other people's tables: scope="col" on a header in the top row, scope="row" on a header at the start of a row. A <th> with neither is guessed, and a scope="col" written on a row header is worse than the guess.

10.6 colspan and rowspan

colspan makes a cell take up several columns; rowspan makes it take up several rows. Both take a positive whole number, both default to 1, and both belong on <th> and <td> alike.

<table>
  <caption>Timetable</caption>
  <tr>
    <th scope="col">Time</th>
    <th scope="col" colspan="2">Weekday</th>
    <th scope="col">Weekend</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">09:00</th>
    <td rowspan="2">Standup</td>
    <td>Focus time</td>
    <td>—</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">10:00</th>
    <td>Review</td>
    <td>—</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Two rules about the arithmetic will save you every debugging session this element causes.

Every row must account for exactly the same number of columns, counting cells covered by a rowspan from above. The second row here has a <th>, a cell spanning two rows and two more cells: four columns. The third row has a <th> plus two cells, which is three written cells plus the one still covered by the rowspan from the row above, making four. Miscount and the table gets a ragged edge, or worse, cells shift a column to the left and every value after them sits under the wrong header.

A cell covered by a span is not written at all. It is not an empty <td>; there is no element there. Writing one pushes the row out by a column, which is the most common way tables go wrong.

rowspan="0" is a legal value meaning "to the end of the row group", and it is worth knowing mainly so you recognise it. colspan="0" was removed and is not supported.

Heavy spanning comes with one honest warning. A table with headers spanning groups, sub-headers beneath them, and data cells that need both is at the limit of what scope can express. It is also at the limit of what a person listening to it from start to finish can follow. When a table needs a diagram to explain it, the better answer is usually two simpler tables.

10.7 headers and id: The Explicit Escape Hatch

When scope cannot express the connection, the headers attribute states it directly. Each cell lists the id of every header that applies to it:

<table>
  <caption>Shipping costs</caption>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <th id="std" scope="col">Standard</th>
    <th id="exp" scope="col">Express</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th id="uk" scope="row">UK</th>
    <td headers="uk std">£3.50</td>
    <td headers="uk exp">£7.00</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th id="eu" scope="row">EU</th>
    <td headers="eu std">£8.00</td>
    <td headers="eu exp">£14.00</td>
  </tr>
</table>

The headers attribute takes a space-separated list of IDs, and for that cell it overrides the automatic algorithm completely. That is both its strength and its danger. It is exact, and it is entirely manual, so a table maintained by hand will drift out of step with itself the first time someone inserts a column and does not update forty headers lists.

Use it in the cases scope genuinely cannot reach:

  • A cell that belongs to a header that is neither in its row nor in its column, as in a table with a block of headers off to one side.
  • Irregular tables where spans make the "nearest header" search ambiguous.
  • Tables with more than two levels of header, where a cell needs a group header and a column header and a row header.

Otherwise prefer scope. It is shorter, it survives editing, and when it is missing the browser falls back to its guess rather than to nothing. The rule of thumb: if you are reaching for headers on a table you generate in a loop, the table is probably too complex, and splitting it is a better fix than annotating it.

Note the empty <td> in the corner. A table with both row and column headers has a top-left cell that is a header for neither, and an empty <td> is the correct thing to put there. A <th> would claim to be a header for something.

10.8 caption

<caption> gives the table a title. It must be the first child of <table>, before any <colgroup>, row group or row.

<table>
  <caption>Population by region, 2025 census</caption>
  <tr><th scope="col">Region</th><th scope="col">Population</th></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">North</th><td>2,410,000</td></tr>
</table>

The caption is the table's accessible name (§10.2's tree measured it), and it is how a user moving between a page's tables can tell them apart. A screen reader's "list all tables" command shows the captions; a page with four tables and no captions shows four entries called "table".

Three practical points.

A visible caption is better than a hidden one. The instinct is to hide it, because the page already has a heading above the table. Resist it. The caption is useful to everybody, and it stays attached to the table when the table is scrolled or copied out. A heading is a separate element that a screen reader may not connect with the table at all.

A caption is not a heading. Do not put an <h3> inside it. It is already announced as the table's name, and a heading inside would appear in the page's heading outline as though it were a section (§6.3).

aria-label and aria-labelledby work on a <table> too, and they are the fallback when the design really cannot show a caption. Prefer the caption. Under §13.3's order of priority an aria-label would override it anyway, which causes confusion when both exist.

Add a <caption> even when it feels redundant, because §10.10 measures what a table without one costs.

10.9 col and colgroup

<colgroup> and <col> describe a table's columns before its rows. They are the only elements in a table that refer to a column directly.

<table>
  <colgroup>
    <col span="2" class="numeric">
    <col>
  </colgroup>
  <tr><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>3</td></tr>
</table>

DOM TREE
<table>
  #text "\n  "
  <colgroup>
    #text "\n    "
    <col span="2" class="numeric">
    #text "\n    "
    <col>
    #text "\n  "
  #text "\n  "
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        #text "1"
      <td>
        #text "2"
      <td>
        #text "3"
    #text "\n"

The span attribute says how many columns a <col> covers. Here the first <col> covers columns one and two, and the second covers column three. <col> is a void element and appears only inside <colgroup>, and <colgroup> appears only after the <caption> and before any rows.

Two things to be clear about.

They carry no semantics. Nothing in the accessibility tree changes when you add them. They do not make a column a header, and they are not an alternative to scope. They exist as a hook for styling and widths, and CSS can set only a small set of properties through them: background, border, width, visibility: collapse.

They are the only way to say "this column is 40% wide" once instead of on every cell in it. That is a real convenience for a wide table, and together with table-layout: fixed it is how a table gets predictable column widths without the browser measuring all the content first.

Whether they earn their place is a judgement call. For a table generated from data, a class on the <col> is cleaner than a class on every <td>. For a hand-written table with three columns, they are ceremony.

The span attribute is the only attribute either element really has. On a <col> the span attribute says how many columns that one <col> covers; on a <colgroup> it does the same for the group, and a <colgroup> with a span may not contain <col> children.

10.10 The Accessibility Tree of a Table, and How It Can Vanish

This is the measurement that justifies every rule above. Two tables, differing only in whether they have a caption:

<table>
  <caption>No headers at all</caption>
  <tr><td>a</td><td>b</td></tr>
</table>

AX TREE
table "No headers at all"
  caption
    text "No headers at all"
  row
    cell "a"
    cell "b"

<table>
  <tr><td>a</td><td>b</td></tr>
</table>

AX TREE
LayoutTable
  LayoutTableRow
    LayoutTableCell "a"
    LayoutTableCell "b"

The second table is not a table. LayoutTable, LayoutTableRow and LayoutTableCell are not ARIA roles at all. They are Chrome's internal marker for "this looks like it is being used for layout", and a node marked that way is not exposed to assistive technology as a table. It has no row or column count, it does not appear in the list of tables, and the commands for moving between cells do not work in it.

Chrome guesses, in other words. The guess is triggered by a table having no <th>, no <caption>, no <thead>, no summary and nothing else that signals data. The heuristic exists because of the layout-table era (§10.12), and it is generally the right call. But it means a genuine data table with plain <td> cells and no caption silently stops being a table.

The defence is the same either way, and it costs almost nothing: give every data table a <caption> and a row of <th scope="col"> headers. Both signal that the table holds data, either one alone is enough to defeat the guess, and each is worth having for its own sake.

The role names to know for the real thing, all of which §10.2 and §10.5 measured: table, caption, rowgroup, row, columnheader, rowheader, cell. Their ARIA equivalents exist (role="table", role="row", role="cell" and so on), and they produce the same tree from <div> elements. That is occasionally necessary and always more work, because none of the automatic header connection, none of the navigation and none of the parser's structure-building comes with it. You would be rebuilding scope by hand with aria-rowindex and aria-colindex. Use <table>.

10.11 Sortable Tables and aria-sort

A sortable table needs three things in the markup, and the third is where people stop too early.

<table>
  <caption>Files</caption>
  <tr>
    <th scope="col" aria-sort="ascending"><button type="button">Name</button></th>
    <th scope="col" aria-sort="none"><button type="button">Size</button></th>
  </tr>
  <tr><td>a.txt</td><td>12 KB</td></tr>
</table>

The control is a <button> inside the <th>, not a click handler on the <th> itself. A <th> cannot take focus, has no button role and does not respond to Enter or Space, so a clickable header cell is a control only a mouse can use (§7.2). Putting a real button inside it costs nothing visually (the button can be styled to fill the cell), and it gives you keyboard operation, a focus indicator and the correct role for free.

aria-sort goes on the <th>, not on the button, and takes ascending, descending, other or none. Exactly one header in a table should have a value other than none at a time, because a table is sorted by one column.

And here is the honest limitation. Chrome's Accessibility.getFullAXTree does not expose aria-sort as a property in the build these measurements were made with, the same gap §13.5 records for aria-current. The tree for the markup above shows columnheader "Name" with a button "Name" inside it and no sort state anywhere, so this is one claim in the section the tool cannot check for you. Real assistive technology does receive it, through the operating system's accessibility interfaces; it is the browser's debugging interface that leaves it out.

The rest of the pattern is behaviour rather than markup. Clicking the button re-sorts the rows and updates aria-sort on all the headers. And because the table's contents changed without a page load, it announces the change in a live region (§13.7), something like "Sorted by name, ascending". Without that announcement, a screen reader user presses the button and hears nothing at all, because the visual change happens nowhere near where their cursor is.

Do not sort by moving DOM nodes into an order different from the visual one. §14.4's rule applies here too: the accessibility tree and the tab order follow the DOM, so a table whose DOM order and visual order disagree is read out in the wrong sequence.

10.12 Layout Tables and role="presentation"

For about a decade a <table> was the only way to put two things side by side, and the web is still full of markup from that time. More to the point, HTML email is still written that way today, because email programs support almost no CSS.

A layout table is a table used for positioning rather than data. It has no headers, no caption, and no relationship between a cell and the cells around it. Exposing it as a table does real harm: the user is told "table with 3 columns and 8 rows", offered cell navigation, and told the column header for each cell, none of which corresponds to anything.

The fix is one attribute:

<table role="presentation">
  <tr><td>Logo</td><td>Navigation</td></tr>
</table>

AX TREE
text "Logo"
text "Navigation"

The table, the row and both cells are gone. All that survives is the text they contained. This is ARIA's presentational children rule. role="presentation" (and its synonym role="none") removes the element from the accessibility tree, and for an element whose children only make sense as part of it (a table's rows and cells, a list's items), it removes those required children too. §13.8 covers the general mechanism; this is its most dramatic example.

Note what it does not do. The content is still there, still drawn, and still focusable if it contains a control. Only the structure is removed, which is exactly right for a layout table: the text was real, and the grid was scaffolding.

Two rules for using it:

  • A layout table gets role="presentation", always. If you cannot avoid the layout table (an HTML email, a legacy template you are not allowed to restructure), this attribute is the entire fix, and it takes seconds.
  • A data table must never get it. This is not a hypothetical mistake but a real and recurring one, made to silence an accessibility linter that complained about a table with no headers. The correct fix for that warning is a <caption> and scope attributes, not deleting the table from the tree.

For a page's layout, none of this applies: use CSS grid or flexbox. The layout table is a compatibility measure for environments without CSS, and only one of those that matters is left.

role="none" means exactly the same as role="presentation". It was added because "presentation" was widely misread as "this is presentational and therefore fine". Use whichever reads better to you; role="none" is the newer spelling and does precisely the same thing.

10.13 Wide Tables

A table with twelve columns does not fit on a phone, and the honest answer is that no markup solves this: the data really is wider than the screen. What HTML can do is make the overflow usable instead of broken.

The markup half of the solution is a scroll container that has a name and can take focus:

<div role="region" aria-labelledby="rev-cap" tabindex="0" style="overflow-x:auto">
  <table>
    <caption id="rev-cap">Revenue by region and quarter</caption>
    <tr><th scope="col">Region</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Q2</th></tr>
    <tr><th scope="row">North</th><td>1200</td><td>1450</td></tr>
  </table>
</div>

TAB ORDER
<div> "Revenue by region and qu"
(leaves the page)

Every part of that wrapper is load-bearing.

overflow-x: auto is what makes the table scroll instead of spilling out of the page. Without it, a wide table makes the whole document scroll sideways, which breaks everything else on the page.

tabindex="0" makes the container a focus stop, as the measured tab order confirms. This is the one place a tabindex="0" on a non-interactive element is not just acceptable but required: a scrollable region that cannot take focus cannot be scrolled with the arrow keys, so a keyboard user simply cannot reach the right-hand columns. Browsers are gradually making scrollable regions focusable by default; until that is universal, state it.

role="region" plus aria-labelledby pointing at the caption gives the container a name and makes it a landmark (§13.6). You can see that in the measurement above: the stop is recorded as <div> "Revenue by region and qu…" and not as a bare <div>, because the caption's text became the region's accessible name. So the focus stop announces itself as "Revenue by region and quarter, region" instead of being an unexplained pause on an anonymous element.

The other approaches are worth knowing, so you can reject them for the right reasons. Reflowing each row into a stacked card with CSS is readable, but it loses the column-by-column comparison a table exists for, and doing it with display: block on table elements destroys the accessibility tree unless the roles are put back with ARIA. Hiding columns below a breakpoint hides data, which is a product decision rather than a CSS one. A pinned first column keeps the row header visible while scrolling and is genuinely good; it is position: sticky on the <th scope="row"> cells, and it is CSS, not markup.

The work is divided the same way as everywhere in this course: the markup establishes what the thing is (a named, reachable region containing a table with headers), and css_mastery decides how it behaves at 375 pixels.

Exercises

1. This table is rendered with the first row bold and centred by CSS. What is wrong with it, and what does a screen reader user hear?

<table>
  <tr><td class="head">Product</td><td class="head">Price</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Skillet</td><td>£48</td></tr>
</table>
Solution

Nothing in the markup says the first row is headers. The cells are <td> with a class, and a class carries no meaning to the browser at all (§2.10). The visual weight was added by CSS, which the accessibility tree does not read.

So the table is not even a table. §10.10 measured it: with no <th>, no <caption> and no <thead>, Chrome classifies it as LayoutTable / LayoutTableRow / LayoutTableCell — internal markers that are not exposed to assistive technology as a table at all. The user does not get "table with 2 columns", cannot use table navigation, and is not told a column header for any cell.

What they hear is the four cell contents read as ordinary text in document order: "Product Price Skillet £48". In a table of forty products that is eighty values in a row with no structure, and the relationship between "£48" and "Price" exists nowhere but on the screen.

The fix is three changes, none of which affects the rendering once the CSS selector is updated:

<table>
  <caption>Cookware prices</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Product</th><th scope="col">Price</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">Skillet</th><td>£48</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<th> instead of <td class="head"> — the element already means "header", and browsers already render it bold and centred, so the class was reimplementing the default. scope on each, turning the browser's heuristic into a statement (§10.5). A <caption>, which names the table and by itself would have defeated the LayoutTable heuristic. And <th scope="row"> on the product name, so each price is announced with both its column and its row: "Skillet, Price, £48".

2. A template renders <table> with a {{#each}} block that emits <tr> elements, and a colleague adds a <div class="loading"> inside the same block to show while data streams in. The spinner appears above the table, unstyled. Explain exactly what happened.

Solution

Foster parenting (§10.4). The table parsing algorithm has a rule no other element has: content that is not permitted inside a table is not dropped and not left where it is — it is moved out and re-inserted immediately before the table.

<div> is not one of the elements a <table> may contain (§2.9 — that list is <caption>, <colgroup>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot>, <tr>), so the parser evicted it. §10.4's measurement shows exactly this: a <div> written between two rows comes out as a sibling preceding the table, with the rows intact inside it.

That explains both symptoms. Above the table, because that is where foster parenting puts it. Unstyled, because every selector written for it presumably starts inside the table — .table-wrapper table .loading matches nothing, since the element is no longer a descendant of the table.

There is a third symptom the colleague has not noticed yet: document.querySelector('table .loading') returns null, so any script that tries to remove the spinner when data arrives fails silently.

The fix is that the spinner cannot be inside the table. Either put it outside:

<div class="loading">Loading…</div>
<table>
  <caption>Orders</caption>
  <tr><th scope="col">Order</th><th scope="col">Total</th></tr>
</table>

or, if it must be positioned within the table's area, put it in a cell that spans the width:

<tbody>
  <tr><td colspan="3" class="loading">Loading…</td></tr>
</tbody>

The general rule for templating a table: at the row level, emit <tr> elements and nothing else — no wrappers, no conditionals that produce elements, no comment nodes from the template engine. This is why every templating language has a "fragment" or "no wrapper" syntax, and tables are the main reason it exists.

3. When is headers the right tool and scope the wrong one? Give a concrete table, and state the maintenance cost you are accepting.

Solution

scope works by a walk: from a cell, look left for the nearest rowheader and up for the nearest columnheader. It is right whenever a cell's headers really are the ones directly above and to the left of it — which covers the great majority of tables.

The headers attribute is the right tool when that walk gives the wrong answer. The clearest case is a three-level header where a cell needs a group header, a sub-header and a row header at once:

<table>
  <caption>Sales by channel and quarter</caption>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <th id="q1" scope="colgroup" colspan="2">Q1</th>
    <th id="q2" scope="colgroup" colspan="2">Q2</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <th id="q1o" scope="col">Online</th>
    <th id="q1r" scope="col">Retail</th>
    <th id="q2o" scope="col">Online</th>
    <th id="q2r" scope="col">Retail</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th id="uk" scope="row">UK</th>
    <td headers="uk q1 q1o">1200</td>
    <td headers="uk q1 q1r">800</td>
    <td headers="uk q2 q2o">1450</td>
    <td headers="uk q2 q2r">910</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Without headers, "Online" appears twice as a column header and the walk cannot tell you which quarter's online figure a cell is — it announces "UK, Online, 1450", which is ambiguous between two columns. With it, the announcement carries all three: "UK, Q1, Online, 1200".

The maintenance cost is real and worth stating out loud. Every headers value is a hand-written list of IDs with no tooling behind it. Inserting a quarter means editing every data cell in the table. A renamed id breaks the association silently — there is no error, the cell simply loses a header. And nothing in the build catches it, because a headers value pointing at a non-existent id is not a parse error.

So the decision is a trade. Accept it for a hand-maintained, structurally fixed table like a specification's parameter list. Avoid it for anything generated in a loop, where the annotation has to be generated too and the generator has to know the grid geometry — at which point it is easier and more robust to reshape the data into two simpler tables, one per quarter, each of which scope handles perfectly.

The other legitimate use is the irregular table where heavy rowspan and colspan make "nearest header" genuinely ambiguous. The same advice applies: it is a signal the table is complex enough to be worth splitting.

4. An accessibility linter reports "table has no headers" on a table used to lay out an HTML email signature. A developer adds role="presentation". A second linter reports the same warning on the product-comparison table, and the same developer applies the same fix. Assess both decisions.

Solution

The first is correct and is the intended use. An email signature laid out with a table is a layout table: no headers, no caption, no relationship between adjacent cells. Exposed as a table it tells the user "table, 2 columns, 3 rows" and offers cell navigation for a grid that means nothing. §10.12 measured what role="presentation" does — the table, row and cell nodes all disappear and only the text survives — and that is exactly the desired result. HTML email is also the one context where the layout table is still defensible, because email clients support almost no CSS.

The second is a serious mistake, and it is worse than the warning it silenced. A product-comparison table is the archetypal data table: every cell means "this product, this attribute". Applying role="presentation" deletes the table, its rows and all its cells from the accessibility tree, leaving a flat run of text. A screen reader user goes from a table they can navigate cell by cell to an undifferentiated stream of product names, prices and feature ticks with nothing indicating which belongs to which. The linter's complaint was correct and the "fix" removed the evidence rather than the defect.

The correct fix for the second table is to give it what it was missing:

<table>
  <caption>Plan comparison</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Feature</th><th scope="col">Basic</th><th scope="col">Pro</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">Storage</th><td>10 GB</td><td>1 TB</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The general lesson is about the shape of the error, not this attribute. A warning that a data table has no headers has two possible responses: add the headers, or declare that it is not a data table. Only one of those is true of any given table, and the truth is a property of the content, not of how loud the linter is. role="presentation", aria-hidden and tabindex="-1" are all attributes whose main real-world use is silencing a tool, and all three make the page worse when applied to something the tool was right about. §13.9's rules exist for exactly this: the first rule of ARIA is to use the native element, and the second is not to change native semantics unless you must.

There is also a smaller point worth making to the developer. Both tables would have passed the linter with a <caption> alone, and §10.10 measured why that matters beyond the linter: a caption is what stops Chrome demoting the table to LayoutTable and makes it findable in the browse-by-table list.

5. Design the markup for a twelve-column data table that must work on a 375-pixel phone. Cover keyboard, screen reader and the case where the user rotates the device.

Solution

Start from the honest position: twelve columns of data do not fit in 375 pixels, and no markup makes them fit. What markup can do is make the overflow reachable, labelled and navigable. So the answer is a horizontally scrolling region, done properly.

<div role="region" aria-labelledby="usage-cap" tabindex="0" class="table-scroll">
  <table>
    <caption id="usage-cap">Usage by service and month, 2025</caption>
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th scope="col">Service</th>
        <th scope="col">Jan</th>
        <th scope="col">Feb</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><th scope="row">Storage</th><td>412</td><td>438</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</div>

The wrapper carries overflow-x: auto, so the table scrolls inside its own box. Without it the whole document scrolls sideways, which breaks the header, the navigation and every fixed element on the page.

tabindex="0" on the wrapper, because a scrollable region that is not focusable cannot be scrolled from the keyboard, and the right-hand columns become unreachable without a mouse. §10.13's tab order measured that the container becomes a stop.
