This is the rare legitimate tabindex="0" on a non-interactive element (§14.3) — it exists because the element genuinely does have a keyboard behaviour.

role="region" with aria-labelledby pointing at the caption, so that focus stop announces itself. A bare focusable <div> is a stop with no name and no explanation, which is worse than not having one.

Every <th> keeps its scope, and the row header is a <th scope="row">. This is what makes the table survivable when scrolled: the user cannot see the "Service" column while looking at December, and the announcement of each cell carries its row header regardless of what is on screen. It is the single most important part of the answer, and it is not a mobile technique — it is just correct table markup, which happens to matter most here.

Pin the first column with position: sticky on the <th scope="row"> cells so the sighted user gets visually what the screen reader user already gets from scope. That is CSS, and it is the one visual affordance that genuinely fixes the wide-table experience.

On rotation nothing needs to change: the region gets wider, the scrollbar may disappear, and the markup is identical. That is the argument for the scroll container over the alternatives — it has one layout that degrades continuously, rather than a breakpoint at which the table becomes a different structure.

Why not the stacked-card reflow, which is the common suggestion. Turning each row into a card with display: block on the table elements destroys the accessibility tree — the table, row and cell roles all disappear, the same way §10.12's role="presentation" does — and it has to be rebuilt with ARIA roles by hand. It also loses the comparison down a column, which is the reason the data is in a table. It is a reasonable answer for a two-column table and a bad one for twelve.

SECTION 11

Forms I — Controls, Labels and Input Types

Forms are the only part of HTML through which a user hands something back. Everything else is a document; a form is a conversation. Forms also have far more built-in behaviour than any other part of HTML:

  • twenty-two input types;
  • a validation engine (§12);
  • a submission algorithm (the browser's rules for what gets sent);
  • keyboard and platform conventions;
  • and an accessibility contract.

They are also the part most often thrown away and rebuilt badly in JavaScript.

The thread running through this section is that the platform has already done the work. A <select> on a phone opens the phone's own picker. <input type="date"> produces a calendar, a date format that suits the user's locale, and three spin controls the user can move between separately. <input type="email"> changes the on-screen keyboard and checks its own format for free. None of that survives being replaced by a <div> with a click handler.

11.1 The Form and Its Controls

A <form> is a container that owns a set of controls and knows where to send them. Two attributes carry that information: the action attribute, which is the URL, and the method attribute, which is how to send it (§12.3).

<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

That is a complete, working, accessible form. It checks the email address, it submits without a line of JavaScript, it works with a screen reader, and on any browser ever made it falls back to a plain HTTP POST. Everything else in this section is a variation on it.

The form control elements are <input>, <button>, <select>, <textarea> and <output>, plus the grouping elements <fieldset> and <legend> and the helper <datalist>. Two properties are shared by all of them and worth stating once:

A control needs a name
Without name attribute its value is never submitted (§12.2). The id attribute is for linking a label; the name attribute is for the server. They are different things and are frequently, harmlessly, given the same string.
A control needs a label
Without one it has no accessible name (§13.3), and a screen reader announces "edit text, blank". This is the most common accessibility failure on the web and the easiest to avoid.

<form> elements cannot be nested. The parser does not merely ignore an inner <form>: it drops it entirely, silently, and the controls inside it become part of the outer form (§1.8). When a layout seems to demand nesting, the form attribute (§12.6) is the answer.

Two attributes on the <form> carry the whole submission. The action attribute is the URL the request goes to, and the method attribute is the HTTP method it uses (§12.3). An omitted action attribute means the current URL, and an omitted method attribute means get, so a form with neither submits a GET to the page it is on. That is occasionally what you want and usually an oversight. The <legend> belongs to <fieldset>, not to <form> (§11.12). It is the one element whose text names a group of controls rather than a single one, and a <legend> must be the fieldset's first child.

11.2 Labels

A <label> connects human-readable text to a control. There are exactly two correct ways to write one.

<label for="postcode">Postcode</label>
<input id="postcode" name="postcode">

<label>Postcode <input name="postcode2"></label>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Postcode"
textbox "Postcode"
LabelText
  text "Postcode"
  textbox "Postcode"

The first uses the for attribute, pointing at the control's id attribute. The second wraps the control and needs no ids at all. Both produce a textbox named "Postcode", which is why the tree above shows them as equivalent.

Prefer the explicit for attribute form. It survives the two things that break wrapping: a layout that needs the label and the field in different grid cells, and a component library that renders them separately. The wrapping form is genuinely useful for checkboxes and radios (§11.6), where the label sits right beside the control anyway.

A label does three things, and only the first is about screen readers:

It names the control
Step 3 of the accessible name computation (§13.3), announced on focus.
It extends the hit area
Clicking the word "Postcode" focuses the field. On a checkbox this roughly triples the target, which matters for anyone with imprecise pointing — and for everyone on a phone.
It survives
Unlike placeholder, it is still there after the user types (§13.3).

Three ways of labelling that are not labels: placeholder (it disappears, and its contrast is low), title (invisible to keyboard and touch users), and a <div> placed next to the field (no connection at all). The first two do produce an accessible name, so they pass simple automated checks while failing real users; §13.3 has the trees.

When a control really has no visible label (a search field whose button says "Search", a table of rows each with a "quantity" spinner), use aria-label, and accept that you have given up the larger click area and the visible text. A visually hidden label is usually better: real <label> markup, clipped out of sight with CSS. It keeps every benefit above except visibility.

The two forms have names worth using in review. An explicit label is <label for="id"> pointing at the control's id; an implicit label is a <label> that wraps the control, with no for at all. An explicit label keeps working when the two are separated in the markup (a table cell, a grid, a component boundary), and it is the one to default to. An implicit label needs no id and cannot drift out of step, which makes it right for a checkbox and its text. Using both at once on one control is the one combination to avoid.

11.3 One Element, Twenty-Two Types

<input> is a void element whose type attribute selects an entirely different control. The complete list:

text
search
email
url
tel
password
number
range
date
time
datetime-local
month
week
checkbox
radio
file
color
hidden
submit
reset
button
image

An unrecognised type attribute falls back to text, which is what makes the newer types safe to use everywhere. An ancient browser shows a text box, a current one shows a date picker, and both submit the same string.

The last four are old ways of writing a button. Use <button> (§11.8) instead, because it can contain markup. <input type="image"> in particular is a submit button drawn as an image; it needs an alt attribute, and it is almost always better as a <button> with an <img> inside.

The types are not cosmetic. Each one gives you three things at once, and the tree shows the third:

<label for="a">Email</label><input id="a" type="email">
<label for="b">Search</label><input id="b" type="search">
<label for="c">Volume</label><input id="c" type="range">
<label for="d">Upload</label><input id="d" type="file">
<label for="e">Brand</label><input id="e" type="color">

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Email"
textbox "Email"
LabelText
  text "Search"
searchbox "Search"
LabelText
  text "Volume"
slider "Volume" orientation=horizontal valuemax=100 valuemin=0 valuetext=50
LabelText
  text "Upload"
button "Upload"
LabelText
  text "Brand"
ColorWell "Brand"

type="search" produced a searchbox rather than a textbox. type="range" produced a slider with its default bounds of 0–100 and a current value of 50. And type="file" produced a button, which is exactly right: the control does not hold text, it opens a picker. On a phone, email, tel and url each bring up a different on-screen keyboard. That is the biggest usability difference in this section, and it costs one word of markup.

Four of the types are worth naming together, because they exist purely to change the on-screen keyboard and the browser's own checks. type="url" demands a scheme and offers a .com key. type="tel" offers a numeric keypad and checks nothing. type="password" hides the characters. type="color" opens the platform's colour picker and always has a value. Note the difference: type="url" checks its value and type="tel" does not, because phone number formats vary too much to check. And type="password" is about display, not security, since the value travels exactly as type="url" or type="color" would.

Three more of the twenty-two are worth naming here. type="range" is a slider, and the value it produces is imprecise by design: type="range" is for a setting where the exact number does not matter, such as a volume. type="file" opens the platform's file picker and is the only type whose value cannot be set from script (§11.7). And note that the alt attribute appears on one input type: type="image", a submit button shown as a picture, where the alt attribute supplies the button's accessible name exactly as it would on an <img> (§8.3).

11.4 Text and Text-Like Types

text is the default and the fallback. The other five in its family differ in what they check, what keyboard they bring up, and what the platform offers to fill in.

email
Validates the format (§12.7). With multiple attribute, accepts a comma-separated list. Mobile keyboards gain @.
url
Requires a scheme, so example.com is rejected and https://example.com is accepted. Worth a hint saying so.
tel
Validates nothing — phone number formats vary too much worldwide for a single rule. Its value is the telephone keypad. Add pattern attribute only if you genuinely know your users' country.
password
Masks the value on screen. It does nothing about transport — that is HTTPS's job — and the value is in the DOM in plain text.
search
A searchbox role, a clear button in most browsers, and a "Search" key on mobile.

Two attributes shape all of them. maxlength both stops typing past the limit and reports a violation; minlength only reports, and only after the user edits (§12.7). The size attribute sets the visible width in characters and is left over from presentational HTML. Set the width in CSS instead, because size cannot adapt to the screen.

Three attributes shape a text field. The size attribute is the visible width in characters, a presentational hint that CSS overrides, so the size attribute is rarely worth setting. The pattern attribute holds a regular expression the value must match, and a pattern attribute should always come with a title explaining the requirement, because the browser's own message quotes neither. The multiple attribute allows several comma-separated values, and it applies to type="email" and to type="file"; a multiple attribute on any other input type does nothing.

11.5 Numbers and Dates

number gives a spinner and rejects anything that is not a number. Its trap is the step attribute, which defaults to 1:

<label for="q">Quantity</label>
<input id="q" type="number" min="1" max="9" step="1">
<label for="w">Weight in kg</label>
<input id="w" type="number" min="0" step="0.01">

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Quantity"
spinbutton "Quantity" valuemax=9 valuemin=1
LabelText
  text "Weight in kg"
spinbutton "Weight in kg"

Without step="0.01", the second field would reject 1.5, because the default step allows only whole numbers (§12.8 measures exactly this). step="any" turns the check off entirely.

number is also the wrong control for things that merely look numeric. Postcodes, credit card numbers, phone numbers and account references are strings that happen to contain digits: they can start with zeros, they have no order, and a spinner on them is nonsense. Use type="text" with inputmode="numeric", which gives the numeric keyboard without treating the value as a number.

range is a slider, and its defining property is that it shows no visible value. Use it only where the exact number does not matter (volume, a rough price filter), or pair it with an <output> (§11.13) that shows the number.

The five date and time types produce real pickers, and the value they submit is always ISO 8601 (the international date format), however it was displayed:

date
2026-08-27
A calendar. Displayed in the user's locale format, submitted as ISO.
time
14:30
24-hour value; displayed as AM/PM where that is the local convention.
datetime-local
2026-08-27T14:30
No time zone at all — the name is literal. Send the zone separately if you need it.
month
2026-08
Expiry dates, billing periods.
week
2026-W35
ISO week numbering. Rarely what anyone wants.

The min attribute and max attribute work on all five, so "no date in the past" is one attribute. The reason the split between display and value matters: a user in Germany sees 27.08.2026, a user in the United States sees 08/27/2026, and your server receives 2026-08-27 from both. Parsing dates written in each country's style is a problem the platform has already solved.

The date and time family is five types, and they differ only in how precise a value they collect: type="date" a calendar day, type="time" a clock time, type="datetime-local" both with no time zone, type="month" a year and month, and type="week" an ISO week. The values are ISO 8601 strings in every case: type="month" gives 2026-03, type="week" gives 2026-W11, type="time" gives 09:00, and type="datetime-local" gives 2026-03-14T09:00 with no offset. That missing offset is exactly why it is called local, and why a booking system needs the time zone alongside it. type="number" belongs to the same group in spirit: use type="number" for a quantity you would do arithmetic on, and a text field with inputmode for a card number or a postcode.

The three numeric constraints work together. The min attribute and the max attribute limit the value, and the measurement in §13.5 shows them becoming valuemin and valuemax in the accessibility tree with no ARIA in the markup. The step attribute sets how fine the steps are, and it is the one that surprises people: step defaults to 1 on type="number", so a price field needs step="0.01" or every decimal value is invalid. A step attribute of any turns the constraint off. All three also apply to the date and time types. There the min attribute is a date or time, and the step attribute counts the type's own unit: days for type="date", seconds for type="time". So min="2026-01-01" on a type="date" field is how you refuse a booking in the past, and step="7" on a type="date" restricts it to one day of the week. (Measured in Chromium: with min="2026-01-05" and step="7", 2026-01-06 is a step mismatch and 2026-01-12 is not; on type="time", step="7" rejects 09:00:05.)

11.6 Checkboxes and Radios

These two look similar and mean opposite things. A checkbox is an independent yes/no. A radio button is one choice from a set.

<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery speed</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="std" checked> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="exp"> Express</label>
</fieldset>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="gift" value="yes"> Gift wrap</label>

AX TREE
group "Delivery speed"
  Legend
    text "Delivery speed"
  radio "Standard" checked=true
  radio "Express" checked=false
checkbox "Gift wrap" checked=false

A radio group is defined by a shared name attribute, and that is the whole mechanism. Same name, same group, one value submitted. Different names give you two independent radios that can both be selected, which is a bug that looks like a styling problem.

Four rules follow from the submission algorithm (§12.2), and they are worth memorising:

Unchecked sends nothing
Not off, not empty — absent. The server must read absence as false.
Always set value
A checkbox with no value attribute submits the string on, which reads badly everywhere it appears.
Give radios a default
A group with nothing checked can be left unanswered and, once answered, cannot be unanswered — there is no way back to "none" without a script or an explicit "no preference" option.
Group them in a <fieldset>
The <legend> is the question; the labels are the answers. Without it a screen reader announces "Standard, radio button" with no clue what is being chosen.

The keyboard behaviour differs too, and it shows why native controls are worth keeping. Tab moves into a radio group once and out of it once; the arrow keys move between the options, selecting as they go. A checkbox gets its own tab stop and toggles with Space. Doing that with <div>s means building a roving tabindex (§14.6) by hand.

The two types in this pair are type="checkbox" and type="radio", and the checked attribute works identically on both. It is a boolean giving the starting state, and after the user touches the control, the checked attribute and the .checked property go their separate ways, exactly as §2.3 measured for value. type="radio" also needs every member of a group to share one name, which is what makes them mutually exclusive. type="checkbox" has no such relationship, and several checkboxes sharing a name simply submit several values.

11.7 File Inputs

<label for="cv">Curriculum vitae</label>
<input id="cv" type="file" name="cv" accept=".pdf,application/pdf">

Three attributes matter. The accept attribute filters the picker to the listed extensions or MIME types. It is a convenience, not a control, since the user can override it and a request need not come from your page at all (§12.13). The multiple attribute allows several files. And capture asks a mobile device to open the camera or microphone directly instead of the file browser.

Two hard requirements. The form must be method="post" with enctype="multipart/form-data" (§12.4), or the file is not sent at all. And the server must check the file's content, not its filename.

The control cannot be pre-filled. Setting value on a file input is ignored, by design: a page that could put a path there could read any file on the machine. That is also why styling it is awkward. The button is drawn by the browser, and the usual technique is to hide the input and put a <label> in front of it, which works because clicking a label activates its control.

The accept attribute filters what the picker offers: MIME types, wildcards such as image/*, or extensions. It is a convenience, not a constraint. The accept attribute changes the dialog's default filter, the user can still choose anything, and so the server must check the type regardless.

11.8 Buttons

<button> has three types, and the default is not the one people expect.

submit
The default. Submits the owning form. A <button> inside a form with no type attribute submits it — which is why an unmarked "Show more" button reloads the page.
button
Does nothing on its own. What you want for every script-driven button inside a form.
reset
Restores every control to its markup value. Almost always a mistake to offer: it sits beside submit and destroys the user's work with no confirmation.

<button> beats <input type="submit"> because its label is its content rather than an attribute, so it can contain an icon, a <strong> or a line break. And it beats a <div> with a click handler in every way at once: it can take focus, Enter and Space activate it, it is announced as a button, it submits forms, it respects disabled, and it appears in a screen reader's list of buttons. §13.9's first rule discusses all of this.

The choice between a button and a link is not a matter of style. A link goes somewhere; a button does something. If the result is a different URL the user could bookmark, it is an <a href> (§7.2). If it changes something on this page, it is a <button>. Getting this wrong breaks middle-click, Ctrl-click, the back button and the screen reader's list of links.

Of the three, type="submit" is the default, and that is the whole trap: a <button> with no type inside a form is type="submit" and will submit it. Write type="button" on any button that is not meant to.

11.9 Select and Its Options

<label for="city">City</label>
<select id="city" name="city">
  <option value="">Choose a city</option>
  <optgroup label="England">
    <option value="bath">Bath</option>
    <option value="york" selected>York</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "City"
combobox "City" expanded=false haspopup=menu
  MenuListPopup
    option "Choose a city" selected=false
    group "England"
      option "Bath" selected=false
      option "York" selected=true

Three things in that tree. A <select> is a combobox, not a list: it carries expanded=false and haspopup=menu, because the options are behind a popup. The options themselves appear inside a MenuListPopup, each with its own selected state. And <optgroup> produced a group named by its label attribute. That attribute is required, and it is the only way to label the group.

An <option> submits its value attribute, or its text if it has none. The first option is selected by default. That is why a placeholder option with value="" is the standard way to force a deliberate choice: combined with the required attribute, an empty value fails validation.

The multiple attribute changes the control entirely. It becomes a scrolling list box with a listbox role and multiselectable=true, and it submits one entry per selected option. Users also widely dislike it, because they do not discover that Ctrl is needed. A group of checkboxes is nearly always the better interface.

<select> has historically been impossible to style, because the popup is drawn by the operating system. The customizable select feature changes that: with the right CSS appearance value, the popup becomes real DOM you can style, and <selectedcontent> is the element that copies the chosen option's markup into the closed control. The styling half belongs to css_mastery. What belongs here is that this mechanism keeps the native meaning, the keyboard behaviour and the mobile picker, which is exactly what a hand-built dropdown throws away.

One more attribute and one new feature. The required attribute works on <select> as it does elsewhere, with one wrinkle: it only means something when the first <option> has an empty value, because otherwise something is always selected and the required attribute can never fail. And the customizable select (the ability to style a <select>'s dropdown with CSS and put rich markup in each option) is arriving with appearance: base-select and the <selectedcontent> element, which copies the chosen option's markup into the button. Treat the customizable select as something to recognise for now: <selectedcontent> is one of the elements jsdom does not implement yet, which is a fair sign of how new it is.

11.10 Textarea

<label for="notes">Notes</label>
<textarea id="notes" name="notes" rows="4" maxlength="500"></textarea>

<textarea> is multi-line text. It is not a void element, and its value is its content, not a value attribute. So a pre-filled textarea has the text between the tags, and every character between them counts, with one exception: the parser drops a single newline straight after the opening tag, as it does for <pre> (§4.11). A second newline, or any indentation, becomes part of the value (measured in Chromium: <textarea> followed by one newline and hello has the value "hello"; with two newlines, "\nhello"). That is why the example above is written with the tags together.

The rows attribute and cols attribute set the starting size in lines and characters. rows is genuinely useful as a hint about how long the answer is expected to be; cols should give way to CSS width. Line breaks are converted to CRLF (carriage return plus line feed) on submission (§12.2).

Two attributes size a textarea, and both are presentational hints CSS overrides. The rows attribute is the visible number of lines, and the cols attribute the visible width in characters. The rows attribute is worth setting anyway, because it decides the box's size before the stylesheet arrives; a cols attribute is rarely worth setting at all.

11.11 Datalist

<datalist> adds suggestions to an ordinary input without limiting it to them:

<label for="browser">Browser</label>
<input id="browser" name="browser" list="browsers">
<datalist id="browsers">
  <option value="Chromium"></option>
  <option value="Firefox"></option>
  <option value="Safari"></option>
</datalist>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Browser"
combobox "Browser" autocomplete=list haspopup=listbox

The input became a combobox with autocomplete=list, the platform's way of saying "there are suggestions, and you may also type something else". The list attribute points at the datalist's id attribute.

This is the right control for "usually one of these, but not always": a city, a job title, a tag. When the value must be one of the options, use <select> instead, because a datalist enforces nothing.

The connection is the list attribute: it names a <datalist> by its id, just as <label for> names a control. A list attribute pointing at nothing silently does nothing, and the list attribute works on most text-like and numeric input types.

11.12 Fieldset and Legend

<fieldset> groups related controls; <legend>, which must be its first child, names the group.

<fieldset>
  <legend>Contact preferences</legend>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="pref" value="email"> Email</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="pref" value="post"> Post</label>
</fieldset>

AX TREE
group "Contact preferences"
  Legend
    text "Contact preferences"
  checkbox "Email" checked=false
  checkbox "Post" checked=false

The group role is named by the legend, and a screen reader announces that name when focus first enters the group. So the user hears "Contact preferences, Email, checkbox, not checked" instead of a lone "Email". For a radio group this is not a nicety: it is the only way the question gets across at all (§11.6).

<fieldset> also has a disabled attribute that passes down to its contents: disabling the fieldset disables every control inside it with one attribute, which is the cleanest way to switch off a whole step of a multi-step form.

Do not reach for it around every pair of fields. A fieldset around a single control adds a level of grouping that means nothing, and a form with six fieldsets is noisier to move through than a form with six labels.

The disabled attribute on a <fieldset> is the only disable in HTML that applies to everything inside: it disables every control within it. That makes the disabled attribute on a fieldset the clean way to switch off a whole step of a multi-step form, and it works together with §12.2's rule: a disabled control is not a successful control, so nothing inside the fieldset is submitted.

11.13 Output, Meter and Progress

Three small elements that are easy to confuse.

<label for="v">Volume</label><input id="v" type="range" name="v">
<output name="shown" for="v">50</output>
<label for="disk">Disk used</label><meter id="disk" min="0" max="100" value="72">72%</meter>
<label for="up">Upload</label><progress id="up" max="100" value="40"></progress>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Volume"
slider "Volume" orientation=horizontal valuemax=100 valuemin=0 valuetext=50
status atomic=true live=polite
  text "50"
text
LabelText
  text "Disk used"
meter "Disk used" valuemax=100 valuemin=0
LabelText
  text "Upload"
progressbar "Upload" valuemax=100 valuemin=0

<output> holds a value your page calculated. Its for attribute lists the ids of the inputs it was worked out from. Critically, and as the tree shows, it is a live region by default (status atomic=true live=polite), so writing a new number into it is announced automatically (§13.7). That makes it the correct element for a running total, and the wrong one for a number that never changes.

<meter> is a measurement within a known range: disk usage, a score, a fraction. It is not a progress bar, and it should never be used as one. It has low, high and optimum attributes that colour the gauge according to whether the value is in a good part of the range.

<progress> is how far a task has got. With a value it is determinate; with no value at all it is an indeterminate spinner, which is the honest markup for "working, no idea how long".

All three need labels like any other control. The text inside <meter> and <progress> is fallback content for browsers that do not draw them, not the accessible name.

11.14 Autocomplete and Autofill

The autocomplete attribute tells the browser what a field means, so it can fill it in from what the user has already told it. It is not a preference but a vocabulary: the specification defines around fifty tokens.

<label for="fn">First name</label>
<input id="fn" name="fn" autocomplete="given-name">
<label for="e2">Email</label>
<input id="e2" name="e2" type="email" autocomplete="email">
<label for="cc">Card number</label>
<input id="cc" name="cc" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="cc-number">
<label for="otp">One-time code</label>
<input id="otp" name="otp" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code">

The tokens worth knowing: name, given-name, family-name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, country, cc-number, cc-exp, current-password, new-password, one-time-code. Prefixes make them more specific: shipping postal-code and billing postal-code tell two address blocks in one form apart.

This matters more than it looks. Autofill turns a twelve-field checkout into two taps, which for a user with a motor impairment is the difference between finishing and giving up. And current-password versus new-password is what tells a password manager whether to offer the saved password or generate a new one. WCAG 2.2 has a success criterion, "Identify Input Purpose", that asks for exactly these tokens.

Browsers deliberately ignore autocomplete="off" on many login and address fields, because sites used it to break password managers. Do not rely on it to suppress anything. The honest reasons to set it are one-off values, like a search box or a code the user reads off a device.

The autocomplete attribute takes a token from a fixed list (email, given-name, street-address, cc-number, one-time-code and several dozen more), and it is what lets the browser fill a form in correctly instead of guessing from your field names. Getting the autocomplete attribute right is also a WCAG requirement: success criterion 1.3.5, Identify Input Purpose, at Level AA, and it is one of the few criteria a single attribute meets outright. That success criterion exists because autofill is an accessibility feature first: for anyone who finds typing slow or error-prone, it is the difference between a usable form and an unusable one.

11.15 The Attributes Nearly Everything Shares

name attribute
What the server sees. Without it, nothing is submitted.
value attribute
The initial value — and only the initial one. Changing it in JavaScript after the user has typed does not update the field, because the live value lives in the DOM property, not the attribute. This is the classic "my reset does not work" bug.
placeholder
A format example, never a label (§11.2). DD/MM/YYYY is a good placeholder; Date of birth is a bad one.
disabled attribute
Unfocusable, unsubmitted, and usually greyed below the contrast threshold. A disabled submit button is a common anti-pattern: the user cannot reach it to find out why it is off. Prefer an enabled button that explains the problem when pressed.
readonly
Focusable, selectable, copyable, and submitted. The right choice for a value the user must be able to read and copy but not change.
autofocus
Focus this control on load. Reasonable on a page whose entire purpose is one field — a search page, a login page — and disorienting anywhere else, because it skips whatever was above it.
inputmode
Which on-screen keyboard, independent of validation. numeric, decimal, tel, email, url, search, none.
enterkeyhint
What the mobile Enter key should say: go, done, next, search, send.

The value rule is worth repeating, because it catches everyone once. input.value in JavaScript reads and writes the current value; input.getAttribute('value') reads the default written in the markup; and input.defaultValue is the property version of the attribute. A form reset restores the default, not the last thing you assigned.

One shared attribute deserves its own note, because it exists for a single, narrow purpose: dirname. Putting dirname="comment-dir" on a text control makes the browser submit the field's text direction alongside its value, as an extra name/value pair. dirname is the only way a server learns whether a user typed right-to-left or left-to-right text, and it is what lets the server store the direction and display the value correctly later (§4.12).

Exercises

1. A signup form uses <input type="number" name="postcode">. List everything wrong with that and give the replacement.

Solution

Leading zeros are destroyed. A number does not have them, so 01234 becomes 1234 — and for a UK-style postcode containing letters, the field rejects the value entirely.

The spinner is nonsense. A postcode has no successor. Incrementing it produces a different, unrelated place.

Scroll changes the value. In several browsers, a mouse wheel over a focused number field alters it. A user scrolling past a filled-in form can silently change their postcode.

step rejects valid input. step defaults to 1, so a postcode with a space or a hyphen fails validation with a message about nearest valid values (§12.8).

It is the wrong keyboard on mobile — a spinner keypad rather than one with the letters some postcodes need.

The replacement:

<label for="pc">Postcode</label>
<input id="pc" name="postcode" type="text" inputmode="numeric"
       autocomplete="postal-code" aria-describedby="pc-hint">
<p id="pc-hint">For example, 1071 XX.</p>

type="text" because it is a string. inputmode="numeric" for the keyboard, with no numeric semantics attached (§11.5). autocomplete="postal-code" so the browser can fill it (§11.14). And a hint via aria-describedby rather than a placeholder, so the format survives typing (§13.4).

The general rule: a value is a number only if arithmetic on it means something. Quantities and prices are numbers. Postcodes, card numbers, phone numbers, years-as-labels and account references are strings.

2. Why does the "Show password" toggle in this form reload the page?

<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="p">Password</label>
  <input id="p" type="password" name="password">
  <button onclick="toggle()">Show password</button>
  <button type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
Solution

Because a <button> with no type attribute defaults to type="submit" (§11.8). The toggle button is a submit button, so pressing it runs toggle() and then submits the form, which navigates to /login.

The fix is one attribute:

<button type="button" onclick="toggle()">Show password</button>

This is worth internalising as a habit: every <button> inside a <form> that is not meant to submit needs type="button" explicitly. The default is the opposite of what most people assume, and the symptom — a page that reloads and loses state — usually gets misdiagnosed as a JavaScript error.

Two improvements while you are here. Inline onclick is best replaced by addEventListener, which keeps behaviour out of the markup and works with a content security policy (§16.10). And the toggle should carry aria-pressed, so the state is announced rather than only shown: <button type="button" aria-pressed="false">Show password</button>, updated whenever it flips (§13.5). Its label should stay "Show password" rather than changing to "Hide", because the accessible name and the pressed state together already say which it is.

3. Convert this to accessible markup and say what each change buys.

<div class="field">
  <div class="label">Delivery</div>
  <div class="radio" data-value="std">Standard</div>
  <div class="radio" data-value="exp">Express</div>
</div>
Solution 
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="delivery" value="std" checked> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="delivery" value="exp"> Express</label>
</fieldset>

What each change buys:

<fieldset> and <legend> produce a group role named "Delivery", so the question is announced when focus enters the group (§11.12). The original <div class="label"> is announced as nothing at all.

Real radios are focusable, have the radio role, carry a checked state, and are operated with the arrow keys as a single tab stop — none of which the original has, and all of which would otherwise need a roving tabindex (§14.6) implemented by hand.

The shared name attribute is what makes them one group and guarantees at most one is selected. data-value did nothing.

Each <label> names its radio and extends the hit area to the word (§11.2).

checked on the first gives a default, which matters because a radio group with no default can be left unanswered and, once answered, cannot be returned to "none" (§11.6).

The form now submits. delivery=std appears in the request with no JavaScript at all (§12.2); the original produced nothing, because a <div> has no name and no value.

The styling is unaffected: the radios and labels are ordinary elements, and hiding the native control while styling the label is a well-trodden CSS technique that keeps every property above.

4. A checkout form has a <select> of 200 countries. A colleague proposes replacing it with a <div>-based dropdown for better styling. Give the strongest technical arguments on both sides and a recommendation.

Solution

For the replacement. A native <select> popup is drawn by the operating system and historically could not be styled at all — no custom fonts, no icons beside options, no two-line entries, no type-ahead search box. For 200 countries, an inline filter is a genuine usability gain, and matching a design system exactly is a real requirement.

Against. The <select> supplies, for free: the mobile platform picker, which is a much better interface than any dropdown on a small screen; keyboard type-ahead, where typing "ne" jumps to Netherlands; the combobox role with expanded and haspopup correctly maintained (§11.9); form submission and validation participation; and rendering above everything else on the page without any z-index fight. Rebuilding it means implementing the ARIA combobox pattern with aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, arrow keys, Home/End, Escape, type-ahead, focus management and a form value — and getting one of those wrong produces a control that is worse than the original in a way that only some users can perceive (§13.9).

Recommendation. Keep the <select>. If the styling requirement is real, reach for the customizable select feature (§11.9), which makes the popup styleable DOM while the browser keeps the semantics, the keyboard behaviour and the mobile picker — the whole point being that you get the appearance without reimplementing the contract. Where that is not yet an option, the honest fallback is a <datalist>-backed text input (§11.11) plus a real <select> beneath it, or simply accepting the native appearance for this one control.

The measurable form of the argument: count the behaviours listed above, and ask whether the team will implement, test and maintain all of them on every browser and screen reader. The answer decides it.

5. Explain the difference between disabled and readonly, and give a case for each.

Solution
disabled

readonly

Focusable

No
Yes

Selectable, copyable

No
Yes

Submitted

No
Yes

Validated

No
Yes

Announced as

"dimmed" / "unavailable"
"read only"

Applies to

Any control, and cascades from <fieldset>
Text-entry controls only

The decisive difference is submission (§12.2): a disabled control contributes nothing to the request, a readonly one contributes its value.

A case for disabled: a "Delivery address" fieldset that is switched off while "same as billing" is ticked. The fields should not be sent, should not be validated, and should not be reachable by Tab — one disabled on the <fieldset> does all three.

A case for readonly: an order reference generated by the server and shown on a confirmation form. The user must be able to select and copy it, and it must be submitted with the rest of the form. disabled would make it uncopyable and would silently drop it from the request.

The trap worth naming: a disabled submit button on an invalid form. The user cannot focus it, so a screen reader user may not find it at all, and nobody is told why it is off. An enabled button that explains the problem when pressed (§12.9) is better on every axis. And when a value must be unchangeable but must reach the server, the belt-and-braces answer is readonly on the visible field plus a <input type="hidden"> — remembering that neither is a security control (§12.13).

SECTION 12

Forms II — Constraint Validation and Submission

§11 built the controls. This section is about what happens when the user presses the button: exactly which controls contribute, exactly how their values are encoded, exactly what the browser checks first, and what you must do on the server no matter what the browser checked.

The reason to be exact is that a form is the only part of HTML that sends something. Everything else in this course describes a document; a form describes a request to a server. Get the encoding wrong and the server never sees a field. Get the validation story wrong and you end up with either a form nobody can submit or a database full of rubbish.

Every submission in this section was captured by pointing a real Chromium at a local HTTP server and recording what arrived. The bodies below are exactly what came over the network.

12.1 A Form Is a Request Builder

Pressing a submit button runs a specified algorithm. In outline:

1
Fire a submit event. If a listener calls preventDefault(), stop — this is the hook every JavaScript form uses.
2
Interactively validate the form, unless novalidate is set or the button carries formnovalidate. A failure stops the submission and shows a bubble on the first invalid control (§12.7).
3
Build the entry list: name/value pairs from every successful control (§12.2), plus the submitter's own name and value.
4
Encode the entry list according to enctype (§12.4).
5
Send it with method attribute to action attribute, and navigate target attribute to the response.

Two facts follow straight from that list, and they are worth fixing in your mind now. The submit event fires before the request is built, which is why calling preventDefault() in a listener is enough to take over completely. And validation happens before the entry list (the list of name/value pairs to send) exists, which is why an invalid form produces no request at all, not an empty one.

One more attribute belongs on the form itself: the target attribute, which names where the response is shown, exactly as it does on a link (§7.6). A target attribute of _blank opens the result in a new tab, and a named target attribute shows it in the <iframe> with that name.

12.2 Successful Controls: What Is Actually Sent

A control adds itself to the entry list only if it is a successful control. The rules are not intuitive, so here is a form containing every interesting case, and the request it produced.

<form action="/submit" method="get">
  <label for="n">Name</label><input id="n" name="name" value="Ada Lovelace">
  <label for="c">Colour</label><input id="c" name="colour" value="grün &amp; blue">
  <input type="checkbox" name="terms" value="yes" checked id="t1"><label for="t1">Terms</label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes" id="t2"><label for="t2">News</label>
  <input type="radio" name="size" value="s" id="r1"><label for="r1">Small</label>
  <input type="radio" name="size" value="l" checked id="r2"><label for="r2">Large</label>
  <label for="e">Empty</label><input id="e" type="text" name="empty" value="">
  <label for="d">Disabled</label><input id="d" type="text" disabled name="skipped" value="x">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="tok123">
  <label for="s">City</label>
  <select id="s" name="city"><option value="">--</option><option value="bath" selected>Bath</option></select>
  <label for="nt">Notes</label>
  <textarea id="nt" name="notes">line one
line two</textarea>
  <button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
  <button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>
</form>

Pressing Save produced this request line:

GET /submit?name=Ada+Lovelace&colour=gr%C3%BCn+%26+blue&terms=yes&size=l&empty=
    &csrf=tok123&city=bath&notes=line+one%0D%0Aline+two&action=save

Six rules, each visible in that string:

No name, no entry
A control without a name attribute is never sent. This is the single most common "my field disappeared" bug, and it is silent.
Unchecked boxes send nothing
news is absent entirely — not news=, not news=off. A checkbox is a presence flag, so the server must treat "missing" as false.
Empty is not missing
empty= is there. A text input always sends its name, even with no value. That asymmetry with checkboxes catches everyone once.
Disabled is skipped
skipped is gone. disabled attribute removes a control from the entry list; readonly does not, which is the practical difference between them.
Only the submitter counts
action=save appears and action=delete does not. Two buttons sharing a name is how one form performs two operations.
Radios send one value
size=l. A radio group is defined by a shared name attribute, and contributes exactly one entry — or none, if nothing is checked.

(The line break above was added to make it readable; the real query string is one line.)

The encoding is worth reading too. A space became +; the ampersand in the value became %26, so it cannot be mistaken for a separator; and ü became %C3%BC, its two UTF-8 bytes in percent-encoded form. That format is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and it is why §3.3's <meta charset> is not optional: the page's encoding decides the bytes the form sends.

The textarea shows one more rule. Its two lines were separated by a single newline in the markup, and they arrive as %0D%0A, a carriage return and a line feed. Form submission turns every line break into CRLF whatever the document contained, so a server that measures lengths or compares hashes against the value it rendered will be off by one byte per line if it assumes otherwise.

The default encoding for all of this is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and it is what produced the output above. application/x-www-form-urlencoded percent-encodes each name and value, joins each pair with =, and separates pairs with &. That is the same format a query string uses, which is why a GET form and a POST form differ only in where the string goes (§12.3).

12.3 GET or POST

method attribute takes two values that mean genuinely different things.

A get request puts the entry list in the query string, as above, and the request has no body. That makes the result bookmarkable, shareable, cacheable and re-runnable. That is exactly right for a search or a filter, and exactly wrong for anything that changes data, because the browser will happily repeat it when the user goes back or refreshes.

A post request puts the entry list in the request body. It cannot be bookmarked, refreshing asks the user first, and there is no length limit worth worrying about. Use it for anything that creates, updates or deletes.

POST /submit
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

name=Ada+Lovelace&colour=gr%C3%BCn+%26+blue&terms=yes&size=l&empty=
    &csrf=tok123&city=bath&notes=line+one%0D%0Aline+two&action=save

Byte for byte, the body of the POST is the query string of the GET. The encoding is the same; only its place in the request changed.

Three practical consequences:

  • A GET form's action cannot carry its own query string. The browser throws it away and puts the entry list there instead, so action="/search?lang=en" silently loses lang. Put it in a hidden input instead.
  • Never put a password or a token in a GET form, because query strings end up in browser history, server logs and Referer headers.
  • The pattern that fixes double submission is POST, then redirect, then GET: answer the POST with a redirect, so the page the user ends up on is safe to refresh.

The HTTP rules underneath (safe methods, idempotence, caching) are backend_and_api_design_mastery's subject. What matters here is that one attribute makes the choice.

The difference restated: a get request puts the entry list in the URL's query, so a get request is bookmarkable, shareable, cacheable and repeatable, and everything in it is visible in the address bar, in browser history and in server logs. A post request puts it in the body, so a post request is none of those things, which is exactly right for something that changes data. The rule comes from what the method means, not from how much data there is: a search is a get request and a purchase is a post request, even when the search is longer.

12.4 enctype: Three Encodings, Two of Them Useful

enctype applies to POST only, and takes three values.

application/x-www-form-urlencoded is the default and is shown above.

multipart/form-data is required as soon as a form contains <input type="file">, because percent-encoding a file's bytes would cost far too much. Each entry becomes its own part with its own headers:

POST /submit
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx

------WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="name"

Ada Lovelace
------WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="colour"

grün & blue

  [terms, size, empty, csrf and city follow, each in the same three-line shape]

------WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="notes"

line one
line two
------WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="action"

save
------WebKitFormBoundarym6aq2FaS2FuIfRgx--

Note that grün & blue arrives as itself, with no percent-encoding, because the boundary string separates the parts instead. A new boundary is generated for every submission; the one above is a real capture, and yours will differ. A part carrying a file gains a filename="…" parameter and a Content-Type of its own, which is how the server learns what was uploaded.

The trade-off is size. Every entry costs a boundary line and two header lines, so a form with twenty short text fields is several times larger as multipart than as urlencoded. Use multipart when you have files and urlencoded when you do not.

text/plain is the third, and it exists for debugging: so a form can email readable text. It is unsafe for anything else, and one capture shows why:

name=Ada Lovelace
colour=grün & blue
terms=yes
size=l
empty=
csrf=tok123
city=bath
notes=line one
line two
action=save

Nothing is escaped. The notes field contained a newline, so the line line two looks exactly like a field named line two. The format has no way to show the difference, and the specification says so: it cannot be parsed reliably. Never point a real endpoint at it.

12.5 The Submitter

The button that caused the submission is the submitter, and it is more powerful than it looks. Besides adding its own name and value (§12.2), it can override five of the form's own settings:

formaction
Send this submission somewhere else. A "Save draft" button beside a "Publish" button, one form.
formmethod
Override GET/POST for this button only.
formenctype
Override the encoding for this button only.
formtarget
Override where the response loads.
formnovalidate
Skip interactive validation. The correct way to build a "Save draft" button on a form whose required fields are not all filled in yet.
<form action="/posts" method="post">
  <label for="t">Title</label>
  <input id="t" name="title" required>
  <button type="submit">Publish</button>
  <button type="submit" formaction="/drafts" formnovalidate>Save draft</button>
</form>

That is a complete form with two outcomes and no JavaScript at all, and the formnovalidate is essential. Without it, "Save draft" would refuse to work until the title was filled in, which defeats the point of a draft.

In JavaScript the submitter is on the event, which is how a listener tells the two buttons apart:

const form = document.createElement('form');
form.innerHTML = '<button name="action" value="save">Save</button>' +
                 '<button name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>';
document.body.append(form);
form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  console.log('submitter:', event.submitter.value);
  console.log('in the data:', new FormData(form, event.submitter).get('action'));
});
form.querySelector('button[value="delete"]').click();

submitter: delete
in the data: delete

The second argument to FormData is the one people miss. new FormData(form) alone does not include the submitter's name and value, because outside a real submission there is no submitter. Passing it explicitly reproduces what the browser would have sent.

Three of those overrides change where and how the data goes: formaction for the URL, formmethod for the method, and formenctype for the encoding. So a "save draft" button can carry formaction="/drafts" beside a submit button that posts to /publish, and a formmethod="get" button can turn one form into a search. formenctype is the rarest of the three, and it exists for the case where one button attaches a file and another does not.

12.6 The Form Owner

A control belongs to a form. Usually that is the <form> it sits inside, but the form attribute removes the need for them to be nested:

<form id="checkout" action="/pay" method="post">
  <label for="card">Card</label>
  <input id="card" name="card">
</form>

<aside>
  <label for="promo">Promo code</label>
  <input id="promo" name="promo" form="checkout">
  <button type="submit" form="checkout">Pay</button>
</aside>

The promo field and the button are outside the <form> in the document, and they submit with it anyway. That matters because forms cannot be nested (§1.8 shows the parser silently dropping an inner <form> altogether), so a layout that put a control in a sidebar, a table cell or a different grid area used to be impossible. The form attribute is the escape hatch, and it works for every element that can belong to a form, including <button>, <select>, <textarea> and <output>.

This relationship is called the form owner, and JavaScript can read it as input.form.

12.7 Constraint Validation: The Attributes

Constraint validation is the browser's own check, run before submission and written entirely as attributes. It costs nothing, needs no script, and works before your JavaScript has loaded.

required attribute
Must not be empty. On a radio group, one member must be checked; on a checkbox, that box itself must be checked.
The type attribute
email, url and number validate their own format for free. This is the cheapest validation in HTML and the reason §11.3 insists on the right type.
pattern attribute
A regular expression the whole value must match — anchored implicitly, so no ^ or $ is needed. Always pair it with a title or a hint, because the browser's failure message says nothing about the required shape.
min attribute, max attribute, step attribute
Numeric and date ranges, and the granularity between them. step defaults to 1 on number, which is why 4.5 is rejected by a bare number input.
minlength, maxlength
Character counts. maxlength also prevents typing beyond the limit; minlength only reports.
novalidate
On the form: turn interactive validation off entirely while leaving the API intact, which is what a custom-error-display implementation wants (§12.9).

One rule catches everybody: minlength and maxlength only apply once the user has edited the field. A value set in the markup is not subject to them. The specification calls this the dirty value flag, and it can be measured:

document.body.innerHTML =
  '<input id="a" minlength="5" value="abc">' +
  '<input id="b" required value="">';
const a = document.getElementById('a');
const b = document.getElementById('b');
console.log('tooShort on a markup value:', a.validity.tooShort);
console.log('valueMissing still applies: ', b.validity.valueMissing);

tooShort on a markup value: false
valueMissing still applies:  true

So a value rendered by the server that breaks minlength submits without complaint. required is unaffected, because it is not a length constraint. This is one of several reasons §12.13 exists.

12.8 ValidityState: Reading the Result

Every form control carries a validity object, a ValidityState, with one true/false flag for each way it can fail and a valid summary. Reading it is how you find out why something failed, not just that it did.

document.body.innerHTML = `
  <input id="a" type="email" required value="">
  <input id="b" type="email" value="not-an-email">
  <input id="c" type="text" pattern="[A-Z]{3}" value="ab">
  <input id="d" type="number" min="1" max="10" step="2" value="4">`;
const flags = ['valueMissing', 'typeMismatch', 'patternMismatch', 'rangeUnderflow',
               'rangeOverflow', 'stepMismatch', 'tooShort', 'tooLong', 'badInput',
               'customError'];
for (const id of ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']) {
  const v = document.getElementById(id).validity;
  console.log(id, v.valid, flags.filter((f) => v[f]).join(',') || '-');
}

a false valueMissing
b false typeMismatch
c false patternMismatch
d false stepMismatch

The d case is the instructive one. 4 sits inside min="1" and max="10", so neither range flag fires, but step="2" counts from min, which makes the valid values 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Chrome's own message for it reads "Please enter a valid value. The two nearest valid values are 3 and 5.", which is a better error than most applications write by hand.

Two flags in that list do not come from attributes. badInput means the user typed something the control cannot even read as a value, such as letters in a number field, and it is why input.value comes back as an empty string in that situation instead of the rubbish typed. customError is set by setCustomValidity (§12.10).

The related methods:

checkValidity()
Returns true or false and fires an invalid event on each failing control. Shows nothing.
reportValidity()
The same, but also displays the browser's bubble on the first failure and focuses it. This is what pressing submit does.
validationMessage
The message the browser would show. Browser-specific and localised to the browser's language, not your page's.

That last point is the one that shapes your design. validationMessage is written by the browser maker, translated into the browser's language, and cannot be styled: the bubble is not a DOM node you can reach. A page in French shown in a Chrome set to English produces English errors. If your product needs consistent, styled, translated messages, you must set novalidate on the form and show errors yourself, using the flags from validity to decide what to say. That is §12.9.

Two methods read the same state from script. checkvalidity returns true or false and fires an invalid event on each failing control, changing nothing visible. reportvalidity does the same and shows the browser's own message on the first failure. So checkvalidity is what you call to decide, and reportvalidity is what you call to tell the user; if you are showing your own messages (§12.9), checkvalidity is the one you want. Note that the flag names describe the failure: rangeoverflow is true when the value is above max, rangeunderflow when it is below min, and it is rangeoverflow rather than rangeok, so every one of these is true in the bad case.

12.9 Showing Errors So Everyone Gets Them

The accessible error pattern has four parts, and each has a reason.

<form novalidate action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required
         aria-describedby="email-hint email-error" aria-invalid="true">
  <p id="email-hint">We use this to send your receipt.</p>
  <p id="email-error" class="error">Enter an email address, like name@example.com.</p>
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

The message is associated, not merely adjacent. aria-describedby links it to the control, so it is announced when focus lands there (§13.4). Note that the attribute takes a list of ids, so a hint and an error can both be attached.

aria-invalid="true" marks the control itself, which is what makes a screen reader say "invalid" along with the name. Set it to false or remove it once the field is corrected; a leftover aria-invalid is exactly the kind of bad ARIA §13.9 warns about.

The message says what to do, not what went wrong. "Invalid input" describes your validator's mood; "Enter an email address, like name@example.com" is an instruction. WCAG's "error suggestion" criterion asks for exactly this.

Focus moves to the problem. After a failed submit, move focus either to the first invalid control or to an error summary at the top of the form: an <h2> plus a list of links, each pointing at the id of a failing field. The summary is the better pattern for long forms, because it says how many things are wrong before the user starts hunting.

The fourth part is the one implementations skip, and it is the difference between a form that is annoying and a form that cannot be used. Without moving focus, a screen reader user presses submit, hears nothing, and has no way of knowing the page changed at all. An inline error message that nobody is sent to is invisible.

Two patterns, and a real form usually wants both. An inline error message sits beside the field, is referenced by aria-describedby, and appears when the user leaves the field or on submit. An error summary sits at the top of the form, lists every failure as a link to its field, and receives focus on a failed submit, which is what tells a screen reader user that anything happened at all. The error summary is the part most often missing, and on a long form it is the more important of the two. Without it, a user is told the form failed and left to find out where, and an inline error message alone stays invisible until they reach the field.

12.10 Custom Constraints

setCustomValidity puts your own rule inside the browser's validation system, instead of next to it.

document.body.innerHTML = '<input id="u" required value="admin">';
const u = document.getElementById('u');
u.setCustomValidity('That name is taken.');
console.log('valid:', u.validity.valid, '| customError:', u.validity.customError);
u.setCustomValidity('');
console.log('valid:', u.validity.valid, '| customError:', u.validity.customError);

valid: false | customError: true
valid: true | customError: false

Two rules. A non-empty string makes the control invalid; only the empty string clears it. And you must clear it before checking again, or the old message keeps failing the field forever. The classic symptom is a form that will not submit even after the user fixes the value. Call setCustomValidity('') at the start of every re-check.

The reason to use it instead of a flag of your own is that it plugs into everything else. A control with a custom error takes part in checkValidity(), blocks submission, matches :invalid, and is found by reportValidity(). Your own boolean does none of that.

12.11 :valid, :invalid, and Why :user-invalid Exists

CSS can style validity, and the obvious selectors are a usability trap.

:invalid matches from the moment the page loads. On a form with three required fields, all three are outlined in red before the user has typed a character: an accusation aimed at a form nobody has tried yet. :valid has the opposite problem, congratulating fields that are merely optional and empty.

:user-invalid is the fix, and it is why the pseudo-class exists. It matches only after the user has interacted with the control and left it, or after a failed attempt to submit. The rule of thumb is short: use :user-invalid for anything the user sees, and keep :invalid for logic that really does care about the state when the page loads. Styling belongs to css_mastery; choosing which state to style is a forms decision, and it belongs here.

12.12 FormData and URLSearchParams

To submit a form with JavaScript, build the same entry list the browser would have built.

document.body.innerHTML = `
  <form id="f">
    <input name="name" value="Ada Lovelace">
    <input name="tag" value="one"><input name="tag" value="two">
    <input name="empty" value="">
    <input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes">
  </form>`;
const data = new FormData(document.getElementById('f'));
console.log('all keys :', [...data.keys()].join(','));
console.log('getAll   :', data.getAll('tag').join('|'));
console.log('missing  :', data.get('news'));
console.log('encoded  :', new URLSearchParams(data).toString());

all keys : name,tag,tag,empty
getAll   : one|two
missing  : null
encoded  : name=Ada+Lovelace&tag=one&tag=two&empty=

FormData follows §12.2's rules exactly. The unchecked checkbox is absent, so get returns null; the empty text field is present; and a repeated name keeps both values, which is why get (the first value) and getAll (all of them) are different methods. Passing it through URLSearchParams produces the urlencoded string byte for byte.

For a fetch, the type of body you pass decides the Content-Type for you. Pass the FormData object and the browser sends multipart/form-data with a generated boundary; pass the URLSearchParams and it sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded. If you set the header yourself, you break the multipart case, because you cannot know the boundary.

12.13 Client-Side Validation Is Not Validation

Everything in this section so far is client-side validation, and all of it is a convenience for honest users. None of it protects anything.

It can be removed
DevTools deletes a required attribute in one click; §12.7's novalidate disables the lot.
It can be bypassed
Nothing obliges a request to come from your page at all. curl does not run your HTML.
It does not know enough
"Is this username taken?", "does this coupon still exist?", "may this user do this?" are server questions.
It misses markup values
§12.7's dirty-value rule means a pre-filled value can violate minlength and submit anyway.

So server-side validation checks everything again, and treats every field as possibly absent, empty, repeated or hostile until proved otherwise. The two layers have different jobs: the client's job is to tell the user quickly, and the server's job is to decide. A useful discipline is to make the server the single source of the rules and generate the HTML constraints from those rules, so the two cannot drift apart.

Anything a value is later inserted into (an SQL query, a shell command, an HTML page (§16.9)) needs escaping suited to that destination as well. Validation and escaping are different operations, and neither replaces the other.

To restate the division: client-side validation is a user-experience feature, and server-side validation is the security boundary. server-side validation must check again every constraint the markup expressed, because an attacker sends the request without ever loading the page.

12.14 Progressive Enhancement

A form that works without JavaScript and works better with it is following progressive enhancement. Forms are where the idea pays off best, because the browser already implements the basic case.

The shape is always the same. Write a real <form> with a real action attribute and method attribute that a server can handle on its own. Then, in script, catch submit, call preventDefault(), send the same entry list with fetch, and update the page in place. If the script fails to load, is blocked, or throws an error before it is attached, the form still submits, because the browser does it.

<form id="signup" action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="em">Email</label>
  <input id="em" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>

document.body.innerHTML = `<form id="signup" action="/signup" method="post">
  <input name="email" type="email" value="ada@example.com"></form>`;
const form = document.getElementById('signup');
form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const body = new URLSearchParams(new FormData(form));
  console.log('would POST to', form.action.replace(/^https?:\/\/[^/]+/, ''));
  console.log('body:', body.toString());
});
form.requestSubmit();

would POST to /signup
body: email=ada%40example.com

requestSubmit() is the right way to submit a form from script, and form.submit() is the wrong one. The old method skips both the submit event and constraint validation, so your own listener never runs. The enhancement reads its target and its method from the markup instead of repeating them, so the endpoint is written down in exactly one place.

The failure this avoids is not hypothetical. On a slow connection, the user pressing the button before the script has finished loading is an ordinary event, and a form built this way submits normally in that window instead of doing nothing.

Exercises

1. A checkout form loses the "gift wrap" preference about half the time. The control is <input type="checkbox" name="gift" value="yes">. The server reads gift and stores true or false. What is happening?

Solution

Nothing is being lost. The server is misreading a checkbox.

An unchecked checkbox is not a successful control (§12.2): it contributes no entry at all. The request contains no gift key whatsoever — not gift=, not gift=off, not gift=false. So "about half the time" is exactly the proportion of customers who did not want gift wrap.

The server code is almost certainly doing something like reading the field and failing on its absence, or defaulting it to a value that is wrong. The fix is to treat presence as true and absence as false:

  • gift present with the value yes → true.
  • gift absent → false.

Two related points. Checkboxes differ from text inputs here, which is where the confusion comes from: §12.2's capture shows empty= present for an empty text field but no news at all for the unchecked box. And if you genuinely need a value in both cases — an audit trail, a partial update where "absent" means "do not change" — the classic technique is a hidden input with the same name placed before the checkbox: <input type="hidden" name="gift" value="no"> followed by the checkbox. Both are sent when it is checked, and the server takes the last value.

Finally, value="yes" is worth keeping. A checkbox with no value attribute sends the string on, which is what browsers default to and which reads badly in server logs.

2. A file upload works for small files and silently drops the file for large ones. The form is <form action="/upload" method="post"> with an <input type="file" name="doc">. Two things are wrong. Name them.

Solution

The enctype is missing. The default is application/x-www-form-urlencoded (§12.4), which cannot carry file content. What the server receives is the filename as an ordinary field value, and nothing else — which is why small files appear to work if the code only ever checked that the field was non-empty. The form needs enctype="multipart/form-data", and it needs method="post", which it already has (enctype is ignored on GET).

There is a size limit somewhere, and it is failing silently. Web servers and application frameworks impose a maximum request body size by default, and exceeding it typically produces a rejected request rather than a truncated one. "Works small, fails large" is the signature. The fix has three parts: raise the limit deliberately to whatever the product actually needs, return a clear error when it is exceeded, and tell the user the limit before they wait for an upload to fail.

Two things worth adding while you are there. The accept attribute filters the file picker to the types you want, which is a usability improvement and not a security control. And the server must validate the file's real content — never trust the filename or the part's Content-Type, both of which are supplied by the client (§12.13).

3. A form uses novalidate and renders its own error messages under each field. QA reports that screen reader users cannot tell the form failed. The messages are correct and visible. What is missing?

Solution

Three things, and the first is the one that produces the exact symptom described (§12.9).

Focus never moves. The user presses submit, the page renders errors below the fields, and focus is still on the submit button at the bottom of the form. A screen reader announces nothing, because nothing about the user's position changed and no live region was updated. As far as they can tell, the button did nothing. Move focus after a failed submit — to the first invalid control for a short form, or to an error summary heading at the top for a long one.

The messages are not associated with their controls. Being visually below a field means nothing in the accessibility tree. Each message needs an id, and each control needs aria-describedby pointing at it, so the message is announced when focus reaches the field (§13.4). Without this, a user who tabs back to fix the field hears the label and nothing else.

aria-invalid="true" is not set. That is what makes the control itself announce as invalid rather than merely having some description. Set it on failure and clear it on correction.

An alternative to moving focus is a role="alert" region containing the summary, which announces itself (§13.7). It is weaker: the user hears the count but is not taken anywhere, so they still have to hunt. Moving focus to a summary that contains links to each failing field gives them both.

Finally, check that the error text says what to do — "Enter a date in the past" rather than "Invalid date". That is a WCAG level AA requirement and not merely good manners.

4. Why does form.submit() skip your validation, and what should you call instead?

Solution

Because submit() is older than both the submit event and constraint validation, and it was specified to submit the form directly: it does not fire the submit event and it does not run constraint validation. A page that attaches a listener and then calls form.submit() from anywhere else has a code path that bypasses its own logic entirely — including whatever preventDefault()-based enhancement it was relying on (§12.14).

Call form.requestSubmit() instead. It behaves exactly as if the user had pressed a submit button: it validates, it fires submit, and a listener can cancel it. It also takes an optional argument — the button to treat as the submitter — so form.requestSubmit(deleteButton) produces the same entry list, and the same formaction override, that clicking that button would have (§12.5).

There is one legitimate use for submit(): deliberately bypassing your own listener, for instance in a fallback path that has already done its own validation and wants the browser's plain navigation behaviour. That is rare and should be commented, because it reads as a bug.

5. Design the markup for a search form that must be bookmarkable, must not lose its lang=en parameter, and must announce its result count to screen reader users. State why each decision is what it is.

Solution 
<search>
  <form action="/results" method="get">
    <input type="hidden" name="lang" value="en">
    <label for="q">Search the archive</label>
    <input id="q" name="q" type="search" required>
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
  <p id="count" role="status"></p>
</search>

method="get". A search is a read, so the result must be bookmarkable, shareable and safe to refresh — all of which follow from the entry list being in the URL (§12.3). POST would give a page that prompts on reload and cannot be linked to.

lang is a hidden input, not part of action. This is the trap the question is built around: a GET form discards any query string on its action and replaces it with the entry list, so action="/results?lang=en" would silently lose lang (§12.3). A <input type="hidden"> puts it in the entry list where it survives.

type="search" and a real <label>. The type gives the platform's search affordances and a searchbox role; the label gives the accessible name (§13.3). No placeholder in place of a label.

required. Stops an empty search round-tripping to the server for nothing. It is a convenience only — §12.13 still applies, and the server must handle q being absent or empty.

<search> wraps it, producing a search landmark so the form can be jumped to directly (§6.9).

The count is an empty role="status" rendered with the page. status implies aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="true" (§13.7), so writing "18 results" into it later is announced without interrupting. It must exist and be empty before the update, which is why it is in the initial markup rather than created when results arrive.

If the form navigates to a new page rather than updating in place, the live region is unnecessary — a page load announces itself, and the result count belongs in the <h1> and the <title>.

SECTION 13

The Accessibility Tree, Roles, States and Properties

Everything in the previous twelve sections has been about one tree: the DOM, built by the parser in §1 and shaped by the content models in §2. This section is about a second tree, computed from the first. Most developers never look at it, and it is the only thing a screen reader ever sees.

That is the whole idea, and it explains why accessibility work so often feels like guesswork. You change some markup, you cannot perceive the result, and you are left reasoning about a structure you have never inspected. The fix is not to try harder; it is to look at the structure. Chrome computes it, exposes it, and will print it for you. The rest of this section is what it says.

Every tree in this section was produced by rendering the markup beside it in Chromium and asking the browser for Accessibility.getFullAXTree, which returns the same data the browser hands to assistive technology. None of them was written from memory, because several are not what a careful person would guess:

  • <output> is a live region (an area whose changes are announced automatically).
  • <input type="file"> is a button.
