  • <select> is a combobox with a popup.
  • <details> contains no button at all.

A course that wrote those from intuition would get four out of four wrong.

13.1 The Second Tree

A browser builds the DOM from your markup (§1.6). It then builds a second structure from the DOM, the accessibility tree, and hands that to the operating system through an interface called a platform accessibility api: UI Automation on Windows, NSAccessibility on macOS, AT-SPI on Linux. A screen reader is an ordinary application that reads the platform accessibility api. It has no access to your HTML, your CSS or your JavaScript. It sees roles, names, states and relationships, and nothing else.

Your markup
Text you wrote. Never seen by assistive technology directly.
The DOM
What the parser built (§1.7). Often not what you wrote — §1.8 is a catalogue of the differences.
The accessibility tree
Computed from the DOM. Fewer nodes, each carrying a role, an accessible name, an accessible description, and a set of states.
Platform API
The operating system's accessibility interface, which the browser publishes the tree into.
Assistive technology
A screen reader, a switch device, voice control, a braille display. Reads the platform API. Never reads your HTML.

Two consequences follow straight away, and the rest of the section depends on both.

The tree is smaller than the DOM. Elements with no meaning contribute nothing. A <div> wrapping a <span> wrapping text produces exactly one node, the text:

<div><span>Plain text</span></div>

AX TREE
text "Plain text"

That is not Chrome losing information. <div> and <span> mean nothing, as §4.14 said, and that is what makes them safe hooks for styling. They are left out of the tree because there is nothing to say about them.

The tree is computed, not stored. Change an attribute and it is computed again. That is why an aria-expanded that JavaScript never updates is worse than no aria-expanded at all: the tree faithfully reports the out-of-date value, and a user is told the menu is closed while it is open in front of everyone else.

The vocabulary for the rest of this section is wai-aria, the Accessible Rich Internet Applications specification, published by the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative. wai-aria defines the roles, states and properties used below, and every role name and aria-* attribute in this course comes from it.

13.2 Roles: Implicit and Explicit

Every node in the tree has a role: the answer to "what kind of thing is this?". Roles come from two places.

An implicit role comes from the element itself. <button> has the role button, <nav> has navigation, <h2> has heading. You get it for free, and you cannot lose it by accident. An explicit role comes from the role attribute, and it replaces the implicit one.

<a href="/x">Link</a>
<a role="button" href="/y">Fake</a>
<button>Real</button>

AX TREE
link "Link"
text
button "Fake"
button "Real"

Read that tree carefully, because it is the most instructive handful of lines in the section. (The bare text line is the newline between the two anchors: whitespace between elements is real content, and the tree says so.) The second anchor is a link. It navigates when clicked, it appears in the browser's list of links, and Ctrl-clicking it opens a tab. But to a screen reader user it is a button: announced as a button, expected to respond to Space, expected to do something on this page rather than go elsewhere. The role attribute changed the announcement and nothing else.

That mismatch is the reason for the discipline in §13.9. ARIA changes what is said about an element. It never changes what the element does. It adds no keyboard behaviour, no focusability, no click handling and no styling. It only relabels the tree, and if the behaviour underneath does not match the new label, you have made the page worse than before, because you have replaced a true announcement with a false one.

The other side is where ARIA earns its value. When no native element exists for what you are building (a tab strip, a tree view, a combobox with custom filtering), the role attribute is the only way to make the tree say what the thing is. Compare the two approaches for the same visual widget:

<div role="tablist">
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="p1" id="t1">One</button>
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="false" id="t2">Two</button>
</div>
<div role="tabpanel" id="p1" aria-labelledby="t1">Panel</div>

AX TREE
tablist orientation=horizontal
  tab "One" selected=true
  tab "Two" selected=false
tabpanel "One"
  text "Panel"

The tablist picked up an orientation nobody wrote, because horizontal is that role's default. The tabpanel is named "One", not by any text inside it, but through aria-labelledby pointing at the tab that controls it, which is how a panel is supposed to be named. And each tab carries selected, a state that has no HTML attribute and exists only in ARIA.

Roles are divided into four families, and knowing which family a role belongs to tells you what else it obliges you to provide.

Widget role
button, checkbox, slider, tab, menuitem. Interactive. Taking one on obliges you to supply keyboard behaviour and to keep its states current.
Document structure role
heading, list, table, article, figure. Describes content. Nearly always already provided by the right element.
Landmark role
banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo, region, search, form. The page's regions; §13.6.
Abstract role
widget, section, input, command, and eight more. Exist only to organise the specification. Authors must never use them in content — role="section" and role="widget" read as though they should work and do nothing at all.

The abstract role trap is worth a moment, because it is silent. role="widget" is not an error, gives no warning, and produces a node with no useful role. There are twelve abstract roles, and two of them, section and input, are ordinary English words a developer reaches for naturally.

Two pairs of terms for the rest of the section. An implicit role is the one an element has by being that element (<button> is a button), and an explicit role is one written with the role attribute. An explicit role always wins over the implicit role, which is what makes §13.9's second rule matter.

Roles also fall into families. A widget role describes an interactive control (button, checkbox, slider, tab), and a document structure role describes content (article, list, heading, table). Landmark roles (§13.6) are a third family. The distinction is worth having because a widget role commits you to keyboard behaviour and states, while a document structure role usually commits you to required children instead: role="list" needs listitem children, and a widget role such as role="tab" needs a tablist around it.

13.3 The Accessible Name

A role says what a thing is; the accessible name says which one it is. "Button" is useless; "Delete invoice 4021" is usable. Working out that name is the most consequential algorithm in this section. It is specified precisely, and almost every accessibility defect in the wild is a name that came out empty or came out wrong.

The specification calls it accessible name computation, and it works down an ordered list, stopping at the first thing that produces a non-empty string.

1
aria-labelledby
The text content of the elements whose ids it names. Wins over everything, including visible content.
2
aria-label
A literal string on the element. Invisible on screen.
3
Native markup
The mechanism the element itself provides: <label> for a form control, alt for an image, <caption> for a table, <legend> for a fieldset, <figcaption> for a figure.
4
Contents
The element's own text, for roles that permit it — a button, a link, a heading, a cell.
5
title
The tooltip attribute, as a last resort. Never available to a touch or keyboard user.

The order is not folklore. Here are all four of the top mechanisms competing on one element:

<span id="lb">labelledby</span>
<button aria-labelledby="lb" aria-label="label" title="title">content</button>

AX TREE
text "labelledby"
button "labelledby"
  text "content"

The button is named "labelledby". The aria-label, the visible text and the title all lost, and the visible text is still listed as a child, because the button's contents stay in the tree even when they did not supply the name. A sighted user reads "content"; a screen reader says "labelledby"; a voice-control user who says "click content" is not understood. That is the argument against aria-label on anything with visible text, and WCAG has a name for it: the visible label must be part of the accessible name.

The native mechanisms in rule 3 are the ones to prefer, because they are visible, they survive translation, and they need no ids. A <label> names its control whether it is connected by the for attribute or by wrapping:

<label for="a">Email</label>
<input id="a" type="email">
<label>Postcode <input type="text"></label>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Email"
textbox "Email"
LabelText
  text "Postcode"
  textbox "Postcode"

Two details in that tree are worth knowing. The LabelText node is Chrome's internal role for the label's own text: the label appears in the tree as well as naming the control, which is why a label reading "Email" and a control named "Email" count as one piece of information, not two. And the wrapping form puts the textbox inside the LabelText rather than beside it. Both name the control identically.

The two attributes that look like labels and are not:

<!-- ❌ neither of these is a label -->
<input type="text" placeholder="Email">
<input type="text" title="Email">

AX TREE
textbox "Email"
textbox "Email"

Both produce a named textbox, so both will pass a simple automated check, and both are defects. The placeholder disappears the moment the user types, taking the only description of the field with it, and every browser styles it in low-contrast grey. The title never appears at all for a keyboard or touch user. They are fallbacks in the name computation precisely so that a badly built page is not silent; they are not designs.

13.4 The Accessible Description

Besides the name, a node may carry an accessible description: secondary text, announced after the name and a pause, for things that do not belong in a label. Format hints, password rules, an explanation of what a destructive button will destroy.

It comes from aria-describedby, pointing at one or more ids:

<label for="p">Password</label>
<input id="p" type="password" aria-describedby="hint">
<p id="hint">At least twelve characters.</p>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Password"
textbox "Password" describedby=hint
paragraph
  text "At least twelve characters."

Two things in that tree. The textbox carries describedby=hint, a relationship recorded as a property, pointing at the node that supplies the description. And the paragraph is still there, unchanged, for everyone to read. aria-describedby does not move or hide content; it links to it. That makes it the right tool for hint text, and the wrong tool for anything only some users should get.

The difference between name and description matters for a practical reason. A screen reader in forms mode announces the name every time focus lands on the control; descriptions can be switched off in settings, and they are announced later. Anything a user must have in order to answer the question is a name; anything that merely helps is a description. "Email" is a name. "We will never share this" is a description.

13.5 States and Properties

The third thing a node carries is its condition. ARIA divides these into an aria state (things that change as the user interacts, like aria-checked and aria-expanded) and an aria property (things that describe the element more permanently, like aria-required and aria-haspopup). The distinction is only a way of organising them; the platform treats them alike, and both are written as aria-* attributes.

Native elements supply most of them without being asked:

<label for="x">Quantity</label>
<input id="x" type="number" min="1" max="9" required>
<label for="d">Locked</label>
<input id="d" disabled>
<label for="r">Reference</label>
<input id="r" readonly>

AX TREE
LabelText
  text "Quantity"
spinbutton "Quantity" required=true valuemax=9 valuemin=1
LabelText
  text "Locked"
textbox "Locked" disabled=true
LabelText
  text "Reference"
textbox "Reference" readonly=true

required attribute, disabled attribute and readonly became required=true, disabled=true and readonly=true with no ARIA in the markup at all, and min attribute/max attribute became the spinbutton's range. This is the normal case, not a special one, and it is the reason §13.9's first rule exists.

ARIA earns its place for a state HTML has no attribute for. A toggle button, one that stays pressed, is not an HTML concept:

<button aria-pressed="false">Bold</button>
<button aria-pressed="true">Italic</button>
<div role="button" tabindex="0">Underline</div>

AX TREE
button "Bold" pressed=false
button "Italic" pressed=true
button "Underline"

The first two are announced as "toggle button, not pressed" and "toggle button, pressed". The third is announced as a plain button, because a role does not bring its states with it. You take on role="button" and get nothing else: no focusability, no Space and Enter handling, no pressed. The tabindex="0" there does the focus half by hand (§14.3). The keyboard half still needs a listener, and the state half needs aria-pressed kept up to date by the same code that changes the appearance.

The states worth memorising, and the mistake each one prevents:

aria-expanded
On the control that expands something, never on the thing expanded. Its absence means "this does not expand"; false means "collapsed".
aria-controls
Names the id of what the control operates on. Support is patchy; treat it as documentation rather than as navigation.
aria-checked, aria-selected, aria-pressed
Three different ideas: ticked, chosen-within-a-set, held-down. Announced even when false, because "not pressed" is information.
aria-haspopup
Warns that activating this opens a menu, listbox, dialog or grid. Native <select> sets it for you.
aria-disabled
Announces disabled while leaving the element focusable and clickable. Useful for a control that must stay discoverable; a genuine trap when you meant disabled.
aria-invalid, aria-errormessage
The failed-validation pair; §12.9 builds the whole error pattern on them.
aria-level, aria-sort
Heading depth outside <h1>–<h6>, and a column's current sort direction (§10.11).
aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuetext
A custom slider's four numbers. aria-valuetext exists because "seventy-two" is not what the user wants to hear when the scale is "Large".

One measured caveat about the tool used throughout this section: Chrome's getFullAXTree does not currently expose aria-current as a property, so the trees printed here will not show it even where the markup sets it. That is a limit of this particular way of inspecting the tree, not of aria-current, which screen readers announce normally and which is the correct way to mark the current page in a navigation list (§7.12). It is worth stating rather than hiding, because "I could not see it in the tool" and "it is not there" are different claims, and a course that mixes them up teaches you to trust a tool further than it deserves.

Three more properties complete the set. aria-disabled, aria-required and aria-level are the ARIA spellings of states the native elements produce for free. So aria-required on an <input required> is redundant, and aria-disabled is only useful on something that cannot carry a real disabled attribute, where it announces the state while leaving the control focusable. aria-valuenow is the current value of a slider, spinbutton or progressbar, and it goes with aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax; the measurement above shows aria-valuenow's native equivalent appearing from min and max with no ARIA at all. And aria-errormessage points at the element holding a control's validation message, the ARIA counterpart of §12.9's pattern; aria-errormessage is only honoured while aria-invalid is also set.

Two terms for the family as a whole: an aria state is something that changes as the user interacts (expanded, checked, pressed, selected), while an aria property is a more fixed fact about the element, such as its label, its level or its relationship to another element. Nothing enforces the distinction. It is worth knowing because the specification groups them that way: an aria state is what you update in an event handler, and an aria property is usually written once. There is also aria-owns, which claims another element as a child in the accessibility tree when the DOM cannot express the relationship. aria-owns is a last resort, because it makes the two trees disagree on purpose, and reordering the DOM is nearly always the better fix.

13.6 Landmark Roles and the Shape of the Page

A screen reader user does not read a page top to bottom any more than you do. They jump around: by heading, by link, and by landmark. Landmarks are the page's regions, and §6 built them out of elements rather than roles. Here is what those elements actually produce:

<header>Site name</header>
<nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/">Home</a></nav>
<main><h1>Title</h1></main>
<aside>Related</aside>
<footer>© 2026</footer>

AX TREE
banner
  text "Site name"
navigation "Main"
  link "Home"
main
  heading "Title" level=1
complementary
  text "Related"
contentinfo
  text "© 2026"

Five elements, five landmark roles, and no role attribute anywhere. <header> became banner and <footer> became contentinfo, but only because they are at the top level of the document. Nested inside an <article>, they are ordinary containers with no landmark role at all, which is correct and often surprising.

<section> is the exception that proves the rule about names:

<section><h2>Notes</h2></section>
<section aria-labelledby="t"><h2 id="t">Notes</h2></section>

AX TREE
heading "Notes" level=2
region "Notes"
  heading "Notes" level=2

The first <section> produced no node at all: the heading is there, the section is not. The second produced a region. A <section> is only a landmark when it has an accessible name, because an unnamed region in a landmark list would be an entry reading "region" with nothing to tell it apart from the other four. The same rule applies to <form>: named, it is a form landmark; unnamed, it is nothing.

That is also the argument for naming every landmark you have more than one of. Two navigation landmarks both called "navigation" are a menu the user has to explore to tell apart; aria-label="Main" and aria-label="Breadcrumb" are a menu they can use. Do not put the word "navigation" in the label: the role is already announced, and "Main navigation navigation" is what the user hears.

13.7 Live Regions

Everything so far is announced because the user moved to it. A live region is the opposite: content that announces itself when it changes, without the user going there. Search results updating, a "saved" confirmation, a validation summary appearing, a countdown.

<div role="status">Draft saved</div>
<div role="alert">Could not save</div>
<output>42</output>

AX TREE
status atomic=true live=polite
  text "Draft saved"
alert atomic=true live=assertive
  text "Could not save"
status atomic=true live=polite
  text "42"

Three things in that tree are each worth more than a paragraph. role="status" implies live=polite and atomic=true, so you do not write aria-live when you use the role. role="alert" implies live=assertive, which means it interrupts whatever the screen reader is currently saying. And <output>, an ordinary HTML form element from §11.13, is a live region by default with exactly status's behaviour, which is why it is the right element for a calculated total and the wrong one for text that never changes.

aria-live takes three values, and the middle one is the only one you usually want.

off
The default. Changes are not announced.
polite
Announced at the next pause. Correct for almost everything.
assertive
Interrupts immediately. Correct for an error that blocks the user and for very little else. Overuse makes a page unusable — every interruption discards what was being said.

aria-atomic="true" says "read the whole region, not just the part that changed", which is what you want for "3 of 12 results" and not what you want for a log that keeps adding lines. And here is the rule that catches everyone: the live region must already be in the DOM, empty, before the change happens. A region inserted at the same moment as its text is often not announced, because the platform had nothing to watch. Render the empty container with the page, and write text into it later.

Two properties belong with live regions. aria-atomic="true" says the whole region should be announced when any part of it changes, not just the changed part, so aria-atomic is what turns "4" into "4 items in basket". And role="alert" is the shorthand for an assertive live region: role="alert" is aria-live="assertive" plus aria-atomic="true", and it is the right role for a validation error or a failure message that should interrupt.

13.8 Removing Things From the Tree

Four mechanisms take content out of the accessibility tree, and the differences between them matter.

<p>Visible and announced</p>
<p hidden>Removed from the page entirely</p>
<p aria-hidden="true">Visible on screen, absent from the tree</p>
<div inert><button>Cannot be reached</button></div>
<button>Can be reached</button>

AX TREE
paragraph
  text "Visible and announced"
button "Can be reached"
hidden attribute
Gone for everyone: not rendered, not in the tree, not focusable. The honest way to hide something.
aria-hidden="true"
Removed from the tree while staying on screen and staying focusable. Correct for a decorative icon beside text that already says the same thing. Never put it on anything focusable — you create a control a keyboard user can reach and a screen reader cannot describe.
inert attribute
The subtree is unfocusable, unclickable and out of the tree, but still painted. This is what a modal dialog needs applied to the rest of the page (§14.8), and doing it by hand with aria-hidden plus tabindex="-1" is how it was done before inert existed.
Presentational children
Some roles flatten their contents by specification: a button's inner markup contributes to its name and stops being separately navigable. You cannot put a heading or a link inside a button and expect either to be reachable.

The mechanism a beginner reaches for, and should not, is CSS display: none, which removes content from the tree exactly as the hidden attribute does. That is fine when you mean it, and a disaster for the "visually hidden" pattern: text meant only for screen readers. The correct technique clips the element to a one-pixel box instead of hiding it, and it belongs to css_mastery. What matters here is knowing why display: none cannot be the answer.

role="presentation" and its synonym role="none" are the fifth mechanism, and they are more drastic than they look:

<table role="presentation">
  <tr><td>Layout</td></tr>
</table>

AX TREE
text "Layout"

The table, the row and the cell are all gone; only the text survives. That is the point. Applied to a table used for layout (§10.12), it stops a screen reader announcing "table, one row, one column" about something that is not data. But it also shows that the role passes down to the structural children that need the parent, so it is not a local change.

The inert attribute is the third mechanism, and the only one that removes an element from both trees (the accessibility tree and the order of focus) while leaving it drawn on screen. The inert attribute on a container makes everything inside it unfocusable, unclickable and absent from the accessibility tree. That is exactly what showModal() applies to the rest of the page (§14.8), and what a hand-built overlay has to do by hand.

13.9 The Rules of ARIA

The specification gives five rules of thumb, ordered by how much time each one saves.

1. Use the native element instead. If a <button>, <a href>, <input>, <select> or <nav> will do the job, use it. You get the role, the states, the keyboard behaviour, the focus handling and the platform's own conventions, in every browser, for free, as §13.5's first tree showed. This is the first rule of aria, and it settles most ARIA questions before they are asked.

2. Do not change native semantics unless you really have to. <h2 role="tab"> destroys the heading. Wrap instead of overriding: put the <h2> inside the element that carries the role.

3. All interactive ARIA controls must be usable from the keyboard. A role="button" that only responds to click is a button a keyboard user can focus and cannot press. If you take on the role, you take on the behaviour with it.

4. Do not put aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element. This is §13.8's trap, stated as a rule because it is so easy to fall into: hiding an icon that happens to be a link produces a focus stop that announces nothing.

5. All interactive elements must have an accessible name. A nameless button is announced as "button", the accessibility equivalent of a link labelled "click here" (§7.10).

Underneath all five sits the sentence to take away from this section: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA. Nothing checks that an ARIA attribute is true. A role="checkbox" whose aria-checked is never updated, an aria-expanded on a menu that JavaScript forgets about, an aria-label left over from a previous design: each is worse than the plain markup it replaced, because a user who cannot see the screen has no way to notice the announcement is wrong. Surveys of the web's home pages have found that pages with ARIA have more detected errors on average than pages without it, and this is exactly why.

The tab pattern is the standard example of the third rule. role="tab" commits you to arrow-key navigation, a roving tabindex, aria-selected on each tab and aria-controls pointing at its panel. Take on role="tab" and you have taken on all of it, because a screen reader will announce the pattern and its user will expect the behaviour.

13.10 ARIA in HTML: What Is Allowed Where

There is a companion specification, aria in html, that says which roles and which aria-* attributes are valid on which elements. It exists because most combinations mean nothing and some do real harm, and its rules can be checked: the html validator in §16.4 enforces them.

Three families of restriction are worth knowing by heart.

Some elements accept no role at all. <html>, <head>, <meta>, <script>, <style> and <title> are not content, so a role on them is nonsense.

Some attributes are prohibited on some roles. A prohibited attribute is the sharp one: aria-label and aria-labelledby are not allowed on an element whose role is generic, which is the role a bare <div> or <span> has. <span aria-label="Warning">⚠</span> looks reasonable, is valid HTML, and names nothing, because a generic node cannot carry a name. Give the element a role first, or use a real element.

Some roles bring required children. role="list" expects listitem children; role="tablist" expects tab children; role="table" expects rows containing cells. Supply the role without the children and you have a list with no items, announced as such.

In practice all three take care of themselves if you use the elements you would reach for by default. This subsection mostly describes what goes wrong when you leave that path, and the aria in html rules are why a validator can tell you before a user does.

Two more terms from this part of the specification. A prohibited attribute is one the specification forbids on a given role. Most importantly, aria-label and aria-labelledby are a prohibited attribute on generic, on paragraph and on plain text, so naming a <div> or a <p> does nothing at all. And the tab pattern is the usual example of required structure: role="tablist" contains role="tab" elements, each of which points with aria-controls at a role="tabpanel". Leave out the role="tablist" and the tabs lose their position information; leave out the role="tabpanel" and the aria-controls points at nothing.

13.11 WCAG: The Standard Behind the Requests

Everything so far is mechanism. WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, is the conformance standard that regulators, purchasing departments and lawsuits actually refer to, and 2.2 is the current version. Its structure is worth knowing, because it is how accessibility work gets specified to you.

Four principles, remembered as POUR:

Perceivable
The information can reach the user's senses. Text alternatives (§8.3), captions (§9.8), contrast, content that survives being resized.
Operable
The interface can be driven. Keyboard access (§14), enough time, no seizure-inducing flashes, findable content.
Understandable
Readable text, predictable behaviour, and help when input goes wrong — the whole of §12.9.
Robust
It works with assistive technology, now and later. Valid markup, correct name/role/value — literally this section.

Under the principles sit guidelines, and under those sit testable success criterion entries, each at level A, AA or AAA. Level AA is the bar in almost every legal and contractual context. A is a floor nobody accepts on its own, and AAA contains criteria that not all content can meet.

The criterion this section exists to satisfy is 4.1.2, name role value: every interface component must expose its name, its role and, when it has one, its state, and must tell assistive technology when they change. Read that back against §13.2 to §13.5 and you have the whole section in one sentence.

WCAG's four principles are worth memorising, because every criterion hangs off one of them: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. perceivable covers text alternatives, captions and contrast; operable covers keyboard, timing and focus; understandable covers language, predictability and error handling; and robust covers valid markup and correct name/role/value, which means robust is the principle this whole course serves. The initials spell POUR, which is how most people remember them.

13.12 Auditing: What Tools Catch, and What They Cannot

Automated tools are genuinely useful and genuinely partial, and being precise about where they stop is what keeps a green report from being mistaken for an accessible page.

The accessibility tree itself
Chrome DevTools' accessibility inspector — the Accessibility pane beside Styles — shows the computed name with every source in the precedence chain, and marks which ones were superseded. It is the fastest way to answer "why is this named that?".
Rule engines
axe-core, and lighthouse, which embeds it. They find missing names, bad contrast, invalid ARIA, duplicate ids, and out-of-order headings.
The validator
Catches the aria in html violations from §13.10 alongside ordinary markup errors (§16.4).
A keyboard
Free, already installed, and finds more real defects than any of the above. Put the mouse down and use the page.

The published figure worth remembering: automated rule engines detect somewhere around a third of WCAG issues in practice. The two thirds they cannot reach are the judgement calls: whether alt text describes the purpose of the image, whether the reading order makes sense, whether an error message tells you how to fix the problem, whether "Read more" is a useful link name. A machine can see every one of those sentences and cannot judge any of them.

So the honest workflow has four steps, and only one is automated:

  • run the rule engine to clear the mechanical failures;
  • tab through the page to find the focus problems;
  • read the accessibility tree for anything whose name or role surprised you;
  • and, where you can, test with an actual screen reader.

NVDA on Windows and Orca on Linux are free; VoiceOver comes with macOS and iOS; JAWS is the commercial one. Half an hour with one of them changes how you see everything in this section, because you stop reasoning about the tree and start hearing it.

Name the tools once, so the vocabulary is familiar. nvda is the free Windows screen reader most testing is done with, and voiceover is the one built into macOS and iOS; between nvda and voiceover you can cover most real usage without buying anything. axe-core is the rule engine behind most automated checkers, and lighthouse embeds axe-core in Chrome's own audit panel, so a lighthouse accessibility score is an axe-core result with a number attached. The browser's accessibility inspector (Chrome's Accessibility pane, Firefox's Accessibility panel) is the one that shows the tree itself, and it is the tool this course used throughout.

Exercises

1. A colleague fixes an accessibility report by adding aria-label="Submit" to a <div> that already has a click handler. List everything still wrong.

Solution

Four things, in descending order of severity.

It is not focusable. A bare <div> is not in the tab order (§14.2), so a keyboard user cannot reach it at all. tabindex="0" would fix the reaching; nothing about aria-label does.

It is not operable. Even focused, a <div> does not respond to Enter or Space. A click handler fires on click, and the browser synthesises a click from those keys only for elements that are natively buttons. The handler would need explicit key handling.

It has no role. A <div> has the role generic. It will not be announced as a button, will not appear in a screen reader's list of buttons, and gives no hint that activating it does something.

The name does not even apply. This is the subtle one from §13.10: aria-label is a prohibited attribute on an element whose role is generic. The name is discarded. The markup looks fixed, the report may even go quiet, and the accessibility tree contains an unnamed generic node.

The fix is rule 1 of §13.9: <button type="button">Submit</button>. That is focusable, operable by Enter and Space, announced as a button, named by its contents, and works in every browser with no JavaScript beyond the handler that was already there. Every one of the four defects above is a thing <button> does for free.

2. Explain why placeholder="Email" passes an automated "form control has a label" check and is still wrong.

Solution

Because the check is asking whether the control has an accessible name, and it does. placeholder is step 3-adjacent in the accessible name computation (§13.3) — a documented fallback, used when nothing better exists. The tree in §13.3 shows textbox "Email", identical to what a real <label> produces. The rule engine sees a name and moves on.

It is wrong for reasons no rule engine can evaluate:

It vanishes when the field has content. The user types, the only description of the field disappears, and they can no longer check what this box was for. This is worst exactly when it matters most — reviewing a long form before submitting.

It fails at low vision and in bright light. Browsers style placeholder text at deliberately low contrast to signal that it is not a value, which puts it below the WCAG contrast threshold in most designs. Raising the contrast makes it look like a filled-in field instead.

It confuses autofill and translation. A field that appears to have a value is harder for password managers and translation tools to handle correctly.

It leaves nothing to click. A real <label> extends the control's hit area — clicking the word "Email" focuses the field, which matters for anyone with imprecise pointing.

The correct pattern keeps both: a <label> for the name, and placeholder only for a format example that is not the name — <label for="d">Date</label><input id="d" placeholder="DD/MM/YYYY">. Better still, put the format in an aria-describedby hint (§13.4), where it survives the user typing.

3. A modal dialog is built with a <div>. The team adds role="dialog" and aria-modal="true". What is still missing, and what does the tree not tell you?

Solution

role="dialog" and aria-modal="true" make the announcement correct. They do nothing whatsoever about behaviour, which is §13.2's asymmetry in its most consequential form.

Missing: a name. role="dialog" with no accessible name is announced as "dialog". Point aria-labelledby at the dialog's own heading.

Missing: focus moves in. When the dialog opens, focus must be moved into it, or a screen reader user is still positioned back in the page behind (§14.8).

Missing: the rest of the page is still reachable. aria-modal="true" is a claim about modality, not an implementation of it. Tab still walks out of the dialog into the page behind, which is the defining bug of hand-rolled modals. The fix is inert on everything else (§13.8) or a focus trap.

Missing: Escape closes it, and focus returns. Neither is free, and returning focus to the control that opened the dialog is the half most implementations forget.

Missing: it is not in the top layer. Stacking has to be managed by hand against every z-index on the page.

What the tree does not tell you: all of it. The accessibility tree will show dialog with modal=true and look completely correct, because every one of those five defects is behavioural. That is precisely why §13.12 puts a keyboard above every automated tool — tabbing once past the last control in the dialog reveals four of the five in about two seconds.

The alternative is §14.8's <dialog> element with showModal(), which supplies modality, the top layer, Escape, the backdrop and the inertness of the rest of the page, and needs only the name and the focus restoration from you.

4. You are asked to add aria-live="assertive" to a search-results container so that result counts are announced. Give two reasons to push back and say what you would build instead.

Solution

Reason one: assertive interrupts. It discards whatever the screen reader is currently saying, mid-word. On a search field that updates as the user types, every keystroke interrupts the announcement of the previous keystroke, and the user hears fragments of numbers and nothing else. polite (§13.7) queues the announcement for the next pause, which is what almost every live region wants; assertive is for errors that block the user.

Reason two: the region is the wrong size. Marking the whole results container live means the entire list is announced whenever any of it changes — potentially dozens of results read aloud. The announcement should be a small, dedicated region containing the summary only.

What to build instead: an empty role="status" region rendered with the page, updated with a short summary.

<label for="s">Search</label>
<input id="s" type="search" aria-describedby="count">
<p id="count" role="status"></p>
<ul id="results"></ul>

The results go in the list; the text "12 results" goes in the status region. Three details make it work. The region is already in the DOM and empty before the first change, which is §13.7's rule — a live region created at the same moment as its content is often not announced. role="status" implies live=polite and atomic=true, so the summary is read as a unit and does not interrupt. And the updates should be debounced, so a fast typist gets one announcement rather than eight.

For a search that navigates rather than updating live, none of this is needed: a page load announces itself.

5. Given the tree below, reconstruct markup that produces it, and say which two attributes are doing work that no element could do alone.

group "Delivery"
  Legend
    text "Delivery"
  radio "Standard" checked=true
  radio "Express" checked=false
Solution 
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="std" checked> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="exp"> Express</label>
</fieldset>

The <fieldset> produces the group role; the <legend> names it, which is the native mechanism at step 3 of the accessible name computation (§13.3) and is why no aria-label appears anywhere. Each wrapping <label> names its radio from the text beside it (§13.3's implicit form), and checked attribute produces checked=true.

The trick in the question is that there are no ARIA attributes at all. Everything in that tree — the group, its name, the roles, both states — came from four ordinary HTML elements. That is §13.9's first rule as a worked example, and it is the honest answer to "which two attributes are doing work no element could do": none of them are, because there are none.

Two details worth noticing in the tree. checked=false is printed for the unselected radio rather than omitted, because "not checked" is information a screen reader announces. And the Legend node appears as well as naming the group, exactly as LabelText did in §13.3 — the text is both a name and content.

SECTION 14

Focus, the Keyboard and Interactive Elements

§13 was about what the page says. This section is about what it does when nobody touches the mouse. Focus is the marker for "the element that will receive the next key press", and automated tools are worst at checking it, because focus order is not a property of the markup. It comes out of several things interacting: the DOM order, tabindex, disabled, inert, shadow roots and the top layer. The only way to know the result is to press Tab.

So every focus order printed in this section was produced by driving a real Chromium and recording where the caret went. Several of them are not what the markup suggests.

More people depend on this than the obvious group. Keyboard-only users, yes, but also anyone using voice control, a switch device, a screen reader or a broken trackpad, or simply someone filling in a form who would rather keep their hands on the keys. Getting focus right is one of the few accessibility investments that visibly improves the experience for everybody.

14.1 What Focus Is

At any moment, exactly one element in the document has focus: the one that receives key presses. document.activeElement names it, and when nothing has been focused it is <body>.

Two vocabulary distinctions do a lot of work later:

Focusable
Can hold focus, whether by click, by .focus(), or by Tab.
Sequential focus navigation
The subset reachable by pressing Tab, in a defined order. Every element in it is focusable; not every focusable element is in it.

tabindex="-1" fills exactly the gap between them: focusable from script, but not reachable by Tab. That makes it the right tool for a heading you want to send focus to after a route change (§14.6), and the wrong tool for a control.

14.2 What Is Focusable Without Being Told

<a href="/a">Link</a>
<a>No href</a>
<button>Button</button>
<label for="i">Field</label><input id="i">
<div>Div</div>
<span tabindex="0">Span</span>

TAB ORDER
<a> "Link"
<button> "Button"
<input>#i
<span> "Span"
(leaves the page)

Five elements in that markup look interactive, and only four are stops. An <a> without an href is not a link: it cannot take focus, has no link role, and does nothing on Enter. It is a common accident when an href is filled in by a template and comes out empty.

The set of elements that can take focus by default is short: <a href>, <button>, <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <summary> inside a <details>, elements with contenteditable, and <iframe>. Everything else needs tabindex.

Two ways of taking a control out are worth knowing exactly, because they look similar and are not:

<button id="a">A</button>
<button id="b" disabled>B</button>
<label for="c">C</label><input id="c" readonly>
<label for="d">D</label><input id="d" disabled>
<button id="e">E</button>

TAB ORDER
<button>#a "A"
<input>#c
<button>#e "E"
(leaves the page)

The disabled attribute removes the control from the sequence entirely; readonly leaves it in, so the value can be read and copied. That difference, plus the difference in what gets submitted (§12.2), is the whole choice between them.

14.3 tabindex, and Why Positive Values Are a Bug

tabindex takes three kinds of value, and only two of them should ever appear in your code.

0
Focusable and in the sequence, at its natural place in document order. What a custom widget needs.
-1
Focusable by script only. For focus targets (§14.6) and for the unselected members of a roving group (§14.6).
Positive
Never. It does not reorder locally — it reorders the entire document.
<button id="one">One</button>
<button id="two" tabindex="1">Two</button>
<button id="three">Three</button>
<button id="four" tabindex="2">Four</button>

TAB ORDER
<button>#two "Two"
<button>#four "Four"
<button>#one "One"
<button>#three "Three"
(leaves the page)

Every positive value goes first, in numeric order, ahead of everything in the document that has no tabindex, including the site's own navigation and skip link. Two buttons with tabindex="1" and tabindex="2" therefore become the first two stops on the page. The value applies to the whole document, so a component that sets one breaks every page it is dropped into, and the numbers would have to be managed across the whole site, which nobody does.

The correct way to change the focus order is to change the DOM order.

14.4 Focus Order Follows the DOM, Not the Screen

<div style="display:flex">
  <button id="second" style="order:2">Second in source</button>
  <button id="first" style="order:1">First on screen</button>
</div>

TAB ORDER
<button>#second "Second in source"
<button>#first "First on screen"
(leaves the page)

CSS moved the boxes; it did not move the stops. The user sees "First on screen" on the left, and Tab goes to the other one. Flexbox order, grid placement, position: absolute and direction can all cause this, and it is the most common way a redesign silently breaks keyboard use: nothing visible changed, so nobody tested it again.

WCAG has a criterion for it (focus order must keep the meaning and the page usable), and the test is free: Tab through the page and watch whether the indicator moves sensibly. When the source order and the visual order really must differ, reorder the DOM and use CSS to position things, not the other way round.

14.5 The Focus Indicator

The browser draws a ring around the focused element. Never remove it without replacing it. outline: none with nothing in its place makes a page unusable by keyboard, and it is still the most common accessibility defect in production CSS.

It gets removed because the ring also used to appear on mouse clicks, where it looked like a mistake. :focus-visible solved that properly. It matches only when the browser judges that a focus indicator should be shown: keyboard focus, yes; a click on a button, no; a click into a text field, yes, because you need to see where the caret is. Modern browsers already draw their default ring through it, so leaving the default alone is a correct choice.

Where you do style it, WCAG's Focus Appearance criterion (2.4.13, at Level AAA) asks that the indicator be at least as large as a two-pixel outline around the element, with a 3:1 contrast between the same pixels focused and unfocused, which rules out a one-pixel grey line on a grey button. The visual technique belongs to css_mastery. The requirement belongs here, because a focus indicator is not decoration: for a keyboard user it is the entire interface.

The indicator is often called the focus ring, and the single worst thing you can do to a page is remove it: outline: none with no replacement leaves a keyboard user with no idea where they are. If the default focus ring does not suit the design, replace it; do not delete it. :focus-visible is the selector that makes this practical, because :focus-visible matches only when the browser judges the indicator should be shown. A mouse click on a button then draws no ring, while Tabbing to it does.

14.6 Managing Focus

Three patterns cover almost everything.

Send focus to a target. After an action that changes what the page is about (a route change in a single-page application, a failed submit (§12.9), a panel opening), move focus to the new content's heading. Give the heading tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus without joining the tab sequence. The user's next Tab then continues from the right place.

Restore focus afterwards. Whatever opened a dialog, a menu or a panel is where focus must go back to when it closes. Store the element before opening, and call .focus() on it afterwards. Skip this and the user is dropped back at the top of the document.

Roving tabindex. A composite widget (a toolbar, a tab strip, a tree) should be one tab stop, with the arrow keys moving inside it. The technique is exactly what its name says: every member carries tabindex="-1" except the current one, which carries 0, and the arrow keys move the 0 and call .focus(). This is not an optional extra; it is what the platform already does:

<button id="a">A</button>
<label><input type="radio" name="r" id="r1" checked> Standard</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="r" id="r2"> Express</label>
<button id="b">B</button>

TAB ORDER
<button>#a "A"
<input>#r1 value=on
<button>#b "B"
(leaves the page)

Two radios, one stop. Tab enters the group once and leaves it once; the arrow keys choose within it. Any custom widget of the same shape is expected to behave the same way, and a tab strip where Tab visits all seven tabs is wrong, even though every tab can be reached.

Two terms for the rest of the section. focus management is the general practice of deciding where focus goes when the page changes underneath it (after a route change, after a dialog opens, after a row is deleted), and focus management is something you have to do, because the browser only does it for real page loads. focus restoration is the specific half that returns focus to where it came from: focus restoration is what showModal() does for you (§14.8), and what a hand-built overlay has to remember to do by storing document.activeElement before it opens.

14.7 Details and Summary

The built-in disclosure widget, with no JavaScript at all:

<details>
  <summary>Delivery options</summary>
  <p>Standard delivery takes three days.</p>
</details>

AX TREE
group
  DisclosureTriangle "Delivery options" expanded=false

Two things in that tree. The whole thing is a group, and the <summary> is a DisclosureTriangle carrying expanded=false. The browser keeps that state up to date, which is the entire argument for using the element. And the paragraph is absent, because a closed <details> hides its contents from the accessibility tree as well as from the screen. The focus sequence confirms the same:

<details><summary>More</summary><a href="/x">Inside</a></details>
<button>After</button>

TAB ORDER
<summary> "More"
<button> "After"
(leaves the page)

The link inside is not a stop while the disclosure is closed. That is correct, and it is something hand-built accordions often get wrong by leaving hidden content focusable.

The open attribute sets the starting state and is updated by the browser as the user toggles, so you can read it to save the state. And a name attribute on several <details> elements makes them an exclusive accordion: opening one closes the others, again with no script.

<summary> must be the first child. It is the only part that is a focus stop, it responds to Enter and Space, and it must be short, because it is the accessible name for the whole group.

Two more things about <details>. The open attribute is a boolean reflecting the current state, and it works in both directions: the browser sets and clears the open attribute as the user toggles, so reading it tells you the state and writing it changes it. And giving several <details> elements the same name makes them an exclusive accordion: opening one closes the others, with no script at all. That exclusive accordion behaviour is all most accordion components are built to do.

14.8 Dialog

<dialog> is the modal that gets everything right. It is worth listing what "everything" means, because each item is something hand-built modals get wrong.

<dialog open>
  <h2>Delete this invoice?</h2>
  <button>Delete</button>
  <button>Cancel</button>
</dialog>

AX TREE
dialog
  heading "Delete this invoice?" level=2
  button "Delete"
  button "Cancel"

A closed <dialog>, one without the open attribute, produces no node at all in the accessibility tree and is not drawn, so leaving it in the markup costs nothing.

There are two ways to open it, and they are not interchangeable. show() opens it non-modal: the rest of the page stays interactive, and Tab walks straight out of the dialog into the page behind, which is almost never what a confirmation dialog wants. showModal() opens it modal, and this is what that gives you, measured by driving the browser:

focus before opening: open
after showModal(), focus starts at: in1
tab cycle: in1 -> in2 -> body -> in1 -> in2 -> body
after Escape, dialog open: false
focus after close: open

Four behaviours in six lines. Focus moved into the dialog automatically, to its first focusable element. Tab cycled within the dialog and never reached the buttons behind it. Escape closed it with no key handler written. And focus returned to the button that opened it. Each of those is a separate defect in the average hand-built modal (§13's third exercise lists them), and here all four are free.

Three more things showModal() gives you. The dialog is promoted to the top layer, above every z-index on the page, so there is no stacking fight. The rest of the document becomes inert, so a click behind it does nothing. And a ::backdrop pseudo-element appears behind it, which is the correct way to dim the page. A separate overlay <div> is not needed, and it is the usual cause of the bug where the page behind scrolls.

close() closes it and sets returnValue. A <form method="dialog"> inside closes it on submit and sets returnValue to the submitting button's value, which is the no-JavaScript way to build a confirm dialog. And closedby lets you declare whether light dismissal applies, meaning whether clicking the backdrop or pressing Escape closes it.

The one thing it does not do for you is the name. Point aria-labelledby at the dialog's heading, or a screen reader announces only "dialog".

A modal dialog is the pattern this element implements, and "modal" means precisely that the rest of the page is inert while it is open. That containment is a deliberate focus trap, the one case where trapping focus is correct rather than a defect, because the user can always leave with Escape. A focus trap with no way out is the worst keyboard defect there is, and it is exactly what a hand-built modal dialog produces when someone builds the Tab cycling and forgets the Escape handler. Two attributes are worth knowing: closedby states what may close the dialog (any, closerequest or none), and light dismiss is the behaviour closedby="any" turns on, where a click outside the dialog closes it. That is the popover default (§14.9), not the <dialog> default.

14.9 Popover

The popover attribute handles the other half of the overlay problem: menus, tooltips, disclosure panels, notifications. These are things that are not modal and should close when you click elsewhere.

<button popovertarget="menu">Actions</button>
<div id="menu" popover>
  <button>Rename</button>
  <button>Delete</button>
</div>

AX TREE
button "Actions" expanded=false

That tree shows the whole mechanism in one line. With the popover closed, its contents are absent and the button carries expanded=false: the browser keeps up to date the state that §13.5 warned would go stale if you kept it yourself. No script is involved. popovertarget connects the button to the panel, and popovertargetaction can force show, hide or toggle instead of the default toggle.

Three values, and the difference is dismissal:

auto
The default. Light dismiss: clicking outside or pressing Escape closes it, and opening another auto popover closes this one. Correct for menus.
manual
Closes only when something tells it to, and does not close its siblings. For toasts and notifications that stack.
hint
A third layer for tooltips: a hint closes other hints but does not close an open auto popover, so a tooltip inside a menu does not dismiss the menu.

Popovers also live in the top layer, so like <dialog> they escape overflow: hidden and every z-index. The distinction to hold on to: showModal() when the user must deal with it; popover when they may ignore it. A popover does not trap focus and does not make the page inert, by design.

The popover api is all of that: a popover attribute on the element, and a popovertarget on the button that controls it. The popover attribute takes two values. popover="auto", the default, gives light dismissal and automatic closing: opening one popover="auto" closes any other that is not its ancestor, and a click outside or Escape closes it. popover="manual" gives none of that. A popover="manual" stays open until something closes it explicitly, which is what a toast notification wants. The button's popovertargetaction chooses what the control does (show, hide or the default toggle), so popovertargetaction="hide" is how a close button inside the popover works. Between the popover api and <dialog>, the rule is: a popover attribute for something that can be dismissed and blocks nothing, showModal() for something that must be answered.

14.10 Inert

The inert attribute marks a subtree as absent for the purposes of interaction: it cannot be focused or clicked, and it is out of the accessibility tree, while still being drawn on screen.

<div inert>
  <button id="a">Behind the overlay</button>
</div>
<button id="b">Reachable</button>

TAB ORDER
<button>#b "Reachable"
(leaves the page)

showModal() applies this to the rest of the document for you, which is why it is rarely written by hand. Where it earns its place is a non-modal overlay, a form step that is not active yet, or a carousel's off-screen slides: anywhere content is visible but should not be usable.

The technique from before inert was aria-hidden="true" plus tabindex="-1" on every focusable element inside, kept up to date by script. It is worth knowing, because you will find it in existing code, and worth replacing, because the two halves drift apart: aria-hidden alone leaves the focus stops behind.

<a href="/x" id="a">Visible</a>
<a href="/y" id="b" aria-hidden="true">Hidden from assistive technology</a>
<a href="/z" id="c">Last</a>

TAB ORDER
<a>#a "Visible"
<a>#b "Hidden from assistive te"
<a>#c "Last"
(leaves the page)

Three stops. The middle link is absent from the accessibility tree (§13.8) and still very much present in the focus sequence, so a screen reader user tabs onto a control that announces nothing at all. That is §13.9's fourth rule, and this is the measurement behind it.

14.11 Keyboard Conventions to Honour

If you build a widget, users expect the platform's keys. These are the ones with settled conventions:

Tab / Shift+Tab
Between components. Never within one.
Arrow keys
Within a composite: tabs, radios, menus, toolbars, trees, grids.
Enter
Activate a link or a button; submit a form from a text field.
Space
Activate a button, toggle a checkbox, open a select. Never a link — Space scrolls.
Escape
Close the thing on top: dialog, popover, menu, autocomplete list.
Home / End
First and last item in a composite.
Type-ahead
Jump to the item starting with the typed letters, in a listbox or select.

The difference between Enter and Space is the sharpest test of whether a control is the right element. A real <button> responds to both; a real link responds to Enter only; a <div role="button"> responds to neither until you write the handler, and the handler people write usually forgets Space (§13.9's third rule).

Two things not to do. Do not add custom single-key shortcuts without a way to turn them off or change them: a voice-control user dictating text triggers every one of them, and WCAG 2.1 added a criterion about it. And do not use accesskey: its modifier key differs between platforms and browsers, and it clashes unpredictably with the shortcuts of assistive technology.

The whole section comes down to one habit, and it costs nothing: put the mouse down and Tab through the page before you ship it. Every measurement above came from doing exactly that, with a script instead of a hand.

The standard for all of this has a name: WCAG 2.1.1, keyboard accessible, at Level A. Every function of the page must be usable from a keyboard. Its companion is 2.1.2, no keyboard trap, which requires that focus can always be moved away again. A keyboard trap is therefore a Level A failure on its own, and it is why a hand-built overlay that cycles Tab without handling Escape is a more serious defect than the missing feature it was added for. Being keyboard accessible is not a separate feature to build. It is what you get by using the elements in this course as they are, and what you lose the moment a <div> takes over from a <button>.

Exercises

1. A designer asks you to add tabindex="1", tabindex="2" and tabindex="3" to the three fields of a signup form so they are reached first. Explain what will actually happen.

Solution

Those three fields become the first three focus stops on the entire page — before the skip link, before the site navigation, before anything in the header (§14.3). Every positive tabindex is ordered ahead of every element without one, document-wide, and the value is not scoped to the form.

The consequences compound. A keyboard user pressing Tab from the address bar lands in the middle of the page with no context. After the third field, focus jumps back to the top of the document and walks the navigation the user has already skipped past. And if any other component on the page also uses a positive value — a third-party widget, a cookie banner — the two sets interleave by number, so the order depends on values chosen by people who never met.

There is also a maintenance problem with no good answer: adding a field between the first and second means renumbering, and a global numbering scheme has to be maintained by everyone touching the page.

What the designer actually wants is for the form to come early. The fix is to move it earlier in the DOM, which fixes the reading order for screen readers at the same time, and to use CSS for placement if it must appear lower on screen — remembering §14.4, that visual order and focus order are then different, which is the problem in reverse.

If the goal is only "let people get to the form quickly", the standard answer is a skip link: a link at the very top of the page, visible on focus, pointing at the form's id (§6.10).

2. A team builds a modal with a <div>, an overlay, role="dialog", aria-modal="true" and a focus trap. List what <dialog> plus showModal() would have given them, and what they still have to write themselves.

Solution

What showModal() supplies, all measured in §14.8:

  • Focus moves into the dialog, to its first focusable element.
  • Tab cycles within the dialog and cannot reach the page behind — no focus-trap code.
  • Escape closes it, with no key handler.
  • Focus returns to the element that opened it.
  • The rest of the document becomes inert: clicks and screen reader navigation behind it do nothing (§14.10).
  • The dialog is in the top layer, above every z-index, so no stacking-context problem and no need for the overlay <div> at all.
  • ::backdrop dims the page behind it.
  • The dialog role and modal state are set by the element.

What is still yours:

  • The accessible name. aria-labelledby pointing at the heading, or it announces as "dialog" (§13's third exercise).
  • Opening it. showModal() has to be called; there is no declarative attribute equivalent to popovertarget.
  • Scroll locking of the page behind, if the design wants it.
  • What the buttons do. A <form method="dialog"> inside gives you returnValue for free, which covers the confirm/cancel case with no JavaScript.
  • Styling, including ::backdrop and any open/close transition.

The honest comparison is not that the hand-built one is wrong — it is that it is eight behaviours implemented and tested by hand, each of which will be broken by some future refactor, against one method call. The <div> version is worth keeping only if it must run somewhere <dialog> does not exist, which is no longer a real constraint.

3. Why is aria-hidden="true" on a link worse than doing nothing, and what should be used instead?

Solution

Because it removes the element from the accessibility tree while leaving it in the focus sequence — measured in §14.10, where the hidden link is still the second of three tab stops.

The result is a control a keyboard user can land on and a screen reader cannot describe. The user hears silence, or at best the bare word "link", with no name, no purpose and no indication of what pressing Enter would do. Doing nothing at all would at least have announced the link's text. This is exactly why it is a numbered rule in §13.9.

What to use instead, depending on the intent:

  • To hide it from everyone, use hidden attribute or CSS display: none. Gone from the page, the tree and the focus order together, with no possibility of drift.
  • To make it visible but not operable, use inert attribute on it or its container (§14.10). Unfocusable, unclickable, out of the tree, still painted.
  • To hide a decorative icon inside a link that already has text, aria-hidden="true" on the <svg> or the <span> is exactly right — because that element is not focusable. The rule is about focusable elements, not about the attribute.

The general form: aria-hidden changes one of the two trees. Whenever a change must apply to both, it needs a mechanism that touches both.

4. A tab strip has seven tabs. Tabbing through it visits all seven. Is that correct? Justify the answer with reference to a native control.

Solution

No. A composite widget should be one tab stop, with the arrow keys moving between its members (§14.6).

The native control that settles it is the radio group, measured in §14.6: two radios, one stop. Tab enters the group, the arrow keys choose within it, Tab leaves. <select> behaves the same way — one stop, arrows and type-ahead inside — and so do the browser's own toolbars. A user's expectation is set by those, and a tab strip is the same shape of control.

Why it matters beyond convention: Tab is the coarse navigation key, for moving between the things on a page. A page whose every list item and tab is a stop makes Tab useless for its actual job, and a user hunting for the form at the bottom has to press it forty times.

The implementation is the roving tabindex: every tab carries tabindex="-1" except the currently selected one, which carries 0. Arrow keys move that 0 to the next tab, call .focus() on it, and update aria-selected (§13.2). Home and End jump to the first and last.

There is one legitimate variation. In the "manual activation" pattern, the arrow keys move focus without changing the panel and Enter or Space activates — which is better when switching panels is expensive. In "automatic activation" the arrow keys both move and activate, which is better when it is cheap. Both are one tab stop; the difference is only what an arrow key does.

5. A single-page application changes the route and swaps the main content. Screen reader users report that nothing seems to happen. Diagnose and fix.

Solution

Nothing did happen, from the user's point of view. A real page load moves focus to the top of the new document and the browser announces the new title. A client-side route change does neither: the URL changes, the DOM under <main> is replaced, and focus is still sitting on the link that was clicked — which may no longer exist, in which case the browser resets focus to <body> and the user's position is lost entirely.

The fix has three parts.

Move focus to the new content. Give the new view's <h1> a tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus without joining the tab sequence (§14.1), and call .focus() on it after rendering. The heading is announced, the user knows where they are, and their next Tab continues from the right place.

<main>
  <h1 tabindex="-1">Invoice 4021</h1>
</main>

Update the document title. document.title is what a browser announces on a real navigation, and what appears in history and in the tab. Set it on every route change.

Announce the transition if focus alone is not enough. A role="status" region (§13.7) saying "Invoices page loaded" covers the gap for users whose screen reader does not announce the focus move clearly. It must already be in the DOM and empty before the change.

Two things to avoid. Do not focus the <main> element itself unless it has a name — it announces as an unnamed region. And do not use aria-live on the whole content area: every route change would read the entire page.

The general principle is the one behind §14.6's first pattern: when the page's subject changes without a navigation, focus is how you tell the user.

SECTION 15

Templates, Custom Elements and Shadow DOM

Every section so far has used the elements the platform ships. This one is about adding your own. Not by imitating them with <div>s and classes, but by extending the list of elements itself, so that <user-card> is as real as <p> to the parser, the DOM, the accessibility tree and form submission.

The three specifications that make this possible are usually grouped together under the name web components, but they solve three separate problems:

  • <template> gives you markup the parser accepts but does not run.
  • Custom elements give you a tag name tied to a JavaScript class.
  • Shadow DOM gives you a hidden subtree whose markup and styles cannot collide with the rest of the page.

They are independent, and each one is useful alone. Most of the confusion around them comes from being taught as one thing.

15.1 Three Problems, Three Mechanisms

Inert markup
You want a chunk of HTML in the document that is not rendered, whose images do not load and whose scripts do not run, ready to be cloned. That is <template>.
A real element
You want a tag with behaviour attached, which the parser upgrades wherever it appears — including in HTML you did not write. That is a custom element.
Encapsulation
You want internal markup that the page's CSS cannot reach and that the page's querySelector does not find. That is shadow dom.

None of them is a framework. There is no data binding, no reactivity and no rendering loop; those are the parts a framework adds. What the platform gives you is the boundary of an element, which is exactly the part a framework cannot give you, because creating elements is the parser's job.

15.2 Template: Markup That Does Nothing

<template id="row">
  <tr>
    <td class="name"></td>
    <td class="qty"></td>
  </tr>
</template>

A <template> is parsed, so its contents become a real DOM subtree. But that subtree lives in a separate document fragment, attached to the element's content property instead of to the page. So it is not drawn, its <img> does not download, its <script> does not run, and its ids do not clash with the document's.

The other thing it does is skip the content-model rules. <tr> outside a <table> is foster-parented out by the parser (§10.4); inside a <template> it is kept, which is why a table-row template is the standard example.

document.body.innerHTML = `
  <template id="row"><li class="item"><b class="n"></b>: <span class="q"></span></li></template>
  <ul id="list"></ul>`;
const tpl = document.getElementById('row');
const list = document.getElementById('list');
for (const [n, q] of [['Bolts', 12], ['Nuts', 30]]) {
  const clone = tpl.content.cloneNode(true);
  clone.querySelector('.n').textContent = n;
  clone.querySelector('.q').textContent = String(q);
  list.append(clone);
}
console.log(list.innerHTML);
console.log('template still empty on the page:', tpl.childElementCount);

<li class="item"><b class="n">Bolts</b>: <span class="q">12</span></li><li class="item"><b class="n">Nuts</b>: <span class="q">30</span></li>
template still empty on the page: 0

Three details. cloneNode(true) makes a deep copy, because you want a new copy each time instead of moving the original. Appending a fragment moves its children and leaves the fragment empty, which is why the loop clones it. And tpl.childElementCount is 0 even though the template plainly contains an <li>: the children live under content, not under the element.

Compared with building the same markup from innerHTML, a template is faster (it is parsed once), safer (no strings are glued together, so there is no way to inject markup; see §16.9), and easier to read, because the markup is markup.

15.3 Defining a Custom Element

An autonomous custom element is a class that extends HTMLElement, registered under a name.

class WordCount extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    const words = (this.textContent || '').trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length;
    this.setAttribute('data-words', String(words));
  }
}
customElements.define('word-count', WordCount);

document.body.innerHTML = '<word-count>the quick brown fox</word-count>';
const el = document.querySelector('word-count');
console.log('instance of WordCount:', el instanceof WordCount);
console.log('data-words:', el.getAttribute('data-words'));
console.log('tag name:', el.tagName.toLowerCase());

instance of WordCount: true
data-words: 4
tag name: word-count

The name is not free-form. A valid custom element name must contain a hyphen, must start with a lowercase letter, and must not be one of a short list of reserved hyphenated names from SVG and MathML (font-face among them). The hyphen is the whole compatibility guarantee: the standard will never define a hyphenated tag, so your name can never clash with a future element. It is also what §2.11 relies on: a hyphenated unknown tag is a custom element, not a typo.

customElements.define may be called only once per name; a second call throws an error. And upgrade is the word for what happens to an element that was already in the DOM when define ran. The parser created it as a plain HTMLElement, and define changes its prototype after the fact and runs its callbacks. That is why a custom element works in server-rendered HTML whose script loads late: the markup is parsed at once and comes alive when the definition arrives.

The kind defined this way is called an autonomous custom element: a new element name of your own, extending HTMLElement. The other kind, a customized built-in, extends an existing element instead (§15.13). An autonomous custom element is the one every browser supports, and the one to use.

15.4 The Lifecycle Callbacks

There are four callbacks, and the order of the first two is not what most people assume.

constructor
The element exists but is not in the document. Must not touch attributes or children — the specification forbids it, and the parser has not supplied them yet. Set up internal state and a shadow root, nothing else.
connectedCallback
Inserted into a document. Where rendering, event listeners and subscriptions belong. Can run more than once — moving an element disconnects and reconnects it.
disconnectedCallback
Removed. Where you undo everything connectedCallback did — every listener on window, every timer, every observer. Skipping this is the standard web-components memory leak.
attributeChangedCallback
One of the observedAttributes changed, was added, or was removed. Fires before connectedCallback for attributes present in the markup.

That last ordering is measurable and it matters:

class OrderProbe extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['level'];
  constructor() { super(); console.log('constructor'); }
  attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
    console.log(`attributeChangedCallback ${name}: ${oldValue} -> ${newValue}`);
  }
  connectedCallback() { console.log('connectedCallback'); }
  disconnectedCallback() { console.log('disconnectedCallback'); }
}
customElements.define('order-probe', OrderProbe);

const el = document.createElement('order-probe');
el.setAttribute('level', '1');
document.body.append(el);
el.setAttribute('level', '2');
el.remove();

constructor
attributeChangedCallback level: null -> 1
connectedCallback
attributeChangedCallback level: 1 -> 2
disconnectedCallback

So by the time connectedCallback runs, every observed attribute has already been delivered. That means the rendering should happen in connectedCallback, and attributeChangedCallback should only record the change, re-rendering only if the element is already connected. Rendering from attributeChangedCallback alone produces an element that renders once per attribute before it is even in the document.

Note that oldValue is null the first time, not undefined and not the empty string. That null exists precisely to tell "was absent" apart from "was empty".

15.5 observedAttributes

attributeChangedCallback fires only for names listed in the static observedAttributes array. The list is read once, when the element is defined, so it cannot be changed later.

class Watcher extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['size'];
  attributeChangedCallback(name, _old, value) { console.log('saw', name, '=', value); }
}
customElements.define('w-atcher', Watcher);
const el = document.createElement('w-atcher');
document.body.append(el);
el.setAttribute('size', 'large');
el.setAttribute('colour', 'red');
el.removeAttribute('size');
console.log('colour is set:', el.getAttribute('colour'));

saw size = large
saw size = null
colour is set: red

colour changed twice and was never reported, because it is not observed. And removing an observed attribute reports a newValue of null, the same "absent" signal as in §15.4. Observing everything is not an option, and you would not want it: the list is what keeps the callback cheap.

15.6 Attributes Are Not Properties

This is the most common source of confusion in custom elements, and it is not specific to them: it is the same distinction §2.3 drew for value.

An attribute is markup: a string, visible in the HTML, readable with getAttribute, and matchable in CSS. A property is a JavaScript field on the object: it can be of any type, and it is invisible in the markup.

For built-in elements, the platform keeps certain pairs in step: id, class, href. For your own element, nothing is kept in step unless you write the code. The convention that works:

class TempGauge extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['celsius'];
  get celsius() { return Number(this.getAttribute('celsius') ?? 0); }
  set celsius(v) { this.setAttribute('celsius', String(v)); }
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.textContent = `${this.celsius} °C`; }
}
customElements.define('temp-gauge', TempGauge);

document.body.innerHTML = '<temp-gauge celsius="21"></temp-gauge>';
const g = document.querySelector('temp-gauge');
console.log('rendered:', g.textContent, '| property:', g.celsius);
g.celsius = 30;
console.log('rendered:', g.textContent, '| attribute:', g.getAttribute('celsius'));

rendered: 21 °C | property: 21
rendered: 30 °C | attribute: 30

The property is a view of the attribute, not a second copy, so the value lives in only one place and cannot drift. The getter turns the string into a number, which is the other half of the job: attributes are always strings.

Reflect only what really is configuration. Anything that is not a string (an array of rows, a callback, a large object) should be a property only. Turning a data table into an attribute string produces unreadable markup and a parse on every change.

15.7 Shadow DOM

attachShadow gives an element a second, private subtree.

class BoxedNote extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    if (this.shadowRoot) return;
    const root = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    root.innerHTML = '<style>p { color: rebeccapurple }</style><p>Inside the shadow</p>';
  }
}
